# A CHRISTIAN AND HEAVENLY TREATISE.

### CONTAINING MEDICINE <note>original: "physicke"</note> FOR THE SOUL: VERY NECESSARY FOR ALL WHO WOULD ENJOY TRUE SOUNDNESS OF MIND, AND PEACE OF CONSCIENCE.

---

->Newly corrected and enlarged by the author,<-
->**Mr. John Abernethy**, now Bishop<-
->of **Caithness** <note>original: "Cathnes"</note>.<-

---

> Behold, this we have searched, so it is: hear it, and know it for your own good. **Job 5:27.**

---

->*AT LONDON*,<-
->Printed by **Felix Kingston**, for *John Budge*,<-
->and are to be sold at his shop in *St. Paul’s Churchyard*,<-
->at the sign of the Green Dragon. 1622.<-

<summary>This is the title page for Bishop John Abernethy's theological and psychological work, which frames spiritual care as "medicine for the soul." It identifies the author's high rank in the Scottish church and cites Job 5:27 as a foundational scriptural authority for the text.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the specific discussion of spiritual deafness in Chapter 33 to the book's general preface ("To the Reader"), which outlines the overarching purpose and structure of this treatise on spiritual health.</meta>

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut headpiece featuring symmetrical foliage, scrolls, and a central human figure or cherub head.</image-desc>

# TO THE READER.

<margin>
The general Method:
1. Description of the sickness.
2. The faculty affected.
3. The causes.
4. Signs and Symptoms.
5. Prognostics.
6. Remedies.
</margin>
You have here the *Soul’s Physic* <note>original: "Soules Physicke"; medicine or healing for the soul</note>. Spiritual *Sicknesses* are described in detail. The *Faculties* <term>the mental or spiritual powers of the soul, such as will or reason</term> (being the parts immediately affected) are briefly mentioned. The *Causes* are distinctly set down, like so many fountains from which diseases spring. The *Signs* and *Symptoms* are particularly specified, like so many branches, leaves, blossoms, and bitter grapes that grow up and arise from any deep-rooted <note>original: "radicall"</note> sickness and impurity. The *Prognostics* <term>forecasts of the likely course of a disease</term> show the difficulties of the cure, along with the danger and all the evils that are likely to follow. The *Remedies* are not gathered from animals, plants <note>original: "vegetals"</note>, or minerals—a whole world of those are not able to ease the soul for even one moment—but from the clear streams of reason and the most pure and perfect Fountain of Divine Scripture. The body and the soul receive their most suitable medicine from their own proper elements: the body from things below, the soul from things above.

<margin>
Diligence of the Author.
</margin>
I have taken great pains to write, correct, and enlarge this treatise. Whatever I have found relevant <note>original: "pertinent"</note> in any ancient or recent writers, I have inserted along with my own findings.

<margin>
Necessity of the Treatise.
</margin>
May it please you to take some effort to read it carefully, for it is for your necessary use, regarding your maladies—both those that are already within you <note>original: "inherent"</note> and those that are looming <note>original: "imminent"</note>; these to be...

<summary>This preface introduces a treatise on spiritual healing, outlining a systematic approach to diagnosing and treating soul-based ailments using Scripture and reason rather than physical medicine. The author emphasizes the diligence used in compiling wisdom from both ancient and contemporary sources.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual health, Soul's Physic, theological medicine, diagnostic method, faculties of the soul, Divine Scripture, spiritual remedies</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues a list of reasons why spiritual health is more important than physical health, likely part of a preface addressed "To the Reader."</meta>

-> # To the Reader. <-

<margin>1. Reason.</margin>
...prevented, the other to be cured. The diseases of the body are in no way as dangerous and deadly as those of the soul. Lazarus's painful sores only harmed his temporary life, but Dives's <note>original: "Diues"; a Latin word for 'rich man,' traditionally used as the name of the wealthy man in the parable of Lazarus and the rich man in Luke 16.</note> lack of self-control <note>original: "intemperancy"</note> cost him eternal life. No physical disease can prevent your glorious resurrection, but if you die of a spiritual disease, it cuts off all hope of future glory and plunges you into that "second death" <note>second death: A biblical term for eternal punishment or separation from God.</note>.

<margin>2. Reason.</margin>
The body may be vigorous; the *Balsam of Life* (which is *Nature's Master Physician*) can cure many ailments without any medicine. But the soul (not having by nature a single drop of the *Balsam of Grace*) can never thoroughly rid itself of any sickness.

<margin>3. Reason.</margin>
This treatise serves everyone alike. For who is not born with the seeds <note>original: "ſeminary"; a place where things are developed or sown</note> of all evil? And who does not have just cause to complain about the many diseases of their mind, which disturb their hearts and consciences and lead to endless destruction?

<margin>4. Reason.</margin>
And what can be better than *a sound mind in a healthy body*? <note>original: "A ſound mind in a whole body"; a translation of the Latin phrase 'mens sana in corpore sano'.</note> We are afraid of the slightest fever <note>original: "ague"</note>, we feel even the smallest toothache, and we are eager to prevent any hidden disease among our vital organs <note>original: "noble parts"; in early medicine, this referred to the heart, liver, and brain</note>. Shall we then neglect those so great and dangerous diseases of our most important part, the soul?

<margin>5. Reason.</margin>
<margin>6. Reason.</margin>
The swallow knows her celandine <note>original: "Celidon"; referring to the greater celandine (Chelidonium majus), a plant long associated with swallows in folklore</note>, the deer <note>original: "Hart"</note> his dittany <note>dittany: A medicinal herb believed in antiquity to help animals expel arrows from their bodies</note>, the dog his grass, the ibis her enema <note>original: "Cliſter" or clyster; an archaic term for an enema</note>, the pigeon her laurel, the stork her oregano <note>original: "origanum"</note>. Shall we then be ignorant of the specific remedies for our soul? We are willing to take medicine made of the bitterest desert gourd <note>original: "Calocynthis"</note>, the most violent antimony <note>antimony: A chemical element used in early medicine, often to induce vomiting</note>, the harshest vitriol <note>vitriol: A term for various metallic sulfates or sulfuric acid used in early chemistry and medicine</note>, the filthiest waste, worms, and beasts...

<summary>This preface argues that spiritual health is far more vital than physical health, noting that while animals instinctively know how to heal themselves with herbs, humans often neglect the "Balsam of Grace" needed to cure the soul.</summary>

<keywords>spiritual health, Lazarus and Dives, Balsam of Grace, natural remedies, animal instinct, soul vs body, early modern medicine</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface "To the Reader," comparing the desperate physical remedies people seek for their bodies with the superior spiritual remedies available for their souls. It argues that physical illness is often a tool used by God to prompt spiritual healing.</meta>

-> # To the Reader. <-

...flies, mice, and such filthy and harmful ingredients <note>original: "wares"</note> (so disgusting to nature and the senses), can we not also embrace the most appropriate remedies for our best part—the soul—made of those finest medicines <note>original: "simples"; individual plant or herb-based ingredients used in traditional medicine</note> of sanctified reason and divine graces?

<margin>People for whom this is most necessary: the sick in soul and the diseased in body.</margin>
The honorable, the strong, the wise, the beautiful, and the healthy may find here what heaps of filthy ailments <note>original: "maladies"</note> lie hidden in their souls, under the carved and painted tombs of their bodies. Those who are physically ill are taught here to first seek health for their souls so that they may more quickly gain health for their bodies. For God places diseases on the body to restrain or punish the diseases of the soul, or to force us to seek spiritual remedies for them. We must not be like King *Asa*, who in his physical illness did not seek spiritual health from God, but relied only on physicians. <note>original: "physician"; this refers to 2 Chronicles 16:12, where King Asa is criticized for trusting only in medical doctors rather than God during a foot disease.</note> If, during a physical illness, the health of the soul is sought first, God will either free you from the disease or else comfort you so that you may bear it with patience. In His own time, you will find it has done you great good, leading to your everlasting benefit.

<margin>
Genesis 20:3, 4, 17.
1 Corinthians 11.
Psalm 32.
2 Chronicles 16:12.
Romans 8.
</margin>

<margin>Pastors and their people.</margin>
The *physician of the soul* <note>The author uses this term to refer to a pastor or minister.</note> will find this treatise very useful for his people when he looks upon them with a compassionate heart—as many diseased patients, like those sick people, *blind, lame, and withered, waiting for the moving of the water at the pool of Bethesda*. <note>A reference to John 5, where the sick gathered at a pool in Jerusalem hoping for a miraculous healing.</note> By preaching the Word—and using his doctrines, applications, exhortations, and comforts stored with a variety of heavenly antidotes and specific remedies—he can lead their minds back to soundness and health. Much time, many...

<margin>John 5:3.</margin>

<sig>A 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: many</meta>

<summary>This page addresses both the healthy and the sick, arguing that physical ailments are often intended by God to provoke spiritual healing. It also encourages ministers to act as "physicians of the soul" by using spiritual remedies to care for their congregations.</summary>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This text is the conclusion of the author's preface "To the Reader," found at the beginning of the volume (Signature A). While the previous page provided (page 491) focuses on the "Deafness of the Ear" in the main body of the work, this preface establishes the author's intent: to prioritize practical spiritual healing over academic debate.</meta>

<page-type>preface</page-type>
<header>TO THE READER.</header>

Many volumes and most sermons are spent on **contemplative** <note>original: "Contemplative"; focused on theoretical or meditative study.</note> and **polemical theology** <note>original: "Polemicall Theologie"; theology concerned with disputes and arguments over doctrine.</note> (the mysteries of <term>commonplaces</term> <note>original: "common places"; standard topics or headings used in theological study.</note> and controversial subjects), but too little is spent upon **practical divinity** <note>The application of religious beliefs to daily life and the care of the soul.</note> to cure the suffering soul—which, of all things, is most necessary.

<margin>Physicians and their patients.</margin>
The physician of the body will often find that a patient’s emotional mind corrupts and disturbs the <term>humors</term> <note>In early medicine, the four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine a person's health and temperament.</note> and spirits of the body; beneath a <term>frail</term> <note>original: "crazie"; in this period, the word meant physically broken or infirm.</note> body often lies an even more diseased soul. A heart full of comfort for the soul is better for a person than a box full of drugs is for the body.

<margin>A particular admonition to the reader.</margin>
If you improve yourself by this treatise, it is the very thing I seek. But if you look upon it with a disdainful eye and a careless mind regarding your soul's health, you are an object of pity. If you respond to my hard work with malicious criticism, first accomplish as much yourself as you find here. It is easier to find fault than to create, to gossip than to paint, and to blame than to build.

If you object to this treatise or its author out of a diseased mind—whether in blindness or in passion—I reject the judgment of such a mind. Just as the woman who was a petitioner appealed from "drunk King Philip" to "sober King Philip" <note>An ancient anecdote about a woman who refused a judgment made by Philip of Macedon while he was intoxicated, demanding he hear her case again when sober.</note>, so do I appeal from my irrational critic to my healthy-minded critic. But whatever you find here that is blameworthy while in a sound mind, I am certain that in wisdom and love you will advise me, excuse it, or amend it.

->Yours in the Lord,<-
->Mr. John Abernethy.<-

<sig>A</sig>
<meta>catchword: Thine</meta>

<summary>In this preface, John Abernethy argues that practical spiritual care is more important than academic theological debates and asks the reader to approach his work with a healthy, constructive mind rather than a critical one.</summary>
<keywords>John Abernethy, Practical Divinity, soul health, King Philip of Macedon, physician metaphor, polemical theology</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the author’s English preface to a formal Latin dedication written in his honor by John Strang, a prominent Scottish theologian. This celebratory poem praises Abernethy for his dual expertise in physical medicine and spiritual divinity.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece at the top of the page featuring symmetrical scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>

# TO THE REVEREND PRELATE JOHN ABERNETHY, <note>original: "Ioannem Abrenethium"</note> Doctor of Sacred Theology, Bishop of Caithness, etc.
->A man most highly furnished with a vast store of learning, and especially most skilled in both kinds of medicine <note>The author refers to "both medicines": the healing of the body (physic) and the healing of the soul (divinity).</note>: when he was publishing anew his book on the **healing of the soul** <note>original: "pfeuchiatria"; a Latinized Greek term for psychiatry/spiritual healing.</note>, enriched with new care.<-

---

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' decorated with vine-like patterns.</image-desc>

If we bestow wonderful praise upon those who heal bodily limbs
With the arts of Apollo <note>original: "Phœbais"; referring to Phoebus Apollo, the Greek god of healing.</note>:
And since a thousand troops of diseases infest the soul—
Evils both more numerous and more serious than those of the body—
How great is the honor rightly yours, most worthy Prelate,
Who supplies medicines for the diseases of the soul?
As much as the body is inferior to the soul, as much as Christ is to the child of Leto <note>original: "Latonia proles"; referring to Apollo. The poet argues that Abernethy’s Christian healing is as superior to worldly medicine as Christ is to a pagan god.</note>,
And as much as fleeting things are inferior to eternal goods:
So much should **Podalirius** and **Machaon** <note>In Greek mythology, the sons of Aesculapius and legendary healers of the Trojan War.</note> give way to this work,
Along with the great school of **Galen** and **Hippocrates** <note>The two most influential physicians of antiquity.</note>.
Could you, as the foremost of physicians, have applied the method
Of physical medicine so skillfully to sacred matters?
Indeed, not even the one from **Epidaurus** <note>original: "Epidaurius"; referring to Aesculapius, the god of medicine, whose primary temple was at Epidaurus.</note> himself
Practices the healing arts more learnedly than you, or understands them better.
Well done! It is your special gift to excel in both kinds of medicine,
So that there may be a healthy mind in a healthy body.
Our one salvation, physician, and medicine is Christ;
You teach Him, and He has taught you.

->John Strang, Doctor<- <note>original: "Ioannes Strangius"</note>
->of Sacred Theology, etc.<-

<summary>This page contains a Latin dedicatory poem by John Strang praising Bishop John Abernethy. Strang argues that Abernethy’s work on "the healing of the soul" is superior to the works of famous ancient physicians because it focuses on eternal rather than physical health.</summary>
<keywords>John Abernethy, John Strang, Bishop of Caithness, spiritual healing, psychiatry, Galen, Hippocrates, Apollo, Aesculapius, divinity vs. medicine</keywords>

<meta>This page consists of commendatory verses written in Latin by colleagues of the author. It transitions from the previous chapter's theological warnings about spiritual deafness to academic and personal praise for the author’s ability to heal both the body and the soul.</meta>

->To the Reader, the Work, and the Author.<-

What Nature can achieve, and what Grace can provide for illnesses—the latter tending to the soul, the former to the body—the author is a minister <note>original: *mystes*, meaning a priest or one initiated into sacred mysteries</note> of both. The same method that Grace has applied to bodily diseases, he also applies to the soul. What the condition is, its parts, its cause, the prognosis, the signs, and the cure—which are so often repeated in this book—these things demonstrate his method. If Grace provides the method, and Grace provides the subject matter, what kind of work should we consider this to be?

It is a noble work. Wherever you go, I promise you life: you shall live, and you shall give life to others. Success to you! The Great Bishop <note>likely referring to Christ as the "Bishop of Souls"</note> recognizes you as a minister of Grace, and even Panacea <note>the Greek goddess of universal healing</note> will praise her own minister. I promise this, and so I fall silent: "A sound mind in a sound body" <note>original: *mens sana in corpore sano*, a famous Latin aphorism from Juvenal</note> is the sum of this book, and it is the sum of my wish for you.

->**Patrick Sands**, Principal of<-
->King James’s University, which is in<-
->**Edinburgh**.<-

---

->An Epigram to the Author.<-

Be of good courage and equal virtue, most worthy leader <note>original: *præsul*, a high-ranking cleric or protector</note>, the star and radiance of your order and your country. No more praise is due to him <note>referring to Aesculapius, the god of medicine</note> who gathered the torn limbs of Hippolytus to return each to its proper place; nor to him <note>referring to Orpheus</note> who called back the shade of Eurydice from greedy Hades, powerful only with his Thracian songs. 

Grace created you a minister, and Nature created you a physician; each Goddess has equipped you with her own gifts. Relying on Grace, you drive away diseases and dispel symptoms; you are a universal cure <note>original: *panacea*</note> for desperate evils. While I stand in awe of you as both Minister and Physician, most learned son of Hippocrates <note>the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note>, I am turned into an Egyptian Harpocrates <note>the god of silence; the speaker is saying he is struck speechless with admiration</note>.

->**Henry of Danzig**,<-
->*St. Andrews* <note>original: Andreapol.</note><-

<meta>This page continues a series of commendatory poems written in Latin by the author's colleagues. ->Another poem to the same author.<-

**B**orn under divine auspices and with the favor of Apollo, 
*The palm and sweet glory of Machaon’s couch.* <note>original: *Palma Machaonij dulce decusque thori*. Machaon was the son of Asclepius and a legendary healer in Greek mythology; "couch" refers to the clinical bed of a patient.</note>
With marvelous skill, you subdue illnesses that are 
Uncertain, desperate, and difficult to resolve.
Hence, as if born from Apollo and the nymph Coronis, <note>Apollo and Coronis were the parents of Asclepius, the god of medicine.</note>
You bear golden signs upon your lofty head.
And now you publish a work more lasting than bronze,
And greater than the proud structures of Memphis. <note>original: *Memphi superba*; a reference to the Great Pyramids of Egypt, often used to symbolize enduring monuments.</note>
You enrich the work of fruitful Nature and her hidden treasures,
And you paint intricate webs with a fine needle.
Therefore, your temples deserve to be bound with a double laurel wreath:
For you cure with your hand just as you piously teach with your voice.

->**George Lynd**, of St. Andrews. <note>original: *G. Lynd. Andreapol.*, referring to Andreapolis, the Latin name for the city and University of St. Andrews.</note><-

### An Anagram on the Author’s Name.

# JOHN ABERNETHY.

->Rearranging the letters:<- <note>original: *Αναγραμματιζομθ'*, a Greek term for the process of creating an anagram.</note>

### Truly healthier, use it well. <note>original: *Sanior sanè, vti benè.* This is a Latin anagram of the name *Ioannes Abrenethivs* (the Latinized spelling of John Abernethy).</note>

->Explanation, and to the Author.<-

**S**o that the mind may be healthier, you truly reveal mysteries:
*Hence you are a healthier minister and a holier Physician.* <note>original: *mystes*, meaning a priest or one initiated into sacred mysteries.</note>
As you truly bring forth wisdom, so you also prepare medicines well:
*This is what your writings proclaim; this is what the anagram reflects.*

->Another way, for the progressing Reader.<-

### Go forth truly healthier, so that you may live well.

->Explanation, alluding to John 5:14.<- <note>John 5:14: "See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you."</note>

Go forth truly healthier, so that you do not sin, but live well;
Thus you will be happy in soul and pleasing to God.

### Honey in breath:

The sweet honey came to you from grace:
Health for the soul, and pleasant to the heart:
Poured into your *breath*, it distills from the same,
To help others, and to impart comfort.
So that all may get what is worth more than money:
The health of their souls, if they will eat this honey.

<meta>This page transitions from the specific discussion of spiritual "deafness" in the previous chapter to a poetic meditation addressed directly to the "Sick Soul." It serves as a compassionate opening to a new section, shifting the tone from instruction to healing and hope.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal band of scrollwork and floral motifs separates the top of the page from the text, and a similar band appears at the bottom. The text is enclosed within a simple rectangular line border.</image-desc>

### To the Sick Soul.

Man's only one, and greatest one, you are
The breath of life, God's lamp of love and light,
A spiritual guest <note>original: "ghostly Guest"</note>, present in every part;
Your house of clay <note>A common historical metaphor for the human body</note> cannot diminish your stature;
Man's honor you shall be, and his best treasure,
His great glory, and dignity beyond measure.

Though you lie blind, mad, and filled with evil,
Hard as a stone, deeply seared, and sorely wounded,
Senseless, corrupt, gangrened, and continually plagued,
And you fall, fret, and faint—and (what is more)
You despair of life, and loathe all remedy,
And look for nothing but endless misery:

Yet come and see: your help springs from heaven.
You are encompassed with balms of saving grace;
The Sun shines with healing in his wings; <note>A reference to Malachi 4:2, "the Sun of Righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings."</note>
The golden oil drips down to comfort you.
Dear soul, why are you so deeply dejected?
Here, for your sores, the proper medicine <note>original: "physicke"</note> is revealed.

<vocab>sick soul, breath of life, God's lamp, spiritual guest, house of clay, balms of saving grace, medicine</vocab>

<summary>This page contains a poetic address to a "sick soul," describing the human spirit's divine origin and its current state of spiritual suffering, while promising heavenly healing. It emphasizes that despite the soul's despair and "wounds," divine grace and "physic" (medicine) are available for restoration.</summary>
<keywords>soul, spiritual healing, grace, house of clay, ghostly guest, medicine, divinity, suffering</keywords>

<meta>This page contains introductory commendatory poems written by various scholars and friends of the author, John Abernethy. They praise his dual expertise in medicine and theology, celebrating his ability to heal both the body and the soul.</meta>

->To the Author.<-

Of known effects, when grounds are sought too precisely,
Young naturalists <note>original: "Naturalists"; students of the physical world or science</note> often prove to be old atheists.
And some who can move nothing, except for the First Mover [God],

# CHAPTER 1. Of Spiritual Sicknesses in General.

...clearly: showing both the sores and the salve <note>original: "salue"; a healing ointment or remedy</note>; and that there is no life without this health. The diseases with which this health is troubled <note>original: "pestered"</note> and undone are many, both dangerous and deadly. For just as from that first divine Curse <note>original: "Malediction," referring to the Fall of Man</note>, all impurities are spread <note>original: "disseminate"</note> through the body (the breeding grounds <note>original: "seminaries"</note> of all following diseases and death), so from that same fountain spring all the fundamental <note>original: "radicall"</note> <margin>Romans 7:24</margin> impurities of that *body of death*, causing in the soul every kind of spiritual disease and leading all toward that *Second death* <note>A biblical term referring to eternal damnation</note>.

The soul is most slavishly occupied in repelling and repairing the accidental <note>original: "incident"</note> ruins of this molded, muddy cottage <note>A common Early Modern metaphor for the physical body being made of dust or clay</note> in which it dwells. It should exert a far greater effort to care for itself, in order to properly obtain both soundness and safety. Most people are burdened and troubled by many things <margin>Luke 10:40</margin> with care and concern for the body. But few, like *Mary*, choose that "good part" (meaning the soul’s health) which shall not be taken away. 

When Christ cured diseased bodies, <margin>John 9:6, 37, 38</margin> he also cured sick souls. When he opened the eyes of the body, he also opened the eyes of the soul. When he healed the lame body, he also healed the lame soul, so that <margin>John 5:5, 14 and 7:23</margin> the diseased might be *completely whole*. 

We are sensitive enough to the slightest illnesses of the flesh, and to the smallest pin prick in the most distant part of the body. But as for spiritual diseases, they are both numerous and most easily caught; they are difficult to avoid <note>original: "eschewed"</note>, even more difficult to detect or feel, and most difficult to help and heal. Their diagnosis <note>original: "cognition"</note> and treatment <note>original: "curation"</note> are both to be considered. And first, in general, they should be examined in their *nature, causes, signs, symptoms, prognoses <note>original: "Prognosticks"</note>, treatments, and remedies.*

# CHAPTER 1. Of Spiritual sicknesses in general.

...[affec]ted character of the affection <term>In this context, "affection" refers to a persistent state of mind, emotion, or disposition</term>. <margin>Jeremiah 13:23</margin> *Can the Black man <note>original: "Blacke-moore"</note> change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Then may you also do good, who are accustomed to do evil.*

Every sin makes a change <note>original: "immutation"</note> in the soul: but every sin is not a mental sickness, but only that sin which stops the soul's functions.

<margin>Original sin is no sickness. Romans 5:14.</margin>
That "sinning sin" (called *Original Sin*) is not properly to be called a spiritual disease; rather, it is something worse. It is that first *Root* and most impure seedbed <note>original: "seminarie"</note> from which all those woeful diseases spring. It is the destructive parent of such a damnable offspring, and it differs from those diseases as the cause differs from the effect.

<margin>Infirmities are not sicknesses. Jeremiah 20:10; Psalm 38:17; John 13:10.</margin>
The infirmities <term>weaknesses or character flaws</term> of the regenerate <term>those who have been spiritually reborn or converted</term>, and the limping <note>original: "claudications"</note> and stumbles of the Saints, are not diseases, except in part. *He who is washed needs only to wash his feet, but is clean every bit.* Because these infirmities do not become excessive or intolerable, they do not lead to an inherent and permanent rot <note>original: "putrifaction"</note>. They do not leave a lasting mark, nor do they rule the person. Instead, immediately <note>original: "incontinent"</note> as they are born or spring up, they are pushed back or driven out. They do not become settled habits <note>original: "affections"</note> or dispositions.

<margin>Romans 7:13, 24.</margin>
And while a spiritual disease is called a *disposition against nature*, by "nature" we do not mean this illegitimate, corrupt, and diseased "second nature" we have acquired. Instead, it means our *first nature* before the *Fall*—that very excellent holiness representing God's Image in all the powers <term>original: "faculties"</term>, functions, and actions of the soul.

<margin>Genesis 1:2, 3; 1 Peter 1:1; Ephesians 4:24; Colossians 3:10.</margin>
It is called *against nature* because: 
1. It exceeds the limits of our original nature; 
2. It does violence to the soul; 
3. It interrupts and clearly troubles its powers, functions, and actions.

<margin>Against nature: Romans 7:23; 1 Corinthians 2:14; Romans 8:7; 2 Corinthians 3:5; Ephesians 4:17.</margin>

<margin>
Romans 5:14 and 7:13.
Ephesians 4:18, etc.

[Sub]stance of the soul; there is neither sickness, impurity, nor mortality. But in the parts of the soul (or rather its faculties) there are properly diseases: such as *Blindness* in the mind; *Hardness* in the heart; and *Intemperance* in the affections, etc. As for the "contents" of the soul—namely, that *Original and native concupiscence* <term>concupiscence: Strong sexual desire or, more broadly in this theological context, the innate tendency of human nature toward sin.</term>—it is the universal cause of all diseases. In the functions of reasoning, judgment, knowledge, opinion, consultation, choice, appetite, desire, etc., are properly found the *Symptoms*.

Since sicknesses reside immediately in the faculties, it follows that not every light affection—whether momentary, passing, tempting, withdrawing, enticing, deceiving, conceiving, desiring, compelled, or sudden—can be called a disease of the soul, unless it remains, resides, and sticks fast to it. Otherwise, it is merely a lighter kind of disposition.

<margin>
They hurt the functions grievously, evidently, immediately, and in themselves <note>original: "per se"</note>.
</margin>
It is said *to hurt and interrupt the functions and actions*: perverting, depraving, and making them altogether repugnant to the purity of reason, the sanctity of God’s image, and the equity of his will—and allowing no action at all (or at least, only a very corrupt one) to be performed. And this it must do grievously, evidently, and immediately, *in itself* <note>original: "per se"</note>, (and not indirectly <note>original: "per accidens"</note> as causes do). For *Causes* beget sicknesses; *Sicknesses*, in turn, beget and bring forth the *Symptoms* as their fruits.

<margin>
They offend God because they are willingly acquired, and God, the internal Physician, is despised <note>original: "contemned"</note>.
</margin>
*Offending of God, etc.* The sicknesses of the body are involuntary and may move others to pity, but none to revenge, because they offend no one, nor do they bring the patient under the authority of any laws. But the soul of man is willingly and maliciously sick. Of its own accord, it makes itself unfit for the service of its rightful owner and master—or at the least, it yields and consents to it. It would rather be sick beside *Pharaoh’s* <note>original: "Pharao's"</note> fleshpots in bondage than be made whole with heavenly *Manna* in a freer service. For the sake of the pleasure of the flesh's sensuality, it delights more in being a slave to sickness than in being healthy for its own good and the honor of God.

<margin>

*Aristotle, Ethics, Book 3, Chapter 5.*

# Chapter 1. Spiritual sicknesses and their differences.

<sig>B 4</sig>

A person with a diseased body does not despise the *Physician*; he seeks him out, calls for him, reveals his sores to him, obeys his advice, and is thankful to him for his health. But the sick mind, just as it delights in its own distress, also does not care for that *Great Physician* of the soul, nor for his *blood*, our most supreme medicine. <margin>Matthew 9:12.</margin> Israel would not acknowledge that God cured them. Nor would Jerusalem be gathered under *Christ’s* wings, <margin>Hosea 11:3. Matthew 23:37.</margin> so that he might warm them with his heat, heal them, and save them with his *Pelican* blood. <note>The pelican was a common Christological symbol in the Renaissance; it was believed the bird would prick its own breast to feed its young with its blood to save them from death.</note> By this willingness to remain sick and this contempt for that great medicine, *God* is offended. The *Physician* is turned into a Judge, and his saving hand into judgment. The soul dies both the first and the second death. <margin>Why are spiritual diseases so perilous?</margin> The first is spiritual, by which the soul is deprived of the presence of *God’s Spirit* (the soul of the soul); it is dead to *God* but alive to *Satan*. The second is eternal, to be fulfilled after death but never ended.

<margin>Use.</margin> Through this, we may see how deep sin lies within us: how we always carry fire in our chest and endless death in our hearts.

---

->*The differences between mental diseases and their description.*<-

<margin>Lawlessness <note>original Greek: "Anomia"</note>. 1 John 3:4. Romans 5:14. Mental diseases differ from original sin and many actual sins.</margin> Original impurity and spiritual sicknesses are both prohibited by the Law; both are sins and transgressions of the Law.

That *Original* impurity is sin and the cause of all sin; but these spiritual sicknesses are sins and the effects of sin. These are the branches and bitter fruits; the other is that most venomous root from which they spring, which in this life can never be fully and finally uprooted <note>original: "extirped"</note>.

<margin>Romans 6:12 and 2:8.</margin> These sicknesses differ from actual sins just as specific cases differ from the general category. For not all actual sins are diseases, unless they reign over a person and obedience is given to them.

**CHAPTER 1. Of spiritual sicknesses,**

to, and the faculties are offered up to serve it.

<margin>Some idiopathic. Some sympathetic.</margin>
The diseases of the soul differ among themselves. Some are *idiopathic* <note>original: "Idiopathetick"; referring to a primary disease that arises on its own within an organ rather than as a symptom of another condition.</note>, originating as a specific suffering arising immediately within the soul and residing there—such as blindness of mind, hardness of heart, and so on. Some are *sympathetic* <note>original: "Sympatheticke"; referring to a condition where one part of the soul or body is affected by a disease in another part.</note>, resulting from a more indirect suffering. These either arise from the body and are shared with the soul—such as that type of "wounded spirit" which arises from melancholy—or else they arise from the soul and spread to specific organs of the body, such as the "poisonous tongue," the "deaf ear," and the "evil eye." In some respects, these may be called *symptomatic* <note>original: "Symptomaticke"; meaning they are outward symptoms of a deeper spiritual issue.</note>.

<margin>Mark 7:22, 23.</margin>
<margin>No spiritual disease exists by itself; it is neither simple nor solitary. *As a simple imbalance* <note>original: "Vt simplex in temperies"</note>.</margin>
Furthermore, it is often seen that the body may have a single disease alone, without the company of another; but in the soul, there is always more than one—indeed, many and diverse diseases at the same time. In the body, there may be one simple and solitary disease, lacking the presence of a direct cause and without any significant *symptom*. But in the mind, every sickness is accompanied and nourished by its own underlying cause <term>continent cause: a medical term of the time for a cause that is actively maintaining the disease</term> and has severe *symptoms* following from it. This is like a *nephritic* <note>original: "Nephriticke"; relating to the kidneys.</note> condition in the kidneys <note>original: "reines"; an archaic term for kidneys.</note>, which has both *obstruction* as the cause and pain <note>original: "dolour"; meaning physical or mental suffering</note> as the symptom at the same time.

<margin>Spiritual diseases are always accompanied by their own causes and by the fellowship of other sicknesses. Acts 28:27. And they are implicated.</margin>
No disease of the soul can exist on its own but is always accompanied by others. For they are either *implicated*—still resting in their own affected parts yet conspiring to the disruption of some common function—as *blindness* in the mind and *hardness* in the heart work together to stop repentance. This malady was long present among the *Jews*: *For their heart grew fat and hard, their ears were dull of hearing, and they closed their eyes, lest they should see with their eyes, hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and should return, so that God might heal them.*

<margin>Or connected.</margin>
Or else they are *connected*, fastened, and coupled together; one of them is always the underlying cause <note>original: "continent cause"</note> of the other, being so near in nature—such close neighbors...

->The causes of spiritual diseases.<-

The causes are various: some are *External*, obvious, and primary <note>original: "primitiue"</note>. The devil in his malice works upon corrupt affections by seducing and poisoning the heart. When he is near, he can seduce like a serpent and bite like a viper. When he is further away, like the *torpedo fish* <note>The torpedo fish or electric ray was known in antiquity for its ability to numb or paralyze its prey through a "narcotic" or numbing touch.</note>, he can inflict his numbing venom through indirect contact. And (no matter how far off he might be) he is that *Dragon whose tail drew a third of the stars out of heaven*. God, in His justice, acts here as a "withdrawing" <note>original: "deficient"</note> cause, abandoning those He chooses and handing them over to Satan's power and to their own wits and wills.

Regarding *antecedent* causes: some are *idiopathic* <note>term: idiopathic—In early medicine, this referred to a primary disease arising within the organ itself, rather than being caused by another condition.</note> and work immediately upon the soul. For example, our innate <note>original: "native"</note> corruption is a universal, internal, and pre-existing cause of all spiritual maladies. Others are *sympathetic* <note>term: sympathetic—A condition where one part of the body or soul suffers in response to an affliction in another part.</note>. For instance, *melancholy* <note>term: melancholy—One of the four humors; an excess of "black bile" was thought to cause sadness, fear, and mental disturbance.</note> in the body, through a sympathy with the soul, works upon the mind, corrupts the imagination, deceives the heart, frightens the conscience, and disturbs the affections.

<margin>Continent or conjoined causes.</margin>
<margin>Romans 6:16, 17.</margin>
As for *continent* <note>term: continent cause—In Galenic medicine, this is the "containing" or immediate cause that is present as long as the disease is present.</note> and *conjoined* causes, these are the ones most closely linked to the sickness itself. An example is the specific act of *giving ourselves as servants to obey sin leading to death*. This is a corruption that is both acquired and embraced...

# CHAPTER I. Of their Signs and Symptoms.

->### Signs and Symptoms.<-

<margin>
Signs are gathered either from causes, effects, the parts affected, or from any result.
</margin>
By **Signs**, we mean anything that might reveal or make obvious the hidden internal illness, either to oneself or to others. This sign may be taken from the **evident cause**, from the **effect** and results of the current disease, or from the **part and faculty affected**.

<margin>
Symptoms are more specific signs. A physical symptom differs from a spiritual symptom.
</margin>
<margin>
What a symptom is. *Symptoma* <note>original Greek: Συμπτωμα</note>.
</margin>
<margin>
Matthew 7:16, 20.
</margin>
<margin>
Evils of guilt <note>original Latin: *Mala culpæ*</note>.
</margin>
By **Symptoms**, we mean those occurrences that may happen alongside and coincide with the illness. All **symptoms** are **signs**, but not all **signs** are **symptoms**. In the body, nothing can be both a **sickness** and a **symptom**, just as nothing can be both a **cause** of a sickness and a **symptom**. A **symptom** may be the cause of another **symptom**, just as one **sickness** may be the cause of another **sickness**. However, a **symptom** itself is neither a sickness nor the cause of a sickness. 

But it is very different in the soul, because the soul is spiritual. Its sicknesses are so subtle, and their gathering, accompaniment, entanglement, connection, and succession are so great and wonderful—and the "mystery of iniquity" <note>A biblical phrase from 2 Thessalonians 2:7, referring to the hidden nature of sin and evil.</note> is so profound—that we must not define **symptoms** as strictly as we do in medicine <note>original: "Physicke"</note>. Instead, we should understand them more broadly, according to the origin of the word: as all those things that are accidental, contingent, incidental, occurring afterward, or happening at the same time as such a disease. These things characterize and describe the disease more vividly in all its wretchedness. *By their works you shall know them, and an evil tree brings forth evil fruit.* They are (for the most part) the specific fruits of more general illnesses and the disturbances of the soul's functions and proper actions.

<margin>
Pathognomonic <note>A medical term for a sign that is specifically characteristic of a particular disease, making a diagnosis certain.</note> and proper symptoms.
</margin>
<margin>
Accidental <note>original: "assident"; signs that usually, but not always, accompany a disease.</note> and common symptoms. Indicative <note>original Greek: Δηλωτικα (Delotika)</note>.
</margin>
Some of these are **Pathognomonic**, and are always accompanying the disease like a shadow follows a body. They begin, continue, and end with the sickness and are inseparable from it. Others are merely **Accidental**, sometimes appearing only at the beginning of the disease and sometimes occurring later. They are not always present, nor are they proper, <note>The text ends mid-sentence; "proper" here likely means "unique" or "exclusive" to one specific disease.</note>

<summary>This page defines and distinguishes between "signs" and "symptoms" within a spiritual context, arguing that while medical definitions are strict, the "sicknesses of the soul" require a broader understanding because of their complexity.</summary>
<keywords>signs, symptoms, pathology of the soul, pathognomonic, accidental symptoms, medical analogy, spiritual illness</keywords>

->### Prognostics<-

Prognostics and their use.

**P**rognostics are signs that reveal the outcome of a disease, or what evils and miseries are likely to follow from it—whether it is curable, incurable, or doubtful. The grounds from which they are collected.

Romans 2:5.
Proverbs 27:22.
</margin>

Universal remedies are those that serve to cure almost all diseases. <margin>Faith.</margin> These include, first, true faith in God and the application of Christ’s blood.

# CHAP. II.
## 1. Blindness of mind.

---

> Revelation 3:17. *You do not know that you are blind.*

-> Description. <-

<margin>The mind's beams. Emanating <note>original: "Emanant"</note> to the creatures.</margin>
The mind's speculative beams, emanating and directed toward nature—which were once so great, so sure, and so clear that they knew all creatures completely, truly, and distinctly, without exception, error, or confusion—became extremely dimmed in that first ruin <note>referring to the Fall of Man</note> and ever since. Yet, through research, study, instruction, science <note>In this context, science refers to general knowledge or systematic learning.</note>, and experience, they are much repaired. 

But the immanent <note>remaining within or inward-looking</note> beams reflected on ourselves—by which we should behold, contemplate, and study ourselves (which is both great philosophy and a beginning of theology)—are far more darkened. 

<margin>Immanent in ourselves.</margin>
<margin>Ascending unto God.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 6:23.</margin>
<margin>Ignorance of ourselves and of God.</margin>
And most of all, those ascending beams that should penetrate toward *God* for man's final safety are not only wonderfully weakened, so that they cannot reach their highest zenith, and strangely stopped by the intervention of so many clouds, but are also so suffocated in the very crystalline humor <note>In early modern medicine, the "crystalline humor" was thought to be the central lens or essential part of the eye that enabled vision.</note> of the mind that man has now become darkness itself <note>original: "darknesse in abstract"</note>. *And if the light that is in the eye is darkness, how great is that darkness?*

These two sorts of blindness are two sorts of most dangerous and deadly ignorances, which are most difficult to help. The first is the ignorance of ourselves, which will be handled first; the other is the ignorance of *God*, which follows next.

### Chapter 2. 1. Blindness of mind.

There are three sorts of ignorance regarding ourselves.

<margin>Negative ignorance of ourselves. <note>original Latin: "Ignorantia puræ negationis: vel Nescientia"</note> Ignorance of pure negation, or lack of knowledge.</margin>
*Negative ignorance:* This is the ignorance of things that are unnecessary, superfluous, irrelevant, impossible, unprofitable, unneeded, or forbidden—things we are in no way obligated to know. For example, we do not need to know how many of the smallest branches of veins, nerves, or arteries are spread throughout the body, or how often we have breathed, eaten, or drunk. We do not need to take note of our minor and completely indifferent actions, words, and thoughts that are of no importance, being neither good nor evil. This sort of ignorance of ourselves is not a vice, nor a sin, nor an evil; it is tolerable.

<margin>Privative ignorance. <note>original Latin: "Ignorantia simplicis priuationis"</note> Ignorance of simple deprivation.</margin>
*Privative and simple ignorance:* This is an ignorance consisting of a mere and simple deprivation. It is a lack of that knowledge that we are born to have, or that should be inherent within us. Just as rest is a bare and simple absence of motion, so we do not know our noble parts or their uses. We do not know the <term>complexion</term> <note>the balance of "humors" or bodily fluids thought to determine health and temperament</note>, humors, and principles of our body. We do not know how the elements are turned into our food, and how our food is turned into our physical substance. We are ignorant of many more excellent things in our body and soul—things of which Adam had knowledge, but which we lost through him. This sort of ignorance of ourselves is miserable, yet it is not a sin; rather, it is a part of our misery and a punishment for sin. We should work to repair this ignorance to some degree, for our own great good and God's glory.

<margin>Corruptive ignorance. <note>original Latin: "Ignorantia malæ & perversæ dispositionis"</note> Ignorance of an evil and perverse disposition.</margin>
*Corruptive ignorance:* This is an ignorance stemming from an evil and stubborn disposition, such as when one has a habit of following false principles and false opinions. This is not a simple and bare deprivation like the previous kind, but a <term>potential deprivation</term> <note>original: "priuation potentiall"</note> that includes a power and tendency toward evil. It is like rot in an apple, which is not only the loss of the fruit's natural heat but also a tendency toward corruption. It is not a simple deprivation (as blindness is), but it retains something of the thing that is being deprived (just as sickness does). For deprivation is negative,

### Chapter 2. 1. Blindness of mind.

...ery in the natural <note>original: "natiue"</note> subject: but corruption adds a positive contrary, establishing <note>original: "founding"</note> that negative state.

<margin>Description of our blindness.</margin>
This blindness of the mind is not only a simple deprivation of self-knowledge, but also a willful refusal to meditate upon ourselves. It is a failure to apply our thoughts to our own lives so that we might become skillful and impartial judges of ourselves. Because of this, we are most unwilling to remember, consider, notice—or even feel—the need to study ourselves continually. And even when we are at our most blind, we still will not acknowledge our blindness. *This is an ignorance of ourselves that is both miserable and abominable.* It is a most fearful plague. <margin>Revelation 3:17</margin> *The Lord strikes many with madness, blindness, and confusion <note>original: "astonying"</note> of heart.* <margin>Deuteronomy 28:28</margin>

---

->*Part affected.*<-

<margin>The mind.</margin>
The faculty of the mind is the part affected here. Within it, reason, understanding, and judgment are eclipsed. They are both unable and unwilling to reflect their own light back upon themselves, as if by a mirror, so that a person might observe and contemplate himself.

---

->*Causes.*<-

<margin>Various causes.</margin>
Just as the causes of physical blindness vary—some being external on the outer membrane <margin>The cornea and the pupil. <note>original Latin: "Cornea. Pupilla."</note></margin> of the eye, some being deeper in the structure, and some being most internal of all (such as in the **crystalline humor** <note>the lens of the eye, once thought to be the central organ of sight</note>, the **optic nerves**, the **visual spirits** <note>an early medical theory that invisible "spirits" carried sensory information through the nerves to the brain</note>, and the brain itself)—so too are the causes of this spiritual blindness toward ourselves. Some are external, and some are internal.

# Chapter 2. 1. Blindness of Mind.

...one's own commendation: that comforting <note>original: "solacious"</note> sorcerer, flattery, the blindfolder of minds—as sweetly embraced as it is smoothly delivered. If it is resisted even a little, it is so pleasing that it is never thoroughly shut out; thus, even if often excluded, it is at last received again. It so pleases, honors, and commends that the mind rejoices at its own praise. It always yields one victory to obtain a greater. It is able to make Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Elder, a tyrant of Syracuse often used in literature as an example of extreme vanity and susceptibility to flattery</note> believe his own spit is sweeter than honey. There is nothing more dangerous; there is nothing that corrupts and blinds the minds of men more easily than flattery.

<margin>Lack of instruction and warning.</margin>
Some lack the means of instruction and cannot get them; some have them and will not use them. There is nothing so unsavory to many as a warning. Neither does a biased <note>original: "affected"</note> mind admit a grave admonition. How long was David ignorant of his own condition until he was skillfully instructed and warned by the Prophet Nathan! 
<margin>2 Samuel 12; 1 Corinthians 14:24–25</margin>
The unbeliever or the unlearned person remains ignorant of the secrets of his own heart until he is rebuked and judged—and then he falls down.

<margin>Prosperity abused.</margin>
Peace and prosperity are good in themselves; but to a base and beastly mind, they are evil. They blind the owner and make him "unhappily happy." Stagnant waters rot the soonest; resting iron rusts the fastest; and resting minds are blinded the most quickly. The body's well-being is the soul's blindfold. 
<margin>Proverbs 1:32; Revelation 18:7; Psalm 30:6.</margin>
*As ease kills the foolish, and the prosperity of fools destroys them,* so it also blinds them. The minds of even the best people are in danger of this, *as David confesses of himself: "In my prosperity, I said, I shall never be moved."*

<margin>Bad examples. Cicero, *On the Orator*, Book 3. "He who seems good to himself by comparison is just like one who, looking at the lame, wonders at his own speed." <note>original: "Qui sibi comparatione, bonus videtur, perinde est, ac si quis ad claudos respiciens, suam miretur velocitatem."</note> Seneca.</margin>
We are too observant <note>original: "sighty"</note> of examples and quick to imitate. These two things move us most: similarity and example. Comparisons blind us; when we judge others to be too evil, we think ourselves to be too good. He who, through comparison with those worse than himself, appears good to himself is just like someone who, looking at a person with a limp, wonders at his own speed. It is a common saying among those who are blinded in evil: *If I am bad, I have many companions.*

### Chapter 2. 1. Blindness of mind.

<margin>Corruption.</margin>
That radical, primary, inbred venom (even the "law of our members" <note>original: "law of our members"; a biblical reference from Romans 7:23 to the sinful impulses that work within a person's body</note>), which is further acquired by the daily and habitual contagion of sin, and most of all hourly spewed in by that tyrannizing Dragon <note>referring to Satan</note>, so perversely affects and infects the mind (being so deprived of light and so depraved by darkness) that it cannot reflect its own beams back upon itself. We are so far not only inclined but declined <note>meaning fallen away or turned aside from what is right</note> that our minds can approve of us in our worst actions and reprove us in our best.

Of mind.
Memory.
Aristotle.
Cicero, *Oratorical Partitions*.
Jeremiah 44:9.
James 1:23, 24.
</margin>
The Memory (that inward scribe) that should retain, record, revolve, and furnish the mind with matter for discourse, is so perverted that it will spend itself on anything rather than on ourselves. Because of this, **we forget our own wickedness. And if we have considered ourselves for a short time, we immediately forget what kind of men we were.**

<margin>
Conscience.
Genesis 42:21.
1 Timothy 4:2.
</margin>

<margin>
Heart and affections.
Luke 19:14.
*Reasonings* <note>original Greek: Λογισμοι (Logismoi)</note>.
Romans 2:15.
2 Corinthians 10:14.
Isaiah 57:20.
2 Peter 2:12.
Jude 1:10.
</margin>
The heart and affections, with a violent *ataxy* <note>original: "Ataxie"; a Greek term for disorder, confusion, or a lack of self-control</note>, create a seditious mutiny and slavish insurrection against the more noble faculty of the soul, like an insolent people rising against their sovereign. The mind, *memory, conscience, will, and affections* do not cooperate with their *reasonings* <note>original: Λογισμοι (Logismoi)</note> to enable a man to know himself. (The mind does not show him the law; the memory does not show him the facts; the conscience does not show him his judgment; the affections and will do not stir everything forward, nor do they cry out, "All this is more than true; and woe to us, we are like a raging sea!") Thus, blinded men become **as natural brute beasts, led by sensuality, and made to be caught and destroyed. And whatever things they know naturally, like beasts without reason, they corrupt themselves in those very things.**

### Signs and Symptoms.

<margin>
He is foolish.
Matthew 23:17, 19.
Luke 12:20.
Titus 1:16.
</margin>
He who does not know himself is not truly wise; he makes a fool of himself at his own expense. Either he does not know *God*, or if he claims to know him, he denies him through his actions. He is persistently arrogant. He maintains no modesty, nor does he keep himself within his own station <note>original: "ranke"; referring to one's proper social or moral place</note>. He undertakes many things that are beyond his strength. He never doubts himself, thinking he understands well enough when he actually understands nothing at all.

<margin>
Arrogant.
</margin>
He forgets himself and loses himself in outward things. He always looks ahead of himself; he scatters his wits on vanities and never brings them home to himself. He can put his house in order, but not his life or his soul—just like *Achitophel* <note>Achitophel was an advisor to King David; the Bible notes that before he committed suicide, he "put his household in order" (2 Samuel 17:23), a metaphor here for focusing on worldly affairs while neglecting the soul</note>. He does not remember his past passions or his perverse opinions. He never fears for himself, unless it is in a crude way, noticing only obvious and open faults. He deals with himself superficially, partially, and sparingly—either making excuses or never asking, "*What have I done?*" He never considers his own natural constitution <note>meaning his inherent character or physical/mental makeup</note> or his inclinations. He does not know his own weaknesses and needs. He cannot kill <term>mortify</term> or control <term>moderate</term> his passions, and he does not care to improve them.

<margin>
Vain.
2 Samuel 17:23.
He forgets himself.
Jeremiah 8:6.
</margin>
He does not consider the evils he is running into or those that have threatened him. He does not feel his own evils, nor does he fear them, and he seeks no remedies for his miseries. He does not prepare himself for future changes and trials. He often falls to the ground and tumbles headlong into the same mistake. He does not lead an orderly life; all his actions are either bad or frivolous. He is a fickle <term>circumstantial weather-cock</term> <note>meaning someone whose character or behavior changes based on external circumstances rather than internal principles</note>, and his goodness comes by chance and luck rather than a virtuous disposition. He is a self-pleaser, saying to himself, "*I am rich and increased with goods, and have need of nothing,*" while in reality, he has nothing at all. He does not consider the beam that is in his own eye <note>a reference to Matthew 7:3 regarding people who ignore their own massive faults while judging others</note>.

His life is evil.

<header>Chapter 2. 1. Blindness of mind.</header>

### Cures and remedies.

<margin>A difficult cure.</margin>
Making a blinded mind able and willing to see and know itself—using its own reflected light—is as difficult and rare as it is easy to misjudge and deceive ourselves. <margin>Jeremiah 17:9 and 8:6.</margin> The heart is deceitful and wicked *above all things: who can know it? No one says, "What have I done?"* Man is a little world <note>the concept of the "microcosm," where the human being reflects the structure of the universe</note>, said the *Philosophers*. Man is the greatest miracle, said *Augustine* (insofar as he is God’s creature). But, as a fallen man, he is the *Devil’s* workmanship; and a man’s tongue is a world of wickedness. <margin>Ezekiel 16:2, 43.</margin> *If the tongue is so wicked, what is the whole person?* <note>original: "Si lingua, quid totus?"</note> To know ourselves, therefore, is a great work and requires a thousand eyes. It is hard to know ourselves, yet it is a blessing.

<margin>Avoid the causes, and fear the evil.</margin>
Shun all the external causes of this blindness and consider deeply the many great evils that follow from it, as can be seen especially among the previously mentioned symptoms and prognostics <note>signs or forecasts of the course of a disease</note>.

<margin>Self-knowledge is commanded. 1 Corinthians 11:31, 32. *Know yourself.* It must be prayed for.</margin>
Remember to keep your eyes reflected upon yourself; it is both God’s counsel and His command: *to judge yourselves*. The pagans <note>original: "Ethnickes"; a term for non-Christians or those outside the Judeo-Christian tradition</note> acknowledged it as an oracle from heaven: *Know yourself* <note>original: "Γνῶθι σεαυτόν" (Gnothi seauton); a famous Ancient Greek aphorism inscribed at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi</note>. Through humble prayer, buy a portion of that *eye-salve* from that true *light* <note>a reference to Revelation 3:18, where spiritual insight is likened to medicinal ointment</note>, so that the eyes of your mind may be anointed and you may see. The pagans labored much in this by the light of nature <note>reason and instinct without divine revelation</note>. You are bound to go beyond them by the light of grace.

<margin>Make a habit of it.</margin>
Begin to acquaint yourself with yourself. Through use and habit, learn to take a view of yourself, so that at length you may attain a perfect ability in seeing and knowing yourself thoroughly. By frequent practice and habit, a child progresses from creeping to walking, from babbling to speaking, and from ink-blotting to perfect writing. Many things are learned through practice and skill that nature does not provide on its own, as is seen in *acrobats* <note>original: "Tumblers"</note> who perform while walking upon a rope. Therefore, how much more should you—who have the light of nature and far...

# Chapter 2. 1. Blindness of mind.

...far more, the light of grace (if you will seek it) must labor within you, so that you are practiced in turning your eyes upon yourself to know your own iniquity. <margin>Jeremiah 3:13</margin>

<margin>Job 39:37. Do it exactly. Proverbs 20:27. Zephaniah 2:1, 2.</margin>
The way to perform this exercise is to use your own mind (*the Lord’s lantern*) to search yourself, as it says in *Zephaniah 2:1: Search yourselves; yes, search yourselves, O nation not worthy to be loved.* The Hebrew word used there signifies three things: First, to gather *your wits* together—wits that were previously scattered outside of yourself on vain things. Second, to winnow <note>original: "fanne"</note> *yourselves* to purge away your spiritual chaff. Third, to *search narrowly*, as if for a lost jewel or a hidden mine.

<margin>Not crudely.</margin>
You must not search crudely <note>original: "groſſely"</note>, looking only for obvious errors and blatant vices. You must not consider little sins to be no sins, nor treat major sins as minor ones. Do not think of secret sins as non-existent, or open sins as insignificant. <margin>Nor superficially.</margin> You must not examine yourself *superficially*, making excuses or acting hypocritically—finding almost nothing to be wrong because of so many clever distinctions, mitigations, qualifications, pretenses <note>original: "colours"</note>, questions, necessities, inconveniences, tolerances, and ignorances. This is turning mountains <margin>But narrowly.</margin> into specks <note>original: "moates." Likely referring to the biblical "mote" or speck of dust in the eye.</note>. Instead, you must search narrowly, even for your smallest errors, secret sins, and private corruptions. These are close to our nature and delightful to our hearts, acting as traitors to *God* and to us. It is harder to find them than to root them out, as *Caesar* said of the *Scythians* <note>The Scythians were nomadic warriors famous for being difficult to locate and trap in battle.</note>. You must test yourself <margin>Substantially. Job 22:5. Lamentations 3:22.</margin> *substantially*, searching every corner. Judge great sins to be infinite and little sins to be great; consider no sin small. And for every sin, say: *It is of the Lord’s mercy that we are not consumed.* Look for all sins, spare no sins, and spend all your time in this, never ending. The more you find, the more you should suspect that there is still more hidden behind.

<margin>2 Corinthians 13. 1 Corinthians 11.</margin>
The Apostle says, *Examine yourselves; again I say, examine yourselves.* He doubles the word *examine*, just as *Zephaniah* doubles the word *search*. This means that when we have finished one examination, we must do it all over again, and

How sweet a sleep follows the recognition of ourselves—how quiet, how comfortable, how free?

# Chapter 2. 1. Blindness of mind.

<margin>Regarding the body.</margin>
Consider, therefore, that from the earth came your parents' food <note>original: "meat"; in Early Modern English, this referred to any kind of food</note>; from food came their blood; from blood came their seed; and from their seed, *your body was made*. And so, from the first to the last, you are made of the earth. The first man is of the *earth, earthy* <note>original: "earth, earthly"; see 1 Corinthians 15:47</note>. You are merely made up of a heap of earth, or constructed like a piece of mud-wall. Our body is corruptible and mortal. *Man's breath departs, and he returns to his earth.* Say with *David, "I was made in a secret place, and fashioned beneath in the earth."* Sin has defaced the body, and thereby it has become the garment of ignorance, the garment of wickedness, the bond of corruption, a living death, a feeling corpse <note>original: "sensible carrion"</note>, a portable tomb, a thief within the home. It flatters because it hates; it hates because it envies; while it lives, it deprives you of life.

<margin>
1 Corinthians 15:47.
"Corruptible, mortal." <note>original: "φθαρτον, θνητον"</note>
1 Corinthians 15:53.
Psalm 146:4.
Psalm 139:15.
And with Job 10:10, 11, 12.
Hermes [Trismegistus] in the *Poimandres*. <note>original: "Herm. in Pam."</note>
</margin>

<margin>Regarding the soul.</margin>
The soul is a real and spiritual substance of *God's* own making, placed in the body and confined there, so that man, partaking of both *God* and the world, might bear the image of both. Being a *mind-endowed body* and a *body-dwelling mind*, he might become a *horizon* <note>The author views the human soul as the meeting point or boundary line between the physical and spiritual worlds.</note> between the bodiless angels and the mindless bodies here below.

<margin>Her place.</margin>
This soul fills the body entirely, diffused into every part—indivisible, incorruptible, undisturbed, and uninterrupted. She is one in substance, yet diversified by various powers, acting on various objects and producing various effects, like the single *Sun*, which is manifold in its operations.

<margin>
Her substance is one.
Her faculties are diverse.
</margin>

<margin>Distinct from the body.</margin>
The body confines her, but the body's beauty, strength, or health will never refine her; neither can food nor any physical element help her. In a sick, blind, or maimed body, she may be whole, sighted, and perfect; and in the weakest body, she may be most active. She in no way depends on the body, but the body depends on her.

<margin>Her powers.</margin>
She is like a careful housewife, guiding everything well at home in the body—attracting, retaining, digesting <note>original: "decocting"</note>, distributing, expelling, and so on. She moves the body, both outside and inside, wherever she pleases. She gives life to the senses, by

<margin>
Her vegetative power.
Motive power, both local and vital.
</margin>

### Chapter 2, Section 1: Blindness of Mind

<margin>Sensitive power</margin>
...through whose windows she <note>The author personifies the soul as "she" throughout this section.</note> views all things outside and brings them home to herself with all their various forms, as she pleases best.

<margin>Common sense and imagination. Fantasy. Dreams. Sensitive memory. Wit.</margin>
She gathers them into one mass and heap. She beholds them, distinguishes them, combines, compares, and evaluates them. In this, she is also not idle when we sleep. She preserves them in their order until she needs them for her use.

Her eye—the body's light and the fuel of nature's laws—reviews and notices these forms in their highest sublimity. From there, she abstracts them, perceives them, reasons <note>original: "discourseth"</note> upon them, compares them, resolves effects into causes, and collects universal natures from many specific examples. It marks the inside of things—the substance, the tree, the root, and the core—just as she previously marked the outside, the circumstances, the bark, the branch, and the sound through the senses.

<margin>Reason. Understanding. Opinion. Judgment. Wisdom.</margin>
When she reasons, this light and eye of hers is called *reason*. When she remains fixed in conclusions, it is *understanding*. When she rests lightly on conclusions, it is *opinion*. When she bases her truth upon principles, it is *judgment*. And finally, judging between good and evil, truth and falsehood (in which she does not fail, nor does she require the skill of the senses), by the many steps of the *stair of wit* <note>original: "wits staire"; "wit" here refers to the general intellect or mental capacity.</note>, the soul ascends to her high degree of *wisdom*.

<margin>Will, heart, affections. Intellectual memory. Conscience.</margin>
By her hand and most delicate fingers, as she finds everything fit or unfit for her use, she takes, rejects, or puts it into practice. In her storehouse, she contains all arts and general reasons. She concurs with *God* in excusing, accusing, pacifying, and frightening, according to the mind's light in all her actions.

<margin>An exhortation to the soul.</margin>
Thus, *O divine soul*, within your cabinet, ten thousand forms may sit at once, and each keeps its true proportion—such as men, beasts, trees, towns, seas, land, heaven, and earth. Fire converts coals into fire. The body converts meat into blood. You convert bodies into spirits, refining the most essential forms <note>original: "subliming the quintessenced forms"; "subliming" refers to the alchemical process of purifying a substance, used here to describe how the soul turns physical sensations into spiritual thoughts.</note> from grosser matters.

# Chapter 2, Section 1: Blindness of Mind
<sig>D</sig>

...forms: transforming them into your nature, to carry them lightly on your celestial wings. Your life-giving <note>original: "quickning"</note> power feeds the senses; the senses feed your intellect <note>original: "wit"</note>. Your life-giving power only wants *to exist*; the senses want *to exist* and *be well*; but the intellect wants *to exist*, *be well*, and *be well forever*. O *Soul, go to your highest sublimity and the farthest horizon of your sight*: and let that *Alpha and Omega* <margin>Revelation 1:8</margin> <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, used as a title for God as the beginning and the end.</note> dwell within the lines of your dimensions. <margin>The Spirit. Luke 1:47, 1 Thessalonians 5:23, Genesis 2:7.</margin>
The spirit is a third part of a person’s being: just as the body is made of the earth, the spirit is made of the sky <note>original: "firmament"</note>. This spirit is inherited <note>original: "extraduce"; referring to the theological theory of "traducianism," where the spirit is transmitted from parents to children.</note>, nourished by the most refined energies of food and the elements of the world. It is the immediate life of the body. It has been given many names among scholars: It is called the *bond* <note>original: "*vinculum*"</note>, because these two extremes—<margin>Star-like spirit. Invisible body. Magnet of the microcosm. Clothing of the soul. Magnetic spark of the world's soul. The bond and vehicle of the soul. <note>original: "Spiritus sydereus. Corpus inuisibile. Magnes microcosmi. Vestimentum animæ. Animæ mundi scintilla magnetica. Vinculum & Vehiculum animæ."</note></margin> the physical, earthly body and the divine, heavenly soul—could not be joined except by a spirit of the skies, which shares the nature of both to link them together. Just as *Christ* is both man and *God*, sharing both natures to join *God* and humanity together. It is called the *vessel* <note>original: "*Vehiculum*"</note> because it carries the soul's faculties so easily through all parts of the body to all the organs, allowing for the quick execution of all its functions and actions. For example, the skill of a musician is instantly conveyed from the intellect of his brain to the furthest joints of his fingers. It has many roles and effects in the body: it is born with the body, feels with the body, and dies with the body, yet it differs from the body in substance and in power.

<margin>Shadow of the Trinity.</margin>
Thus, recognize in yourself a *physical body*, a *sky-like spirit*, and a *divine soul—a shadow of the Blessed Trinity*. The difference is this: in us, there are three essences in one person; but with *God*, there are three Persons in one essence.

# Chap. 2. 1. Blindness of mind.

...by the examination of ourselves, according to the four cardinal virtues: *Justice, Fortitude, Prudence*, and *Temperance*. The volumes of moral philosophy are filled with these. If we try and sift ourselves according to these virtues, we shall find many things worthy of blame; for, like wandering stars, we have (except for brief moments) forsaken the path <note>original: "eclipticke line"</note> of the golden mean and have wandered among all the extremes of vice.

<margin>Inconstancy. "What he sought, he now despises; what he lately threw away, he seeks again. He fluctuates, and his whole life is inconsistent in its order." <note>original: "Quod petijt, ſpernit, repetit quod nuper emiſit. Æſtuat, & vita diſconuenit ordine toto." — Horace, Epistles 1.1</note></margin>
The greatest and best part of our actions are but outbursts <note>original: "eruptions"</note> and impulses caused by circumstances. Indecision <note>original: "Irresolution"</note> begins them; instability follows them. Our actions are contradictory; we are not always like ourselves. We run from ourselves and rob ourselves of our own identities. Appetite and opportunity, along with the changing times, carry us like the wind.

<margin>Weakness. Vanity. Cares.</margin>
Good things in our hands are made worse through our weakness; we are weak in virtue, in truth, in extremes, and in the face of sudden news. Our thoughts are vain, breeding vain designs and even vainer desires; they produce empty beliefs and even more foolish hopes. Cares trouble us with things that serve us more when we are dead than when we are living; we do not take as much care for what we are within ourselves as for what we are in the public knowledge of men.

<margin>Troubles.</margin>
We are more troubled by small and light occasions than by greater affairs. We are bothered by fantasies, dreams, shadows, foolishness, anger <term>choler</term>, sorrow, joy, lies, deceptions <note>original: "impostures"</note>, and tales—even by nothing at all. As Greece and Asia were set on fire for an apple <note>A reference to the Judgment of Paris, the mythological cause of the Trojan War.</note>, we let the greatest evils arise from the smallest grounds. And the circumstance or accident moves us more than the substance.

<margin>False contentment.</margin>
We place our satisfaction <note>original: "contentment"</note> in the most frivolous trifles <note>original: "toyes"</note>, without which we could easily live. We feed on opinions and dreams. Animals do not satisfy themselves with nothing, but only with that which is present, tangible <note>original: "palpable"</note>, and real. We run, we rush, we rave, and build castles in the

<summary>The author argues that human behavior is characterized by instability and a lack of self-awareness, noting that people frequently abandon the "golden mean" of virtue for trivial impulses and public reputation.</summary>
<keywords>cardinal virtues, moral philosophy, inconstancy, vanity, human weakness, Trojan War, self-examination, golden mean</keywords>
