<meta>This page continues the discussion on the vanity of human existence and the necessity of deep spiritual self-examination, moving from moral philosophy to the internal work of the Holy Spirit.</meta>

the air. We live, we flee, we die, and a tiny speck <note>original: "mote"</note> at the last is the reward of our life's work. <margin>Psalm 62:9</margin> *Every living person is altogether vanity.* <note>original: "Vniuerſa vanitas omnis homo viuens."</note> And as *God* has all good in essence, and all evil in understanding only, so we are quite the opposite: we have all our good in our imagination <note>original: "fansie"</note> and all evil in essence.

<margin>Desires.</margin>
We cannot choose what we should; what we have chosen and obtained does not content us. Present things are loathed; we long <note>original: "bleat"</note> after things absent, unknown, and yet to come.

<margin>Pleasures. *From the very fountain of delights, something bitter rises up.* <note>original: "Medio de fonte leporum, ſurgit amari aliquid." — Lucretius</note></margin>
We cannot enjoy our good things and delight in our pleasures without some mixture of evil and grief.

<margin>Sorrow. *There is a certain pleasure in weeping.* <note>original: "Eſt quædam flere voluptas." — Ovid</note></margin>
We often let our highest pleasure cause a dejection of heart, just as sorrow is also never pure; in sorrowing, there is some pleasure.

<margin>Spiritual consideration of ourselves goes deeper.</margin>
The spiritual consideration of ourselves goes beyond the previous two methods. It searches most deeply: it evaluates <note>original: "ranges"</note> those who are of the best natures, the most civil behavior, and the most respectable profession, as well as those who are endowed with a supernatural decrease of sinfulness and some measure of inward graces. It pierces to the lowest bottom of the best regenerate <term>regenerate</term> <note>Spiritually reborn or restored to a state of grace</note> heart and spies spots in the face of innocence; it shows that despite all that is done well already, *Christ* still has something against them. <margin>Revelation 2:4, 14</margin> It finds blemishes even among the truest streams of grace. We are commanded to make this consideration of ourselves, unless we are reprobates <term>reprobates</term> <note>Those rejected by God or hardened in sin</note>. <margin>2 Corinthians 13:5</margin> *Test yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you—unless indeed you fail the test?*

<margin>Wrought by the Spirit. Proverbs 16:2; 1 Corinthians 2:10.</margin>
This is accomplished not only by the *Word* of God, but also by the most secret search of the *Holy Spirit*, who *weighs the spirits*. He reveals both the *things of God to us* and our own most secret faults <note>original: "spots"</note> to ourselves.

Here is required great humiliation, frequent meditation, and strict examination, with frequent short, fervent prayers <note>original: "ejaculation" — brief, sudden outbursts of prayer</note> and lifting up...

<margin>The benefit of knowing ourselves.</margin>
O man, why should you wear yourself out trying to know the sea and land, the stars and everything else, and yet not know yourself? It is one of the best parts of wisdom to know yourself. When Demonax <note>A Greek Cynic philosopher.</note> was asked when he began to practice philosophy, he answered, "When I began to know myself."

<margin>It makes us humble.</margin>
It will beat down your pride. Philip of Macedon <note>The father of Alexander the Great.</note>, to restrain and hold down his pride, appointed someone each day to wake him with these words: "Arise, O King, and remember you are a man."

<margin>And wise. To know nature.</margin>
It is great wisdom and great philosophy to know ourselves. It leads us to the true knowledge of our nature. Basil <note>original: "Basilius"; likely Saint Basil the Great.</note> says, "Be mindful of nature, and you shall never be proud. Observe yourself, and you shall be mindful of nature."

<margin>And God. "Man is a model of God in a small image." <note>original Latin: Exemplarqué Dei homo est in imagine parva.</note></margin>
It leads us to the true knowledge of God. The perfect knowledge of yourself shall sufficiently lead you, as if by the hand, to the knowledge of God.

<margin>It prevents judgments. Zephaniah 2:1, 2. 1 Corinthians 11:31. Epictetus's Handbook <note>original: "Epict. Enchir."; the Enchiridion or Manual of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus.</note>.</margin>
It prevents God's judgments. *Examine yourselves, even examine yourselves, O nation not worthy to be loved, before the decree is issued.* <note>Zephaniah 2:1-2</note> *If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.* <note>1 Corinthians 11:31</note> If you desire to become good, first believe that you are bad.

<margin>Lamentations 3:40.</margin>
It is the beginning and foundation of grace and repentance. *Let us search and test our ways, and turn again to the Lord.* <note>Lamentations 3:40</note>

<margin>More benefits. Psalm 16:7. Psalm 4:4. 1 Corinthians 11. 2 Corinthians 13:5. 1 Timothy 1:15, 16, 17. Romans 7:24, 25. "Looking to yourself." <note>original Greek: Σκοπῶν σεαυτὸν; a reference to Galatians 6:1.</note></margin>
It is a blessed gift of God for which to give praise; He gives us that counsel, *our inner thoughts also teach us in the night.* <note>original: "reines"; referring to the kidneys or "reins," historically believed to be the seat of emotions and secret thoughts. See Psalm 16:7.</note> It casts out and keeps out sin. It prepares a person properly for Communion. It assures a man that he is no castaway <note>original: "reprobate"; one rejected by God.</note> and makes him thankful to God for that assurance. It preserves him from many temptations (Galatians 6:1). It helps others who fall (likewise).

# CHAPTER III.
# The other blindness of mind, or ignorance of God.

---

> Isaiah 42:19 and 56:10. *Who is blind but my servant?*

---

-> Description <-

<margin>To what extent God is to be known.</margin>
Our knowledge cannot comprehend *God* as He is; yet we ought to understand Him as He has revealed Himself to us: partly through His works, and partly through His Word. *Adam* could have known Him perfectly in this way. But we cannot do so, for our miserable blindness and ignorance of *God*—and of His will and ways in *Christ* for our salvation—is so great and so profound.

<margin>Holy ignorance. Romans 11; Deuteronomy 29:29; Romans 12:3; Unspeakable words <note>original: Αρρητα ρηματα (Arrhēta rhēmata)</note>. 2 Corinthians 12:4.</margin>
Ignorance of *God*, insofar as He has obscured and hidden Himself from us, is no sin. As the scripture asks, *Who knows the mind of the Lord?* Or who knows the exact moment of Christ's second coming? This type of ignorance concerns the secrets of *God* and is a "holy ignorance." Secret things belong to *God*, and revealed things belong to us. It concerns things that are above, meaning that which is *fitting to understand*. An example of this was *Paul's* experience of hearing words that cannot be spoken. We must know all that we need to know and all that we are permitted to know; we should consider ourselves happy if *God* admits us to His court, even if He does not admit us to His private counsel <note>A metaphor: being a member of the royal household (the "court") versus being a member of the inner circle of advisors (the "counsel")</note>.

<margin>Perverse ignorance.</margin>
But the ignorance of *God*—insofar as He has most clearly and carefully revealed Himself through His works and Word—is not a simple *lack of knowledge* <note>original: neſcience</note> or a general want of

<summary>This page defines two types of ignorance regarding God: a "holy ignorance" of things God has intentionally kept secret, and a "perverse ignorance" of what God has clearly revealed through His Word and creation.</summary>

# CHAPTER 3. 2. Blindness of mind.

...of knowledge. It is not a simple privation <note>original: "priuation," meaning an absence or lack</note>, or a mere want of that specific knowledge that we should have had. Instead, it is an ignorance joined with a **perverse disposition**, by which the mind is not only blinded against **God** and godliness, but also plainly rebels against them. There are some notions left since the Fall concerning **God**, good, evil, life, right, wrong, truth, and falsehood; however, they are generally corrupted, maimed, and covered with dross. They are like carved stones in the heap of a ruined palace, serving only to make us inexcusable.

<margin>It is native and acquired.</margin>
This perversely disposed ignorance of **God** (in which we are all born and by which we are corrupted) quickly begins to increase, strengthen, and grow in degrees the further it spreads, like a fire. It becomes a compound blindness, made up of both native and acquired ignorance, and it continues to increase until it passes all bounds.
<margin>It grows.</margin>

<margin>Excusable ignorance.</margin>
The specific types of this ignorance are categorized according to its degrees. One kind is, in part, **excusable**; the rest are more **inexcusable**. **Excusable ignorance** is that which is unwitting <note>original: "witlesse"</note> but not willful; in this state, the will is deceived and errs only because of the mind's blindness.
<margin>1 Timothy 1:13; Philippians 3:15; Acts 17:30; John 9:41.</margin>

Thus **Paul** says: ***God* had mercy on me, because I did it ignorantly.** And, **If any be imperfect in the faith, they should be supported. If you are otherwise minded, *God* will reveal the same to you.** And, **The time of this ignorance, *God* overlooked.** This refers to the Gentiles. Also, **If you were blind, you would have no sin.** But take note: this simple ignorance is not altogether excusable, since it is our duty to know that which we are ignorant of. However, it is excusable in part compared to willful ignorance or sins committed against knowledge. The servant who knows his master’s will shall be beaten with many stripes, but he who does not know it shall be beaten with few.
<margin>It excuses not the whole [guilt], but only a portion. <note>original: *Excusat non a toto, sed a tanto*</note></margin>
<margin>Luke 12:47.</margin>

<margin>Inexcusable and malicious ignorance.</margin>
**Inexcusable ignorance** is malicious and willful. **They say unto *God*, "Depart from us, for we do not desire the knowledge of your ways. Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him?"** Because of this, **they willfully do not know.** They regard...
<margin>Job 21:14; 2 Peter 3:5; Romans 1:28; Psalm 14:1; John 12:4; Genesis 6:5.</note>

It uses the metaphor of a ruined palace to describe the remaining but corrupted natural knowledge of God in humans.</summary>

The second part is *not to know God*. Many are willingly ignorant so that they may sin more freely. Vanity of mind causes willful blindness to grow until *the foolish heart becomes full of darkness*, and at last becomes *finally a reprobate mind*. This leads to that *spiritual intoxication* <note>original: "ebrietie"</note> and the *power of delusion* <note>original: "efficacie of delusion"</note> that causes people to *believe lies*.

Our natural ignorance of *God*—his godhead, his power, and so on—is less than our ignorance of *Christ* and of the grace found in him. By the greatest light of human reason, the gospel is considered altogether nothing but foolishness.

---

->*Parts affected.*<-

<margin>
The mind.
</margin>
The mind is the faculty chiefly affected here, to a greater or lesser degree, and the rest of the faculties are affected by association. By the light of nature, the *mind* possesses some principles and common notions by which *God* may be known. However, the *mind* is narrow and weak—like the eye of an owl before the *sun's beams*. It can only know him in general terms, but not in specific detail.

<margin>
Common notions <note>original Greek: "Κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι"</note>.
Apprehension <note>original Greek: "Κατάληψις"</note>.
Aristotle in *Metaphysics*.

Acts 14:14.
Acts 17:24.
</margin>
For example, principles such as *there is a God* and *God is to be worshipped* are common, obscure, and imperfect. The men of *Lystra* knew that there was a *God* by their common natural light, but they erred in the specific application because they tried to offer sacrifices to *Paul* and *Barnabas*. Through reason, the blinded *mind* may attain this natural sight of *God*, but only with great difficulty and many helps; it is obtained by few and takes a long time to achieve. Even when it is attained, it is mixed with many errors and the *suppressing of the truth in unrighteousness* <note>original: "withholding of the truth in unrighteousnesse"</note>. Without the supernatural remedies of grace to strengthen and perfect it, the mind must continue to remain in darkness.

### Chap. 3. 2. Blindness of mind.

...to continue and grow in their ignorance. Many things that should be known are unknown, either by negligence to know, or sluggishness to learn, or bashfulness <note>original: "shamefastnesse": being too shy or modest to ask questions</note> to inquire; such ignorance has no excuse.

->Signs and Symptoms.<-

<margin>He is an atheist. Galatians 4:8.</margin>
He who is thus blinded and ignorant of the true **God** either impiously has no **God** or superstitiously has too many gods. His heart is haughty, and the usual word of all his thoughts is, *There is no God*. Or if he acknowledges that there is a **God**, he still denies His providence and presence, and says in his own mind, *God has forgotten, He hides His face, He will not look out, He will never search*. He has toward God no love, no fear, no trust, because he does not know Him. He either (like an atheist) never worships **God**, or else (like the **Athenians**) does it ignorantly <note>original: "Ignoto Deo": To the unknown God</note>. As for godliness, he either denies it, mocks it, or counterfeits it for profit. No man gets a paralyzed <note>original: "palise": palsied</note> hand through a blinded eye. But the blinded mind has a paralyzed heart and is senseless of sin and wrath, and of the silent <note>original: "deafe"</note> strokes of a punishing <note>original: "reuenging"</note> conscience. His conscience always sleeps; or if it stirs, he has enough fleshly songs to sing it back to sleep. From the beginnings <note>original: "preludies"</note> of sins, he comes to a habit of them, so that at last he cannot repent, nor change his dark <note>original: "Morian": Moorish or Ethiopian, referring to Jeremiah 13:23</note> skin, nor cleanse his leopard spots. He is wise to do evil and ignorant to do good.

# Chapter 3. Section 2: Blindness of mind.

<margin>Natural knowledge is a tutor <note>original: "Pedagogue"</note> that leads to the light of grace.</margin>
...by supernatural light, sight, and divine contemplation <note>original: "Theorie"; from the Greek *theoria*, meaning a looking at or contemplation of the divine</note>. By natural light, we are led—as if by a tutor—to know God, his Divinity <note>original: "Godhead"</note>, goodness, wisdom, power, providence, some articles of our faith, and the Ten Commandments. Thus, we are fitly prepared to be taught by supernatural contemplation.

<margin>The knowledge of God is three-fold.</margin>
You must understand that the knowledge of God is either purely *Natural, Scriptural, or Spiritual.*

<margin>Natural knowledge is two-fold: Inborn and acquired.</margin>
Again, natural knowledge is either *inborn or acquired.*
Inborn knowledge is naturally grafted into the minds of all people. Through principles known by nature, they may understand that there is a God.

<margin>Acquired knowledge.</margin>
Acquired knowledge of God is gathered from his works and creatures. These act as many *characters* <note>original: "Characters"; symbols or written signs</note> and footsteps of the *Deity*, imprinted everywhere and in everything, and understood by the things that have been made.

<margin>Romans 1:19-20. "And every blade of grass represents the presence of God" <note>original: "Præsentémque refert quælibet herba Deum"</note>. Psalm 19:1. Job 12:7, 8, 9, and 10.</margin>
Consider God, not by physical sight, but by his works. The heavens sound out the glory of God; their greatness and brightness suggest <note>original: "insinuates"</note> to us the power and glory of the Master-builder <note>original: "Work-master"</note>. Indeed, all creatures resemble the majesty of the Creator. *Ask now the beasts, and they shall teach you; and the birds of the heaven, and they shall tell you; or speak to the earth, and it shall show you; or the fish of the sea, and they shall declare unto you. Who is ignorant of all these, or does not know that the hand of the Lord has made them? In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind.* The creatures are the "Book of Nature," as said *Anthony the Hermit* <note>original: "Antonius Eremita"; Saint Anthony the Great, an early Christian monk</note>. When he was criticized for his lack of books, he answered the philosopher: "My book, O philosopher, is *the nature of things created.*"

<margin>Nicephorus, Book 1, Chapter 43. Dionysius, *On Mystical Theology* <note>original: "l. de myst. Theol."</note>, Chapters 2 and 7.</margin>
There are three ways our minds collect the knowledge of God from the light of nature and from creatures:
1. By the way of *excellence* <note>original: "Via eminentiæ"</note>: when we attribute to God (by a certain similarity) whatever is excellent in creatures. For example, when we count God the most wise, the most just, the most merciful, and so on.
2. By the way of *negation* <note>original: "Via negationis"</note>: when we remove from God whatever is defective or

<margin>The way of excellence. The way of negation.</margin>

# ### Chapter 3, Section 2: Blindness of Mind.

...other. And in Judas, after the betraying of Christ.

<margin>The harmony of the world.</margin>
Behold the order, progress, and end of all causes: the complete harmony of the universe, where there are so many opposites, yet such harmony among them. Everything comes from one, and everything returns to one <note>original Latin: "Omnia ab uno, omnia ad unum"</note>.

<margin>Predictions.</margin>
Behold the prediction of future events; the strange signs and wonders that have occurred, along with their outcomes, which proclaim a higher power.

<margin>This appears through the analogy of a ship.</margin>
If you see a well-equipped ship at sea, coming into its home port and sailing smoothly before the wind, wouldn't you quickly conclude that there is a captain <note>original: "Governor"</note> within it who guides it? In the same way, when you behold this beautiful universe with all its decorations and continuous motions, you may say that there is an internal and supreme Mover behind it.

<margin>A clock.</margin>
If you look into a clock, you see that one wheel is moved by the next wheel; that one is moved by another wheel, and that by yet another, until you reach the weight <note>original: "poize"</note>. And then you must conclude that a craftsman formed it and made everything move, while he himself remains unmoved.

<margin>Yourself.</margin>
If you consider yourself, notice how the veins from your liver provide nourishment. Your nerves from the brain allow for movement. Your arteries from the heart sustain your life; in them, you perceive a spirit, and by that, a pulse which you cannot stop, even to save your life. Observe the wonders of your brain, of your heart, and of your other vital organs <note>original: "noble parts"</note>, and see how wonderfully you are made.

<margin>Psalm 139:14. A tree.</margin>
Does not the tree that your eye sees lead your mind to the root, which is unseen beneath the earth? Does not a river lead your thoughts to its source and its first springs? And should not created things <note>original: "the Creatures"</note> lead your mind to the Creator?

<margin>A cottage in India. Psalm 8:1.</margin>
If you enter into India <note>In this period, "India" often referred generally to any distant, newly explored land, including the Americas.</note> and, in some newly discovered part there, spy a cottage, wouldn't you say, "Here are the footsteps of men"? And who does not see the footsteps of God throughout all the world? *How excellent is his name throughout all the world!*

### Chapter 3, Section 2: Blindness of Mind.

<margin>It is a wrong way to know God through the devil. Plutarch in his treatise, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original: "de defec. oracul."</note>.</margin>
It is a fair and seemly thing when a man is drawn to God by the *inward light* of his mind and the *outward sight* of the world. But it is a backwards way to be led forward by the devil's hand. An example of this is that governor <note>original: "president"</note> in Sicily, an atheist, who believed there was a God only because there was a devil, after he asked his *idol* for an answer to a question he had delivered in a sealed envelope.

<margin>The universal consent of all people.</margin>
Go through every corner of the world and search through all ages; behold all kingdoms, and even the very dens and caves of the most barbarous people, wherever mankind has lived. You will find this universal consent among them: that there is a God. This truth is written and read in every climate; it is engraved and deeply ingrained in man. People in newly discovered lands, though they may be without kings, laws, houses, or clothes, are never found to be without some knowledge of the Godhead. It is so natural for man to know the author of life and the cause of nature that all of antiquity agrees with this. <margin>The testimony of antiquity.</margin> The *Indian Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanes"</note>, the Persian Magi, Pythagoras, and Plato,* as well as all the most ancient poets—*Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, Pherecydes, Theognis, etc.*—always begin their works with *Jupiter*.

He is that only and universal *Unnamed One* <note>original: "Innominat"</note> who is above every name. # Chapter 3. 2. Blindness of mind.

<margin>Polytheism is atheism <note>original: "πολυθεοτης eſt αθεοτης"</note>.</margin>
...did not in their hearts acknowledge them, but only did so to please the people and the King. To have many gods is to have no God; for the gods of the **Gentiles** <note>In this context, non-Jewish people or pagans.</note> were either noblemen who had died, or devils falsely taking the name of gods upon themselves, or else they were simply stars.

<margin>The Gentiles did not receive this knowledge from the Jews.</margin>
While it might be said that the **Gentiles** received their knowledge of God from the **Hebrews**, the answer is: 1. The **Jews** did not spread the mysteries of their religion among the infidels. 2. The pagans <note>original: "Ethnickes"</note> mocked the Jewish religion.

<margin>God is seen and praised in his works.</margin>
Therefore, say with **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure from antiquity associated with wisdom and the "universal nature."</note>: *Lord, shall I contemplate you in things above, or in things below? You have created all things, and this universal nature is nothing else but your image.* But rather say with **David**: *Bless the Lord, all you his works, and let my soul bless the Lord.*

<margin>Psalm 103:22.</margin>
<margin>The school of nature has three types of students: Epicureans, Philosophers, and Christians.</margin>
The "school of the creatures" <note>The study of God through the natural world.</note> contains three types of students. 
1. Wordly **Epicureans**, wallowing sensually among the creatures; they feed themselves like beasts and are filled with **vanity**. 
2. **Curious heads**, busy with dark and troublesome questions; they are filled with **variety** <note>Likely referring to the fragmented and conflicting opinions of secular philosophy.</note>. 
3. Spiritual **Christians**, using the creatures as if they did not use them, and are filled with **truth** <note>original: "verity"</note>. 

Be you of this third type, who both sees God and enjoys him best through his creatures. You can perceive this more sensibly than the Orator <note>Referring to the Roman statesman Cicero.</note> could declare when he said: *The benefits that we use, the light that we enjoy, and the spirit that we breathe—we see that they are given and shared with us by God.*

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
<margin>Nature teaches only that God exists, but not what he is.</margin>
This natural knowledge of God teaches only in general that there is a God. However, it does not explain who he is or how he should be worshipped. Yet, this kind of knowledge is granted to men to draw them toward a further and better search for God. As **Paul** said: *As I passed by and beheld your devotions <note>Your objects of worship.</note>, I found an Altar where it was written, "Unto the unknown God." Him, whom you then ignorantly worship, I show to you: God who made the world and all things that are in it, etc. That they should seek...*

<margin>Acts 17:23–29.</margin>

<summary>This page argues that while nature reveals the existence of God, it cannot reveal his true identity or the proper way to worship him. It distinguishes between the empty curiosity of pagan philosophers and the spiritual understanding of Christians who see God's hand in creation.</summary>

# Chapter 3. 2. Blindness of mind.

And because there is nothing more in such a person except only *natural and scriptural knowledge*, he may become a shining lamp, but not a burning coal. He may enlighten others but not inflame himself; he may reveal to others their inward slumber, deadness, darkness, and hardness. Yet he himself remains within the depths of his soul, which is darkness itself—darkness in the abstract—and he is one who cannot see far off. This knowledge is only very general; it is merely a pedagogy <note>the method and practice of teaching</note> and a manuduction <note>original: *manuduction*; a leading by the hand or guidance</note> toward a more holy and heavenly knowledge that follows.

The spiritual knowledge of God is that Spirit of revelation, wisdom, and spiritual understanding. By this, although a person sees no more than what is in the Scriptures, they see those same things more clearly and better than through the Scriptures alone. Their enlightened eyes see supernatural truth more deeply than the simple letter of the Scripture can direct them. This is brought about by the secret illumination of the *Spirit*. And by that *Anointing* which he has received and which dwells in him, the Spirit teaches him of all things; and it is true and not a lie. He is made truly taught of God <note>original: *theodidaktoi*</note> and is truly acquainted with the mysteries of salvation. He also knows the dimensions of it: the breadth, length, depth, and height. He has a glorious and comforting, transforming sight of God's face. His light makes him both a shining lamp and a burning coal: he is at once both enlightened and inflamed. He determines matters of conscience with judgment and sincerity. He does all things with a gracious manner of single-mindedness and sincerity of heart, in all circumstances, for God's glory, his own good, and the good of others. In times of confusion, he has the noblest <note>original: *bravest*</note> resolutions. In afflictions, he makes the right use of the greatest evils.

### CHAPTER IV.
## Madness of Mind.

<margin>Ecclesiastes 9:3</margin>
> **2 Timothy 3:9.** *Their madness shall be evident to all men.*

### Description.

<margin>
Romans 1:21, etc.
Titus 3:3.
Galatians 3:1.
2 Peter 2:16.
2 Timothy 3:1 and 9.
</margin>
The mind is like a vessel that can never be empty: if it is not filled with the heavenly knowledge of ourselves and of God (the two fountains of true wisdom and happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>), it is replete with strange, mad imaginations and concepts, from which flow the floods of all wickedness and vice. For there is no evil that can be either thought or performed that must not be ascribed to this disease of madness and folly. Just as these great armies <note>original: "troups"</note> of impieties of the **Gentiles** <note>Non-Jewish people; in this context, the author refers to the pagan nations of antiquity</note> against God and nature sprang from a **mad** and foolish heart, it also stems from this: that men are unwise. The **Galatians'** <note>The people of Galatia, whom the Apostle Paul rebuked for being "foolish" for abandoning his teachings</note> fall flowed from their foolishness. The mute beast <note>Referring to the donkey of the prophet Balaam, which spoke to stop his reckless path</note> forbade the Prophet's madness. And all the wickedness of men in these last days and perilous times begins with their **madness**, and these sins are nothing else but the symptoms of it.

This is not like that madness that proceeds from the body's physical imbalance <note>original: "distemper"</note> and is cured by natural **medicine** <note>original: "physike"</note>; nor is it like the rage of those who are **afflicted by tarantism** <note>original: "Tarantat," referring to a historical dancing mania believed to be caused by the bite of a tarantula</note> and are cured

If those who run into fires, waters, depths, and dangers to the risk of their bodies are considered **furious** <term>furious: in this context, meaning insane or dangerously mad</term>, then they are to be considered much more mad who willfully throw themselves into endless dangers by their idle and foolish **conceits** <term>conceits: private opinions or fanciful notions</term>.

<margin>
Vain Opinion.
Galatians 5:8.
Ephesians 4:17.

The first and immediate work of this madness of mind is an imagined opinion. It proceeds from a mind deluded <note>original: "illuded"</note> by the imagination, which the diseased person thinks to be both true and good, when in itself it is both false and evil—the very vanity of the mind.

<margin>
Opinion is either true or false, good or evil.
True and good.
False and good.
False and evil.
</margin>
Opinion, as it is always weak <note>original: "infirme"</note> and uncertain in its own nature, is either true or false in regard to its **object**, and either good or evil, wise or foolish, in respect to its **effect** and **end**. Even if an opinion were completely false, if it leads to no evil, it is less foolish and less to be concerned about. For a man to consider his swarthy <note>original: "blacke"</note> wife beautiful <note>original: "faire"</note> makes him loving; to consider himself worse than he is makes him humble; to account all things for the best procures peace for himself. His opinion may be false, but it is not very foolish. Such opinions and imaginations are not to be cured. 

But if an opinion is both false and tends toward ill effects and ends—to the offense of himself, of others, or of God—and if they are the imaginations of **wicked enterprises**, then it is foolish and to be cured, if it is possible.
<margin>

->Treatment and remedies.<-

<margin>
Instruction in the truth.

The sowing of the seeds of grace in the minds of youth, so that they may be nourished in the faith by careful instruction and holy education, serves greatly to avoid this madness. This is how Timothy was guided from the start <note>original: "prevented"; in Early Modern English, this meant to be anticipated or helped in advance through divine grace or early guidance</note>, having learned the Holy Scriptures from childhood. When they reach greater maturity, they must be nurtured in religion and (if need be) disciplined through correction. Folly is bound in the heart of a child, but the rod of teaching will drive it away from him. Train a child in the way he should go <note>original: "in the trade of his way"</note>, and when he is old, he will not depart from it.

<margin>
Shun common sensual opinions.
Proverbs 30:32.
</margin>
*If you have been foolish in lifting yourself up, and if you have thought wickedly, lay your hand upon your mouth.* And hereafter, do not be carried away by the stream and swift river of general madness.

<margin>
Suspect opinions.
</margin>
Be suspicious of that which pleases the senses, for sensuality gives rise to many imaginations. Distrust common notions <note>original: "vulgar conceits"</note> supported by public applause and popular custom. Suspect a novelty of opinion as the untimely birth of an idle brain.

<margin>
Search for the truth of opinions.
</margin>
Search and examine all opinions that occur. With a quick and clear spirit, seek out the motives, causes, natures, effects, and ends—even down to the root. There may be a thousand opinions on one thing, of which only one is true. One truth may be overshadowed by a thousand lies. Truth, like a pearl, may be scattered and covered among heaps of many superfluous ashes; and like gold, it may lie hidden in the deepest mines. Therefore, set your mind at liberty and free it from all men's opinions. Let it expand in a noble universality to search for the truth in everything—a truth that is not obvious to everyone.

<margin>
Withdraw your mind from worldly opinions.
</margin>
Withdraw <note>original: "sever"</note> your mind little by little from the world's opinion and (like the stars) walk in a contrary course. And like a wise traveler, do not choose the fairest,

[foolish]ness: our wisdom, being enmity against God. To show the greatness of this, the Apostle uses the abstract words **foolishness** and **enmity** (Romans 8:6-7).

**Unbelief** <note>original: "Incredulity"</note> occurs when a person either does not believe the **truth of the promises of grace in general**, or else does not believe that the **truth and grace belong to them specifically** and particularly. This is that **temporary faith**, which still remains a form of unbelief; because although they know and love the truth, they do not make true use of it by applying it to the heart. This is found in many reprobates <note>original: "reprobates"; those rejected by God or hardened in sin</note> who know the Word and consider it sweet, like a **love song**. From this often proceeds that **gust** <note>original: "guſt"; a taste or relish</note> or **taste of the heavenly gift** and that **power of the world to come**, yet without truly possessing it in the heart.

### CHAPTER 5: The Evil Heart of Unbelief <note>original: "incredulity"</note>

<margin>Mark 9:24</margin>
...[having] <note>completing the word from the previous page</note> of the heart; but along with it, some unbelief <note>original: "incredulity"</note> and doubting. As the weeping father of the child said: *Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.* This is characteristic of weak Christians. It is an infirmity and disease which they daily lament and would gladly have amended. This is their true, saving, sincere <note>original: "unhypocritical"</note> faith, mingled with doubting. 

<margin>
It is not the nature of faith. 
Romans 4:20.
</margin>
However, this doubting is not part of the nature of their faith (unlike the previous types of unbelief, which are part of the nature of dead and temporary faith). Instead, this doubting—though mingled with saving faith—is not a weakness of the faith itself, but a fruit of the **unregenerate** <note>term: unregenerate—the part of a human nature that has not yet been spiritually renewed or "born again."</note> part of the person; it stands in opposition to faith.

<margin>
It does not reign. 
None are charged with it.
</margin>
But because this doubting and portion of opposing unbelief does not "reign" or rule over the **elect** <note>term: the elect—those chosen by God for salvation</note> as the previous types do, the elect are not labeled as incredulous or unfaithful. Furthermore, God does not hold it against them <note>original: "lay it to their charge"</note> if they labor and strive against it to have it corrected.

---

### *The Part Affected*

<margin>
Mind.
Heart.
Titus 1:15.
Conscience.
Affections.
</margin>
The parts of the person affected by this are:
1. **The mind**: specifically in its understanding, which lacks **illumination** <note>term: illumination—spiritual insight or divine enlightenment</note> and awareness of the truth; and in its judgment, which lacks a full consent that the truth is good.
2. **The heart**: which will not and cannot specifically choose the truth of grace for itself. It fails to grasp, apply, or claim that grace for itself in a firm, personal way as its own proper and relevant good.
3. **The conscience and affections**: through a shared connection <note>original: "sympathy"</note>, the conscience is also defiled, along with all the emotions and desires.

---

<margin>
Worldliness. 
Luke 8:11.
</margin>
An abundance of worldly means—a choking of the Word of God with cares, with riches, and with luxurious liv[ing]...

## Cures <note>original: "Curation"</note> and remedies.

<margin>
Cautions for various unbelievers. Acts 17:18, 22, 28. Acts 2:14.
</margin>
In the curing of unbelief <note>original: "incredulitie"</note>, this caution should be observed: If it is like a *Pagan’s* unbelief, you must begin your cure with natural principles from philosophy and nature. If it is like a *Jew’s* unbelief, deal with him at first with principles and grounds from the *Old Testament*. If it is like the unbelief of a *common Christian*, deal with him with grounds from the *Evangelists* <note>The authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note>. A *Pagan* denies all Scripture. A *Jew* denies the *New Testament*. An *unbelieving Christian* <note>original: "Infidell-Christian"</note> denies that the truth and grace of the *New Testament* belong to himself in particular. A *Pagan* admits only the light of nature, reason, and history <note>original: "stories"</note>. A *Jew* admits only the *Old Testament*. A *Christian* admits the whole Scripture.

<margin>
Remedies against general unbelief. Natural and supernatural truth <note>original: "Verity"</note>.
</margin>
Consider that truth is more extensive than nature, sense, and reason can reach. For just as there are natural truths, there are also supernatural truths that are invisible yet believable, of which reason is not capable until they are revealed. But once revealed, reason understands and approves of them; like the eye that sees nothing in darkness, but when the sun has risen and shines, it reveals and makes manifest all visible things to the eye. Nature and sense are the servants of reason, <margin>Truth compared with sense, nature, and reason.</margin> and reason is the handmaid of truth. Truth enlightens reason, and reason strengthens <note>original: "roborates"</note> truth. Reason will not reject faith, but reason declares that there are many things beyond reason's capacity and nature's limits, and therefore they are to be believed.

<margin>
Submit reason to Divine truth <note>original: "verity"</note>. To go mad even while using reason <note>original: "Et cum ratione insanire"</note>.
</margin>
You must not say, "This or that is not agreeable to nature, sense, or reason; therefore I will not believe it." For this is to imprison truth within nature, sense, and reason. Therefore, learn to submit reason...

### CHAPTER 5. *The evil heart of Unbelief <note>original: "Incredulity"</note>.*

<margin>Example.</margin>
For example:
1. Nature says, *Nothing can be moved by itself.*
2. Sense says, *The heavens are moved.*
3. Reason says, *Therefore they are moved by another.*
4. Faith says, *This "other" is God.* And I believe the same as it is written in the Scriptures, *Psalm 148:6.*

<margin>Romans 1:20.</margin>
The 1st, 2nd, and 3rd are natural truths <note>original: "verities"</note>; the 4th is a supernatural truth. *For the invisible things of God—that is, his eternal power and Godhead—are seen by the creation of the world, being considered through his works.*

<margin>Example.</margin>
Another example:
1. Nature says, *From nothing, nothing can be made by natural means.*
2. History and sense say, *From nothing—yes, even from opposites <note>original: "contraries"</note>—Christ made great things.*
3. Reason says, *He worked, therefore, by a virtue and power above nature: namely, by his divine power or Divinity.*
4. Faith says, *I believe he is both God and man: as it is written, Philippians 2:6–7.*

The first is a natural truth; the second, an historical and sensory <note>original: "sensible"</note> truth; the third, a logical truth; the fourth is above all these, a heavenly truth.

And consequently, because God cannot lie, it follows that the Scripture of God contains perfect truth: and that all that is written therein is to be believed. <margin>Reason is the unbeliever's <note>original: "infidels"</note> teacher <note>original: "Pedagogue"</note>.</margin> Against unbelievers, reason is to be used as a teacher <note>original: "Pedagogue"</note> to bring them to the school of faith. Reason, drawing from nature, kindles little sparks which Theology turns into great flames to give light to faith. <margin>As also testimony.</margin> Reason and testimonies have great force to persuade unbelievers. Reason is one witness, sufficient enough; a high number of witnesses is a manifold reason.

# CHAPTER 5. The evil heart of Unbelief. <note>original: "Incredulity"</note>

The tree seeks the earth for nourishment; the magnet <note>original: "Loadstone"</note> seeks the North Pole for rest; the deer <note>original: "Hart"</note> seeks the rivers of water; the earth seeks the rain; the stomach seeks food. Yes, a very strange voice.* God shall take hold of you as His own more than you are able, through your desire, to take hold of Him as your own. This can be seen in *Abraham*, who practiced this overcoming <note>original: "convincing"</note> power of faith and, beyond hope, believed in hope.

*Reason* said to him, "God's promise is impossible: your body is dead, your wife’s womb is dead, and God's promise is uncertain." But faith affirms with an overcoming power: God gives life to <note>original: "quickeneth"</note> the dead; he speaks of things that do not exist as if they did. God is willing, true, and able to perform his promises. I will give glory to God and believe. It is as if he were saying: God’s power is above nature, his wisdom is above reason, and his truth is above my doubting. I am, therefore, fully assured.

<margin>

The word "hardness," <term>Hard</term> <note>original Greek: "Σκληρὸς" (skleros)</note>. Mark 16:14 and 10:5. Matthew 19:8. <term>Hardening or induration</term> <note>original Greek: "Σκληρωμα" (skleroma)</note>.

Why it is called hardness of heart.
</margin>
<margin>
<term>Thorn</term> <note>original Greek: "Ἄκανθος" (akanthos)</note>.
A painful and cancerous scirrhus <note>original Latin: "Schirrus dolorificus & cancrosus"</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap T featuring floral patterns.</image-desc>This hardness of heart is like a scirrhous tumor—hard and insensitive (whether it is internal, in the liver or spleen, or external, in any part of the body). It grows hard through the drying up of the internal moisture <note>original: "humidity"</note>, leaving behind sticky <note>original: "clammy"</note> and glue-like dregs which block the passages and shut out the animal spirits <note>In the medical theory of the time, "animal spirits" were fluids in the nerves responsible for sensation and movement</note>, by which that part of the body becomes unfeeling. Similarly, in spiritual hardness, the fluid of grace, light, and reason is dried up <note>original: "exciccat"</note>. The poisonous dregs of sensuality remain and block all entrance to the heavenly graces of the Spirit, and so the heart remains senseless. If any humor of bile <note>original: "bilious humour"</note> is mixed with this physical hardness, it is called a painful and cancerous scirrhus. Likewise, when God adds the terrors of conscience to hardness of heart, it is felt horribly and most painfully.

<margin>
Why it is called <term>hardening</term> <note>original Greek: "πώρωσις" (porosis), referring to a callosity or the formation of a callus</note>.
Ephesians 4:18.
Paul of Aegina, Book 3, Chapter 73 <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note>.
</margin>
It is also called a stony hardness (called by physicians a *tophus* <note>original: "Tophos", a hard deposit often found in joints</note> or a callosity). It also signifies a tough, insensitive hardness, like that white, hard, and dry substance that knits together <note>original: "conglutinates"</note> broken bones. It may also be called a sort of festering discharge <note>original: "apostumate Sanies"</note> and matter, clotted <note>original: "coagulate"</note>

Hardness of heart is either:
1. Natural and inbred, born with us all.
2. Or else it is acquired and voluntary, which is a desperate, willful drying up and extinguishing of those smaller sparks left behind in nature's light and common graces. By this, many make themselves hard like an adamant stone and willfully estrange themselves from God. *The wicked are strangers from the womb; even from the belly they have gone astray and spoken lies.*
3. Or else it is inflicted by the hand of God as a punishment. God hardened the heart of Pharaoh when he gave him over fully to himself and the devil.

Hardness felt.

Hardness of heart, again, is either felt or not felt at all. Hardness felt is when we see and feel with sorrow our own dullness and deadness of heart, which cannot relent or dissolve into unfeigned repentance at the threats or promises of God. This happens to God’s children in their state of grace as a branch of our inbred corruption, and we are always fighting against it until death extinguishes it.

<header>CHAPTER 6. Hardness of heart.</header>

## Causes.

<margin>
How God hardens.
Exodus 4:21.
Deuteronomy 2:30.
Joshua 11:20.
Romans 9:18.
Exodus 9:16.
Psalm 119:8, 11, 51.
Romans 1:24.
2 Samuel 24.
2 Samuel 12.
Isaiah 6.
Isaiah 48:4.
1 Samuel 2:25.
Romans 9:18.
</margin>
God hardens justly as a punishment for sin. (As the potter may do as he pleases with his own clay) to show his power and to declare his name throughout all the world. He does this by ceasing to support a person with grace; by giving man over to his own lusts; by giving him over to *Satan’s* power; by blindfolding him; and by striking the heart daily through the Word, his judgments, his blessings, the motions of the Spirit, and the pricks of conscience. If these do not break the stony heart to contrition, then through its own corruption, the heart is hardened. It is like an anvil <note>original: "stithie"</note>: the more it is beaten, the harder it becomes. All this proceeds from the Lord’s foreknowledge. However, he does not harden his own people in the same way he hardens the reprobate <note>those rejected by God and destined for damnation</note>. He hardens his own to humble them under a sight and sense of their own corruption, and to sharpen their appetites for the heavenly *Manna* <note>spiritual nourishment provided by God</note>.

<margin>
How Satan hardens.
2 Corinthians 4:4.
</margin>
*Satan* hardens the heart by tempting and persuading it to refuse grace and to continue in sin or impenitence.

<margin>
How man hardens.
Exodus 8:15 and 9:34.
Jeremiah 4.
Ephesians 4:18.
2 Corinthians 3:14, 15.
Ephesians 4:17.
Jude 19.
2 Chronicles 36:13.
Jeremiah 5:3.
Hebrews 3:13.
Psalm 1.
Deuteronomy 2:30.
Acts 28:26.
</margin>
Man hardens himself by his own inbred <note>innate or natural</note> corruption. First, by abusing rest, peace, and prosperity. Secondly, by delighting in the "heart's veil," which is the mind's blindness, weakness, vanity, sensuality, and lack of the Spirit. Thirdly, by resolving not to repent. Fourthly, by yielding to the deceiving baits of sin. Fifthly, by continuing in the custom of sin without remorse, and by frequently repeating the act of sinning with delight and long habit. Sixthly, by clinging to the contagious company of graceless persons. Seventhly, by feeding their own hearts with self-love. Eighthly, by sleeping in carnal security <note>a false sense of spiritual safety while living in sin</note>.

1. God hardens by withholding grace (Deuteronomy 2:30).
2. Satan hardens by stealing away grace (2 Corinthians 4:4).
3. Man hardens by refusing grace (Psalm 95:8; Proverbs 28:14).

<summary>This page outlines the three agents of spiritual hardening: God, who hardens as a just judgment; Satan, who hardens through temptation; and man, who hardens himself through habitual sin and self-love. It emphasizes that while God hardens the reprobate for destruction, he temporarily hardens his own people to lead them to humility.</summary>
<keywords>hardness of heart, sovereignty of God, Satan, free will, sin, repentance, grace, reprobate, carnal security, spiritual discipline</keywords>

Upon this hardness grows a callous layer <note>original: "sward"</note> of unfeeling fatness that dulls the heart and makes it altogether insensitive; it spreads to the eyes and blinds them; it enters into the ears and shuts them. This willful hardness increases over time to such an extent that it is forced to vent its own stoniness by infusing an "iron sinew" into the neck—so that neither judgment nor mercy can bend it—and a "brazen brow" onto the face (a stony brow, a steel brow, a harlot’s brow), so that no rebuke will cause the person to blush at open acts of wickedness. Shame is no longer in his face, nor is there any sting in his heart.

As for that hardness which is felt and mourned, it is rarely without a piercing sorrow. It is full of trouble, grief, inner conflict, and a desire to improve; it is only that the spiritual means <note>spiritual practices such as prayer, scripture, and worship</note> have been long neglected. This is merely a temporary state. It may involve much ignorance, but less ill-will; those who are affected by this are more willing in spirit than they are able to feel. They are distressed with themselves because they are not as grieved by sin as they would like to be, and they are not as moved by God's mercy as they should be.

Remedies for felt hardness.
</margin>

1. Fear hardness of heart as the greatest punishment that God can lay upon you.
2. Frequently and thoroughly examine yourself and your specific, personal sins until your eyes are opened so that you may see yourself completely.

# CHAPTER VII.
## The spirit of slumber.

---

> Isaiah 29:10. *The Lord has covered you with a spirit of slumber.*

---

->Description.<-

<margin>
What it is.
</margin>
<margin>
A spirit of stupor <note>original Greek: Πνεῦμα κατανύξεως (pneuma katanuxeos)</note>.
Romans 11:7, 8.
</margin>
Just as physical sleep binds up all the senses and the vital energies <note>original: "animall spirits"; in early modern medicine, these were believed to be subtle fluids that transmitted sensory information and movement through the nerves</note>, this *spirit of slumber* binds up the soul, preventing any awareness of sin or feeling of grace. It is a most profound drowsiness, depriving a person of all awareness and feeling. And *Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching</note> says that it is such a habit of the soul by which it is so given over to sin that it cannot be brought back to a better state.

<margin>
Types and degrees of slumber.
Song of Solomon 5:2.
</margin>
<margin>
Ephesians 5:14.
</margin>
And just as there are various types and degrees of sleep-inducing diseases in the body, so there are various specific types of this *slumber*. The *godly*, because of their remaining corruption, sleep to some extent while their heart *remains awake*. Some others (like the ungodly) are in a deeper sleep—indeed, a dead sleep—to whom it is said, *Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead*. Their sleep cannot be easily broken; they are like those who are oppressed with sleep-inducing diseases, such as <term>lethargies</term> <note>persistent drowsiness</note>, <term>caros</term> <note>a state of deep, stupor-like sleep or semi-coma</note>, <term>catalepsies</term> <note>a condition characterized by muscular rigidity and lack of response to stimuli</note>, <term>catophoraes</term> <note>a medical term for a coma-like state or constant inclination to sleep</note>, or <term>typhomanes</term> <note>a state of lethargy combined with delirium, often associated with fever</note>, which are all deadly unless they are quickly cured. And just as all these deadly sleeps proceed from a cold humor <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids thought to determine health and temperament; "cold" humors were associated with sluggishness</note> or vapor filling the brain and oppressing the vital energies and senses, so this deadly *spirit of slumber* occurs when men have...

<summary>This page defines the "spirit of slumber" as a spiritual stupor that deadens the soul to sin and grace, comparing it to various medical sleep disorders of the time.</summary>

Carnal presumption of mercy—thinking they can obtain mercy as easily as anyone else, whenever they please, and in whatever manner they think best. *“When he hears the words of this curse, he blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall have peace.'”* They wish not to live well, but to die well like Balaam <note>a prophet in the Book of Numbers who desired the peaceful death of the righteous despite his own disobedience</note>. They think, in their own imagination, to create a heaven as they please and make the way there as wide as they like, *promising themselves liberty while they are the servants of corruption.* They think they may pass as easily as they please through the womb to grace, through grace to sinful indulgence <note>original: "wantonness"</note>, and through indulgence to glory—*turning the grace of God into indulgence.* They offer to the Lord *the unclean, the blind, the lame, the sick, and the torn,* and they consider inward and spiritual holiness to be nothing but *a weariness and something to be scoffed at <note>original: "snuffed at"</note>.*

<margin>Mental.</margin>
...that they be neither unlawful nor immoderate. **Mental sobriety** is a moderation of all our joys, confidence, desires, designs, delights, hopes, and inquiries; ensuring that they are bounded by honesty, reason, and religion. <margin>Prayer.</margin>
Be diligent in prayer and strive in it. Watchmen keep watch best when they are talking; acquaint yourself with the Lord, and keep yourself awake by conversing with Him. Let the body stir up the spirit, and the spirit the body. Give no rest to your soul, and let your soul give no rest to that *Holy One of Israel*. Incessantly urge Him, like the persistent widow <note>Referencing the Parable of the Persistent Widow in Luke 18:1–8, who refused to stop asking for justice.</note>; do not leave Him until, like *Jacob*, you receive a blessing <note>Referencing Genesis 32, where Jacob wrestles with an angel and refuses to let go until he is blessed.</note>.

<margin>Suspect Satan. 2 Corinthians 2:11. 1 Timothy 3:6 & 6:7.</margin>
Carefully recognize and always remember *Satan's* deceits <note>original: "circumuentions"</note>; do not be ignorant of his schemes <note>original: "machinations"</note>. On every occasion, suspect his traps <note>original: "pageants"</note> and snares. The tempter has a thousand ways to tempt; he desires nothing so much as for us to take some grains of his *Laudanum* <note>original: "Laudanum"; a tincture of opium used as a sedative. He wants us to fall asleep just once so that he may sow his weeds <note>original: "tares"</note> and spread his traps <note>original: "gins"</note>. There is not one person whom he does not assault, whether to tempt *Judas* or to strike <note>original: "buffet"</note> *Paul*. <margin>2 Corinthians 2:17. 1 Peter 5:8.</margin> Let us watch, therefore, because our adversary goes about continually *like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour*.

<margin>A skillful Physician. Isaiah 58:1.</margin>
...but a sleeping man can hardly help himself. It is appropriate that he have some skillful *craftsman* <note>original: "Artisan"</note> or *Scribe* trained in the kingdom of God, who can raise his voice like a *Trumpet* to administer these remedies with further instruction, warning, conviction, and encouragement. This person should also use discretion, considering all the circumstances of the cure: such as the time, place, person, and the nature and severity of the illness.

<margin>Trials <note>original: "Crosses"</note>.</margin>
If none of these things will prevail—just as doctors send their incurable patients away to mineral or metallic baths, or leave them to *God and nature* <note>original: "Deo, & naturae"</note>—so I leave those (who cannot or will not be cured) to their Maker. They must be awakened either by some heavy trial <note>original: "cross"</note> or some deeper wound of conscience. And if these things do not wake them, I expect they shall soon fall into a remedy beyond all cure: an unquenchable bath of fire and brimstone, which is the "second death." In that place, there is no more sleeping in sin nor waking to grace, but only endless weeping and gnashing of teeth.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### A cauterized conscience.

> 1 Timothy 4:2. *Whose conscience is cauterized (or burned) with a hot iron.*

---

->Description.<-

<margin>Conscience deals only with specific details.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral flourishes and a circular border within a square frame.</image-desc>
Conscience does not deal with generalities, as the mind does; but only with every particular thought of the mind, desire of the heart, word of the mouth, and action of the body.
<margin>Job 16:19.</margin>
It has a *witness in heaven*, with whom we are said to *know together* <note>original: "conscire"</note>:
<margin>Why it is called *syneidesis* <note>original: "συνειδησις"</note> or conscience. 1 John 3:20, 21.</margin>
and for this reason it is called conscience: meaning a private knowledge shared with someone other than ourselves—and this other person is only God. It combines two secret-keepers <note>original: "secretaries"</note> for one thing, and two sets of knowledge for one matter; so that we can know nothing ourselves alone.
<margin>Why it is called *synteresis* <note>original: "συντηρησις"</note>. It is God's deputy.</margin>
It is also called a *preservation of the moral spark* <note>original: "συντηρησις" or "synteresis," a theological term for the innate habit of practical reason that keeps us from total moral ignorance</note> of the light of nature, or the light of the law, to convict us in all our actions. God has appointed it to pass judgment before Him and with Him; either for us or against us. This is for the advancement of His own people so they may be converted, and so the wicked may be left convicted <note>original: "conuinced"</note>. At the last, it shall testify against them, how often it warned them, though they would not listen; a sentence which God, in His own time, will confirm <note>original: "ratifie"</note> against them.
<margin>It gives testimony. Romans 2:15.</margin>
It gives testimony regarding all our thoughts, words, and deeds. It is that Notary who always has the pen in his hand to record what is done. From him, nothing can be hidden, and no one can be set free.

<margin>Why called cauterized. 1 Timothy 4:2. The use of cauteries.</margin>
In the wicked, the conscience becomes "cauterized," or seared with a hot iron. In using this word, the Apostle Paul alludes to medical cauterization <note>The use of a hot iron or chemicals to burn tissue.</note>, which is used for: 1. Branding or marking any part of the body with a hot iron. 2. Cutting away any rotten or gangrenous part. 3. Turning any decaying part into a dead, senseless scab <note>original: "escarre," a piece of dead tissue that eventually falls off.</note> that soon falls away. 4. Treating venomous bites, carbuncles, venereal <note>sexually transmitted</note> or plague-ridden boils, and stubborn tumors that otherwise refuse all help. When a diseased part cannot be helped by softening, ripening, drawing out infection, or cutting, then the only option is cauterizing—either through heat or chemical means—as the situation requires.

<margin>A cauterized conscience is guilty. 1 Timothy 1:19.</margin>
Thus, a cauterized conscience is: 1. A conscience stained and branded with inseparable, past <note>original: "bigane" or "bygane"</note>, unrepented marks and signs of guilt and corruption. 2. A conscience that has been cast off, put away, or cut away; so that in regards to its duties, it neither truly nor holily witnesses, accuses, nor excuses. All past light, feeling, and life (of both reason and grace) have turned into a hard, calloused, rotten, dead, and crusty lack of feeling.

<margin>Senseless. Ephesians 4:19. Filthy. Ephesians 4:18; Romans 1:28.</margin>
3. A conscience that is rotten, venomous, ulcerated, diseased, filthy, and gangrenous, whereby a person most boldly dares to fall away and commit any sin with greed. 4. A conscience that is, at first, without feeling, so long as the filthy, senseless...

<margin>Consciences. Romans 2:15.</margin>

It is a tragedy acquired by the increasing corruption of one's nature, as will be seen in the specific causes that follow.

<margin>Sins wasting the conscience.</margin>
Sins against the conscience, or (as *Augustine* calls them) "sins that waste the conscience"—which are committed with a full mind and resolution, even greedily, and reign over the whole person—their habit, over time, brings on a strange wasting away and empties the conscience of all light and life. In its place grows an incurable abscess <note>original: "apostumation"</note> and rot, to be seared <note>original: "feared"</note> with a hot iron.

<margin>Hardness of heart.</margin>
Hardness of heart and the fury of uncontrolled <note>original: "inordinate"</note> passions work together to enable sins to waste the conscience even more. These (in a circular effect) increase both the hardening of the heart and the searing of the conscience.

<margin>Satan poisoning.</margin>
Just as Satan blinds, he also numbs and poisons the conscience. *Judas* was first a devil, then repossessed again by the devil, until his conscience was fully seared to the highest degree.

<margin>God deserting.</margin>
God deserts the sinner and punishes the previous abuse of the natural or enlightened conscience.

<margin>Blindness of mind. Titus 1:15.</margin>
Increased blindness of the mind, joined with an evil heart of unbelief <note>original: "incredulity"</note> (by which the light of conscience is extinguished), brings on a festering sore throughout the entire conscience, which is then seared: *To those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure, but even their minds and consciences are defiled.*

<margin>Madness of mind. Psalm 10:3. Isaiah 28:15.</margin>
Crazed <note>original: "brain-sick"</note> and foolish opinions (directly against the true meaning of God’s Word) treat empty verbal prayer as true devotion. They think seeking help from witches is an acceptable remedy for any trouble. They believe that swearing by created things in a true cause is not a sin. They claim that true religion is merely being overly strict <note>original: "preciseness"</note>; greed is just being practical <note>original: "worldliness"</note>; pride is just self-respect <note>original: "honesty"</note>; fornication is just a youthful phase; and swearing is a brave and gentlemanly way to speak. They believe that even though they sin against God, they can escape judgment. In a moment, he will not be able to endure himself, but must either burst or most desperately end his life, as did *Ahithophel* <note>original: "Achitophel"</note> and *Judas*.

<margin>A dangerous situation.</margin>

If this disease is neglected for a long time, it becomes almost incurable. It is useless to say, after many years, "God is merciful; I have sinned." Pharaoh, Saul, and Judas all cried out, "I have sinned" <note>original Latin: "Peccavi"</note>. Yet Pharaoh’s heart was hardened and he perished. Saul consulted with a witch and was cast away. Judas despaired and took his own life. This condition is cured with great difficulty; almost no one escapes it. For a person so affected either falls into a depraved <note>original: "reprobate"</note> mind or rushes toward a desperate end. He had no desire to reform himself, but he will have a raging mind to destroy himself. His hardened <note>original: "indured"</note> heart can endure the harshest rebukes and corrections from others, but he cannot endure himself.

<margin>The many evils of a seared <note>original: "feared"; in this context meaning cauterized or hardened</note> conscience.</margin>
A seared conscience can never be a friend; it is always a person's greatest enemy. It is the Lord’s sergeant, constantly arresting and bringing its owner before God. It is his jailer, keeping him in tight irons and ensuring he appears on that great day of judgment. It acts as a thousand witnesses to accuse him, the judge to condemn him, the executioner <note>original: "hang-man"</note> to punish him, and flashing firebrands to torment him. It remains a forerunner and enforcer of God’s most righteous judgment. When God awakens it, it will become extremely cruel and fierce, like a ravenous beast.

<margin>A false sense of peace.</margin>
The judgment of the conscience may (by God's permission) be suppressed for a time and to a large extent, and its final sentence may go unheard. But in the end, it rages and is invincible; it cannot be fully or finally extinguished.

<margin>Genuine terror.</margin>
At last, it will lift up its voice like a trumpet and thunder with an authentic, divine echo of condemnation from God’s judgment seat <note>original: "tribunall"</note>.

<margin>A book opened. Revelation 20:11, 12.</margin>
Although it is a "closed book" in this life, yet after the death of the body—and even more so after the body's resurrection—it will be an "opened book." God will enlighten it and stir it up by His mighty power. It will plainly disclose the oldest and most hidden sins <note>original: "abominations"</note>, along with countless millions of endless sorrows. And in this life, it shall

## *Healing and remedies.*

<margin>Fear of judgment and death.</margin>
If you seek incessantly for honors, riches, and pleasures—which must eventually be left behind—and for the helping and easing of the least pain of your body, which is returning to the dust: how much more should you care to be relieved of this festered conscience, the greatest malady that can befall a person? Consider often these two most terrible days—death and Judgment—in which everyone must give an account. In those moments, a seared conscience shall be a great enough condemnation on its own. On the contrary, we must labor for a sound and whole conscience, which *is a continual feast* <note>Proverbs 15:15</note> and the only surest comfort in life, in death, and after death.

<margin>Proverbs 15:15. Let this be a wall of brass, etc. <note>original Latin: "Hic murus aeneus esto, &c." From Horace, meaning a clear conscience is an impenetrable defense.</note> Knowledge and application of the Word for use. 1 Peter 2:2; Psalm 119:18; Proverbs 2:4; Psalm 119:66; Galatians 3:10.</margin>
Endeavor for a daily increase of true light. Let that *sincere milk, sweeter than honey*, be your daily nourishment <note>original: "diet-drinke"</note>, so that it may dwell in you plentifully. Like David, desire the opening of your eyes, that you may understand the wonders of God's Law. Make a daily search of the Scriptures, as if looking for gold in the mines of the earth. Labor for spiritual wisdom, so that you may have—along with your enlightenment—the right use of it in all your specific actions. Let your conscience be healed, lightened, and directed by it in all your affairs. Be always meditating upon this judicial sentence of the Law: *Cursed is every man who does not continue in all things which are written in the Book of the Law to do them* <note>Galatians 3:10</note>. Apply this justly deserved curse to yourself, so that your prideful, preoccupied, and ignorant mind, and your hardened heart (the poisoners of conscience), may finally be startled into awareness.

<margin>Examination. Lamentations 3:40, 41, 42; Zephaniah 2:1.</margin>

# CHAPTER IX.
## A wounded spirit.

---

->*Proverbs 18:14. But a wounded spirit, who can bear it?*<-

---

### Description.

<margin>
What it is.
How it occurs.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial T featuring scrolling foliage.</image-desc>The deepest wound of the spirit is caused by trouble of conscience or distress of mind: when a man's conscience is disquieted before God, wherein the power to excuse oneself is too small, and the power to accuse is too great.

<margin>
The lowest degree.
</margin>
The lowest degree of this wound is when a man is in suspense and doubts his spiritual standing <note>original: "good estate"</note> before God, and is in a simple fear and grief over his own condemnation (a common condition among the <term>regenerate</term> <note>Those who have been spiritually reborn or converted to the faith.</note>).

<margin>
The highest degree.
</margin>
The greatest degree of this is when a man is (in his own sense and understanding) without any hope of salvation. This is more than simple fear; it is even a kind of fearful desperation.

<margin>
Three types of this wound.
</margin>
There are three types of this wound. 1. It either arises directly from the soul. 2. Or it arises directly from a <term>melancholic body</term> <note>original: "melancholike body"; referring to the historical medical theory of the four humors, where an excess of "black bile" was thought to cause deep sadness or depression.</note>. 3. Or it is a mixture, arising from both.

<summary>This page defines the "wounded spirit" as a state of extreme mental and spiritual distress caused by an overactive, accusing conscience. It categorizes the condition into varying degrees of severity, from simple doubt to total despair, and identifies its origins in the soul, the body, or both.</summary>

<keywords>wounded spirit, conscience, distress of mind, salvation, despair, regenerate, melancholic, spiritual health</keywords>

### Part affected.

<margin>
The Conscience.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial T featuring vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>The part affected here is primarily the conscience, whose disturbance <note>original: "perturbation"</note> spreads through all the faculties of the soul, as will clearly appear hereafter.

### Causes.

<margin>
God acts to declare His justice against the wicked and His mercy toward the godly.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial G featuring scrolling foliage.</image-desc>God, by His own will, causes this wound to be inflicted to further manifest His power. This is done both in justice toward the wicked—starting their hell here on earth and sealing their just condemnation, as seen in Cain, Saul, and Judas—and in mercy toward the godly, such as Job and David. These righteous people often feel no comfort, but only perceptible signs <note>original: "sensible tokens"</note> of God’s displeasure. They think their situation is hopeless and that they have entered into some stage of despair.

<margin>
To test their faith and to refine it.
To rebuke <note>original: "snib"</note> their sins.
To prepare them for glorious feelings.
To help them know themselves and value His presence more.
To know what Christ felt for them.
</margin>
He does this to test their faith and to chastise their sins. In this, He is not an <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The direct producer of an effect.</note> but a <term>deficient cause</term> <note>Theological term for when God allows an effect to happen by withdrawing His supporting grace or presence, leaving the person to their own weakness.</note>, leaving men to themselves and exercising their faith with temptations before He sends them glorious feelings of joy. God hides Himself under a cloud to humble His own children through the knowledge of themselves, making them value His presence more and cling to His strength. He pursues them with His wrath to cause them to flee to His mercy and to understand what Christ felt for them, who drank the dregs of that most bitter cup of which they only drink the drops.

<margin>
Satan, by God’s permission, magnifies sin more than mercy.
</margin>
Satan (that roaring lion) labors by all means to bring the conscience first to senselessness and then to despair. He continually casts cruel and impure thoughts into the heart, even the hearts of the most innocent. He is shrewd and cunning; he magnifies a lesser sin to hide a greater one, and he magnifies any great sin more than <note>The text continues on the next page: "...the mercy of God."</note>

<summary>This page explains that a wounded spirit primarily affects the conscience and is caused by God to manifest His justice toward the wicked and His refining mercy toward the godly. It also notes how Satan exploits this distress to drive the soul toward despair.</summary>

Melancholy.
</margin>
Melancholy (caused by dark fumes and black vapors arising from a diseased <note>original: "distempered"; in the medical theory of the time, an imbalance of bodily fluids or "humors"</note> body) corrupts the imagination so strangely that the heart, emotions <note>original: "affections"</note>, and conscience are greatly disturbed. This creates a tendency to imagine evil in everything, to interpret all things for the worst, to apply every bad thing to oneself, and to imagine a thousand mountains of unavoidable <note>original: "uneschewable"</note> miseries against oneself—accounting oneself to be the greatest sinner and to lie most heavily under God’s eternal displeasure.

<margin>
A false trouble of conscience.
</margin>
In this case, the conscience is not truly touched by a sense of sin, but by a perverted imagination; yet it mimics a troubled conscience very closely. Such a person never addresses his sins specifically, but only in general and in a confused mass. Often he is more affected by the smallest sins and imaginary sins than by the greatest and most real ones. As for God’s wrath, he does not understand it correctly; but because he hears it is such a great evil, he is afraid of it (for every evil frightens him in a confused way). Indeed, he is afraid of a picture on the wall, the crowing of a rooster <note>original: "cocke"</note>, and the rustling of a leaf. He will be strangely terrified by his own thoughts and dreams. Melancholy is the devil’s bait, just as Saul’s evil spirit (the devil) took advantage of his parched <note>original: "adust"; a medical term for humors "burnt" by heat</note> and melancholic temperament.

<page-num>120</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 9. A wounded spirit.</header>

<margin>
Symptoms of blasphemous temptations suggested by Satan.
</margin>
When the devil wounds the conscience with filthy, suggested thoughts, they enter the mind rapidly and are forced upon it violently. They are unavoidable and recur again and again, entering the mind perhaps a thousand times in a single day. These thoughts are conveyed to the mind from the outside. Consequently, the memory is weakened, the senses are dulled, and the brain is confused <note>original: "confounded"</note>. These vile thoughts are directly contrary to the light of nature, and even more so against the light of grace, as they involve thinking irreverently about God. They are conceived with fear, and feelings of trouble and fainting follow. They are cast into the mind, not born there. They can happen to both the bad and the good; even the most upright citizen <note>original: "Civilian"; a person of high secular morality but perhaps lacking spiritual depth</note> and the most sincere believer <note>original: "fairest professor"</note> may be depressed <note>original: "in the dumps"</note> by them. The godly cannot promise themselves freedom from these thoughts, but when they experience them, they loathe them.

<margin>
Symptoms of blasphemous temptations arising from ourselves.
</margin>
There is another kind of impure thoughts, most vile and filthy, that are not so much injected or suggested by Satan; instead, they come more directly from a person's own heart. These come with more leisure, less violence, and more moderation. They are not so far against the light of nature. They do not cause fear, fainting, or physical sickness, nor is the person shocked <note>original: "amazed"</note> by them. They arrive more systematically, arising from the hearts of those with degenerate <note>original: "reprobate"</note> minds. They do not distress the conscience because the mind approves of them; they belong more to a madness of the mind or to a seared <note>original: "cauterized"</note> conscience than to a truly wounded conscience.

<margin>
Symptoms of common trouble affecting the godly.
</margin>
When those who are godly and born again <note>original: "regenerate"</note> experience a trouble of conscience that is more common and less violent, they feel sorry for not feeling as much sorrow as they should. They are grieved by their own hardness of heart and troubled by doubts. They complain of infirmities, needs, weaknesses, imperfections, omissions, and moral slips. They lament that God’s graces are not as sweet to them, and their own sins are not as bitter <note>original: "sowre"</note> as they ought to be.

<margin>
Symptoms of a melancholy trouble.
</margin>
If the trouble of conscience seems to stem from melancholy <note>a condition traditionally believed to be caused by an imbalance of "black bile," resulting in deep sadness or delusional fears</note>, the imagination will produce monstrous ideas:

...thinking himself often to be a beast (such a one was *Nebuchadnezzar*). Sometimes he thinks he is a pitcher, a sow, a dog, or a dead body. Such people may imagine their nose to be monstrously big, their buttocks to be made of glass, or their belly to be full of little cats, etc. He who is affected this way will apply every evil thing to himself. He will have many horrors, fears, and despairs, even regarding his salvation. He fears every man, every creature, and even himself; he fears most when there is least cause for fear. He is displeased with himself and with his own actions. This trouble is not burdened with a specific sense of sin and divine wrath (as a true trouble of conscience is). It lacks courage in everything, whereas a true trouble of conscience can be most courageous in many godly matters. This condition may be cured with medicine <note>original: "Physicke"</note>, but a true trouble of conscience scorns all physical medicines. This passion takes a long time to develop and comes on more slowly than true spiritual trouble does.
