# CHAPTER 9. A wounded spirit.

<margin>
Remedy if the trouble stems from a supposed sin against the Holy Spirit.
1 Timothy 1:13.
Acts 3:17.

What the sin against the Holy Spirit is.

Three things are present in the sin against the Holy Spirit.

Signs that it has not been committed.
</margin>
If your trouble comes from a supposed sin against the *Holy Spirit*—because you think your sins were committed against your own knowledge and conscience, or because you have opposed the truth—you must consider that *Paul* persecuted the truth; *Peter* denied the essential truth; and *David* sinned against his knowledge and conscience. And yet none of these committed the sin against the *Holy Spirit*, which is a total apostasy <note>original: "vniuersall apostacie"; a complete abandonment of faith</note> and a general denial of the truth and the whole religion, attacking it despite the illumination of the mind and conscience. Therefore, three things are required to commit this sin: First, knowledge. Second, a resolute and purposeful malice. Third, an opposition against the whole truth. This sin cannot be committed out of weakness, suddenly, or unawares; but only through spiteful malice, clear knowledge, and settled resolution. Consider this: if you would not want to commit that sin, then certainly you have not committed it. Or if you fear or regret <note>original: "rewest"</note> that you have fallen into it, and wish to be free of it, then certainly you are most free of it.

<margin>
Remedies if the wounded spirit comes from temptations of blasphemy.
Bernard, *Book on Conscience*. <note>original: "Bar. l. de Consci." likely referring to Bernard of Clairvaux</note>
Remember they are the devil's sins, not yours; they are your burdens.
</margin>
If the wound proceeds from temptations of blasphemy, involving filthy and abominable thoughts in the mind, leading you to judge yourself as nothing else but a devil incarnate because of these filthy fantasies that are so "terrible regarding faith, and horrible regarding the nature of God" <note>original: "Terribilia de fide, horribilia de diuinitate"</note>: Remember they are not your personal sins, but your crosses <note>burdens or trials to be endured</note>. They are the devil's sins, and he must answer for them—not you, for you neither created them, nor approved of them, nor consented to them. They are outward thoughts from an external cause; they do not come from ourselves, nor from our own corruption. Therefore, do not fear them.

<margin>
Reject them.
James 4:7.
</margin>
Let them go as they come; do not struggle against them, but reject them as abominable. Do not give weight to the terror they cause. Say with Christ in a similar temptation, "Away with you, Satan; resist the devil" <note>original: "Auoid, Satan, resist the deuill"</note>. Say, "Away with him and such false absurdities." Always consider them Satan’s sins, and not your own.

# CHAPTER 9. A wounded spirit.

<margin>Protest your innocence.</margin>
...your own; appeal to God, and protest your innocence of heart. Say with *Paul*, "*I do the evil I do not want to do*" <note>original: "I doe the euill I would not"; referring to Romans 7:19</note>: do not dwell on these thoughts in your mind any longer.

<margin>

</margin>
And even if I were to concede <note>original: "giuing, but not graunting"</note> that they are your personal and specific sins, remember that if you repent, they proceed from your unregenerate part <note>term: unregenerate part; the part of a person's nature not yet spiritually renewed or reborn</note>. They are pardonable in Christ; if you can say with a sorrowful heart, "*It is no longer I that do it, but sin that dwells in me.*"

<margin>Beware of idleness. Seek out holy and pleasant company.</margin>
Beware of idleness and solitude. Seek out holy company, with holy joy and the singing of Psalms. *Eve*, *David*, and *Christ* were all tempted when they were alone; open your heart and share your condition <note>original: "estate"</note> with some faithful and suitable friend.

<margin>
Strengthen your mind with the light of grace. Colossians 3:18. Psalm 1:2 & 119:11. Proverbs 20:18. & Psalm 119:24. Matthew 4:10.
</margin>
Watch over your own heart and guard it by letting *the Word dwell abundantly in your heart*. Exercise yourself in meditating on the Law of God. Strengthen your heart with the counsel of the most wise God, rather than your own intellect. Oppose these thoughts with the light of grace, saying as *Christ* did in a similar temptation, "*It is written...*"

<margin>Be zealous in doing good.</margin>
The more these vile thoughts enter your mind, the more zealous you should be in doing the opposite; seek God's glory by all means. Be diligent in the duties of your specific vocation <note>term: particular calling; one's specific profession, social role, or God-given station in life</note>.

<margin>Be constant in prayer.</margin>
Above all things, be constant <note>original: "instant"</note> in prayer for mercy and for light: to discern truth from falsehood—to reject the one and yield to the other.

<margin>
If this malady proceeds from "wasting" sins, use the remedies against impenitence.
</margin>
If this malady proceeds from sins that have wasted the conscience <note>term: wasting the conscience; committing serious sins that deaden or destroy one's moral sense and spiritual peace</note>, use every means to correct your lack of repentance (as described in the section on the cure for impenitence). And use all the remedies for comforting a distressed conscience lying under the weight of sin and wrath, as previously described.

<margin>
If it proceeds from melancholy, the remedies are repentance and comfort. Psalm 34:7–8.
</margin>
But if it proceeds from a melancholic <note>term: melancholious distemper; an imbalance of "humors" in the body, which at the time was believed to cause depression, anxiety, or intrusive thoughts</note> physical condition (as it most frequently does), you must repent and renew your repentance; you must also be comforted with the promises of mercy. As the "*Angel of the Lord camps around those who fear him, and de-*" <note>The text continues on the next page: "...delivers them."</note>

# CHAP. 10.

<image-desc>A rectangular decorative woodcut headpiece featuring symmetrical scrolling foliage, floral patterns, and central vine motifs.</image-desc>

### CHAP. X.
### Callous <note>original: "Dedolent"</note> Impenitence.

> *Ephesians 4:19. Who, being past feeling, have given themselves over to wantonness.*
> *Romans 2:5. The heart that cannot repent.*

---

### Description.

<margin>
Romans 2:5.
Repentance has 2 parts.
Contrition must have a threefold sorrow: first from the heart, secondly for sin, thirdly toward God.
2 Corinthians 7:9, 10.
Contrition <note>original Latin: "Contritio"</note> must be accompanied by four things.
Jeremiah 3:13.
1 Corinthians 11:31.
1 John 1:9.
Jeremiah 15:20.
Job 42:6.
</margin>
Impenitence—the state of having a heart that cannot repent—will be better understood if true repentance is first rightly explained. True repentance has two most essential parts: Contrition and Conversion.

Contrition is a sorrow of the heart toward God for sin; that is, for the offense against God, which draws the heart back to Him. It is not a "worldly sorrow," which is felt only for the punishment and harm <note>original: "skathe"</note> caused by sin. Contrition must be accompanied by: 
1. The knowledge of sin; 
2. The hatred of sin; 
3. The judging and condemning of ourselves for sin; 
4. An act of humiliation and confession of sin; 
5. A love for God; 
6. And a hope for mercy in Him.

<margin>
Repentance is given the names of contrition.
^a Jeremiah 4:4 and Hosea 10:12.
^b Joel 2:13.
^c Acts 2:37.
^d Psalm 51:17.
^e Jeremiah 31:18, 19.
^f Ezekiel 36:32.
^g Job 42:6.
^q 1 Samuel 7:3.
</margin>
In Scripture, this is called ^a *the breaking up of the fallow ground* of our hearts; the ^b *tearing of the heart*; the ^c *piercing of the heart*; a ^d *contrite spirit*; the ^e *lamentation of Ephraim*; a ^f *shaming and confounding*; the ^g *loathing of ourselves*; and a ^q *longing after the Lord.*

In regards to this sorrow, the Latin writers <note>original: "Latines"</note> give repentance...

<header>CHAP. 10. Callous <note>original: "Dedolent"</note> impenitence.</header>

<margin>
Repentance from punishment. <note>original Latin: "Pœnitentia a pœna"</note>
Regret. <note>original Greek: "Μεταμέλεια"</note>
Matthew 27:3.
</margin>
...a name derived from that sorrow <note>original: "dolour"</note>, with which the heart is punished. The *Greeks* derive the term from the care, concern, and anxiety that accompany contrition.

<margin>
Conversion in three things.
^a Ephesians 4:23.
^b Colossians 3:6.
^c Romans 6:4.
</margin>
As for *Conversion*, it must be a changing and turning of the heart to God by ^a *regeneration* <note>term: spiritual rebirth</note>. 2. A turning from all sin by ^b *mortification* <note>term: the "putting to death" of sinful desires</note>: and 3. A constant turning to God in that grace of ^c *vivification* <note>term: being made spiritually alive</note>, and a rising up to a new life.

<margin>
Names of repentance taken from contrition.
^d Jeremiah 4:4.
^e Isaiah 55:7.
^f Acts 26:18.
^g 1 Thessalonians 1:9.
^h Acts 26:20.
^i Isaiah 1:16, 17.
Jeremiah 4:1.
Change of mind. <note>original Greek: "Μετάνοια"</note>
</margin>
This is the ^d *circumcision* of the heart, that ^e *turning* to God, a ^f *turning from darkness* to light and from the power of Satan to God; a turning from sin to serve the ^g *living God*; that ceasing to do evil and learning to do well. In regard to this turning, Repentance is called by the Hebrews *Teshuva* (Jeremiah 4:1), a word borrowed from those who have gone long astray and are now returning, after a warning, to the King's highway. It is called by the *Greeks* *Metanoia* <note>original: "Μετάνοια"</note>, an amendment of former foolishness, or a changing of the mind from worse to better.

<margin>
What repentance is.
The seven effects thereof.
2 Corinthians 7:11.
</margin>
So, repentance is a constant sorrow in the heart for offending God through sin, with a hearty turning from all sins to God. This is accompanied by seven effects and signs: *care for amendment*; *clearing* oneself from the guilt of others; *indignation* against yourself; *fear* of offending God; *great desire* to prove yourself to him; *zeal* for his glory; and *revenge* against your own corruption.

<margin>
What impenitence is.
Romans 2:5.
An unrepentant heart. <note>original Greek: "Ἀμετανόητος καρδία"</note>
Romans 2:5.
How it is said that the impenitent cannot repent.
Jeremiah 18:11, 12.
Ephesians 4:18.
</margin>
And by contrast, *Impenitence*, or a heart that cannot repent, is a lack of either this sorrow, or this turning, or both. Not only is it a simple absence of repentance, but also a perverse disposition whereby the heart neither can nor will repent. So, a heart that cannot repent is one that both lacks repentance and can hardly be brought to it—indeed, it is one that has within itself a malicious quality directly opposed and contrary to repentance.

<header>CHAP. 10. Callous <note>original: "Dedolent"</note> impenitence.</header>

<margin>
Past feeling. <note>original Greek: "Ἀπηλγηκότες"</note>

Impenitence is either obvious or else covered by false repentance.

^a Matthew 27:3.

Various types of false repentance.

Hebrews 12:17.
Exodus 8:8, 15; 9:27; and 10:16.
Joel 2:13.
Isaiah 58:5, 6.
</margin>
...sorrow for sin, and are past feeling, having ceased from all grief <note>original: "dolour"</note> and having no sense of pain. Under **Impenitence** is included not only common and open impenitence, but also every kind of delayed and false repentance. Such as the desperate repentance of ^a **Judas**, who felt regret but did not convert. The feigned repentance of **Ahab**, who repented hypocritically. The temporary grief and tears of **Esau**. The feigned humiliation of **Pharaoh**. The tearing of the clothes rather than the heart. The punishing of ourselves and the afflicting of our souls for a day—bowing down the head like a bulrush and lying down in sackcloth and ashes—without inward remorse or a true turning to God.

So, a person who is grieved (no matter how intensely) for sin but does not turn to God; or someone who turns from one sin to another; or one from whom sin turns away because of physical inability <note>original: "impotency"</note>; or one who turns from many sins but not from all (as **Herod** did); or one who turns from all outward sins (as the secular citizen <note>original: "Civilian"</note> or the moralists do); or one who turns from sin either because he is weary of it, or through the light of reason, or for fear of punishment, or for the love of virtue—and not through the special grace of true contrition <note>term: sincere remorse for sin</note> and regeneration <note>term: spiritual rebirth</note>—none of these can be said to truly repent. Instead, they still remain under that heavy calamity and disease of impenitence.

***

### Part affected.

<margin>
Heart.
</margin>
The part affected is chiefly the heart, which refuses to be contrite and broken with sorrow, but instead continues to take pleasure in unrighteousness and refuses to return to God. The rest of the soul's faculties sympathize: the mind does not acknowledge sin, the conscience exists in a senseless state of numbness, and all the affections follow their own impulses <note>original: "sway and swinge"</note>.

***

## Prognostics <note>original: "Prognosticks"; a forecast of the likely outcome of a disease or situation.</note>

<margin>
Cases that are less dangerous or more dangerous.
Proverbs 29:1.
2 Corinthians 2:16.
The Word as a fragrance <note>original: "savour"</note> of death to him.
</margin>

If impenitence proceeds from mere ignorance, it is more easily helped. But that which is joined with knowledge against conscience, and confirmed by habit, becomes deep-seated <note>original: "inveterate"</note> and most difficult to help: *sin becomes a habit; an old disease is hardly cured; and a sore long neglected festers even deeper. He converts the fragrance <note>original: "savour"</note> of life into the fragrance of death.* It convicts <note>original: "convinceth"</note> him more than it converts him. Sudden sounds cause fearful awakenings, but familiar <note>original: "usual"</note> sounds do not disturb. The cannon-shot of the Law <note>The moral law/Ten Commandments</note> astonishes at first, but the habitual <note>original: "usual"</note> impenitent hearer is not frightened by even its greatest thunder.

<margin>
The case of delayed and recovered repentance.
Proverbs 28:13.
</margin>

The more repentance is delayed, or impenitence is covered with false repentance, the more dangerous it becomes. *He who hides his sins shall not prosper; but he who confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy.*

Matthew 11:20.
2 Chronicles 33.
2 Peter 2:21.
Luke 22:32.

For it shall be easier for *Tyre, Sidon,* and *Sodom* on the day of judgment than for them. If he has fallen into impenitence after having previously professed religion and now renounces <note>original: "forswears"</note> the true religion, his condition is very grave. Yet, like *Manasseh, Solomon,* and *Peter*, he may obtain recovery, provided he does not make a final denial of Christ. But for the one who reaches that degree of malicious impenitence—to fall away from religion universally and entirely—there is no hope for such a person, because they do not only fall, but they fall away completely.

<margin>
The case of relapse.
</margin>

If a man, after some grievous sin, comes to repentance and yet falls into the same sin again, his impenitence the second time is more dangerous; it is like a second stroke <note>original: "apoplexie"</note>, which is exceedingly perilous. Cure delayed is dangerous.
Augustine.

Impenitence should be prevented and cured with promptness <note>original: "expedition"</note>. A sore long neglected becomes more deeply festered. It is full of distractions, infirmities, sickness, pains <note>original: "dolours"</note>, troubles, and cares of the mind. It is most fitting, therefore, to turn to God in youth, when the intellect <note>original: "wit"</note> is swiftest, memory strongest, and the prime and best fruits of our life should be dedicated to God.

Charity begins at home <note>original: "Charity beginneth at it selfe"</note>. For a man to be a lover of himself is natural; to love himself with integrity is a virtuous thing; to love himself with piety is a thing of grace. This lawful self-love is the guide of moral virtues and a host to divine graces; the end of which is that it may be well with those who love themselves in this manner.

### Part affected.

<margin>Heart.</margin>
The part affected is chiefly the heart, which draws all the rest of the faculties into its own **disorder** <note>original: "ataxie," referring to a state of confusion or lack of order</note>. By this, it is so pestilently infected that it prefers its own appetites and desires above all things.

<margin>Blindness.</margin>
The less a man knows God, the more he loves himself; and the more he comes into His presence, the more he hates himself. *The wicked has made a boast of his own heart's desire, and the covetous man blesses himself, yet he condemns the Lord; the wicked is so proud that he does not seek God; he always thinks that there is no God.*

When we do not know our weakness, vileness, wickedness, and littleness—and not only our general infirmities and miseries common to all mankind, but also when we do not know our own specific and personal faults and imperfections—we cannot help but foolishly love ourselves. Also, because we do not know ourselves entirely, and do not realize that the soul and mind, and the happiness of it, is far more precious than the body, our affections are set more on the one than on the other.

<margin>Unbelief.</margin>
The cause affects the effect more than the effect can affect the cause. The craftsman loves his work more than the work can love the craftsman. The self-lover does not believe that he is God's handiwork. He has no sure, confident dependence upon God's providence. He thinks he is his own workmanship and that he has made his own fortune. Because he does not trust that God loves him, he relies all the more on his own self-love. He takes more pains—or rather, more pleasure—to love himself in order to provide all his necessities, so that he may live well without God, as if he did not need His help.

### Signs and Symptoms.

<margin>
He cares only for himself.

1 Corinthians 10:24 and 13:5.

And nothing for others.
Philippians 2:4, 21.
</margin>
This is the fountain of all vile and wicked desires <note>original: "affections"</note>. The self-lover lives in pleasure, and for pleasure; it is the only aim of his life. The world is his paradise, sensuality is his happiness, his body is his sanctuary, and his stomach <note>original: "belly"</note> is his God. He sets his mind on earthly things and desires what is below. He is never content with enough; in craving more, he envies those who have more. He loves and covets this world only to spend it on his pleasures. He worships himself as his own idol and is always partial to himself and focused only on his own interests.

He always seeks his own interests, but not the good of *Christ*, the *Church*, the *country*, nor his *neighbors*. He thinks he is born for himself and must live for himself. If he stands, he does not care who falls. He confines all his love within himself and employs all his intellect to make his good deeds return back to himself <note>original: "retrograde," a term from astronomy describing a planet appearing to move backward; here, it means self-serving</note>. He will not let the lamp of his love shine upward to God, nor forward to his friends, nor backward to his enemies, nor inward to his soul, nor downward to the poor. He loves himself better than God, this life better than the next, his body better than his soul, and his pleasure better than his body. He is a fool at his own expense <note>original: "charges"</note>.

Like *Narcissus* <note>A figure from Greek mythology who fell in love with his own reflection and died because of it</note>, he falls in love with his own shadow and is, like *Suffenus* <note>A poet mentioned by the Roman writer Catullus who was famous for thinking his own bad poetry was magnificent</note>, pregnant with his own self-importance. He is both the lover and the person loved; his love is both the giver and the receiver, and it is twice blinded. He is his own parasite and flatterer. He admires himself and speaks arrogant things; if he notices any mistake in himself, he—like *Manius* <note>A character in Horace's writings known for overlooking his own faults while criticizing others</note>—is quick to forgive himself.

<margin>
*What we desire is holy* <note>original: "Quod volumus sanctum est"</note>.
</margin>
This love is foolish, wicked, and worthy of blame. Whatever he does, he confirms this old saying: "What we want to be right, is right." He only values God’s will as far as it benefits him. He will enjoy listening to preaching just to satisfy his "itching ears" <note>A biblical reference to people who seek out teachers who tell them only what they want to hear (2 Timothy 4:3)</note>, right up until the sermon starts rebuking his sins. At that point, he recoils.

<margin>
He lacks contentment.
</margin>
He is never truly content because he never seeks what is actually good for the soul. He hunts for external things that look good on the outside but are harmful to those who are already morally corrupt. He is never at peace with himself; he has secret battles within and finds a conflicting tide inside his chest: his appetite persuades him toward one thing, while his reason argues against it. He is never truly happy; he rejoices based on his physical senses but feels sorrow in his conscience. He cannot bear to be alone and hates solitude. When he is most physically quiet, he is then most disturbed by the rebellion of his foolish passions and the outcries of a tormenting conscience.

---

<margin>
The many great evils that result from self-love.
*Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book 9, Chapter 8.*
</margin>
This is a most dangerous and almost incurable plague of mankind. These people sweetly love themselves and kill themselves at the same time. They are even more hated by God because they are so beloved by themselves. The self-lover will hurt both himself and his neighbors while following his perverse passions. Self-love was the ruin of the fallen angels, the cause of confusion for humanity, and the root of all mischief. It built *Babylon* <note>Symbolic of human pride and rebellion against God</note>, it corrupts the whole world, it promotes the assembly of Satan, and it fills up hell.

### Curation and remedies.

<margin>
How far nature allows self-love: namely, in necessary things.
</margin>
Remember that *Nature* is generous, allowing you to love yourself and please yourself in all things that are *Necessary*, and it offers them readily and abundantly to your hand. This it does for all people equally and impartially. If your body is covered and kept warm with a coat, Nature does not care about its color or how fine the fabric is. If your stomach is satisfied with food, it does not care about the delicacy of it.

<margin>
*Nature is content with little* <note>original: "Natura paucis contenta"</note>.
How far God allows self-love: namely, in lawful things.
*Acts 15:28.*
*1 Corinthians 9:27.*
*Matthew 6:29.*
*Psalm 104:15.*
</margin>
But God is even more generous, and allows you to love yourself and please yourself within broader limits and with a more favorable boundary. Thus, you may use what you please—so long as you do not exceed integrity, moderation <note>original: "mediocrity"</note>, reason, charity, the benefit of others, the scope of your profession, the healthy laws of men, and the freedom of Divine Laws. He allows things that are not only necessary, but also decent and delightful. *Nature* allows Solomon nothing but a simple gray coat, but God allows him to be gloriously dressed. *Nature* allows a man’s stomach nothing but water, but God allows wine to gladden the heart of man.

The restrainers of self-love.
*To each his own* <note>original: "Suum cuique"</note>.
</margin>

2. Look to your neighbor, and do not damage charity: Do as you would be done to.

# CHAPTER XII.
# Rotten Hypocrisy. <note>original: "Putride"</note>

> *Matthew 23:27. Whited tombs, which are within full of all filthiness.*

---

->Description.<-

<margin>
What hypocrisy is.
Hypocrisy <note>original: "ὑπόκρισις" (Greek)</note>.
Jeremiah 42:20.
One thing is hidden, another appears. <note>original: "Aliud subest, aliud apparet" (Latin)</note>
Hypocrite <note>original: "ὑποκρίτης" (Greek)</note>.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring foliate motifs.</image-desc> Hypocrisy signifies a simulation, or a disguise. We pretend things to be what they are not, and we conceal things that actually are. Or, hypocrisy is the pretending to be another person. The word "hypocrite" properly signifies a *stage actor* <note>original: "Stage-player"</note> who takes on another person’s identity—as when a slave plays the part of a king, or when someone pretends to be more holy than they are, or someone who puts on another's face or clothing.

<margin>
Matthew 6:16.

How it is filthy.
Hypocrisy is a rotten plague. <note>original: "Putrida tabes hypocrisis" (Latin)</note>. Bernard of Clairvaux.
Corruption, decay <note>original: "φθορά, φθίσις" (Greek)</note>.
</margin>
In the path of religion and godliness, and in the public profession of it, hypocrisy is a most filthy wasting disease <note>original: "consumption," often referring to tuberculosis in this period</note>. It is like a painted tomb, inside of which there is nothing but rottenness. It is a decay; it is the same thing in the soul that a wasting disease is in the body, which is a universal draining of the "balsam" <note>original: "Balasame," meaning the vital healing essence</note> of life. So, hypocrisy is a universal decay of the soul's lamp of light and life, and of reason and grace.

<margin>
Two types of hypocrisy.
</margin>
Hypocrisy occurs either in worldly matters or in religion.

<margin>
Hypocrisy in worldly things:
1 Peter 2:1.

The wisdom of the serpent instructed the simplicity of the dove. Wisdom without simplicity is maliciousness, and simplicity without reason and wisdom is foolishness. That imperial saying, "He who does not know how to dissemble does not know how to reign" <note>original: *Nescit regnare, qui nescit dissimulare*</note>, is to be understood as a King's clemency, who must use connivance regarding some minor offenses. This was the wisest King’s counsel: *“Do not pay attention to all the words that people say, lest you hear your servant cursing you. For often your own heart knows that you yourself have likewise cursed others.”* Neither are the stratagems and warlike policies of Joshua, nor the threatening trials and sagacity of Solomon, hypocrisy. We pass by this kind of hypocrisy, as it is not to be insisted upon in this place.

<margin>
Hypocrisy in religion and its foundations.
</margin>
Hypocrisy in religion involves a false union of diverse and contrary things: of two parties, of two actions, and of a twofold relation.

<margin>
Two contrary things.
</margin>
The two things are:
1. One thing in appearance—imagined, represented, signified, and professed through some show, form, or representation—without any actual substance or meaning. (According to this, all hypocrisy may be called a show or form, consisting more or less of a hollow formality.) 
2. There is another thing, in reality, different or contrary to the first, lurking and secretly hidden under the false show; because of this, all hypocrisy may be called private or hidden.

<margin>
2. The Parties.
</margin>
The two parties are: one, the actor in his performance, playing the part of the stage actor <note>original: "stage-Player"</note> and deceiving with his mask <note>original: "vizard"</note>. The other is the deceived observer. Sometimes the very same person may play both roles...

The two actions of hypocrisy are: either imagining <note>original: "conceiting"</note> and representing a thing to oneself; or else an external profession of some secret thing that either is not so, or is not so to that extent, or does not exist at all in reality as it is imagined, or else is not expressed in the way it is conceived in the mind.

<margin>
Twofold relation.

"To lie is to go against one's own mind with a deliberate will." <note>original Latin: *Mentiri est ex proposito voluntatis contra mentem suam ire.*</note>
</margin>
The twofold relationship is false: when the thought represents something and does not prove the truth, nor the truth the thought, there is a simple falsehood and error. And when the words, writing, facial expression, or action do not resemble or prove the thought, there is a manifest lie. Hypocrisy always involves a contradiction: either between the truth and the thought, or between the thought and its expression <note>original: "signification"</note>. Conversely, in truthfulness <note>original: "veracity"</note>, integrity, and sincerity (the opposites of hypocrisy), there is a constant uniformity in truth, thought, word, and deed: their "yes" is "yes," and their "no" is "no."

<margin>
Psalm 32.

Degrees and types <note>original: "specials"</note>.
1. Grace more imagined than it is in reality.
2. Grace imagined that does not exist at all.
</margin>
There are three degrees and types of hypocrisy. Sometimes more grace and godliness are imagined to be in the heart than actually exist. This is characteristic of the regenerate <note>those who have been spiritually reborn</note>; the other two types are common to all. Sometimes the true saving graces of God are imagined to be in the heart when they are not there at all, whereby the hypocrite seems to himself, and to others as well, to be a member of the true Church. He possesses, in fact, the common graces of the Spirit, but he mistakes them and considers them to be special and saving graces. His form of godliness is Satan’s middle ground <note>original: "Mediocrity"</note> between the two extremes of careless impiety and hopeless despair.

<margin>
3. Grace professed that is neither in reality nor in imagination.
</margin>
And sometimes that grace and godliness—which is neither truly within the heart nor even imagined to be there—is publicly professed.

### Chapter 12. Rotten Hypocrisy <note>original: "putride," meaning decaying or morally corrupt</note>.

<margin>He fears the inconveniences of true godliness. Isaiah 59:15.</margin>
The way is too straight <note>original: "straite," meaning narrow or difficult</note>, too narrow, and full of thorns. He will not fight against his own corruptions, the devil's temptations, and the world's troubles, arguing that *he who turns away from evil makes himself a prey.* <note>original: "maketh himselfe a prey," a reference to Isaiah 59:15, implying that being good makes one a target for the wicked.</note>

For these reasons, he thinks the safest and best course is not to be "precise" <term>precise: a term often used in the 17th century to describe Puritans who were overly strict or scrupulous in religious observance</term> or too stubborn in his piety. Instead, he maintains a middle ground <note>original: "mediocrity," here meaning a moderate or lukewarm path</note> that fits his worldly attitude and the current customs of the day, so as not to trouble his mind any further. Based on this foolish idea, and hoping for the best, he gambles with his soul.

<margin>A misunderstanding of sin, justice, and mercy; and false evidence of them.</margin>
He is full of a foolish misunderstanding of sin, judgment, and mercy. To him, sin is minor and easily forgiven; justice is small and avoidable; and mercy is above all of God’s other works, his truth, and his promises—something to be obtained at the first call. He presumes upon mercy. He thinks that prosperity, outward peace, and an inward, hollow taste of *godliness* are certain signs of mercy. He convinces himself he is holy enough because he is happy and secure enough. He makes no further progress in piety, but contents himself with "common graces" <term>common graces: general blessings such as health or intellect shared by all people, rather than the specific saving grace required for salvation</term>.

<margin>A bad conscience.</margin>
His conscience is too loose and unlimited, strong enough to digest any sin. He favorably downplays, excuses, interprets, and justifies his actions. He has reconciled the accusing and excusing powers of his conscience so that one hardly interferes with the other. He thinks that a little grace can be gained while much sin is committed, as long as there are some "good intentions" or hopes involved. He does not lack theoretical principles of divine truth, but when it comes to practicing them, he has his own reservations, exceptions, and limitations. He follows them only as far as they agree with his worldly well-being; when they interfere with his plans, he stops or turns away from his faith.

<margin>❦ Matthew 13:21.</margin>
Therefore, he is a temporizer <term>temporizer: a person who changes their behavior or opinions to suit the current circumstances or for personal gain</term>. The guides for this broad conscience are social examples, customs, public opinions, worldly wisdom, and basic natural ideas of right and wrong. He will not subject his conscience to the full yoke...

The heart that is removed from God, and is not content to be ruled by the straight form of his truth, is content to be entangled with a more easy form of piety taught by the rules <note>original: "precepts"</note> of men and the "doctrines of demons" <note>original: "diuels"</note>. As it is said: *“Because this people come near unto me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me was taught by the rules of men.”*

## Signs and Symptoms.

<margin>
Signs and symptoms of secret hypocrisy.
His blindness.
</margin>
He who is subject to secret hypocrisy focuses his eyes too much upon his own worthiness and graces; he admires himself more than his peers. He looks too little and too seldom at his own needs and weaknesses. He is not thoroughly acquainted with the slowness of his race and the smallness of his progress toward so high a prize <note>A common biblical metaphor for the Christian life as a race for the prize of salvation.</note>.

<margin>
His carelessness.
</margin>

### Prognostics <note>predictions or signs of how a condition will develop</note>.

<margin>
The danger of secret hypocrisy.
</margin>
If secret hypocrisy is not cured in time, the egg will hatch into a cockatrice <note>a mythical serpent that could kill with a single glance</note>. It will eventually make even the best man embrace some groundless eccentricity <note>original: "singularity"</note> and degenerate into the madness of indefensible <note>original: "unwarrantable"</note> opinions—opinions that take deep root, spread dangerously, and cause harm under a deceptive appearance <note>original: "plausibly"</note> of truth. This happens because of his secret pride, as he gazes upon his own spiritual gifts <note>original: "graces"</note> with excessive admiration. Yet, because this happens only to a "chosen child" <note>an "elect" person destined by God for salvation</note>, he still has the hope of recovery and mercy at the end.

<margin>
The case of opportunistic <note>original: "temporizing"</note> hypocrisy in a reprobate.
</margin>
As for the double-minded or opportunistic hypocrite: if he is a reprobate <note>someone rejected by God and destined for damnation</note>, he will never change. However, his suffering in the "second death" <note>eternal punishment in Hell</note> will be lessened because he restrained himself from committing even more sins.

<margin>
In a chosen child.
</margin>
A chosen child, before being born again <note>original: "regenerate"</note>, might be an open atheist—like the thief on the cross who later repented, or a fierce persecutor like Saul, who became the preacher Paul. He might also start as either a blatant <note>original: "grosser"</note> or a merely formal hypocrite <note>one who follows the outward forms of religion without inner faith</note>. In His own time, God may use that hypocritical "form of godliness" as a teacher <note>original: "Pedagogue"</note> leading toward true grace. There is hope for such a person to change, especially if he is willing to take advice and is responsive <note>original: "tractable"</note> to using all the spiritual tools <note>original: "means of grace"</note> available.

<margin>
Dangers.
Revelation 2.
</margin>

### *Cure and Remedies.*

<margin>
Remedies for secret hypocrisy.
Know yourself.
</margin>
If your heart is ensnared in secret hypocrisy, turn your eye away from your supposed worthiness toward the many dregs of your corruptions, weaknesses <note>original: "infirmities"</note>, needs, failures <note>original: "omissions"</note>, dullness, lack of zeal, carelessness of conscience, shrinking from your service, and fear in your calling. Retrace your steps <note>original: "Run the back trace"</note>; notice how faintly you have run toward eternal life, and how feebly you have sought for that great prize. See how justly you have deserved to be plagued with some fearful abandonment by God <note>original: "desertion"</note>, casting you into some hateful <note>original: "odious"</note> sin, and awakening your old guilt from before your conversion <note>original: "unregeneration"</note> with millions of fresh stings—like so many awakened lions ready to tear your heart with fresh remorse. Closely observe <note>original: "Narrowly mark"</note> the self-satisfaction you feel in your own spiritual gifts. Of this sort, the highest degree is that fearful fall into the sin against the Holy Spirit.

---

### *Part affected.*

<margin>
Mind.
Heart.
Affections.
</margin>
Because this malady is a compound evil and varies by specific types—being sometimes in matters of faith and other times in the way we live our lives—the soul is affected accordingly. If the apostasy is in religion, the mind is first affected. If it is in conduct <note>original: "conversation"</note>, the heart and affections are first affected. When any one part is first affected, it draws in the rest of the faculties through sympathy, so that not one function of the soul remains free; rather, to a greater or lesser degree, sooner or later, directly or indirectly, they are all infected.

### Causes.

<margin>
God is a just <term>deficient cause</term> <note>A "deficient cause" refers to an agent that allows an effect to happen by withholding something—in this case, God withholding grace—rather than actively performing an evil act.</note>.
</margin>
The deficient cause of man's falling is God. He justly deserts whoever he wills, and in whatever measure it pleases him, in order to try, correct, or punish them according to his wisdom. We stand by grace; the lack of grace is the occasion of falling, whether it is withheld from the start or withdrawn later.

<margin>
Satan is an unjust <term>efficient cause</term> <note>An "efficient cause" is the primary agent that actively produces an effect or brings something to pass.</note>.
Ephesians 6:12.
1 Peter 5:8.
</margin>
Satan is the active cause of a person's fall. As it is said:
> *For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, and against the worldly governors—the princes of the darkness of this world—against spiritual wickedness in high places.* <note>Ephesians 6:12</note>

He moved *Judas* first to treason, then to desperation. He caused *David* to count his people <note>referring to the census in 2 Samuel 24, which was seen as a sin of prideful self-reliance</note>; he buffeted *Paul*; he desired to "sift" *Peter*, and sifted him too much when he made him deny his Master. Through his transformations, deepness, methodical stratagems, and temptations, he blinds the imagination and corrupts the heart and affections. He makes sin seem small and pleasant. He makes the sinner presume too much on God's mercy, on Christ's death, and on his gracious promises. He persuades the sinner that they already have faith before they sin and shall not lose it when they sin—and that they shall have enough time and power to repent well enough once they have sinned. His purpose is to make the heart sin without any sense of conflict, drawing the person toward <term>Epicurean</term> <note>In this context, someone who ignores God to live a life of worldly pleasure and indifference</note> contempt, final <term>defection</term> <note>a total desertion of faith</note>, or hopeless desperation.

<margin>
His craft.
Matthew 4:9, 10.
2 Samuel 15:2.
</margin>
He uses our own flesh and the world as deputies and instruments in all his suggestions. He observes our disposition and our strongest natural or habitual inclinations; he uses the "tide" of our own <term>humors</term> <note>In historical medicine, the four "humors" or bodily fluids were thought to determine a person's temperament and personality</note> to throw us headlong into sin. If he finds people addicted to voluptuousness, covetousness, or ambition, he follows the momentum of their appetites. And because <term>concupiscence</term> <note>strong desire or lust, often specifically relating to worldly or sexual urges</note> follows the <term>complexion</term> <note>the physical constitution or temperament of the body</note> and temperature of the body, he takes his advantage...

<margin>
Various forms of falling.

The unregenerate fall in one way.

<header>CHAPTER 14.</header>

## CHAPTER 14.
### The Gangrene of Heresy.

---

->2 Timothy 2:17. *Whose word shall eat away like a gangrene.* <note>original: "fret as a Gangrene"</note><-

---

->Description.<-

<margin>
Why it is called heresy.
*Hairesis* <note>original Greek: "αἱρεσις"</note>: from *haireo* <note>original Greek: "αἱρεω"; meaning "to choose" or "to take"</note>.
</margin>
<margin>Sect. <note>original Latin: "Secta"</note></margin>
Heresy is essentially an option or election (from a word that signifies "to make a choice"). This was once a commendable <note>original: "laudable"</note> word among the philosophers and was used to describe a proper form of learning, faction, study, or course of life, which the Romans <note>original: "Latines"</note> call a "Sect." Now, it is a word of contempt, and the name "Heretic" is a word of great disgrace. It refers to one who goes astray from sound and wholesome doctrine and continues stubbornly in his opinion, caring nothing for the approved truth and peace of the Church.

<margin>
Four things in heresy:
Error.
</margin>
<margin>
Conviction.
Contumacy.
Augustine, *Against the Manichaeans*. <note>original Latin: "Aug. con. Man."</note>
</margin>
<margin>Propagation.</margin>
Four things must occur to make a complete heretic: 
1. **Error** regarding the truth, whether it concerns the Head, **Christ**, or his body, the **Church**, or else those necessary things that belong either to the **Head** or the body. 
2. **Conviction** by the **Church** based on the Scriptures. 
3. **Contumacy** <note>original: "Contumacy"; meaning stubborn resistance to authority or refusal to reform</note>: For those who will not correct their pestilent and deadly opinions, but instead insist on defending them, are heretics. 
4. To this is often joined **Propagation**, in spreading their opinions abroad as masters and teachers of error.

<summary>This page defines heresy by its Greek etymology ("to choose") and explains how it evolved from a neutral philosophical term into a religious term of disgrace, identifying four specific criteria that constitute a "heretic."</summary>
<keywords>heresy, etymology, Church doctrine, contumacy, 2 Timothy 2:17, Saint Augustine, sect, religious error</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of heresy, distinguishing the "heretic" from the "schismatic" and the "simple believer," and expands on the metaphor of heresy as a medical "gangrene."</meta>

<page-num>203</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 14. The Gangrene of Heresy.</header>

<margin>
There is a difference between a heretic and one who holds a heresy.
Augustine, *The Usefulness of Belief*, Chapter 1. <note>original Latin: "Aug. lib. de vtil. cred. c. 1."</note>
</margin>
There is a great difference between the **heretic** and the person who believes his heresy. For, if out of simplicity and a gullible heart (having been deluded by **heretics**) he yields to the error without stubbornness, and once warned of it, does not argue but gives way and repents, he is not to be called a **heretic**.

<margin>Difference between a heretic and a schismatic.</margin>
There is also a difference between the **heretic** and the **schismatic**. A **schismatic** separates himself from the unity, peace, and body of the **Church** regarding his lifestyle, order, or discipline. A **heretic** offends against the truth <note>original: "verity"</note>, while the **schismatic** offends against charity. Often, the same person offends against both; thus, he is both a **heretic** and a **schismatic**.

<margin>
Heresy is a disease.
Chrysostom, *On the First Epistle to the Corinthians*, Homily 15. <note>original Latin: "Chrys. in Epist. ad Corin. 15."</note>
"Those who cause trouble" <note>original Greek: "οἱ ταραχήχητι" [likely a variant of *hoi tarassontes*]</note>.
2 Timothy 2:17.
Why it is called a gangrene.
"Gangrene" <note>original Greek: "Γαγγραινα"</note>.
</margin>
**Heresy** is a most deadly and contagious disease, as it was said of some that they were sick with the **Manichaean** heresy. It is most truly called by the **Apostle** a **gangrene**, which is a death <note>original: "mortification"</note> of the affected area. It results from a lack of vital heat and spirit, which is either repelled or kept from the area (by constraints, bruising, or obstruction), or else choked or extinguished (by an abundance of humors, inflammation, obstructions, blocked natural perspiration, piercing cold, or by a poisonous quality). Just so, the **heretic** maliciously rejects grace, and God justly withholds it from him. His foolish imaginations, his violent affections, his heart frozen in the dregs of sin, and the devil's injected venom choke and extinguish his inherent common light and ordinary graces. Thus, he becomes wholly gangrenous; and in his devilish and malicious opinions conceived against the divine truth, he becomes most poisonous and obstinate.

<margin>
How it spreads.
"It has a spreading nature" <note>original Greek: "Νομην εχει"</note>.
"Spreading" <note>original Greek: "Νομη"</note>: 1. "Eating ulcers" <note>original Latin: "ulcera depascentia"</note>.
Pliny and Dioscorides.
Matthew 16:6, 12.
Revelation 8:7 and 9:2.
Hebrews 12:15.
</margin>
This **gangrene** is said to "fret" or spread by eating up and consuming the parts around it. **Heresy** is of a spreading nature and infectious to the whole body of the **Church**, like poison, leaven, or fire and smoke rising out of the bottomless pit, and like a root of bitterness springing up.

God turns the evil of heresy to the good of His **Church**. Because of it, the **Scriptures** are searched more diligently. The condemnation of **heretics** has revealed what the **Church** truly believes, and what truth is contained in healthy doctrine. The falsehood of heresies and the light of the truth (like two opposing opposites) argue against one another. The heresy appears more disgusting because of the truth <note>original: "verity"</note>, and the truth appears clearer because of the opposing heresy. One becomes more hated, and the other more loved.

# CHAPTER 14: The Gangrene of Heresy

Heresies are exposed so that they may be avoided, and not accepted.

Satan blinds.
2 Corinthians 4:4.

</margin>
> The god of this world blinds the minds of infidel heretics: *so that the light of the glorious Gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should not shine unto them. That Arch-apostate Heretic <note>This refers to the Antichrist or the figure of the Man of Sin</note>, who is an adversary and exalts himself against all that is called God or that is worshipped, so that he sits as God in the Temple of God, showing himself to be God, comes by the effective working of Satan, with all power and signs and lying wonders, and in all the deceptiveness of unrighteousness among those who perish.*

<margin>
Self-love.
Augustine, chapter 1, *On the Usefulness of Belief* <note>original Latin: "August. c. 1. de uti. cred."</note>.
Pride.

3 John 1:9.
Bede.
</margin>
The dominance of self-love in men's hearts—caring too much for themselves, being discontented with their current situation, and swelling with a great desire for worldly goods, but especially for glory and power—has infected many with this gangrene. For example, *Diotrephes*, who loved to have preeminence in the Church, fell deep into heresy and is called a **proud arch-heretic** <note>original Latin: "Heresiarcha superbus"</note>.

<margin>
Discontentment.
Impatience.
Tertullian.
Valentinus.

His Gangrene.
Abyss <note>original Greek: "Βυθὸς"</note> as father.
Silence <note>original Greek: "Σιγὴ"</note> as mother.
</margin>
It is found by experience that other raging passions of the mind have bred and watered the seed of heresy in the hearts of many. For instance, *Valentinus*—a Platonist and Pythagorean philosopher and a professor of the truth, a man of great wit and eloquence—confidently expected to be made a Bishop. When he saw himself frustrated in this by the promotion of someone better, he began out of indignation to wander from the truth and became a clear heretic. He professed many devilish opinions, such as: thirty *Aeons* <term>Aeons: in Gnostic belief, these are divine powers or beings that emanate from God</term> involved in the generation of the gods; and his "two beginnings" of all things <note>The "Abyss" and "Silence" mentioned in the margin</note>. He taught that Christ's body was not a real body, but a celestial and spiritual body, and was born not *of* the Virgin, but *through* the Virgin <note>Meaning Christ passed through Mary like water through a pipe, without taking his humanity from her</note>. He taught that faith was natural, that works earned merit, and finally, he denied the Resurrection. From him proceeded the heretics called the *Valentinians*.

<margin>
Apollinaris and his errors.
</margin>
*Apollinaris* <note>Apollinaris of Laodicea, who taught that Christ had a human body but a divine mind rather than a human soul</note>, a Presbyter, having been excommunicated by *George*...

**George**, Bishop of Laodicea, was so inflamed with passion and confidence in his own intellect that he quickly embraced and devised new heresies. He claimed that the true Church must have perfect and angelic holiness, and that the power of the Sacraments depended upon the dignity and holiness of the Minister. He held many other errors, and from him flowed the **Donatists**.

Transmigration of souls <note>original Greek: "Μετεμψυχωσις"</note>.

**Marcion**, an immoral man <note>original: "whoremonger"</note> who was excommunicated by his father (a godly Bishop), quarreled with the Church’s severity. Because of this, he began to oppose the truth and embraced the entire heresy of his master, Cerdo. He professed two gods and claimed that Christ's humanity was merely illusory <note>original: "phantasticke"</note>; that his body was not made of the Virgin Mary's substance; and that he only suffered for us through a kind of delusion. He turned all the doctrine of Christ into a tragic fable, claiming everything was only an appearance. He also affirmed that the matter of the physical world was co-eternal with God. He denied the Resurrection and held that the souls of the damned <note>original: "reprobate"</note> should be saved. He defended the idea of the soul passing from one body to another (reincarnation) and the repetition of Baptism as often as anyone fell into sin.

He declared plainly that Christ was not God, nor co-eternal with the Father, but was a creature made from nothing. The **Arians** held that Christ was like God in substance <note>original: "homoiousios"</note>, but not one with him in substance <note>original: "homoousios"</note>. <sig>P 4</sig>

<margin>
Purge their passions.
</margin>
And because they are not moved by the truth itself, nor by any true zeal to hold onto such bad opinions, but only by certain worldly, physical <note>original: "fleshly"</note>, and sinful emotional motives—and natural, blinded imaginations which serve as the foundation and fuel for their "gangrene"—they should first be driven from these strongholds and breeding grounds <note>original: "seminaries"</note> before they are dealt with regarding any specific point of heresy. For example: their self-love, general madness of mind, emotional outbursts, greed, ambition, discontent, indignation, overconfidence in their own cleverness, their seared <note>original: "cauterized"</note> conscience, and hypocrisy should be helped and cured first (according to whichever traits dominate them). Otherwise, it will be extremely difficult to stop the stream before the fountain is dried up, or to cure the gangrene before the fluids <note>original: "humours"</note> that feed it are emptied and cleared out.

2 Timothy 1:13
Hebrews 4:12

2 Timothy 2:25
</margin>
Once their <term>cacochymic</term> heart is purged of all emotional passions—and the "bad juice" that flows to the affected part is removed, diverted, or driven back—it is most appropriate, after this prior preparation, to deal with the gangrene itself. This is done through that wholesome and healing *doctrine* and that *sharp two-edged sword that is alive and powerful in its action, and enters through:* make many "incisions" of clear convictions so that they may cut deeply into the gangrene. Every now and then, treat <note>original: "foment"</note> and wash the affected part with warm instructions, exhortations, and loving warnings so that the deep-seated, crude error may be weakened <note>original: "attenuate"</note>. Apply the most sharp <term>Egyptian ointment</term> of threats and warnings of divine punishment <note>original: "comminations"</note> to eat away and dry up the heretical rot. This should be done often and repeatedly until the gangrene is consumed and the good, living heart of flesh appears.

<margin>
Excommunication.
</margin>
But if it does not yield to these remedies, then as the proverb of *Hippocrates* <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> states: *those things which are not cured by iron are cured by fire* <note>original: "quae ferro non curantur, ignis curat"</note>. First, the church censures...

<summary>This page describes the "medical" process of curing heresy, advising that the heretic's underlying character flaws and passions must be treated before their doctrinal errors can be corrected with Scripture. It concludes that if persuasive "surgery" fails, the final resort is the "fire" of church discipline and excommunication.</summary>

# CHAPTER 14: The Gangrene of Heresy
<sig>P 4</sig>

<margin>
Titus 3:10, 11
</margin>
The censures of the Church must be used, and specifically by those who have authority: *After a first and second warning, a heretic is to be rejected, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned. This is as Paul did with Hymenaeus, whom he delivered to Satan so that he might learn not to blaspheme.* <note>Referencing 1 Timothy 1:20</note>

<margin>
The Magistrate's power.
</margin>
If the heretic rejects <note>original: "contemne"</note> the judgment <note>original: "sentence"</note> of the Church and continues in his perverse opinion to corrupt others, the civil authority <note>the "Magistrate"</note> must seize him. The Magistrate has power over both schismatics—as they are the authors of division <note>original: "schisme"</note> and disturbers of both the ecclesiastical and political states—to restrain and correct them, and over heretics, especially those who have risen from within that Church. They are to punish such people, not only because they are convicted of error or stubbornness <note>original: "contumacy"</note> in defending it, but primarily because they spread their "gangrene" (either privately or publicly) to the subversion of others and the disruption of public order.

### CHAPTER 15

## The Plague of Discontentment

->1 Kings 8:38: *When everyone shall know the plague in his own heart.*<-

***

->Description<-

<margin>
Contentment
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial T featuring scrolling vines and leaves.</image-desc>
The mind should strive to attain that happy state in which it may freely enjoy itself at all times, with sound contentment and peaceful balance. It should be like a pair of scales whose plates, beam, and needle <note>original: "tongue"</note> keep a very equal and steady course. In prosperity, the mind should not be raised too high by pride, a flighty mind, self-satisfaction, or excessive joy; nor should it be too dejected when our desires and delights are frustrated <note>original: "crossed"</note>. If the mind is slightly disturbed or suddenly overwhelmed, it should resolutely return to its steady state again. It should not always labor for ease or hope to never be shaken; rather, it should endeavor to make itself firm and strong against everything that might assault it—whether by pulling it down or puffing it up. This is one of the essential aspects of the soul’s integrity and health.

<margin>
1 Kings 8:38.
Discontentment.
</margin>
The opposite of this is the *plague of discontentment*. It is a universal, epidemic plague and a most heavy calamity for everyone. It does not spare even the wealthiest and most powerful, and it gnaws at the hearts of the greatest princes.

How many thousands does it every day assail, making their lives invisibly miserable? Their death is more sudden and cursed, and their souls (which is worst of all) are most damned. It is a storm, causing many a person to suffer shipwreck; it is an *internal battle* <note>original: "intestine battell"</note>, banishing all peace. It is a <term>titubation</term> <note>a staggering or stumbling of the mind</note>, a grief, and an offense of the mind; it is an enemy to that *evenness* and balance of mind. It is a bitterness of the heart, more bitter than wormwood and gall. It is a vexation of the spirit, and this is that *darkness* of the heart that is accompanied by much grief, sorrow, and anger: a sickness indeed, tormenting the heart (Ecclesiastes 5:17).

---

->Part affected.<-

<margin>
Heart.
Mind.
Affections.
</margin>
The heart (or the will) is chiefly affected here: either when it is frustrated by losing an enjoyed good or failing to get a desired good (whether it be truly good or only appears to be so), or else when it is annoyed by some present or looming evil (whether it be truly evil or only appears to be so). Sometimes the heart will be under a constant, stubborn discontentment; at other times, it is held in hesitation and suspense. Because there is a reciprocal relationship between the heart and the mind—the mind first informing the will, and the will thereafter forcing the mind to anxiously meditate and deliberate upon the heart's grief—it happens that the mind, as well as the heart's affections, are grievously tormented with this plague.

A prejudiced idea <note>original: "prejudiciall conceit"</note>.
Genesis 4:27 & 31.

Many are mastered by a prejudiced idea, thinking others sit in their light and that the sin of others eclipses their own candle. Real troubles <note>original: "Crosses"</note>.

Troubles disquiet the soul, whether they are real or imagined, present or feared. They greatly astonish and beat down the weak mind, bringing it much distress, and often leading to rage and despair. This happens even more when the poor mind is obsessed with common, mistaken opinions about adversity and a false valuation of things based only on their outward appearance.

<margin>
Imaginary troubles.
</margin>
It often happens that even where there is no obvious cause for grief, and a complete freedom from all external evils, some will still be tormented by millions of imaginary discontents—forging and faking troubles in their own thoughts to bother their own minds. This arises from a <term>melancholic</term> <note>historically, "melancholy" referred to a physical imbalance of "black bile" thought to cause gloom and irrational fear</note> disorder of the brain; the "fouleness" of the physical organ foolishly distracting its functions.

<margin>
Sin.
</margin>
But there is nothing that brings greater distress to the mind than sin, that *enmity* against God and ourselves. It begins with a false sense of satisfaction but ends with a much more real discontent. It is silent at first with a deceptive truce, smiling smoothly in the beginning; yet afterward, it becomes a violent executioner of deserved vengeance, both within and without. It provides troops of furies to set the whole soul on fire—which the sinner may avoid for a time, but can never truly escape.

He interprets every wrong in the harshest possible way, and nothing can satisfy his rage except revenge.

### Cure and remedies.

<margin>
Do not fret over the faults or welfare of the wicked. Consider God’s providence: Psalm 73:17, etc., and your own more happy and heavenly condition.
</margin>
Do not afflict yourself for the faults of others, nor fret with envy at their social standing <note>original: "estates"</note>, no matter how prosperous they are. Do not give in to your grudging thoughts, considering that God’s providence disposes all things most wisely. Enroll yourself as a scholar in God’s school; go into his *Sanctuary* and there learn from his Word that he orders all things most justly. Ask for your eyes to be opened to consider your own heavenly status, and then you will despise all the vain and profane pomp of others. Learn to think lightly of the misdemeanors of others; do not grieve over them like **Heraclitus** <note>a Greek philosopher known for weeping over human folly</note>, nor inhumanely make a pastime of them like **Democritus** <note>a Greek philosopher known for laughing at human folly</note>. Instead, either improve what you can, or patiently endure and wisely overlook <note>original: "dissemble"</note> what you cannot help.

<margin>

</margin>

Avoid all impossible, irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent"</note>, and idle business; for he who takes too much upon himself gives fortune much power over him. *Do not concern yourself with great matters or things too difficult for you.* <note>Referencing Psalm 131:1: "neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me."</note> Draw your mind away from too many outward distractions and back to itself. However, do not fall into a lowly carelessness, and do not be lazy in your necessary and honest tasks <note>original: "adoes"</note>.

</margin>
Consider that you are a pilgrim in a dangerous place. While sailing on this glassy sea <note>A biblical metaphor for the world or the heavenly realm, found in Revelation 15:2</note>, remember that you may encounter a storm. Never be so fixed in one condition <note>original: "estate"</note> that you become impatient with change; on your journey, any accident may befall you. Therefore, anticipate the worst in all things: foresee trouble and prevent it, or else learn to be strong against it when it arrives. For example, when **Anaxagoras** <note>a Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note> was told that his son had died, he answered calmly, "I knew well that he was mortal." He who prepares himself by anticipating the worst will never have to say at the end, whatever happens, "I never expected it."

<margin>

</margin>
Remember that we are all prisoners of fortune, subject either to ourselves or to others, and enslaved to a thousand causes of discontent. Human life is both a warfare and a form of bondage; everyone is a prisoner—some in golden chains, others in iron ones. Some are slaves to poverty, some to riches, some to honor, and some to lowly status <note>original: "basenesse"</note>. Learn, therefore, to view even the best things as nothing but golden chains and burdens held by golden ropes; the captivity is the same as that found in rusty shackles <note>original: "gieues," archaic for gyves</note>.

Look at it more in its substance than in its outward appearance <note>original: "accident"</note>; in the core, rather than in the bark; and in the end, rather than at the beginning. For trials to sinners are instructions; to sluggards, they are compulsions; to the virtuous, they are theaters in which they display their virtues; to wise men, they are a source of good and steps toward greatness and happiness. This was the case for Joseph, who was lost so that he might be found. They are the fruits of sin and God's messengers.

It is a remedy for a sick mind—a remedy that is not pleasant, but effective <note>original: "soueraigne"</note>; bitter to the body, but sweet to the soul; pleasing in its very unpleasantness.

Learn to fence in the practice school before you fight in the fields. Use meditation for this, thinking about the worst and making yourself ready to receive it. A man forewarned is half-armed. A good sailor prepares for a storm. A wise Captain prepares for war during times of peace. See to it, therefore, that no evil surprises you; stand on your guard, foresee what is to come, and be resolved for all accidents.

### CHAPTER 15. The Plague of Discontentment.

Do not struggle against God or against yourself. Do not be a fool, ignorant of where trials <note>original: "crosses"</note> come from, nor a rebel, murmuring with impatience against the Author of them. *Make a virtue of necessity*; draw good out of evil. Kill *Goliath* with his own sword, and find profit in pain.

Be truly honest within yourself, and you will be more peaceful in adversity than the wicked are in their prosperity. A heavy trial and a sick conscience create great torment. If your "lesser part" (your physical life or worldly estate) is subject to the whims of fortune, keep your core principles <note>original: "the principle"</note> under your own control. If your trial impoverishes you, do not let it make you wicked; if it afflicts you, do not let it cast you down from your integrity <note>original: "probity"</note>, virtue, and grace.

<margin>Resolution. Meditation.</margin>
Time and habit are the remedies used by the lower sort of people when facing trials. But let resolution and meditation make you strong. Be content in your trials because they come from God. Be thankful because they are medicines for the soul. Be cheerful because they are steps toward your glory. This world is your "hell"; your heaven is yet to come. If your worldly status were better, your standing with God might be worse. It is a fortunate evil that forces one toward good, and the next best thing is an evil that prevents something worse.

<margin>An enjoyment of God. 1 Kings 8:38.</margin>
But the last and best remedy against all forms of discontentment is a sweet enjoyment <note>original: "fruition"</note> of God, which you may have by seeking Him through prayer to be your portion and your all in all. The heart of man is triangular <note>original: "three-nooked"</note>, while the world is round; a circle cannot fill a triangle. Only God can do it, who fills all things with His presence. *Plato* said, *"The mind is not satisfied nor quieted until it returns to the place from which it came"* <note>A common Renaissance paraphrase of Platonic thought; original Latin: "Mens non satiatur, nec quietatur, donec redeat illuc unde uenit."</note>. Let your heart be happy in itself and keep your blessing in your own breast; draw your mind from the outer edge of the world to God, the center. He is a comfort that is matchless, changeless, eternal, omnipresent, above all accidents, and free from all uncertainties. God alone is a thousand joys and a world of happiness, the only life and light. *Algerius* <note>Pomponio Algerio (c. 1531–1556), a martyr who famously wrote from his prison cell about the spiritual "light" and "sweetness" he experienced despite his confinement.</note> the Martyr found more light in the dungeon than there was in all the world outside.

<margin>The sweetness of this enjoyment.</margin>
Here is your secret Manna <note>A reference to the "hidden manna" of Revelation 2:17, signifying internal spiritual nourishment.</note> without murmuring, and a Paradise—

# CHAPTER 16.
## The Grief of Impatience.

> Psalm 42:5, 11. *Why are you cast down, my soul, and disquieted within me?*
> Psalm 73:21. *Certainly my heart was vexed, and I was pricked in my reins.* <note>original: "reines" — an archaic term for the kidneys, often used in the Bible to refer to the seat of deep emotions or the conscience.</note>

---

### Description.

<margin>
What impatience is.

Insensibility: natural or Stoic.

Patience.
</margin>
Impatience is an unwilling endurance of any kind of thing that troubles us. The opposite extreme is insensibility: whether it is natural, as found in those who are brutish and born like blocks of wood; or voluntary, which is a Stoic-like pressure placed on the heart to exempt it from all kinds of grief. The middle virtue is patience, which is a willing suffering of any trouble.

<margin>
Two kinds of impatience.
</margin>
There is one sort of impatience toward God, which occurs when we grumble under the burdens <note>original: "crosses" — trials or hardships seen as a "cross to bear."</note> He sends; this implies a dislike of God or of His actions toward us, even if we otherwise seem to endure them fairly well. There is another sort toward men, regarding their persons, status, actions, or the injuries they cause when they offend us.

<margin>
3. Degrees of impatience.
2 Thessalonians 2:1, 2.
To be shaken or unsettled <note>original: σαλευεῖν</note>.
Agitation.
To be moved or shaken <note>original: σείεσθαι</note>, alluding to that figure, a solid shape <note>original: στερεον σχημα — likely referring to a cube, which is stable on all sides.</note>.
</margin>
The heart is sometimes agitated like a ship in a tempest and finds no rest, but is rolled up and down like a ball. The opposite of this is to establish the heart so that, under all evils, it may lie steady <note>original: "close"</note> like a four-squared stone. James 5:8.

<summary>This page defines impatience as the unwilling endurance of trouble, contrasting it with both "insensibility" and the virtue of patience. It distinguishes between impatience directed toward God's providence and impatience directed toward other people.</summary>
<keywords>impatience, patience, insensibility, Stoicism, spiritual trials, stability of heart, Psalm 42, Psalm 73, James 5:8</keywords>

<header>CHAPTER 16. The Grief of Impatience.</header>

<margin>
Hebrews 12:3.
Psalm 42:11.
Fainting.
Colossians 1:11.
Losing control of ourselves.
Luke 21:19.
</margin>
At other times, the heart grows weary and faints under the burden; the opposite of this is being *strengthened with all power* <note>original: "corroboration with all might"</note>. Sometimes, again, a person goes out of their mind, as it were, with rage, grumbling, and complaining against everything. He loses possession of himself and of his sound mind and senses, and almost does not know what he is doing or what he should do. The opposite of this is *possessing our souls with patience*.

### The Part Affected.

<margin>
Psalm 39:3.
Psalm 73.
</margin>
The heart is the part chiefly affected here, when it is deeply grieved by the lack of the good things it desires <note>original: "affecteth"</note>, and by the presence of the evil that it hates. As David says of himself, *My heart was hot within me, and while I was musing, the fire kindled*. Sometimes the heart is impatient at the misfortunes of those whom we love, as well as at the success of those whom we dislike. For example, David fretted at the prosperity of the wicked.

### Causes.

<margin>
The lack of good things.
Exodus 15:24.
Exodus 16:2.
Numbers 11:4, 5, 6.
</margin>
Besides the common external causes—such as God being a just "deficient" cause <note>A "deficient cause" refers to God justly allowing a trial to happen by withholding His immediate comfort or intervention.</note> and the devil being an unjust "efficient" cause <note>An "efficient cause" is the active agent that produces an effect; here, the devil is seen as the active stirrer of unrest.</note>—the lack of things we once enjoyed, or that our hearts earnestly desire and currently need, stirs up impatience. This happened when Israel grumbled against Moses, saying, *What shall we drink, or what shall we eat? Who shall give us meat to eat? ### Signs and Symptoms.

<margin>
He can tolerate no one.
Judges 15:16.
Exodus 16:7.
</margin>
The impatient man is like a mad dog who spares no one, but bites everyone who comes toward him. He curses either the Creator, or the creation, or both. He is always murmuring, complaining, and quarreling. He turns from a friend into an enemy; he uses the law and his own power for revenge. If he is restrained from doing so, it is only because he is a coward and lacks the courage, not because he knows he should refrain as a Christian.

He has a fragile <note>original: "flexible"</note> nature, easily dismayed by evils. He feels the whip of discipline, but cannot see the hand of the one who strikes <note>meaning he focuses on the pain rather than God's purpose in it</note>. He has a weak back for even the lightest burden. Lacking one thing, or feeling a single pain, troubles him more than enjoying many blessings can comfort him. In his grief, he has "hanging hands, weak knees, and halting feet," being completely disheartened and discouraged. He takes everything in the worst possible way and cannot find any relief without lashing out in fury. Anguish weighs him down, and even a small thing will cause him to abandon a righteous cause.

### Prognoses <note>original: "Prognostickes"</note>.

<margin>
A case for healing.
It is a great evil not to be able to bear evil. <note>original: "Magnum malum non posse ferre malum. Senec."</note>
</margin>
Impatience is most difficult to cure in the ignorant and the faithless, but it is more easily helped in those who are guided by reason or by grace. It does not help resolve evils but rather increases them. It is like a lime-rod <note>a twig coated with birdlime, a sticky substance used to catch small birds</note> to a bird, or a hook or a net to a fish, or iron chains to a thief, or a heavy burden on a weak back: the more one struggles, the more harm is done. It makes external evils seep into the soul and become internal.

When the people became grumblers, their bodies fell in the wilderness, and the Lord sent fiery serpents among them, which caused them to be destroyed by the Destroyer. Even Ahithophel and Judas, in their impatience, hanged themselves.

### Cures and Remedies.

<margin>
Stoic apathy is a false remedy.
</margin>
The Stoic *apathy*—which attempts to suppress the heart by exempting it from all grief—is a false and fanciful cure for impatience. It is actually good for us to feel our troubles to some degree. However, we should learn that even if they affect us, they should neither overwhelm nor master us; instead, we must make good use of them.

By this, we are moved to take the Lord’s side and to know His strength within us, resolving not only to die in holiness, but to die for the sake of holiness.

We should not value the suffering body too highly; it is merely the instrument of the spirit. Why should a skilled craftsman complain too much about damage to his tool? Or a brave man at the breaking of his weapon? The body is made to serve the soul. It is only a borrowed garment, by which our spirits appear upon their stage to act their part in a comedy or tragedy. The Spartan <note>original: "Lacedemonian"</note> children whipped one another (sometimes to death) without showing any sign of pain, in order to enable, encourage, and accustom themselves to suffering for their country. And what should we not suffer to sit upon the eternal throne? Anaxarchus, while being pounded in a mortar by the tyrant Nicocreon, would never admit that his mind was affected, saying, "Strike, strike; you do not strike Anaxarchus." <note>original: *Tunde, tunde; Anaxarcum non tundes.* Anaxarchus was a Greek philosopher who asserted that his essence was separate from his physical body.</note>

Prayer.
James 5:13.
Psalm 50.
</margin>

It is most effective, when experiencing the current situation and the disturbance of impatience, to force yourself to fall down in devotion before God. *Is any among you afflicted? Let him pray.* You have the Lord’s promise: *Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I shall deliver you, and you shall glorify me.* God shall either ease your body of the burden or ease your heart of the grief, and with His secret comforts, He shall sweeten the sharpest crosses. Along with this, join a loving heart toward God.

## CHAPTER XVII.
## The Excess of Intemperance.

> *James 5:5. You have lived in pleasure on the earth and in wantonness; you have nourished your hearts as in a day of slaughter.*
> *1 Timothy 5:6. But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives.*

### Description.

<margin>Who are intemperate.</margin>
<margin>The object is bodily pleasure.</margin>
<margin>Pleasures are either common or particular <note>original: "proper"</note>.</margin>
<margin>According to the nature of the individual, not the species. <note>original: "Secundum naturam individui, non speciei"</note></margin>
A person is said to be intemperate if they are devoted to enjoying delights and pleasures immoderately. And just as the object of impatience is grief, the object of intemperance is bodily pleasure—whether related to nourishment or reproduction <note>original: "nutritive, or generative"</note>—and especially that which concerns the sense of touch. 

There are some pleasures that are natural, necessary, and common to all, shared with the beasts: such as the pleasure of food and drink <note>original: "meate and drinke"</note> in response to hunger and thirst. Others, however, are neither common nor natural, but are external <note>original: "adventitious"</note> or acquired, and specific to certain people according to their habits and the lack of discipline <note>original: "unruliness"</note> in their minds. These become, in a way, natural to them. 

Regarding natural pleasures, fewer people are said to be intemperate; but regarding particular <note>original: "proper"</note> pleasures, there are many: such as those who are excessively devoted to specific types of food, drink, sexual indulgence <note>original: "venery"</note>, and other special kinds of bodily pleasures. These are things they could otherwise very well live without, and are activities they either should not enjoy at all, or at least not to the extent that they do.
