<margin>Types and degrees of intemperance. *Aristotle's Ethics, Book 3, Chapter 11.* Gluttons <note>original Greek: "γασρίμαργοι"</note>. Drunkards <note>original Greek: "φιλοπόται"</note>. Those with unnatural lusts <note>original Greek: "φιλοπαῖδες"</note>. Lovers of delicacies <note>original Greek: "φιλόψοι"</note>.</margin>
Some people are intemperate in common pleasures, such as those who are "belly-mad" <note>original Latin: "ventrefurentes," referring to extreme gluttony</note>; others are intemperate in specific, personal pleasures, and these are more rightly called intemperate than the first group. Some are intemperate in only a few things, while others spare no pleasure at all. Some are not seen as intemperate until they are provoked by powerful and significant temptations <note>original: "objects"</note>, while others are much more deserving of the name because they stir themselves up, or are easily moved by the slightest occasion.

---

### The Part of the Mind Affected.

<margin>The sensitive appetite.</margin>
The sensitive and concupiscible appetite <note>The "concupiscible appetite" is the part of the soul that pursues what it perceives as good or pleasurable.</note> is most affected here. It is infected and delighted by the most widespread and varied sense: the sense of touch. In this vice, the will is more active and ready than it is during bouts of impatience.

---

### Causes.

<margin>God as a withholding cause. Romans 1:21, 25, 26. Romans 1:28.</margin>
Those who forsake God (neither glorifying him as God nor being thankful, but loving the creature more than the Creator) are, in His justice, given up to the intemperance of vile affections. *For as they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God delivered them over to a depraved mind, to do those things which are not proper.*

<margin>Satan as an active cause. Ephesians 2:2.</margin>
The prince who rules in the air (<note>Satan</note> *the spirit that now works in the children of disobedience; that unclean and insatiable spirit*) carefully waits, using all his intended malicious cunning and power. He acts as a devouring lion, a poisonous dragon, and a mad dog with a hellish bite to inflame everyone whom he finds abandoned by God. There is no tool he uses more effectively than intemperance to gain thousands of souls to serve as eternal fuel for his infernal flames.

<margin>Idleness. Satan's pillow <note>original Latin: "Pulvinar Satanae"</note>. 2 Samuel 11:2. Ezekiel 16:49, 50. Leisure has destroyed both kings and prosperous cities before <note>original Latin: "Otium & reges, &c." referencing Horace</note>.</margin>

<margin>Blindness. 1 Thessalonians 4:5.</margin>
Many have their minds so blinded that they do not know how far both God and reason have bounded and limited their pleasures. They think they may live as they please, following their own lustful desires <note>original: "lust of concupiscence"</note>, like the Gentiles who do not know God. They delight in the works of darkness and, like men who do evil, they hate the light.

<margin>Wisdom of the flesh. James 3:15. 2 Peter 2:10, 12, 13. Galatians 5:17, 19. Ephesians 2:3. 2 Timothy 3:2, 4.</margin>
The earthly, sensual, and devilish wisdom of the flesh makes men arrogant <note>original: "stand in their own conceit"</note> and leads them to follow their fleshly nature in the lust of uncleanness. They act like natural brute beasts led by their senses, considering it a pleasure to live luxuriously every day, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and the mind. Here, the belief in some false "good" blinds the eyes of the intellect; the desire for our own vain opinions forces our emotions toward insolence. And self-love—that *Circe* <note>In Greek mythology, the enchantress Circe turned men into swine; here she represents how self-love transforms humans into slaves of their animal instincts.</note> to everyone, making men lovers of pleasure more than lovers of God—holds the heart firmly to desired delights and makes it obsessed with every pleasure.

### *Signs and Symptoms.*

<margin>Foolishness. Laertius. Except for the palate <note>original Latin: "Nisi pallati"</note>.</margin>
The intemperate are fools, whom *Diogenes* mocked because they had locked pantries but "open" (undisciplined) bodies. And as *Demades* said of the *Athenians*, that they never consulted about peace except when they were wearing their mourning clothes; so these people never think of temperance except when they are in the middle of a sickness and under a doctor's care. They follow animals in every point of sensuality, and go beyond both beasts and devils in their own carefully devised <note>original: "excogitate"</note> delights.

<margin>Beastliness. Insatiability. Bodin, Book 4 of *The Republic*, Chapter 1. Giovio <note>referring to historians Jean Bodin and Paolo Giovio</note>.</margin>
They are always experiencing strange lusts, like women suffering from *Malacia* <note>original Latin/Greek: a medical term for abnormal cravings or "pica"</note>; they sharpen their appetites more often than they sharpen their knives. They are always inventing strange delights for themselves and provoking their own desires. A single forest will satisfy many elephants, but both sea and land can scarcely furnish enough to satisfy the appetite of the intemperate. *Muley Hassan* <note>original: "Muleasses," the 16th-century Hafsid King of Tunis</note>, who was cast down from his empire because he was so intemperate, wandered in exile through Italy and Germany; a hundred crowns would not suffice to make a single sauce for him. He later had his eyes burned out by his sons and died miserably.

<margin>They banish strength, wit, and grace. Luke 8:14.</margin>
Their minds are effeminate; they appear to be born only for the sake of their bellies. They fill the body and empty the soul; their pleasures are enemies to their wisdom and blind their eyes so that they have no fellowship with virtue or with grace. The pleasures of this life are those "thorns" that choke the sown Word so that it brings forth no fruit.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Things should be considered not as they appear, but as they truly are: not through the senses, but through reason; not at their beginning, but at their end; not as they arrive, but as they leave. *Potiphar’s wife* and *Amnon* looked at pleasures as they were coming, seeing only sweetness and comfort; but *Joseph* and *Tamar* looked at them as they were departing, seeing only filthiness, brevity, loathsomeness, shame, grief <note>original: "dolour"</note>, misery, and remorse.

<margin>Where there is honey, there is gall. <note>original Latin: "Ubi mel, ibi fel."</note> Macrobius. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, final book.</margin>
Voluptuous sweetness is never without its own gall, poison, and the painful stings of future remorse: it is sweet at first and bitter in the end. In *Rome*, the priests of *Angeronia* <note>The Roman goddess of silence and relief from sorrow.</note> sacrificed in the *Temple of Volupia* <note>The Roman goddess of pleasure.</note>. On her altar, the image of *Angeronia* was also placed to show that grief is the fellow companion of pleasure. *Dionysius* the Tyrant gave a taste of his great happiness to *Damocles* the parasite <note>original: "Paraſite"—meaning a sycophant or professional guest.</note>. In the midst of his imagined happiness, he caused a sharp, glittering sword to hang down from the ceiling of the house by a small string over his head. This terrified him so much that the fear of danger eclipsed his present delights. There is no excessive pleasure that lacks imminent and real danger and grief.

<margin>No fate lasts long; grief and pleasure take turns, but pleasure is shorter. <note>original Latin: "Nulla sors longa est: dolor ac voluptas invicem cedunt, brevior voluptas." Seneca, *Thyestes*, Act 3.</note> Other motives. Erasmus in *Apophthegms*. Proverbs 7:21. Proverbs 7:22, 23.</margin>
Voluptuous men are like *Aesop's* dog, which snatched at the shadow and lost the substance. Many seek their happiness in their pleasures and reap nothing but misery. Voluptuousness is a net, woven of many vices, that traps foolish men like birds. It is like that immoral woman who, with her great craftiness, caused the foolish young man to yield, and enticed him with her flattering lips: *He follows his goddess like an ox going to the slaughter, and like a fool to the stocks for correction, until a dart strikes through his liver; like a bird hastening to the snare, not knowing that he is in danger.*

<margin>Plutarch in *Moralia*.</margin>
The delights of the wicked are like the trivial and distracting games of cards and dice played by those in chains—deceiving both time and themselves while death is at the door. The devil is a fisherman: sin is his hook, pleasures are his baits, and fools are his fish.

**Demosthenes**, when he heard *Lais* <note>A famous and expensive courtesan of ancient Greece.</note> ask ten thousand drachmas <note>original: "drachmes"</note> of money for her company for only one night, answered, "I will not buy repentance so dearly." Pleasures are most carefully to be avoided because they both harm and deceive.

<margin>
Temperance.
Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 6, Chapter 5.
Jerome, in his *Epistles*.
Epicurus.
</margin>
But *Temperance* is a preserver of wisdom, the mother of health, a quencher of vice, and a creator of riches; it provides *Platonic* suppers that are both frugal and wholesome. It is a pilot for the ship and a skilled rider to bridle appetites and rule the body. It makes a man wise, willing, and able to rule himself and to use his pleasures at his own discretion—to lead them, and not to be led by them. Temperance banishes some pleasures, while others it regulates and brings to a healthy moderation. It does not engage with pleasures for their own sake; it knows that moderation is best: to take not as much as you *would* like, but as much as you *should* have.

<margin>
Motives for temperance.
It rules the body.
It is moved by pity.
Bruison, Book 1, Chapter 9, citing Quintus Curtius.
Aeneas Sylvius, Book 3, *Commentaries on the Deeds of Alfonso*.
</margin>
*Alexander the Great* looked upon a helmet full of water presented to him in the middle of extreme thirst while traveling with his army. He refused it, saying, "If I alone drink, these men will be grieved." *Rodolphus* the Emperor, in his battle against the *Bohemian* King, almost perished from thirst along with his entire army. In the meantime, a peasant <note>original: "rustick"</note> tending his harvest offered him a drink. He refused it, saying, "I thirsted for my army, not for myself." But *David* did even better; he longed for a drink of water from the well of *Bethlehem*, which was obtained by the hazard of three of his mighty men. When it was offered to him, he poured it out as an offering to the Lord and said, <margin>2 Samuel 23:15, 17</margin> *“Is not this the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives?”* Therefore, he would not drink it.

If those great rulers <note>original: "stately Potentates"</note> restrained themselves in their extreme needs, even from lawful desires (denying themselves something as simple and necessary as water) out of consideration for others, then why should we not abstain from that which is both unnecessary and unlawful? We should do so out of respect for God and the offense against Him, as well as for our own sake and the good of both body and soul.

<summary>This page defines temperance as the "preserver of wisdom" and illustrates the virtue through historical examples of self-denial by Alexander the Great, Emperor Rodolphus, and King David. It argues that if great leaders could refuse necessary water for the sake of their men, others should easily refuse unlawful pleasures for the sake of God and their souls.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER 17. The Excess of Intemperance.</header>

<margin>
What is true abstinence?
2 Peter 1:6.
</margin>
True abstinence is when someone, because of the love they have for God and for their own well-being, restrains themselves—not only from unlawful things, but sometimes also from things that are lawful and permitted. If it is associated with fellow virtues and graces, such as faith, knowledge, patience, and goodness, it is a confirmation of our calling and election. Otherwise, sobriety is not commendable. For those who abstain from food but still do evil are like devils, who do not eat but are full of sin. Or, if we abstain for selfish reasons rather than for conscience, it is not true temperance—for example, when we abstain more for physical health than for spiritual holiness.

<margin>
Accustom yourself to temperance.
Motives for it.
Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, Book 1, Chapter 9.
"It is a virtue to have abstained from pleasing goods." <note>original Latin: "Est virtus placitis abstinuiße bonis."</note>
Aulus Gellius, Book 17, Chapter 19.
"Endure and abstain." <note>original Greek: "ἀνέχου καὶ ἀπέχου" (anechou kai apechou).</note>
</margin>
Accustom yourself to command your pleasures. Rule them by reason and not by sensuality, and especially by divine law. Even in lawful pleasures, maintain moderation; practice some abstinence, by which you shall be better able to refrain from unlawful desires and make your lawful delights more pleasant. For over-indulgence <note>original: "saciety" (satiety)</note> breeds loathing, and when sweet things are rare, they delight all the more. If anyone exceeds moderation, even the most pleasant things shall become most unpleasant. Reason and moderation have always argued for temperance among the pagans <note>original: "Ethnicks"</note> to command their unbridled lusts. And seeing that of all vices, impatience in the face of evil and intemperance in the pursuit of pleasure are both the most common and the greatest, **Epictetus** said that if any man would imprint these two words in his heart—"Endure" and "Abstain"—they would greatly serve the cause of temperance and tranquility.

<margin>
Overcome pleasures, and how.
"Not by flight nor by absence, but by the vigor of the mind and constant presence." <note>original Latin: "Non fuga nec absentia: sed vigore animi & constanti præsentia."</note> Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book 2.
</margin>
Enter into battle with your foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> delights: not by fleeing or avoiding them entirely, but by the strength of the mind and constant courage, through true and moderate use. This is the constant and settled resolution of the heart against all intemperance, achieved sometimes by reason and sometimes (more strongly) by divine grace.

<margin>
A resolution against intemperance through reason.
</margin>
It should always be the firm purpose of a wise person to appoint reason as the mistress over their lusts. We should harden our minds and withdraw them far from the allurements...

<summary>This page defines true abstinence as a spiritual discipline motivated by love for God and clarifies that physical restraint without moral virtue is meaningless. It cites classical thinkers like Aristotle and Epictetus to emphasize that reason and moderation are the keys to mastering one's desires.</summary>

# CHAPTER XVIII.

## The Frenzy of Passion.

->Romans 7:5. *The passions of sin were at work in our bodies.* <note>original: "members," referring to the parts of the body or the physical nature of man.</note><-

### Description.

<margin>
**What are passions?**
Aristotle, *Politics*, Book 8.
**They are either good:**
Psalm 4.
^a Philippians 2.
2 Corinthians 7:9.
Psalm 119:32.
^b Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 3.
^c Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 4.

^f Plato, in *Philebus*.

Passions are overwhelming movements and disturbances of the heart. They are natural; and like fire and water, they are bad masters but good servants. They provide pleasure and take away the boredom from the practice of goodness. We are commanded to *Tremble and sin not.* ^a *And with fear and trembling, work out our own salvation.* ^b They are *sparks of fire* to kindle virtue. ^c They are a whetstone of fortitude <note>meaning they sharpen one's courage</note>. ^d They are horses which draw the Soul in her coach to the enjoyment of her sweet objects. ^e They are the water that carries the oil of grace upward, away from the filthy dregs of the earth. ^f They are the nerves <note>original: "nerues," meaning the sinews or strength</note> of the Spirit. They are the armed soldiers who attend their Captain. They are the spurs to stir up a sluggish heart to its own task. And they are the wind, moving the ship of the body wherever the Pilot of the mind directs, guided by the Compass and Chart <note>original: "Card," referring to a mariner's compass card or chart</note> of nature's and grace's light.

<margin>
**Or evil.**
</margin>
But they become a most evil malady and breed much mischief when they form a friendship with the senses and rebelliously tyrannize over reason, causing it to yield...

If they are smaller, they are easily digested and expressed by words and tears; but if they are greater and most strong, they cause astonishment <note>meaning a state of being stunned or paralyzed with shock</note> and choke the entire powers of the soul.

And although they are internal <note>original: "immanent," meaning inherent or remaining within the soul</note> acts of the soul and certain motions, yet because they create some stirring and alteration of the body and mind, they are called *passions*. If they turn away from *reason* or *grace* and disturb the calmness of the mind or heart, they are called *perturbations* <note>meaning disturbances or agitations</note>. And because they corrupt judgment, seduce the will, and lead to vice, they are to be regarded as sores and sicknesses of the soul—such as the passion of vileness, the passion of concupiscence <note>meaning strong or lustful desire</note>, and the passion of sins.

1 Thessalonians 4:5.
Romans 7:5.

<header>CHAPTER 18. The frenzy of Passions.</header>

<margin>Affections <note>In this context, "affections" refers to the emotions, passions, or desires of the soul.</note>.</margin>

## Part affected.

The parts affected are the natural affections of the soul, which were once created good but thereafter lost their holiness and rectitude <term>moral uprightness or righteousness</term>. In respect to the other more noble and principal faculties <note>such as reason and will</note>, they are but base. They are compared to the feet of the soul—both paralytic, gouty, and full of many passionate sores which disturb both the head and the heart, and sympathetically affect the conscience, the will, and the mind.

---

<margin>
God as a deficient cause <note>A "deficient cause" refers to God's role in evil not as an active creator of it, but as a judge who withholds his restraining grace, allowing sin to take its natural course.</note>.
Romans 1:21, 24, 26, 28.
</margin>

## Causes.

God justly gives up many to their hearts' lusts of uncleanness so that, out of a conscienceless and remorseless mind, they may do those things that are not convenient <term>unfitting or improper</term>. This he does, more or less, according to the measure of his anger, inflicting this malady by degrees, as it pleases him, upon those who are unthankful.

<margin>
Satan as an efficient cause <note>An "efficient cause" is the primary agent that brings something about.</note>.
1 Chronicles 21:1.
Acts 5:3.
Ephesians 2:2.
</margin>

Just as it is the humor <term>disposition or temperament</term> and inclination of man to be passionate, either by nature or by present occasion, so Satan concurs with the stream of their distorted inclination to urge them on and make them stronger in their fury. The *Devil* stood up against *Israel* and provoked *David* the King to be more ambitious and, by vainly trusting in himself, to *number Israel* <note>Referring to the biblical census of Israel which was seen as a sin of prideful self-reliance</note>. *Judas* was driven by his insatiable covetousness to betray his *Master*. Likewise, *Ananias* and *Sapphira* had *their hearts filled by Satan* to lie to the *Holy Ghost* and keep back part of the price of their possession. The prince that rules in the air—the spirit that now works in the children of disobedience—is the fire to kindle, the bellows to blow, the fuel to feed, and a diligent agent to bring all disordered passions to the most pernicious <term>destructive</term> effects and ends.

### Signs and Symptoms.

<margin>
His words.
*Laertius.*
</margin>
The passionate man's speech is the mirror representing his passions. If anyone charges him with this, "Speak, so that I may see you" <note>original: *Loquere ut te videam* — a quote often attributed to Socrates or Diogenes Laertius, suggesting speech reveals one's character</note>, his outbursts will reveal the true nature of his heart. <margin>*Job* 32:19.</margin> *As Elihu in his zeal, so he in his passion, has his belly like wine that has no vent, and like new wineskins that burst.* The center of his speech, and the axle upon which his talk mostly turns, is his passion—whether it be brawling, boasting <note>original: "vanting"</note>, indecency <note>original: "wantonnesse"</note>, bragging, quarreling, or the like. <margin>His actions.</margin> Just like words, his actions are the cracks and crevices through which the sparks of his passions glint; they are the leaves and fruits of that tree of bitterness. His will.

### *Prognostics <term>prognostics: signs or symptoms that forecast the likely course of a disease</term>.*

<margin>A dangerous case.</margin>
Uncontrolled passion is a most sharp and violent disease: always dangerous and deadly, but even more so if the mind's inclination, a heart lacking grace, a physically distempered body, habit, and the presence of the tempting object all occur together.

<margin>Resulting evils to the soul.</margin>
Most of all, the greatest evils spring from the fountain of passion. The soul is disquieted, the intellect is ruined <note>original: "wit defaced"</note>, grace is extinguished, and the whole man is made a fool before the world, an enemy to himself and to others, and liable to judgment before God.

<margin>To the body. Proverbs 14:30. Proverbs 17:22. Caelius <note>original: "Celius" — likely Caelius Aurelianus, a 5th-century Roman physician</note> book 1, chapter 18 & book 3, chapter 15. Proverbs 17:23.</margin>

Chrysippus <note>a Stoic philosopher who allegedly died of laughter after seeing a donkey eat figs</note> and Zeuxis <note>a Greek painter who supposedly died of laughter while looking at a painting he had made of an old woman</note> died laughing. Sophocles the poet and Philippides the Athenian died instantly from joy. If passions that constrict <note>original: "coarct" — to tighten or squeeze</note> the heart—such as fear, despair, and sadness—are too intense, they endanger the body. *A sorrowful mind dries the bones and produces diseases.*

# CHAPTER 19.
## The Fury of Anger.

<margin>Ephesians 4:26.</margin>
> Be angry, and do not sin.
> Anger is a brief madness. <note>original: *Ira furor brevis est*</note> —Horace <note>original: *Flaccus*</note>.

### Description.

<margin>What anger is.</margin>
<margin>
Since all vices were considered diseases, they called the quick-tempered "sickly." <note>original: *Cum omnia vitia essent in morbis, iracundos morbosos nominauerunt*</note>
Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 4.
</margin>
Anger is a disordered disturbance <term>perturbation</term>, thirsting for revenge for an injury. It is rightly considered a disease. Since all vices are ranked among illnesses, those who are angry are sickly, suffering from a state of fury and madness.

<margin>The two movements of anger.</margin>
The first movement of anger is an involuntary irritation <note>original: "chafe"</note> when encountering an injury, occurring without any intent or purpose of revenge. The second movement is voluntary, involving a settled desire for revenge. The first is a natural weakness and is almost inevitable. The second is an acquired evil.

<summary>This page concludes a discourse on mastering one's passions through spiritual meditation and begins a study of anger, defining it as a "brief madness" or disease and distinguishing between involuntary irritation and the sinful desire for revenge.</summary>

Sinful anger differs from all other sorts of anger which are called lawful.

The **Anger of God** is essential and most just. **Christ**, in His humanity, was angry in a most sinless way—such as when He looked around at the people with anger, while also mourning for the hardness of their hearts.

The **anger of zeal** always keeps its eye on God’s glory, the public good of the Church or Commonwealth, and the personal benefit of the one who was harmed or the one who did the harm. It never decays into malice. It does not hate the person because of their fault, nor does it love the fault because of the person. ^b It is modest, mild, charitable, and free of bitterness in speech and behavior. ^c It maintains decency toward all parties according to their social rank. ^d And just as its manner is appropriate, its subject matter is weighty and just. It concerns either God’s glory, ^e the preservation and defense of ourselves—our lives, our property, and our reputations—or the proper repelling and correcting of injuries received. (It utterly rejects all private revenge.) It involves the protection of others through the law of charity, or the correction and improvement of others. In this, Eli failed; the lukewarm anger of Eli was a result of his lukewarm zeal. <note>Eli was a High Priest in the Bible who failed to properly discipline his corrupt sons (1 Samuel 2).</note>

This appears most in lawful defense, whether of oneself or others—just as **Moses’** anger ^f was directed against the Egyptian whom he slew.

<margin>
Degrees of anger:
*Ira* (Anger).
*Iracundia* (Irritability).
</margin>
There are degrees in *anger*: Some are angry upon some sudden occasion, and some are habitually angry. There is an anger without a voice, an anger with a voice, and an anger with both words and voice. Again, anger is either hidden and subdued, or hidden and nourished, waiting for the opportunity for revenge. It is also either silent or out in the open—shown by the face, by speaking, or by doing.

<margin>
"There are a thousand types of this manifold evil." Seneca, *On Anger*, book 1, chapter 4. <note>original: "Mille species sunt mali multiplicis"</note>
</margin>
Some are quickly angry and quickly appeased; some are slow to get angry and slow to be reconciled; some are the opposite, quickly angry but slowly pleased; and some are slow to get angry and quickly pleased.

<margin>
The essence of anger, and the ground of it.
Seneca, book 2, *On Anger*, chapter 32.
"It is sweet to return pain." <note>original: "Dulce est dolorem reddere"</note>
Genesis 27:42.
"A composite evil." <note>original: "Compositum malum"</note>
Nazianzen.
Acts 5:17; 1 Corinthians 13:4. *Zeal* <note>original: ζῆλος (zēlos)</note>.
Aristotle, book 1, chapter 1, *On Animals*. "Anger is, as it were, a burning, from being on fire." <note>original: "Ira quasi ura ab urendo"</note>
Who are said to be angry.
Aristotle, *Ethics*, book 4, chapter 5.
</margin>
*Anger* arises from a battle of two contrary <term>perturbations</term> <note>disturbances or intense emotions</note> attacking the heart at the same instant. The grief and dislike of the offered and offending injury causes the heart to contract itself and draw back the thinnest blood and purest spirits from the nearest and furthest parts of the body. Because of this, the face grows pale and dark, and great heat gathers around the heart. This internal flame immediately breaks out again with an enlarging of the heart, driven by the desire and delight for revenge, which immediately appears with a different <term>visage</term> <note>original: "visour"; the outward appearance or "mask" of the face</note> in the face.

So, between the grief at the injury (which constricts the heart) and the delight of being revenged (which enlarges the heart), the intensity of both—and the suddenness of this mixed motion, with the agitated heat boiling out—kindles anger. If it is vented by any word, deed, or resolution, it is more quickly quenched. But if the flame is forcibly restrained in any way, it makes the agony so fervent that the heart almost bursts. It is a fiery passion, involving a kindling of the blood around the heart. Those who are most properly called "angry" are those who are quickly stirred up—both against those they should not be, and for the wrong causes—more severely and for longer than is appropriate, and those who are slower to be reconciled unless revenge follows.

</margin>
Drunkenness, as it darkens the wit and perverts the imagination, also stirs up anger <note>original: "choller."</note> more than any other emotion. This happens because of the similarity of the "sulfurous" heat found in both alcohol and in the bilious humor <note>The "bilious humor" (yellow bile) was believed to be a hot, dry bodily fluid that caused irritability and anger.</note>; these combine to make a greater flame, igniting the heart at the smallest injury. *Cambyses*, King of *Persia*, was incensed during his drunkenness at the gentle correction of his favorite official *Praxaspes*, and killed *Praxaspes’* son. *Alexander the Great*, while drinking wine, killed his most loving friend *Clitus* in a fit of foolish fury.

A mind too delicate.
</margin>

For example, some will be irritated by a speck of dust on their hat; likewise, *Myndirides* the *Sybarite* was grieved because...

He who is quick-tempered <note>original: "hasty to anger"</note> commits folly, and he who is of a hurried mind exalts folly. "Proud, arrogant, and scornful" is the name of the one who acts with overbearing pride in his anger. But the wrath of a King is like the roaring of a lion; he who provokes him to anger sins against his own soul.

-> Prognostics <-

<margin>
A dangerous case.
*Seneca, On Anger, book 1, chapter 1.*
Proverbs 19:19.
</margin>
If the habit of this fury is not prevented, or treated at its source <note>original: "seminary"</note>, the cure will be extremely difficult. If it begins to carry us away perversely <note>original: "overthwart"</note>, the return to health will be hard. No plague has cost the human race more <note>original Latin: "Nulla pestis humano generi pluris stetit."</note>. There was never so dangerous a pestilence to mankind as this is. He who is possessed by this fury—even if you rescue him—his anger will only return again.

<margin>
Resulting evils to a man’s self.
1 Timothy 2:8.
*Plutarch; Stobaeus, Sermon 18.*
*Aristotle, book 5 of the Politics, chapter 10.*
</margin>
It blinds the intellect <note>original: "wit"</note>, deforms the body, and exposes it to contempt and danger. It makes the soul furious; it subverts men's estates, families, commonwealths, and kingdoms, and makes one lose his life with his own sting. It defaces God's image, quenches grace, and stops prayer. Marcus Cato said that an angry man and a madman differ in nothing but the duration of time <note>original Latin: "temporis mora"</note>. It is "the beginning of madness" <note>original Latin: "initium insaniae"</note>, said Ennius, and "the beginning of repentance" <note>original Latin: "initium pœnitentiæ"</note>, said Seneca. It begins with rashness and rage and ends with repentance and sorrow, which outweighs the temporary pleasure of revenge. It is more irrational than hatred, because hatred is separate from the physical pain <note>original: "dolour"</note> that always accompanies anger and keeps the wound fresh <note>original: "green"</note>. And though anger has in it some poisonous sweetness, yet it torments its owner and possessor with pangs, like vipers gnawing and gnashing within their mother's belly <note>The author references an old biological myth that baby vipers chewed their way out of their mothers, killing them.</note>. It brings on deadly sicknesses and often does more hurt to the one who feels it than the original injury did.

In his anger, Saul slew Ahimelech <note>original: "Abimelech"</note> the Priest, burned the city of Nob, and killed men, women, children, and livestock, along with eighty-five priests; and all this he did based on an imagined injury. "...and if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with goodness." <note>A reference to Romans 12:20–21.</note> This is just as **Philip**, the **Macedonian King**, did with **Nicanor**, who had wronged him. Philip not only turned a blind eye <term>original: "connivance"</term> to Nicanor’s insults <term>original: "calumnies"</term> but also won him over with a generous gift. Through this, he changed the man’s attitude and made him praise the King instead. On that occasion, the King said to **Smicythus**, an associate of **Nicanor**, "Do you not see that it is in our power to be spoken of well or ill?" He did the same with various others; through patience and mercy, he showed himself to be a skilled physician of diseased and furious minds. For a victory is truly glorious when the one who caused the injury is caught and made to yield by a kindness—or when an enemy is transformed into a friend. The greater the fault, the more excellent the pardon; and the more justified the revenge would have been, the more praiseworthy is the mercy shown.

<margin>
How to use rebukes and corrections without anger.
</margin>
Do not smother anger <term>original: "choller"</term> within; do not fret inwardly or let anger become a part of you by hiding it. It is better to vent it a little so it can burn itself out, rather than letting it smolder. "All vices are less dangerous when they are out in the open." <note>original: "Omnia vitia in aperto leuiora sunt." From Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*, 56.10.</note> But if the offender takes advantage of your indulgence and mercy, and becomes even bolder in offending, then you must follow a specific path: first, a mild warning; then, a sharper and private rebuke; and finally, a lawful and sensible punishment <term>original: "castigation"</term>. We must proceed to this punishment as if to a medicine, without any rage—not because revenge is pleasant, but because it is useful. 

Corrections should be used less often than warnings so that they remain as intimidating as a thunderclap. The fox must not see you acting like a lion every day, for then habit will drive away his fear. Let no one see a donkey’s ears under your lion’s skin—meaning, let no one see the folly within your fury—for that will only make you more despised. And if you choose to use any lawful anger to correct serious wrongdoings, it must not be common (used often for small reasons or toward everyone), or it will lead to contempt. It must not be indirect or done by whispering behind someone's back, for fear of encouraging them to offend further. It must be direct,

[Correction should be] directed toward the person who offends, so that they may feel its impact. It must be productive, punishing what has happened in the past and providing a warning for what is to come. It must be medicinal for the sake of improvement, serious without mocking laughter, earnest without being treated like a game, and swift without delay.

<margin>

</margin>
Make use of all the wrongs done to you, and use them to test yourself and your virtues and graces. If you are justly injured ("It is a judgment" <note>original: "Iudicium est"</note>), accept it and improve yourself. This is like when the courtier **Smicythus** accused **Nicanor** to **King Philip** for slandering him; the King answered, "**Nicanor** is not considered among the worst men in **Macedonia**; it should therefore be considered whether I am at fault or not." But if you are unjustly injured, the one who has done the wrong will eventually be ashamed.

<margin>
Accustom yourself to bridle anger.

Anger is softened by habit. <note>original: "Vsu lenienda ira."</note>
**Seneca.**

We are sick with treatable evils. <note>original: "Sanabilib^s egrotamus malis."</note> **Seneca**, *On Anger*, book 2, chapter 13. **Plutarch**.
</margin>
Habit (that "second nature") makes many things familiar and easy to endure or perform. Just as King **Mithridates**, by the custom of taking poison (beginning with a little), was able to digest so much of it that, at length, he could not be poisoned. Learn bit by bit to tolerate anger <term>original: "choler"</term>. Many have learned through practice what nature did not teach: some to walk upon ropes, some never to laugh, some almost never to sleep, some to carry intolerable burdens, and some to stay long under the water without breathing; and all this for unworthy reasons. But you should accustom yourself to the tempering of this furious passion much more for the tranquility of your mind and the happiness of your soul. It is our own fault if we do not improve.

**Socrates** attained great gentleness and moderation of his passions through practice. He used to practice frustrating and inconveniencing himself so that he might learn to suffer the injuries of others more calmly. He made his own nature teachable by taming <term>original: "dantoning"</term> his own desires. In his extreme thirst (even when a drink was present), he would only look at it, commanding his desire even in the presence of the thing he wanted. **Plato** and those ancient philosophers did the same, teaching the remedies for anger through their own example and practice.

<summary>This page argues that discipline should be medicinal and swift, and that individuals can train themselves to resist anger through habit and self-denial, citing examples like Mithridates and Socrates.</summary>

# CHAPTER 19. The Fury of Anger.

<margin>
Premeditate injuries.

Count them common.

"Assume in your mind that many things must be endured by you." <note>original: *Præsume animo multa tibi esse patienda.*</note> Seneca, book 3, *On Anger*, chapter 37.

Consider the weaknesses of others and what may happen.

Plutarch, *On Restraining Anger*.

And your own weaknesses as well.

"Am I not also like this?" <note>original: *Nuncubi & ego talis?*</note>
</margin>

Prepare your mind by thinking ahead about injuries; by doing so, your mind may be strengthened against every provoking accident as if with an *Antidote*. "Foreseen weapons hurt less." <note>original: *Tela præuisa minus nocent.*</note> No one is offended because he is cold in winter, or because he vomits at sea, or because he is crowded in a public street, because these things are foreseen, common, and almost inevitable. Assume in your mind that many things must be endured. You can be in no place where occasions for anger <term>original: "choler"</term> will not arise. The mind is to be made strong by thinking ahead. Meditate on the weaknesses of others. Let nothing happen beyond your expectation: no one is without their deficiencies. Whatever wrong happens, let it be something you have already accounted for. When the report came to **Anaxagoras** of his son's death, he was less grieved because he had already contemplated his son's mortality. Think also upon your own weaknesses, speak to your own conscience, and consider how often you have provoked God and man to anger. And because others are just like you, sympathize with them rather than becoming enraged, and say with **Plato**, "Am I not also an offender like others?"

<margin>
Do not be suspicious or gullible.
</margin>

Beware of being too gullible: suspect the truth of every report and do not let your ears be easily swayed by gossips <term>original: "tale-bearers"</term>. Do not willingly believe what you hear with reluctance; the most false deceptions often have the most convincing appearance <note>original: "colour"</note> of truth. Test before you trust. We will find many innocent if we begin to judge before we get angry; give way to time, so that it may bring things to light. Take the side of the person who is absent and keep your mind in suspense; do not allow suspicion to add fuel <term>original: "furnish coals"</term> to your anger.

<margin>
Do not be inquisitive <term>original: "curious"</term>.

"Do you not wish to be angry? Then do not be inquisitive." <note>original: *Non vis esse iracundus? ne sis curiosus.*</note> Seneca.
</margin>

Likewise, avoid unnecessary inquisitiveness, which nourishes suspicion. For a thousand wrongs—in thought, word, and intention—have been imagined that never actually did any harm. If the injured party had known about them, he would have distressed himself unnecessarily. For example, King **Antigonus** asked those two subjects who spoke evil of him to move further away from his tent, lest he should hear them and become angry with them.

<margin>
Harden your mind against supposed injuries.

"The mind must be treated harshly, so that it does not feel a blow unless it is heavy." <note>original: *Durè tractandus animus eſt, ut ictum non ſentiat nisi grauem.*</note> Seneca, book 2, *On Anger*, chapter 11.
</margin>

Amend your loathing and disdainful mind, which is provoked almost to vomit at every imagined trifle. Consider that it is too delicate and refined, jumping at every straw, childish, weak, womanish, and (due to the scarcity of true injuries) indulgent <note>original: "lascivious"</note> and moved by every toy. The mind is to be treated harshly so that it feels no blow but that which is severe. Give it no rest, correct it, do not let it yield to sudden opinions, nor mistake imagined injuries for real ones. Do not bestow your thoughts upon wicked things, bridle your desired and delightful pleasures, and do not let a thing offend you if it does not actually harm you.

<margin>
If you have a hot-tempered <note>original: "cholericke"</note> disposition.

If inclined to self-love, pride, lack of self-control, or greed.
</margin>

If your body has a hot-tempered <note>original: "cholericke"</note> disposition (which disquiets and affects your spirit), seek appropriate medicine for that physical imbalance. If self-love, pride, indulgence, or greed incline you toward anger <note>original: "ire"</note>, turn to the specific remedies for those faults.

<margin>
Kind interpretation, gentleness, sincerity of mind <note>original: *candor animi*</note>.

"Anger must be limited in many ways." <note>original: *Circumscribenda multis modis ira.*</note> Seneca, book 3, *On Anger*, chapter 11.

Matthew 1:19 and 26:60.
1 Corinthians 13:7.
</margin>

Limit and lessen every injury in your own mind; gather excuses from every circumstance. Always look at the lack or presence of the injurer’s will and intelligence. If he is a child, let his childhood excuse him. If he is your father, let reverence restrain you. If he is an enemy, he has only done what he was expected to do. If he is a friend, he will readily make amends. If she is a woman, she is the "weaker vessel" <note>A common biblical reference from 1 Peter 3:7 reflecting the era's view of gender</note>. If he is a King, it is folly to resist. If it is a beast, it is beastly to be grieved by it. If it is a disaster, it is God who does it. If he is a good man, do not believe he meant harm. If he is an evil man, do not be surprised. Interpret things for the best, and take all things in a positive light. Be always ready (out of your loving sincerity and kind interpretation) to avoid magnifying wrongs and suspicious thoughts, whatever is said or done. If a matter is doubtful, judge for the best; if it is evil, suspend your judgment; and if the wrongs touch you closely, lessen them by finding excuses.

<margin>
Consider the danger and ugliness of anger.
</margin>

Consider the danger and ugliness <note>original: "deformity"</note> of anger: what deadly diseases have sprung from it, such as fevers, paralysis <note>original: "palsies"</note>, stomach pains <note>original: "collickes"</note>, pleurisy <note>original: "plurifies"</note>, strokes <note>original: "apoplexies"</note>, inflammations, bile-related <note>original: "cholericke"</note> issues, and digestive <note>original: "cæliacke"</note> disorders...

Just as the Spartans made their children look at their slaves when they were drunk to move them to hate that vice, look also at your own deformity when you are angry. It is the counsel of Plato, Sextius, Seneca, and many others, that the angry person should look at themselves in a mirror. They hoped that seeing their own deformity might make them dislike their passion. This is a better preventative <note>original: "preſeruatiue"</note> than a cure, for he who goes to the looking-glass to change himself has already begun to change his mind.

And just as God for Christ’s sake freely forgave you, so should you forgive. Oh, fearful sentence: if we do not forgive small things to our brothers, great things will not be forgiven us by God.

Consider there is no true object of anger in the whole world.
Seneca, Book 2, *On Anger*, chapter 10.
All things are either to be lamented, or scorned.
*Either everything is to be laughed at or wept over. <note>original Latin: "Aut ridenda omnia aut flenda."</note> Seneca, Book 2, *On Anger*, chapter 10.*
Or amended.

The whole world lies in sin and is set to do evil. Anger is a public vice, and what should more mitigate the ire of the wisest than a crowd of sinners <note>original Latin: "turba peccantium"</note>? All the evils in this world are either to be mourned with Heraclitus (who was always lamenting the misery of those who lived poorly, or rather, who perished poorly <note>original Latin: "malè viventium, immo, malè pereuntium"</note>) or to be laughed at with Democritus <note>Heraclitus and Democritus were known as the "weeping" and "laughing" philosophers, respectively.</note>, who esteemed everything as mere vanity and believed there was no serious truth in anything. Where then is the place for anger <note>original Latin: "Ubi istic iræ locus est?"</note>? Socrates, when someone struck him with his foot and was urged by another to strike back, answered, "If a donkey had kicked me with his heel, should I kick back with my heel?" Where then is the place for anger? All things are to be scorned or lamented—or better yet, amended. It is best, therefore, to bear patiently and peaceably (as far as possible) with every occurrence that provokes ire. At the very least, one should be a rebuker of offenders rather than an enemy, and look upon them with pity, just as a physician would look upon his patients.

Augustine, *On the Conflict between Virtues and Vices* <note>original Latin: "Aug. de conflict. & viti."</note>.

He did all and suffered all for our sakes, so that we might be moved by his immovable patience and compelled to follow in his footsteps. Do you think that the one who injured you, or the injury itself, is unworthy of being tolerated? Yet remember that Christ is most worthy, for whose sake and command you should do it. Do not think you can outdo Christ in seeking revenge. He himself has not yet fully revenged his own blood, nor the blood of his *saints*.

<margin>

2 Corinthians 7:11.
</margin>
No one has given you greater cause for displeasure than you have given yourself. Your best wisdom is nothing but enmity against God and against yourself. You have brought upon yourself more shame, more guilt, more harm <note>original: "skathe"; an archaic word for damage or injury</note>, and more danger than the whole world could have done to you. At the very instant when you are stirred to anger <note>original: "choller"; one of the four humors, historically associated with a quick-tempered or irritable disposition</note>, turn your flaming eyes upon yourself and be greatly offended with—yes, even revenged upon—yourself. Abhor yourself even to the dust, no, even to the depths of hell; in an instant you shall be silent, and your fury shall be diverted from another person toward yourself. He who is angry at himself ceases to be angry at another.

<page-num>293</page-num>

# CHAPTER 19. The fury of Anger.

<margin>
Remember your mortality.
Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* <note>original: "Arift. ethic."</note>
</margin>
Remember your mortality and that you must die: keep your decaying flesh and rotten bones in your recent memory. And since you are mortal, do not hold onto immortal anger. As our bodies are mortal, it is not fitting that those who are wise should keep immortal anger. You must let it go at the last—the sooner, the better.

<margin>
Delay a little.

"Before you give in to anger, go through the Greek Alphabet in your mind." <note>original Latin: "Antequam indulgeas irae percurre tecum Alphabetum Graecum."</note>
Plutarch, *Memorable Sayings* <note>original: "Plutarch. in Apoph. fulg. l. 7. c. 2."</note>.
The Greek Alphabet.
</margin>
In the midst of this passion, it is impossible to quench the fire in a single instant. At first, your fury will neither forgive nor yield. Gain only this much: that it may breathe a little and judge a little. Delay is a great remedy for anger; it will cease if it is held in suspense. The counsel of Athenodorus the philosopher to the Emperor Augustus Caesar against anger was: "Before you satisfy your anger, repeat the Greek Alphabet to yourself." This is a remedy not for hidden, lingering, and secret resentment, but for that fervent, explosive <note>original: "gunpowdered"</note>, and sudden anger. In this interval of time, the intensity settles and reason begins to prevail. If one is moved to repeat the Alphabet in the midst of his fury, the victory is begun even as the repetition starts. But instead of the Alphabet, it would be better to repeat some more serious sentences of Scripture, and best of all to offer a prayer. Delaying the execution of anger is always most excellent. Socrates, Plato, and Archytas of Tarentum <note>original: "Architas Tarentinus"</note> practiced the same; they would do no harm while in their anger, but would say, "I would punish you, were I not angry."

<margin>
Seneca, *On Anger*, book 1 <note>original: "Sen. l. 1. de ira."</note>.

<margin>
Aristotle's remedy to Alexander.
Aelian, book 12, *On Various Histories* <note>original: *de var. histor.*</note>.
</margin>
The remedy that *Aristotle* gave to *Alexander* was this: Anger should not be directed toward those who are equals, but toward those who are greater; and you have no equal. He might just as well have said that anger should not be directed toward inferiors, for that is base; nor toward superiors, for that is contemptuous and most unlawful. It follows that if anger must exist, it must be toward equals. And *Alexander* had no one to match him.

<margin>
King Philip's remedy consisted of clemency.
Magnanimity.
Prudence.
Erasmus, book 4, *Apophthegms* <note>a collection of sayings or anecdotes</note>, regarding Philip, King of Macedonia <note>original: *Eraſ. l. 4. apophtheg. de Phil. Mac. R.*</note>.
</margin>
King *Philip* cured his anger against a slanderer <note>original: "calumniator"</note> when he was counseled either to kill him or to banish him. He said he would not, lest the man, wandering among many people, should speak evil of him. In that he did not kill him, it was clemency <note>original: *Clementia erat*</note>. In that he disregarded the man's insults, it was magnanimity <note>original: *Magnanimitas erat*</note>. In that he did not banish him, it was prudence <note>original: *erat prudentia*</note>; it was his wisdom that the man should not go abroad to spread more slander.

<margin>
Wise admonitions.
</margin>
Admonitions should be given mildly, without any hint of harshness, so that our advice does not become useless through roughness. An angry person should not be provoked into making the injury worse or defending his own rage, nor should he be pushed to rebuke his counselor for even greater faults. He would be unwilling to have his wound reopened by a rough and merciless surgeon <note>original: "Chirurgion"</note>. Harsh treatments <note>original: "Corrosives"</note> are hated because of their sharpness. The more wisdom, discretion, seriousness, grace, affection, and gentle persuasion <note>original: "insinuation"</note> that are used, the more effective the help will be. There is no remedy more effective for anger than the speech of a wise and serious friend.

</margin>

### CHAPTER 20.
# The Passion of Hatred.

> *Galatians 5:19–20. The works of the flesh are manifest, which are hatred, discord, jealousy <note>original: "emulation"</note>, and wrath.*
> *Proverbs 10:12. Hatred stirs up contentions.*

### Description.

<margin>
Hatred differs from envy: Plutarch, in his book *On the difference between hatred and envy* <note>original Latin: "Plut. in l. de different. odij & inuid."</note>.
</margin>
Hatred differs from envy, for envy does not extend beyond mankind; but hatred is also found among animals. This can be seen in the *Aegithus* and the *Achantis* <note>In ancient natural history, these were types of birds (likely a hedge-sparrow and a goldfinch) believed to have a natural, perpetual animosity toward one another</note>, who always hated each other while they were living. Even when they are dead, their blood cannot be mixed together; if it is put together, it will separate itself immediately <note>original: "incontinent"</note>. Again, there is some hatred that is lawful <note>such as the hatred of sin</note>, but there is no envy that is lawful. Many people may hate themselves, but no one can envy themselves.

<margin>
And from anger.
</margin>
Hatred differs from anger, because anger is more sudden. Anger may turn into hatred, but hatred cannot be turned back into anger. In hatred, the initial grief is lessened <note>original: "relented"</note>, but the desire for revenge may remain fresh. Anger is always young, and the older it gets, the weaker it becomes; but hatred becomes aged, and the older it is, the stronger it grows. It is not worn away, but increases <note>original: "waxeth"</note> through the years.

<summary>This page defines the passion of hatred by distinguishing it from envy and anger, noting that hatred is a long-lasting, strengthening passion that even exists in the natural world between certain animals.</summary>

Regarding lawful hatred: in God, it is essential and most just, whereby he hates sin and the sinner so that he deserts him in order to punish him. In humans, it is a commendable quality and a characteristic of those who love and fear God. *You who love the Lord, hate evil.* This is what David professes of himself: *Do I not hate them, O Lord, who hate you? And do I not earnestly contend with those who rise up against you? I hate them with a sincere <note>original: "unfained"</note> hatred, as if they were my utter enemies.* It is commanded by God: *Hate the evil, and love the good.* Hate the vices, but not the men; nor should you love the vices for the sake of the men. It is not the part of a wise man to hate those who err; otherwise, he would have to hate himself. For as wicked men are God’s creatures, we should love them; but their vices—and the extent to which they defile themselves with wickedness—should be abhorred.

<margin>
The hatred of enmity.
</margin>
The hatred of enmity occurs:
1. When we hate the evil (as the fault <note>original Latin: *Culpa*</note>) committed by the party offending us, or those whom we love.
2. Because of this evil, we hate the party as our enemy.
3. We desire some evil (as a punishment <note>original Latin: *pœna*</note>) to befall him.

<margin>
The hatred of abomination.
</margin>
The hatred of *abomination* is when we love the person, and out of that love, we hate and detest every kind of evil (whether it is a fault <note>original Latin: *Culpa*</note> or a punishment <note>original Latin: *pœna*</note>) that may befall him or be committed by him.

# CHAPTER 20. The Passion of Hatred.

## The Part of the Person Affected.

<margin>
The natural emotion of hatred.
Psalm 139:21, 22.
Isaiah 30:22.
Philippians 3:8.
</margin>
The immediate seat of this mental disturbance <note>original: "perturbation"</note> is the natural emotion of hatred. Its purpose is to stir up the mind and heart to rightly abhor or shun all evil, whether it is absent or present. The highest degree of this is a holy abomination and disdainful contempt. The lowest degree of it is a low and slight estimation of anything because it is wicked <note>original: "naughty"; in this period, it meant worthless or morally bad</note> or filthy. When this emotion becomes imbalanced and immoderate—either hating what should be loved, or hating too little or too much beyond the just and lawful measure—then the soul is diseased.

---

## Causes.

<margin>
God most justly.
Psalm 105:25.
</margin>
The hearts of all people are in the hands of God; he moves their emotions as it pleases him. *He turned their heart to hate his people, and to deal craftily with his servants.* He does this to increase the guilt of the wicked toward their destruction, and to correct sin in his own people for their own good.

<margin>
Romans 1:28, 29, 30.
</margin>
This is one of those emotions that are "not fitting" <note>original: "not convenient"; meaning unsuitable or improper behavior</note> and that accompany the "reprobate mind" to which God gives many over.

<margin>
Satan.
John 8:44, 47.
1 John 3:12.
</margin>
Those who remain in their "first generation" <note>meaning their natural, unregenerate state of original sin</note> and have not yet tasted that "new birth" remain under the devil's parentage and are like him in all his lusts, but especially in hatred. As Christ said to the Jews: *You are of your father the devil, and you will do the lusts of your father; he has been a murderer from the beginning.* Accordingly, it is said of Cain that he was of that wicked one and killed his brother out of hatred.

<margin>
External occasions that stir the conscience and thoughts <note>original: "conceit"</note>.
Matthew 10:22.
</margin>
The wicked stumble at every opportunity and turn the best things into the causes of the worst emotions. As Christ says: *You shall be hated by all men for my name's sake.*

It explores the causes of hatred, attributing it to divine judgment, the influence of Satan on the unregenerate, and the world's reaction to Christ.</summary>

# CHAPTER 20. The passion of Hatred.

<margin>
1 John 3:12.

Truth begets hatred <note>original: *Veritas odium parit*</note>.
John 15:19.
</margin>
And Cain hatefully killed his brother. Why did he kill him? *Because his own works were evil, and his brother's were good. Every man who does evil hates the light.* And the reason is stated: *lest his deeds should be exposed.* Whatever they find that disturbs <note>original: "moleſtation"</note> their sleeping conscience, they abhor and hate. The world hates Christ *because he testified about it, that its works are evil.* Truth begets hatred, not because of itself, but because of the perversity of men's hearts; when truth is spoken, hatred proceeds from it, which is the poison of friendship. Just as the world loves its own, it also hates the godly *because they are not of the world.* Instead, the godly appear to the wicked to have abandoned them, and consequently, they have exposed and convicted the wicked of their own wickedness. As Christ says, *I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.*

<margin>
Self-love.
Deuteronomy 22:13.
2 Samuel 13:15.
</margin>
From the deepest desires and delights, the deadliest hatred often follows <note>original: "enſueth"</note> because of the strength of self-love. For example, carnal love grounded on lust turns into hatred once the lust is gone. If the love simply stopped when the lust vanished, it would not be a marvel; but that it should turn into hatred seems strange. This is like the man who takes a wife, and after he has slept <note>original: "lien"</note> with her, he hates her. Another example is Amnon, who was so distressed and fell sick for the love of his sister Tamar; but when he had slept with her, he immediately hated her exceedingly. The hatred he felt for her was greater than the love he had previously felt. 

Seeing that this strange transformation <note>original: "metamorphosis"</note> occurs not only in unlawful love but also in that which is lawful, the cause cannot be blamed on love itself. Rather, it is caused by the lust within that love. When a man has his pleasant delights so suddenly extinguished in the object of his affection, he takes the opportunity to be revenged for this hasty ending <note>original: "annihilation"</note> and the choking of his pleasure. All hatred is derived from love, especially self-love, just as all negation comes from affirmation. We hate anything because it corrupts what we esteem as good, and do...

Anger.

Augustine, *Book of Definitions*.
Augustine on Matthew.

One great wrong, or many smaller wrongs left unaddressed, or a wrong that has rooted itself in the heart for a long time, first kindles anger. Once the heat and agitation of the boiling <note>original: *ebullient*</note> blood around the heart is cooled, the pain is softened <note>original: "relented"</note>, but the desire for revenge remains. In this way, anger turns itself into hatred. Hatred is an old anger, gathered from many causes and lasting a long time. *Anger is a speck in the eye, hatred is a beam in the eye; but if you nourish the speck, it will become a beam.* <note>original: *Festuca in oculo, ira est; trabs in oculo, odium est, sed si nutrias festucam, trabs erit*</note>.

Bernard on the *Song of Songs*.

Genesis 26:27.
Genesis 37.
1 Kings 22:8/3.

Hatred is pulled by two horses, Power and Pomp; Fear is in charge of the one, and Envy is in charge of the other. The carriage of hatred races fiercely toward mischief; it is not stopped by innocence, nor delayed by patience, nor hindered by shame. Fear has the greatest power and is almost natural and unavoidable as long as the fear remains. Abimelech and his men of Gerar hated Isaac because they feared him. His eyes are evil because God is good; he rejoices at the destruction of the one he hates, *and is moved with joy when evil comes upon him.* His words are words of hatred: if he says he loves God, he is a liar. He cannot speak peaceably to the one he hates; and even if he can, he only disguises <note>original: "colour"</note> his hatred. He stirs up arguments <note>original: "contentions"</note> and will not hesitate to divorce <note>original: "repudiate"</note> his own best-beloved wife. He is a fool, even when he thinks himself wisest, and he hates anyone who corrects <note>original: "rebuker"</note> him.

### Curation and remedies.

<margin>
Occasions removed.
Plutarch.
</margin>
The causes and occasions of hatred should be removed: take away the fuel <note>original: "matter"</note>, and the fire shall be quenched; take away the occasion, and the hatred shall stop. And because hatred is so easily kindled and so slowly cooled <note>original: "slackened"</note>, injuries should be tolerated with more patience.

<margin>
Rebuke.
Leviticus 19:17.
</margin>
Hatred is forbidden: *You shall not hate your brother in your heart*; and the remedy is attached: *You shall plainly rebuke your neighbor, and not allow him to sin, or allow sin to rest upon him.* In this way he will improve <note>original: "amend"</note>, so that you will have no more reason to hate him, but rather to love him.

<margin>
Remedy to cure your enemy's hatred.
Proverbs 25:21, 22.
Matthew 5:44.
Romans 12:20.
</margin>
And if you would redeem the hatred of your enemy and turn it into love, overcome him with your favors <note>original: "benefits"</note> or kindness. *If the one who hates you is hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink; for you shall heap burning coals upon his head, and the Lord shall reward you.* And if you can do no more, do at least this: in a time of need, help up the donkey <note>original: "Asse"</note> of the person who hates you. Commit the outcome to God—trust in the Lord <note>original: "Spera Domino"</note>—and the Lord shall reward you. David cured the hatred that Saul felt toward him in this way, through his gentleness and kindness.
<margin>
Exodus 23:5.
Proverbs 25:22.
1 Samuel 24:17, 18.
</margin>

<margin>
Another remedy.
Psalm 86:17.
</margin>
Always remain reconciled with God, so that His favor and mercy may be extended toward you. When those who hate you see this, they may be softened in their hearts and ashamed to continue in their malice. Pray to God with David, saying: *Show a sign of Your goodness toward me, so that those who hate me may see it and be ashamed, because You, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.*

## CHAP. 20. The passion of Hatred.

<margin>
Consider that the person you hate may be helpful.
</margin>
The person we hate most, we may be forced to love again as someone who, by God’s providence, is made helpful <note>original: "steadable"</note> to us in due time. The world is inconstant; time is changeable. *Joseph*, once hated most by his brothers, was loved again most tenderly when necessity moved them.
<margin>
Judges 11:7, 11.
</margin>
The Elders of Gilead hated *Jephthah* <note>original: "Iphtah"</note> and expelled him from his father’s house; but when the time of trouble came, he became their beloved leader and captain. Therefore, love as if you might one day be an enemy, and hate as one who is destined to love again.

<margin>
Consider your mortality.
</margin>
Keep your mortality in mind: how does your hatred profit you now? It torments the mind and makes the conscience guilty <note>original: "culpable"</note>. What will it profit you at your death, when the hatred dies but you remain condemned?
<margin>
Ecclesiastes 9:6.
</margin>
And what will it benefit you when *your hatred has perished, and you no longer have any share forever in all that is done under the sun?*

<margin>
Consider the object and cause of your hatred.
</margin>
Look at the object and the cause of your hatred; consider them with a wise eye and distinguish between them. There is the person who is hated, the person who hates, the occasion that was offered, and your own hatred itself.
<margin>
The hated person.
</margin>
The hated person is at ease while you, the hater, are tormented. You imagine the hated person to be evil or to have done evil; if so, the disadvantage will be his. The guilty should be tormented, not you who are innocent.
<margin>
The person hating.
</margin>
The hater is yourself, and you should work above all else to ensure you live in secret peace of heart, free from all discontent and needless irritation <note>original: "molestations"</note>. While you consider the hated person guilty, do not make yourself (the hater) guilty before God.

<margin>
The occasion. Romans 8:28.
</margin>
As for the occasion offered (if you are truly wise), draw good out of evil; for there is nothing so bitter that it lacks its own sweetness. God turns all things to the best for those who love Him.
<margin>
Redirecting your own hatred.
</margin>
And as for your own hatred, it is the only thing that should be hated. You must learn to transform and redirect <note>original catchword: "Divert"</note> it. Turn it away from the people and toward their behaviors; then, move from hating their behaviors to pitying their souls.

If he loved us first so greatly and so undeservedly; if he is more necessary to us than our own life, so pleasant, so profitable, such a sufferer of injuries from us and for us (as Christ gave himself to be a ransom for us); if he has not only punished but also pardoned our offenses; if he has delivered us from so many evils of body and soul, of guilt and punishment—past <note>original: "bygane"</note>, present, and to come—and shared himself with us, with so many millions of graces here and degrees of glory hereafter; if Christ has loved us even unto death and has most willingly suffered such excessive pain to deliver us from that endless pain; should we not (considering that he is both so excellent in himself and so infinitely <note>original: "without dimension"</note> loving toward us) convert our hatred into love? Should we not meet him with some true measure of corresponding affection? And with some proportionate, grateful, and effective recognition, should we not stir up our hearts and say to our own soul:

<margin>
Psalm 103:2, 3, 4, 5.
</margin>
> *My soul, praise the Lord, and forget not all his benefits: who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your infirmities; who redeems your life from the grave and crowns you with mercy and compassion; who satisfies your mouth with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.*

## CHAP. XXI.

### The consumption of Envy.

---

> Proverbs 14:30. Envy is the rotting of the bones. <note>original: "Prou. 14. 13."; this quote actually appears in Proverbs 14:30.</note>

### Description.

<margin>
Envy is a consumption.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'I' in a square frame decorated with foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>
It is justly called the rotting of the bones; it is so painful to the mind and hurtful to the body. Like a chronic fever <note>original: "feuer hecticke"; a persistent, wasting fever often associated with consumption or tuberculosis</note>, it consumes a man and brings him to his end, just as the rotting of the marrow does when it lies within the bones.

<margin>
What it is.
Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, Book 4.
Matthew 20:15.
Proverbs 28:22.
and 22:9.
and 23:6.
</margin>
It is a sorrow <note>original: "dolour"</note> for the good of others. Christ explained it well when he said, *Is your eye evil because I am good?* Those eyes are said to be evil, unlucky, and bewitching, "which have a double pupil" <note>original: "que geminam habent pupillam"</note>; whereby their sight is not simple. In the same way, the envious person misunderstands and spitefully <note>original: "sinisterly"</note> misinterprets another man's happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>.

<margin>
Envy has two objects:
Happiness.
</margin>
It is a complex and confused passion, having two types of objects. The first of these is the welfare and happiness of another, for which the mind feels sometimes a sadness and discontented grief, and sometimes a hatred, and sometimes both. This happens because that good which we dislike in others is either something we lack and wish to have, or we fear some evil will come of it to ourselves or to others whom we love, or we think the person 

<margin>
Unhappiness.
</margin>
envied is unworthy of it. The other object of envy is a rejoicing at the unhappiness of another.

<summary>This page defines envy as a destructive "consumption" that wastes the body and mind, characterizing it as grief over others' success or joy in their failures.</summary>

<margin>
The envious man rejoices in adversity and is sad in prosperity. <note>original Latin: "Inuidus aduerdis gaudet, mæſtuſque ſecundis."</note>
Socrates and Antonius Melissa in *Sententiae*, Section 70, Part 1.
</margin>
The envious man rejoices at the evil things that happen to others and is sorry at their good fortune.

It is a source of distress <note>original: "moleſtation"</note> for good people when they see the happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> of the wicked; it is a disease for wicked people when they see the prosperity of the good.

---

->The part of the soul affected.<-

<margin>
Natural emotions <note>original: "affections"</note>.
</margin>
Envy is not a simple but a complex disturbance of the mind <note>original: "perturbation"</note>. It does not have a natural emotion <note>original: "affection"</note> as its immediate source. For in the beginning, God did not create any feeling of envy in the human soul. That perverse passion appeared in humanity only after the Fall. It is rooted in other natural emotions and arises out of them—namely, greed <note>original: "auarice"</note>, pride, and hatred—as can clearly be seen in the causes described below.

---

->The causes.<-

<margin>
The prosperity of others.
Envy is the smoke of glory. <note>original Latin: "Fumus gloriæ, inuidia eſt."</note>
Envy is bleary-eyed. <note>original Latin: "Inuidia lippa eſt."</note>
Like fire, it seeks the highest places. <note>original Latin: "Tanquam ignis ſumma Petit."</note> Titus Livius.
The opponent of the fortunate. <note>original Latin: "Antagoniſta fortunatorum."</note>
Blister beetles <note>original: "cantariades," likely cantharides</note>.
Those who flourish in virtue. <note>original Latin: "Qui virtute florent."</note>
The neighbor's flock has a larger udder. <note>original Latin: "Vicinumque pecus grandius uber habet."</note> Ovid.
</margin>
The envious person finds his first opportunity in the prosperous and happy state of others. Where there is no light, there is no shadow; and where there is no happiness, there is no envy. Envy is bleary-eyed; it cannot bear to look at the brightness of others. Like fire, it attacks the highest things. It is rightly called the opponent of the fortunate. Blister beetles (which are bred from donkey dung) are always drawing, blistering, and causing sores <note>original: "attractiue, veſicatiue, and vlceratiue"</note>; they delight in eating away and consuming the finest wheat and the most beautiful blooming roses. In the same way, envy follows those who are famous and flourish through virtue. And the closer the envied person is, the more the envious person is provoked. Proximity and prosperity are the parents of envy. It is dim-eyed and cannot see far off; yet up close, it sees too perversely through the spectacles of a wicked imagination, making everything seem larger and more abundant than it actually is. Ambition.
</margin>

<margin>
Hatred.
Augustine.
</margin>
These three crave a fourth to join them: *Hatred*, hating him who has the thing we love. All these conspire to beget envy. It occurs in regard to superiors because the envious man is not equal to them; in respect to inferiors, lest they become equal to him; and in respect to those who are equal, because they have been made equal. So *Saul* envied *David's* success <note>original: "felicity"</note>; *Rachel* envied *Leah's* fertility <note>original: "fecundity"</note>; and *Cain* envied *Abel's* piety and grace.

His objects, and how he works on them.

If he knows the misery of someone he dislikes, he will rejoice to have such a subject upon which to exercise his "pity" <note>The author implies a false or condescending pity here.</note>. He aims at the highest and disdains the lowest. He makes himself unfortunate with other men's fortunes and thinks himself decaying when others prosper and rise. His ears are itching to hear of others what his tongue would gladly speak. The praises of others pierce his heart. He is like the devil, who envies that man should attain to the glory which he himself lost—not because he was ever in hope to get it again, but only because he once had it, he disdains that anyone should have it now.

<margin>

John Chrysostom in his *Homilies*.

It is the root of all evils, the fountain of mischief, the breeding ground <note>original: "seminary"</note> of sin, and the source of offenses. It is an endless evil; it transforms a man’s mind into a devil's spirit. Through envy, the fall of the world and Christ's death were brought about. ### Cures and remedies.

<margin>
Carefully consider the causes <note>original: "occasions"</note> of your envy.
Plutarch.
</margin>
If the causes <note>original: "occasions"</note> of envy were removed, it would soon cease. Take away the fuel, and the fire will go out. But it would be extremely unreasonable for anyone to become unhappy just to cure another’s envy. This is because the nature of envy is not directed simply toward a person, or toward prosperity without considering the person; rather, it is directed toward the person specifically because they enjoy and live in their current happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>.

<header>CHAPTER 21. The consumption of Envy.</header>

<margin>
Points for consideration.
"Envy feeds on the living; after death it rests."
<note>original Latin: *Pascitur in vivis livor, post fata quiescit.*</note>
</margin>
For as soon as happiness leaves the person who is envied, or the person envied dies and leaves their happiness, envy stops on its own accord. It is the duty of a virtuous person to make it stop willingly before it stops out of necessity. Imagine the happiness of others in your mind abstractly, as a temporary circumstance <note>original: "separable accident"</note> enjoyed only for a short time—like a borrowed loan that might belong to someone else tomorrow. Consider again the happy person apart from their happiness: see them in your mind as a mortal human, perhaps to be stripped bare tomorrow, fleeing from the very things you envy in them and rushing toward the grave. Their best things are only "in the making" <note>original Latin: *Fieri*</note> and incomplete. Wait with patience for the end of the comedy or tragedy. And if that person is godly, they are to be crowned with glory, while you lie condemned in torment with devils because of your devilish envy.

<margin>
Love, and the motives for it.
1 Corinthians 13:4.
Romans 13:10.
</margin>
We must use diligence to achieve or renew our spiritual rebirth <note>original: "regeneration"</note>, which shows itself most clearly in love that does not envy: *It is not puffed up, it does not seek its own benefit, it endures all things.* We are all members of one body serving each other, united to one Head [Christ]. The good fortune of others benefits us too, if only we could see it. The strength of one person serves the needs of another. Resenting the happiness of another member is nothing but attacking our own well-being. Love your friends in God, and your enemies for God’s sake. If you think that anyone provokes you to envy, consider it your required duty to pray for them as a Christian. Include them in your private prayers, and your envy shall cease.

<margin>
Closely examine the prosperity of others.
Psalm 73:3.
</margin>
If those who are good—or at least not of the worst sort—are prosperous, it makes men's minds fret a little. But if the wicked or unworthy flourish, it increases the passion of envy much more. Their painless <note>original: "bondless," likely referring to an easy death without struggle as described in Psalm 73</note> death, vigorous life, well-fed bodies, and abundance that exceeds their desires—along with their lawlessness, arrogance, blasphemy, and daily increase in riches—provoke even the godly to impatient fretting.
