<margin>
Points for consideration.
God's providence.
</margin>
fretting. The chief remedy is to enter with *David* into the sanctuary and school of God. Learn by His Word and Spirit that He orders all things most wisely and justly: He corrects you with the lack of the good things that others have, and tests others with the benefits that you lack. Consider that expected endless happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>, prepared for the godly, which makes them despise <note>original: "contemne"</note> all earthly vain pomp as being unworthy of envy. Who can charge God with folly for bestowing on anyone more than is appropriate <note>original: "meete"</note>? Who can challenge Him for unrighteousness because He gives someone less than is due? Consider that no one has pure <note>original: "sincere"</note> blessings, unmixed and free from the presence of troubles: the person who has the most impressive appearance may have the greatest sorrow. Considering one should keep us from envying the other.

<margin>
Walk worthy of the light.

Romans 13:12, 13, 14.

## CHAPTER 22.
### A trembling heart.

---

> Deuteronomy 28:65. *The Lord shall give you there a trembling heart.* 1 Samuel 14:15, 16.
> *Psalm* 55:4. *My heart trembles within me.*

---

->Description.<-

<margin>The object of fear.</margin>
**E**xtreme fear forces the heart to tremble because of those looming <note>original: "imminent"</note> evils that the mind unwillingly perceives as being opposed and contrary to our will and well-being.

<margin>Fear is a sickness.</margin>
Fear is a pitiful disturbance <note>original: "perturbation"</note> and is most unseemly for a man; for it is a shame for a man to be called fearful and to be sick with such a foul <note>original: "filthy"</note> sickness.

<margin>
The object of fear is some terrible thing.
*Aristotle's Ethics, book 3, chapter 6.* <note>original: "Arist. eth. l. 3. c. 6."</note>
*In the same book, chapter 7.* <note>original: "Ibid c. 7."</note>
*Luke 21:11, 26.*
</margin>
The object of fear is some evil that is disliked and detested as harmful <note>original: "noisome"</note> and looming (even if it is only so in appearance and perhaps will never happen). It is therefore called "the expectation of evil"—specifically, an evil that our mind perceives as terrible, or as Christ calls such evils, "fearful things" that we would gladly avoid <note>original: "eschew"</note>. Those who take their own lives <note>original: "put desperate hands on themselves"</note> (which is one of the most terrible evils) do not fear death because they have no desire to avoid it; instead, they seek it as if it were something good.

<margin>
All the types of fear compared together.
</margin>
The *blind* fear is foolish; the *natural* fear is piteous. The *carnal, servile, and desperate fears* are impious and faithless. The *filial* <note>original: "filiall"; the respectful fear a child has for a parent</note> fear is godly and faithful. The *blind* and *natural* fears are more neutral <note>original: "indifferent"</note>. The *carnal* and *servile* fears are forbidden; the *filial* is commended and commanded.

The *servile fear* <note>fear of punishment rather than love</note> acts as a schoolmaster <note>original: "pedagogue"</note> to the ungodly, driving them toward *desperate fear*. But to the *godly*, it is a schoolmaster leading them to *filial fear*.

<margin>
Psalm 55:19.
Isaiah 57:11.
How the godly and ungodly fear.
</margin>
The godless may be without any kind of fear because they experience "no changes" <note>referring to a lack of trials or shifts in fortune that would make them think of God</note> and because God "holds his tongue for a long time." But the godly always fear. The ungodly may have all the types of fear in their full measure, except only for the *filial* fear, of which they can have no part. The godly may be troubled with *blind* and *natural* fear, ensnared in *carnal* fear, and terrified and prepared by *servile* fear—but they are encouraged and comforted by *filial* fear.

The ungodly begin with no fear and come to *carnal* fear; from the *carnal*, they proceed to the *servile*. This often increases until it becomes *desperate*. This, again, never ceases until it becomes endless. But in the godly, the *carnal* and *servile* fears are converted into the *filial*. The more a person wanders from God, the greater their *servile* fear is; but the closer they are to God, the less it becomes.

Antipathies <note>natural aversions or irrational dislikes</note>.

Some will be frightened by a mouse, some by a cat, some by cabbage, some by water, and some at the sight of bleeding. The cause of all this cannot be expressed; it is inborn <note>original: "insit"</note> and inherent. But more evidently, men may have their imaginations corrupted by the influence of the "vapors of melancholy" <note>Early Modern medicine believed "black bile" produced fumes that affected the brain's ability to process reality</note>. These cursed fears—*carnal, servile, and desperate*—are the children of unbelief. They cannot lead to salvation, nor can those who hold them seek or receive pardon. It is a woeful and wicked <note>original: "naughty"</note> fear that obtains no mercy, where faith is lacking and that faithful and true fear of God is despised. Consequently, those bad fears that disturb the soul follow most justly as punishments. *If you will not fear this glorious and fearful name, The Lord Your God, the Lord shall give you a trembling heart.* He who does not trust in the Creator with holy fear will find that every creature brings him tempests of terror.

<margin>
An evil conscience.
Proverbs 28:1.
Psalm 53:5.
</margin>
There is nothing more capable of breeding fear than an evil conscience resulting from a shameful life. *The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion.* *The workers of iniquity fear when there is no cause for fear.* Sin creates an evil conscience; an evil conscience terrifies; and the heart becomes afraid of God, the judge of sin.

This was true of **Adam**, although he would not confess it when he said, *I was afraid because I was naked.* He expressed a false cause, for he was naked before; he concealed the true cause, which was an evil and terrifying conscience. Even the greatest criminals <note>original: "malefactors"</note> do not lack secret terrors in private. The most wicked conscience hates God the most; and because it hates Him, it always fears Him and flees from Him. The greatest source of joy, they turn into the greatest source of fear and terror. They see nothing in Him but power, judgment, and wrath. They do not look at sin as it offends God, but only as it offends themselves by bringing about judgments. They fear to sin only because they fear the punishment of sin. A bad conscience provided fear to **Belshazzar** <note>The Babylonian king who saw the "writing on the wall"</note> and to **Felix** <note>The Roman governor who trembled when the Apostle Paul spoke of judgment</note>.

### *Signs and Symptoms.*

<margin>
The vivid traits of the fearful.
Nahum 2:10.
</margin>
The heart melts, the knees knock together, sorrow is in the loins, and paleness <note>original: "blacknesse"—referring to a dark or livid complexion caused by blood rushing away from the face</note> is in the face. They change many colors like the chameleon; and even if the face shows nothing, a trembling mind still lurks within. Fear closes the pores, constricts the spirits <note>In Early Modern medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried life and sensation through the body</note>, and ruins one's strength. The hair stands on end, and the voice is interrupted—fear is the bond that ties the tongue. A cold sweat will cover the body. The soul is so compressed and draws so far into itself that it almost suffocates itself. Their sleep is interrupted; their eyes are open but do not see; they hear, but are not attentive; they speak, but expect no answer.

<margin>
"Disease is like a holiday to the fearful" <note>original: "Morbus timidis est loco festi"—meaning they use illness as an excuse to avoid action</note>.
"It is impossible to fear and be angry at the same time."
"The fearful never set up a trophy of victory" <note>original: "Timidi nunquam statuêre trophæum"</note>.
Claudian, *The Gothic War*.
John 12:42.
</margin>
At home and in times of peace, the fearful are courageous, but in times of crisis they are nothing. They are bold in words but worthless <note>original: "naughty"</note> in deeds. They tremble even before the trumpet sounds. They delight in whatever allows them to hide. They cannot be angry at anything, and they dare to undertake no great thing. They trouble themselves over every trifle, even "at the bite of a flea" <note>original: "In pulicis morsu"</note>.

->*Cures and remedies.*<-

<margin>
Bad remedies for fear.
</margin>
Fear is cured in many bad ways: when it is either hidden or only slightly altered, as **Saul's** fear was soothed with music; or when one forces themselves beyond their fear in terrible dangers, either to ambitiously acquire some honor or to avoid some greater punishment (as those who are desperate do). Sometimes fear is suffocated by anger and fury, by drunkenness, or by the hope of victory. Other times it is smothered by the encouragement of skill <note>original: "Art"</note> or experience, as seen in soldiers. 
<margin>
"Ignorance is always bold" <note>original: *Semper audax inscitia*</note>.

</margin>
Ignorance holds down fear; the hope of gain prevents fear from being felt.

<margin>
Judges 4:8.
1 Samuel 22:23.
</margin>
Present protection and safety lessen it: as when **Barak** desired the company and protection of **Deborah** the prophetess. This was the comfort (but not the cure) that **David** gave to **Abiathar**: *Stay with me, and do not fear; for with me, you shall be in safety.* 
<margin>
Psalm 55:6.
</margin>
Similarly, **David** wished for the wings of a dove to fly away from his fear.

<margin>
Future things are uncertain.
</margin>
Do not trouble your mind with evils before they arrive: they may just as easily never come as come. Fears and hopes deceive both alike. All things in time come and go by turns. There are millions of unexpected events <note>original: "aduentures"</note> hidden within the hand of God’s providence; the smallest accidents...

Present to yourself in your premeditation some more fearful dangers that may happen to you. Learn in your thoughts to wrestle against them. While you have leisure, give yourself some "false alarms," against which you can devise some advantages ahead of time. This allows you to arm yourself and be provided with a retreat, so that when real perils are imminent, they may be more familiar and you less afraid.

You must boldly attempt something if you wish to be worth anything; it is the part of a man to nobly <note>original: "generously"</note> endure accidents.

For a four-squared stone stands evenly on whichever side it falls. Wisdom is the mother of courage.

<margin>
Points of premeditation.
</margin>
Learn to practice in the fencing school before you fight in the field. Premeditate seriously upon frightening evils before they arrive; even the sharpest and most bitter things are made sweet by digesting them beforehand. Always be prepared for the worst, and then imminent evils shall frighten you less. Consider that nothing can happen to you except from a divine, wise, and fatherly hand. The most bitter trials are the best remedies, prepared by the wisdom of that Great Physician for our poor souls' worst maladies. Settle your heart in the love of God, expecting that even your greatest feared evils (if you are good) shall serve for your greatest good.

Be dying every day by resolving to die daily. Death’s messengers—accident, sickness, and old age—attend us every day. The first two are sudden and final <note>original: "peremptory"</note>; the last allows for more delay. Wrestle with death in your mind before you must wrestle with him in your body. Consider death to be always present. Do not be like the Epicurean <note>A follower of Epicurus; here, one who fears the total end of existence.</note> who fears death out of a fright of non-existence. Nor should you be like the person of the world who fears dying because of future misery. Nor be like the half-Christian <note>original: "Demi-Christian"</note> who fears death because they are in doubt about what will happen to them—whether they will be miserable or simply cease to exist. Nor be like the convicted atheist who, when dying, looks downward and sees three terrible sights: Death, Judgment, and Hell—two to be passed through, and the third to remain in eternally. Instead, be like a courageous and comforted Christian who looks upward and sees, as Stephen did, the heavens opened to receive you and the glorious angels waiting to carry your soul there. Be like one who can die, dares to die, and wishes to die, knowing that after death he shall continue to exist and shall be blissfully happy forever.

<margin>

1 Corinthians 15:56.
</margin>

An innocent life and a deep, studied knowledge of the virtues of death give the strongest confidence against the fear of it. Ask God for the lesson of how to *number your days* <note>Psalm 90:12; a prayer for wisdom regarding the brevity of life.</note>. Live well so that you may die well, and so that you may have little to do when you are dying except to die. If your concern is great to live well, you may be less concerned about dying well. ## CHAP. XXIII.
### The Heaviness of Sorrow.

> *Proverbs 12:25. Heaviness in the heart of man brings it down.*
> *Proverbs 14:10. The heart knows the bitterness of the soul.*

---

->Description.<-

<margin>What sorrow is.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop-cap 'S' with vine and leaf patterns.</image-desc>Sorrow is a passion of the heart, arising upon the perception <note>original: "apprehension"</note> of some present or near, attacking and harmful <note>original: "noisome"; meaning injurious or noxious</note> evil. It differs from fear, which perceives evils as they are in the future; sorrow perceives them as they are present.

<margin>
It is a sickness.
Jeremiah 10:19.
</margin>
The Jewish people, in their mourning, acknowledged it to be a sickness, saying, *“This is my sickness, and I will bear it.”*

<margin>
Division.
2 Corinthians 7:9, 10, 11.
</margin>
Sorrow is either godly or worldly.

<margin>
Godly sorrow for sin, and the seven effects of it.
2 Corinthians 7:11.
</margin>
Godly sorrow is either for sin or for trouble. Sorrow for sin is not hurtful; it causes repentance leading to salvation, which is not to be regretted. It brings forth all seven effects of true repentance: namely, *care for improvement <note>original: "amendment"</note>, clearing oneself from the guilt of others, indignation against ourselves, fear of offending God, a great desire to prove ourselves to God, zeal for his glory, and vengeance against our own corruption.* Nothing is so suitable a cause for mourning as sin, which is to the wicked

Their sorrow is not to be regretted <note>original: "sorrowed for"</note>. *“The heart knows the bitterness of its own soul, and a stranger shall not share in its joy.”* Thus, the heart can simultaneously experience both great sorrow for sin and unspeakable joy in God. This sorrow is felt more deeply by the individuals themselves than it is known to others.

<margin>Esther 4:2.</margin>
It is a comforting <note>original: "comfortable"</note> sorrow to mourn for one's own sins—both past and present (Romans 7:22, etc.)—and for the temptation of sins that are near <note>original: "imminent"</note> (1 Peter 1:6). It is also good to sorrow for the sins of others, as did Lot (2 Peter 2:8), David (Psalm 119:158, 136), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 13:17), Ezra (Ezra 9:3), Christ (Mark 3:5; Luke 9:41), and Paul (Romans 9:2; 2 Corinthians 2:4). They are marked on the forehead with the letter *Tau* <note>The Hebrew letter used as a mark of protection in Ezekiel 9:4; often interpreted by early Christians as a sign of the cross.</note> (Ezekiel 9:4). God looks upon them with favor (Isaiah 66:1). They do not need to stand mourning outside the gate of mercy but may boldly enter in, as they are most welcome to God. He is unlike the Persian Kings, who could not tolerate any mourners or mourning clothes in their presence.

He sighs within himself while waiting for the redemption of his body; he sympathizes with the troubles of others and of the Church.

If godly sorrow becomes excessive and turns into a total heaviness that oppresses all the faculties of the soul—or if it is an anguish and trouble of conscience where the heart is nearly swallowed up by too much grief—in that case, it should be cured by the remedies for a wounded spirit.

<margin>
Worldly sorrow faked <note>original: "fained"</note>.
</margin>
As for worldly sorrow, it is either faked or real. Faked sorrow is that which has only the outward appearance <note>original: "countenance"</note> and show of grief. It is sometimes used in the profession of religion, as by those who *look sour* and those who *afflict their souls for a day, bow down their heads like a bulrush, and lie down in sackcloth and ashes* (Matthew 6:16; Isaiah 58:5). Sometimes it is used at funerals: some do it out of imitation or affectation; some by hiring and recruitment <note>original: "conduction and hiring"</note>; and others by command. This ceremony began with the Egyptians and Chaldeans. The Greeks borrowed this custom from the Egyptians, and the Romans from the Greeks, who concluded their funeral mourning by saying *the final "hail and farewell"* <note>original: "Supremum Salue & vale"</note> to the corpse.

<margin>
Matthew 6:16.
Isaiah 58:5.

Herodotus.
Diodorus.

"Hail forever to me, greatest Pallas, and forever farewell," etc. <note>original: "Salue æternum mihi maxime Palla, æternumq́; vale, &c."</note>
Virgil, *Aeneid* Book 11 <note>original: "Virg. Æneid. 3."</note>.
Jeremiah 9:17.
</margin>
It was used in Israel as well (2 Chronicles 35:24). This lamentation for the dead should not be faked or immoderate (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Instead, it should be decent, without the ceremonies of non-believers <note>original: "infidels"</note> (Leviticus 19:27 and 21:5; Deuteronomy 14:1). It should be true and moderate (Acts 8:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:13; 2 Samuel 3:31 <note>original: "1. Sam. 3. 31"</note>, etc.). Mourning should be greater for the most worthy (John 11:33) and less for those who are unworthy (Jeremiah 22:19; Acts 5:6, 10).

<margin>Real sorrow.</margin>
Real worldly sorrow (which causes the death of both body and soul) is that which is immoderate. It does not humble the heart naturally <note>original: "kindly"</note>, but instead disquiets, disturbs, and unsettles <note>original: "distempers"</note> it. This may proceed from outward evils and losses—which even the best people can be troubled by, such as David and Joshua (Psalm 42:5; Joshua 7:10)—or from inward evils, most commonly from melancholic moods <note>original: "melancholious humours"</note> and, worst of all, from an evil conscience.

<margin>
Psalm 42:5.
Joshua 7:10.
</margin>

<margin>
Melancholy <note>original Greek: Μελαχ.</note>.
It is a sickness.
</margin>
This is a most miserable sickness of the soul.

Anguish of the heart <note>original Greek: Συνοχη καρδιας (Synoche kardias)</note>.
Sorrow comes from dissolving <note>original Greek: Λυπη παρα το λυειν (Lype para to lyein)</note>.
Psalm 42:4.
Job 39:16.
</margin>
"Sorrow is a most great evil" <note>original Greek: ἐστιν ἡ λύπη κακον (estin he lype kakon)</note>. "All sorrowful grief is a sickness to a man" <note>original Greek: Ἅπαν τὸ λυπεῖν ἐστι δυσχερης νόσος (Hapan to lypein esti dyscheres nosos)</note>. *And truly says the wisest man, "Heaviness in the heart of a man brings it down"* (Proverbs 12:25). It brings the heart down because it wastes the natural, vital, and animal spirits <note>In early modern medicine, these "spirits" were thought to be subtle fluids that carried life and thought through the body.</note>. Because sorrow, by troubling and afflicting the heart, consumes it; its spirits are wasted, partly by the contraction of the heart, whereby the spirits are choked (according to which sorrow is called "anguish" or "tightness of the heart"), and partly by the "dissolution" of the spirits (whereby sorrow is called *dissolution*) because it dissolves the spirits, and consequently wears away the body, and sometimes resolves it into tears or sweat. It is also aptly called "a pouring out of the heart like water" (Psalm 42:4).

### Part affected.

<margin>
The natural affection of sorrow.
2 Corinthians 7:11.
John 16:20.
</margin>
Just as fear relates to a future and imminent evil, the natural affection of sorrow relates to evil as something present. One should be rightly grieved by present evil and be just as careful to avoid it. Sorrow should be both moderate and rightly provoked by that which is truly evil. And as the evil is great in scale, so should the mourning be continuous and rise (if the evil requires it) to the level of lamentation. This is the immediate seat of this perturbation <note>term: emotional disturbance</note>: when someone is either grieved by that which is not evil in itself, or by something that is not as great an evil as it appears, or when one is grieved more intensely or longer than they should be. In those cases, it creates a perceptible sorrow <note>original: "dolour"</note> and pain in the heart. The heart is the next thing affected by this overly stirred passion, and through a shared connection <note>original: "sympathy"</note>, the mind is agitated <note>original: "exagitate"</note>.

### Causes.

<margin>
God.
Lamentations 1:12, 13.
1 Samuel 2:33.
</margin>
God inflicts heaviness and sorrow of heart, justly punishing the former insolence of those who have provoked him. As Jerusalem confessed: *“Behold and see, if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow, which is done unto me, wherewith the Lord hath afflicted me in the day of his fierce wrath. He hath made me desolate and daily in heaviness. Again, he hath filled me with bitterness and made me drunken with wormwood”* <note>Wormwood is a plant known for its extremely bitter taste, often used in the Bible as a metaphor for suffering and grief.</note>. That is, he has made me lose my senses with great anguish and sorrow. He corrects the hearts of his own people with sorrow to teach them better how to grieve for sin and to value the joys of his Spirit more highly.

<margin>Satan.</margin>
Satan is ready to be employed as that evil and malicious spirit, directed and permitted at the commandment of God to execute His will against the wicked. *As the evil spirit was sent from the Lord upon Saul and vexed him with sorrow and grievous pangs.*

<margin>
External trouble.
Genesis 30:1.
1 Kings 21:4, 6.
</margin>
External troubles, pains <note>original: "dolours"</note>, disgraces, disappointments, and the loss of friends, parents, wives, children, honors, profits, or pleasures all move this passion. But it is felt all the more if your mind is infected with self-love or habitual <note>original: "customable"</note> impatience, by which the mind is made weak and is not prepared or armed for both good and bad fortune. Indeed, not only do the losses of things we once had grieve us, but the lack of things we most desire moves us just as much. For example, when Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, she said to him in the anguish of her heart: *“Give me children, or else I die.”* King Ahab’s spirit was sad because he could not obtain Naboth’s vineyard.

<margin>Melancholy nourishment <note>original: "nutriment"</note>.</margin>
Among external causes, those things that cause a melancholic imbalance <note>original: "distemper"</note> must also be numbered. In particular, this includes any "melancholy food," such as bread and drink made with darnel <note>Darnel is a weed that, when accidentally ground into flour, could cause dizziness, sickness, or a feeling of intoxication.</note>, staying awake too long, immoderate sexual activity <note>original: "venery"</note>, idleness, solitude, and remaining too much in...

<header>CHAP. 23. The heaviness of Sorrow.</header>

...in one place (which has thick air), too much raw food <note>original: "crudity"</note> and drink without meat, and such things: these are the prior causes of the bad humor of melancholy.

<margin>
Melancholy and how it works.
</margin>
The imagination and fantasy are often, without any external cause, greatly disturbed by the fumes and blackish vapors of "atrabilious" <note>original: "atrabilious," meaning related to black bile</note> humors and scorched <note>original: "adust"</note> melancholic blood. This breeds many strange terrors and unstoppable sorrows. This happens because the brain and its ventricles (the instruments of judgment) are corrupted and darkened by the cloudy, vaporous spirits arising from that bubbling blackish puddle, which obscures our naturally clear "animal spirits" <note>In the medicine of this era, "animal spirits" were believed to be a refined substance that carried thoughts and sensations through the nervous system.</note>. 

It is not so extreme at first, but it grows over time. This does not cause a simple absence of light, but a thick and persistent darkness. Over time, it becomes a habit in the brain, corrupting the mind's understanding <note>original: "conceit"</note>. Because of this, it constantly breeds fearful and sorrowful passions and creates false, distorted shapes, causing great anguish. The imagination sends mournful (though false) reports to the heart. The heart then responds with the same melancholic feeling, turning all joy into misery, all hope into fear, and all confidence into despair.

<margin>Answering a concern.</margin>
One might wonder how any coarse humor in the body can affect the simple soul. But the answer is easy: the soul itself is not so much affected as its functions are corrupted and disturbed. That "firmamental spirit"—which is the bond and vehicle of the soul <note>original: *vinculum & vehiculum animae*</note>, through which the soul’s abilities work and its functions are carried out—is infected and corrupted by the contagion of the most subtle, vaporous spirits of melancholy. And as this spirit is affected, so are the actions and passions of the soul. Just as when the eye looks through green spectacles, everything appears green because of that medium, so too, when the spirit is corrupted, all functions of the imagination and passions are corrupted.

<summary>This page explains how the physical "humor" of melancholy produces vapors that darken the brain and heart, leading to irrational fear and despair. It clarifies that while the soul is pure, its functions are distorted by these physical vapors, much like looking through colored glass.</summary>

### Cures and Remedies

<margin>
Sorrow should not be fought against or concealed at first.
Plutarch.
</margin>
The violence of sorrow should not be fought against at first because it is such a furious and untamed <note>original: "undaunted"</note> beast. It is harder to overthrow it by resisting than to tame it by following its course. Nor should sorrow be concealed too much. It is like a fire: the more it is covered, the more it rages. If hidden griefs do not find an outlet <note>original: "vent"</note>, they will burst the heart within. It is no small relief to a sorrowful heart to have a faithful friend into whose ears one may pour out <note>original: "disgorge"</note> some of their grief.

<margin>
Causes removed.
Isaiah 38:13, 14, 20.
Genesis 45:27.
Or replaced.
</margin>
The easiest remedy for sorrow is to remove its cause. If it comes from evil, that evil should be removed, as when Hezekiah’s death was delayed. If it comes from the loss or lack of something good, that good should be restored, as when Jacob found his son Joseph again. Alternatively, even if the evil remains or the good is still absent, a greater evil might be avoided—just as a merchant at sea avoids death by throwing some of his cargo overboard <note>original: "losing of some of his wares"</note>—or a greater good might be obtained, as when Paul rejoiced in his chains because of his hope for a reward in heaven.

<margin>
Tears mitigate sorrow only slightly.
"One is filled with tears, and grief is poured out" <note>original: "Expletur lachrymis, &c."</note>.
Genesis 45:2, 14, 15, and 46:29.
Various kinds of tears.
</margin>
Tears appear to mitigate sorrow slightly, and shedding tears is a kind of easing of grief. There are various types: some are for joy, which show kindness; some are for misery; some are for both joy and misery (such as the tears of repentance, which are called "the food of the soul"); and some are for deception, which are tears of hypocrisy <note>original: "dissimulation"</note>. Even though tears arise from a grieving heart and trickle <note>original: "distill"</note> from weeping eyes, they are the least effective medicine <note>original: "unfittest salve"</note> one can use to cure sorrow. Although they somewhat relieve the heart of the one who is grieving (even though they...

...[though] they are womanly, they move the hearts of others to compassion. They tie the hands of the Almighty <note>original: "Omnipotent"</note>; they silence the accuser, pacify the adversary, overcome the invincible, and are able to change vengeance into mercy.

<margin>
Time is a remedy, but a poor <note>original: "base"</note> one.
*Seneca, Epistle 63.*
*Seneca, Epistle 97.*
"For it is either feigned or foolish" <note>original: "Aut enim simulatus aut stultus est"</note>.
*Seneca, Epistle 63.*
Weariness in mourning is a shameful <note>original: "vile"</note> remedy for sorrow.
</margin>
There are many who, when their hearts are too weak or their burden too heavy <note>original: "strong"</note>, find that neither reason nor religion is able to help them; and yet, *time* will eventually overcome their sorrow. Time is the physician for all sorrow. He who finds no end to his mourning through counsel will find it through time. The reason is that no one can mourn both intensely <note>original: "greatly"</note> and for a long time. If sorrow becomes deep-seated <note>original: "inveterate"</note>, it is mocked, and not without cause. It is a foolish thing, therefore, to reject so many excellent remedies and, in the meantime, to allow time—the consumer of all things, and perhaps of you before your grief—to have more power over you than wisdom and piety. For a wise person, being simply worn out by mourning is the most shameful remedy for grief. It is far better to stop your sorrow before it stops with you <note>meaning: before the emotion simply exhausts itself naturally</note>.

<margin>
*Job 16:2.*
More suitable remedies.
</margin>
It is not always possible to have the cause of sorrow removed (which, if it could be done, would instantly ease the grief). Friends are often found to be "miserable comforters" <note>a reference to Job 16:2</note>, or else provide no comfort at all. Tears are not always at one's command, and they provide little benefit. To wait for the medicine <note>original: "physic"</note> of *time* is uncertain, as we do not know whether time will consume us or our grief first. It is therefore most necessary to establish some excellent <note>original: "exquisite"</note> remedies to cure sorrow in the heart while the external and previous cause of it remains.

<margin>
Remedies of two sorts.
Remedies by redirection <note>original: "revulsion"</note>.
Gathering the heart <note>original: "Recollection"</note> by a wise and noble estimation of the soul.
</margin>
Just as physicians deal with agitated humors <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were thought to control health and temperament</note> in the body which are in violent motion—when they cannot be easily purged or quickly changed, some they call back to their own source, and others they draw aside to a more convenient place—so too are the proper remedies of sorrow either by *redirection* <note>original: "revulsion," a medical term for drawing a disease from one part of the body to another</note> or *diversion* <note>original: "derivation"</note>. By *redirection*, the heart gathers itself together and directly calls itself back home, to itself, from the evils...

<header>CHAPTER 23. The Heaviness of Sorrow.</header>

<margin>
A disdaining of evils.
</margin>
...evils that provoke it to passion. This occurs when the mind esteems itself so serene, so high, so excellent, and so worthy that it scorns to be affected by any kind of evils, viewing them as inferior things—so base, so wicked <note>original: "naughty"</note>, and unworthy of the agitation <note>original: "commotion"</note> and enslavement of a divine mind. The evils, again, are accounted either as not being evils at all, or else as so small and light (no matter how great they might actually be) that they are thought unworthy of causing the soul to be molested and pained by them.

<margin>
A contempt of sorrow.
</margin>
The royal mind disdains to complain of them, judging sorrow for them to be against nature (defacing nature's beauty), against equity (reproaching nature's law, which has made all things changeable), against piety (murmuring against the providence of God), and against our own utility (killing under a false appearance <note>original: "killing under color"</note>):

<margin>
Judges 4:18-19.
</margin>
Just as *Jael* killed *Sisera*, covering him with a blanket and driving the nail into his brain all the way to the head. <note>The author compares sorrow to the biblical figure Jael, who offered Sisera comfort and shelter only to kill him in his sleep.</note> Consider sorrow to be a viper, bred in our own bosom. It makes one weak <note>original: "effeminates"</note> and covers one with indecent shame. It dries up the bones and eclipses the light of our good fortune. It sours <note>original: "tarteth"</note> the sweetest things that we enjoy, poisoning our best virtues and deeds, and making our whole life bitter. This remedy <note>The practice of disdaining or holding sorrow in contempt.</note> is rare and excellent, but very difficult <note>original: "difficill"</note>; yet the ancient philosophers taught it—such as the *Platonists*, *Stoics*, and *Peripatetics*—and many have achieved it, as is recorded of *Socrates* at his death.

<margin>
Remedies by diversion <note>original: "derivation"</note> and more easy.
</margin>
Remedies by *diversion* <note>original: "derivation"</note> occur when the heart is turned away from the evil that grieves it toward some other object, so that it may be moved to have more joy in that new object than it had sorrow in the evil; or it may be made, in a certain manner and measure, to forget the evil. These kinds of remedies are both easier and more common. In physical medicine <note>original: "bodily physick"</note>, hemorrhages, fluxes, inflammations, discharges <note>original: "defluctions"</note>, and the like are cured by diversion—turning the flowing stream from a more dangerous part of the body to another that is less perilous.

This is used for both smaller and greater evils.

<summary>This page outlines two philosophical and psychological remedies for grief: "disdaining" sorrow by viewing it as an unworthy and destructive passion, and "diversion," which involves refocusing the mind's attention on more joyful subjects.</summary>

# CHAPTER 23. The Heaviness of Sorrow.

<margin>
The mind is to be led away, etc. Seneca <note>original: "Abducendus est animus, &c."</note>. See John 14:2.
</margin>
When a surgeon <term>original: "Chirurgion"</term> is to open a vein, or lance an abscess <term>original: "Apostume"</term>, he will make his patients (for fear of fainting) withdraw their sight, close their eyes, look away, or behold some other thing; so that by diverting their sight, their imagination may be somewhat diverted. Soldiers in battle have their minds diverted from all peril by the hope of victory. Many running to their death have diverted their minds from all sorrow in dying: some by considering the miseries of life; others for reputation <note>original: "estimation"</note> and glory, to show courage. The *Martyrs* have not been afraid, nor their minds cast down in the flames of fire; and *that* was because their minds were diverted from the flame to their crown and the *high price of their calling*. Common people <note>original: "Vulgars"</note> will say to their neighbors distressed with sorrow: *Forget it, think upon some other thing.* The mind is to be drawn to other studies, thoughts, cares, and businesses; and finally, it is often to be cured with a change of place.

<margin>
Preparation of the mind:
</margin>

<margin>
By premeditation and resolution:
</margin>
The mind should be prepared before it falls into the conflict of sorrow and be made ready and strong for all grievous and distressed accidents. Thus, when they come, they may find the heart made firm, and the heart may find them less terrible. Premeditation and the expectation of evil make the mind gather its own forces and make perfect preparation for the storm. He who exercises himself with the thought <note>original: "conceit"</note> of evils finds the real conflict with them easy. Whatever is long looked for falls more lightly, and things are half-finished in their violence by the time they arrive. It is good for the mind never to be over-confident <note>original: "secure"</note>, lest suddenly surprising evils make it miserable and leave it desperate. Resolution of mind gives the safest advantage in this.

<margin>
And strengthening <note>original: "corroboration"</note> of it by virtue and grace.
</margin>
If one should object that it is a torment to the mind to think on evil before it comes, the answer is: it is no pain, but a pastime; and the unspeakable comfort in the time of trouble does more than repay the effort <note>original: "recompence the trauell"</note>. [for]tified and furnished castle: stocked with his own provision of proper goods (not with the goods of the body or fortune, for they provide little help), namely virtue and grace. Socrates so delighted in virtue that no kind of sorrow ever altered his countenance. But the inward jubilee of the mind, in the kingdom of grace, excels; which consists not in food, nor in drink, nor in such bodily trash, but in *righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit*, <margin>Romans 14:17; Psalm 4</margin> which keeps the soul so firm that no encountering evils can deject it.

### Remedies drawn from reason.
<margin>
Use reason as a remedy for sorrow <note>original: "Rationem habe, pro doloris remedio"</note>. Epictetus. Antoninus and Maximus, *Sermon on Cleansing Sorrow* <note>original: "Ser. cle. dolore"</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
Proverbs 12:25.
</margin>

When evils befall you, it is impossible to be altogether devoid of passion (as beasts are, who have no reason); neither should you be like a fool, who cannot use reason. Instead, act like a man indeed, to whom reason is given against evils, either to avoid them or else to endure them. Seek your remedies from within yourself, collecting them from reason. Use reason as a remedy for your grief <term>original: "dolour"</term>. From reason may be drawn many exhortations, persuasions, many counsels, and many comforts. *Heaviness in the heart of a man brings it down, but a good word makes it glad.*

### Examples and specific instances of this.

<margin>
The death of friends.
</margin>

<margin>
Ecclesiastes 7:3.
</margin>

Marcia, at the death of her worthy son Metellus, was almost brought to death by sorrow; but she was restored by the counsels and comforts of Seneca, which he drew from reason. If you are stricken with sorrow for the death of any most dear friend, gather your comforts from grounds such as these: It is a law <term>original: "Statute"</term> of God and nature to die. All things are governed by a divine power. Sorrow does not benefit the dead. *The day of death is better than the day of life.* <note>The author likely references Ecclesiastes 7:1: "the day of death than the day of one's birth."</note> *All things rise only to fall*, and everything is drawing to an end.

<margin>
Loss of goods.
</margin>

If you are in sorrow for the loss of worldly goods, reason affords grounds for comfort: such as the fact that the loss is small. You had contentment when you did not have the thing you now lack. Your loss may be repaired twofold in your own time; nature is content with little. All things are only lent by God and are to be restored at his will.

A consideration of the diversity of trouble.
Punishments.

Consider that all calamities are either *punishments, corrections, trials,* or *martyrdoms.* Punishments are either universal—touching all of humanity equally, such as common troubles (Genesis 3:17), sicknesses (Psalm 39:10–12), and death (Romans 5:12, Psalm 9:7)—or they are particular exemplary judgments that happen to those who are wicked <term>facinorous: exceptionally wicked or atrocious</term> (Luke 23:41, Numbers 25:14, 1 Corinthians 10:11).

Corrections.

Trials.

Tertullian.

By this, as if by a "cloud of witnesses," others (who are so hard to believe) may be encouraged to believe the truth through the unspeakable kindness of God. **Cicero** sets down three weapons of the mind against all trouble and grief, which he could never understand nor practice as well as those who are Christians: *Resolution, Constancy, and Inward Speech* <note>original: "Contentio, confirmatio, sermo que intimus"</note>. *Resolution* (or rather, intention) is nothing but a focused determination, by which the mind is made ready and prepared against every trouble. *Constancy* (confirmation) is a strengthening of the mind against all contrary opinions, doubts, fears, and sluggishness; it is simply steadfastness. As for *Inward Speech*, **Cicero** did not know it—not through a lack of wit, but through a want of grace. This is a speech held partly with ourselves and partly with God in prayer. We speak with ourselves as **David** did when he said, *Why are you cast down, my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Still trust in God.* (Psalm 42:5). And as that...

### CHAPTER 24.
# Violent Desperation.

---

> Job 7:15. *My soul chooses rather to be strangled and to die, than to be in my bones.*
> 2 Samuel 17:23. *Ahithophel <note>original: "Achitophel"</note> put his household in order, and hanged himself.*

### Description.

<margin>Holy desperation.</margin>
<margin>1. Regarding sin. <insert>61 335</insert></margin>
Desperation is either holy or unholy. Holy desperation is when one despairs of his own strength and, in the anguish of his conscience, thinks there is no remedy for him but either to perish in his sins or else, by speedy repentance, to run to his God as his gracious Father. Or, it is when a person under calamity despairs of all strength and help in himself or in the world, and takes his only refuge in God. <margin>2. Regarding affliction.</margin> <margin>2 Corinthians 1:9.</margin> As **Paul** says of himself, *We received the sentence of death in ourselves, so that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead.*

<margin>Unholy desperation.</margin>
Unholy desperation is a passion <term>In this context, "passion" refers to a powerful, often overwhelming emotion or state of suffering in the soul.</term> that brings strange disturbances <note>original: "pertubations"</note> to the soul, and it is understood <note>original: "taken"</note> either more broadly or more strictly. In the broad <note>original: "ample"</note> sense, it is a disease and grief without any expectation of a better condition <note>original: "case"</note>. <margin>Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica*, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 40, Article 4. <note>original Latin: "T. Sec. Secundæ. dist. 40. Art. 4."</note></margin> For desperation is not simply a lack <note>original: "privation"</note> of hope and of all expectation of relief, but it is a retreating <note>original: "retiring"</note>

<summary>This page defines two types of desperation: "holy desperation," which leads a person to abandon self-reliance and turn to God, and "unholy desperation," which is a destructive emotional state characterized by a total loss of hope.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER 24. Violent Desperation.</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

...bringing a retreat from the thing desired because of an imagined impossibility.

<margin>Final.</margin>
Unholy desperation is either final or temporal. Final desperation is that which is incurable; it happens only to those rejected by God <note>original: "reprobates"</note> and to those who die without any hope of comfort.
<margin>Temporal.</margin>
Temporal desperation is a rejection of hope and comfort in a significant way, but it is neither total nor final. This can happen even to God's children.

<margin>Desperation strictly taken, what it is.</margin>
Desperation in its strictest sense (as it is commonly understood) is a terrifying passion <term>In this context, "passion" refers to an overwhelming and agonizing emotional state.</term> and agitation of the soul. By this, the distressed person thinks he can find no relief or help except in death; consequently, he resolves to commit suicide <note>original: "put violent hands into himself"</note>, either to take revenge upon himself or to be freed from some heavier calamity.
<margin>Two ends.</margin>
He is too sensitive to his burden and too impatient with his suffering <term>The "cross" refers to the specific trials or afflictions a person must bear.</term>. He desires death either as a punishment for himself or as a relief.
<margin>Desperate desire of death.</margin>
It is a punishment if he is angry with himself; it is a comfort (though a wretched one) if he is only suffering within himself. He does not desire death as the godly do, *who desire to be released and to be with Christ.* Neither does he endure his afflicted life with patience while looking toward death with hope. In his burning sorrow, he does not simply desire death or impatiently beg for it from God, as **Job** did:
<margin>Job 6:8, 9. Job 7:15.</margin>
> And chooses rather to be strangled and to die, than to remain in his body <note>original: "in his bones"</note>;
But he also goes further; what Job only contemplated <note>original: "did choose"</note>, this person carries out with his own hands as his own executioner <note>original: "hang-man"</note>, acting out of utter impatience.

<margin>Sudden. Advised. Under wrath, cross, or melancholy.</margin>
Desperation, understood in this way, is either a sudden impulse or something longer meditated upon. Furthermore, it occurs either under the sense of God’s wrath, as with **Judas**, or under the weight of affliction <note>original: "under the cross"</note>, as many of the Pagans used to do. Or else, it happens during a fit of intense depression <term>In the Early Modern period, "melancholy" was a broad medical term for conditions ranging from deep sadness to severe clinical depression and psychosis.</term> or temporary insanity <note>original: "phrensy"</note>, as can happen to any man who has lost his mind and does not know what he is doing.

### *Part affected.*

<margin>Diverse faculties.</margin>
This fearful disturbance <note>original: "perturbation"</note> is a complex <note>original: "compound"</note> evil, and has its specific place among various faculties of the soul. There is a deprivation of all joy and hope, trust and confidence in the present or future good, which is loved. In place of these, the emotions <note>original: "affections"</note> of sorrow and fear are excessive, whereby the heart becomes horribly impatient at the present or future evil which it hates, and is altogether unbelieving <note>original: "incredulous"</note>. The conscience is mortally wounded, and the mind is fully eclipsed with the blackish fumes arising from the burning lake of secret terrors.

### *Causes.*

<margin>
Misery.
Jeremiah 8:3.
Revelation 9:6.
Appian.
</margin>
A misery considered beyond remedy—and that can be helped in no other way but by death—stirs up this passion; examples include a troublesome life, the fear of a worse death, or the extreme of any fear and danger. For instance, *Mithridates* (comfortless under his unfortunate circumstances) first attempted to kill <note>original: "dispatch"</note> himself with poison; but when he could not accomplish this (because he had always used his own antidotes, which are still called *Mithridate*), he commanded *Bitallus*, his captain, to kill him.

<margin>
God as a withdrawing cause.
1 Chronicles 10:14.
Satan as an active cause.
1 Samuel 16:14, 22:18, and 28:8.
</margin>
Many (as they justly deserve) are deserted by God and have foolishly yielded themselves to Satan’s servitude, suffering that "old serpent" to lie too long in their bosoms. At length, he begins to awaken them by biting them through the heart until they can find no rest except in their own most foolish ruin. Thus the devil entered into *Judas*—first to betray his Master, and then to commit suicide <note>original: "put violent hands upon himself"</note>. ...witch, and at last killed himself.

<margin>Melancholy.</margin>
Burned <note>original: "adust"</note> melancholy is the messenger of great despair; its blackish fumes make people's spirits seem as if they are drunken. The mind conceives strange, deceptive <note>original: "illuding"</note> imaginations. Even if they are entirely free from any actual external trouble <note>original: "calamity"</note>, their corrupted imagination presents thousands of imagined <note>original: "conceited"</note> trials to the heart. They sometimes imagine they have committed the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit; that they are rejected by God; that armies of disasters are coming for them or have already seized them; and other such thoughts. The heart and emotions (always affected by what the mind reports) are so extremely terrified and distressed that they wait for the melancholic mind’s decision on what to do. Since the information provided was nothing but sorrow and fear, the resolution is nothing other than final despair and a violent death.

<margin>Madness of mind defends self-murder.</margin>
Many are preoccupied with a madness of mind and a foolish opinion that desperate self-murder is lawful. Some think it shows great courage; others see it as an ancient practice of the greatest and most excellent people of every nation. Some think it is a proof <note>original: "testification"</note> of their love—as did the wives of *Seneca, Fulvius, Labio, Scaurus,* and *Paetus* <note>original: "Petus"</note>, who died only to follow their husbands into death and to witness their kind affection to the world. Others argue that whatever they may justly desire, they may just as rightfully do when it is in their own power. They believe the most voluntary death is the most honorable <note>original: "fair"</note> death, and that when they take their own life, they take only what belongs to them, breaking no laws and offending no other person. They think they may apply to themselves what is said of medicine <note>original: "physic"</note>:

<margin>Extreme remedies for extreme evils <note>original: "Extremis malis extrema remedia"</note>.</margin>
For extreme diseases, extreme remedies should be used—and other such foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> ideas swarm in their minds. By these thoughts, they are moved to believe that one of the greatest sins is perfectly lawful, while in the meantime, their hearts are filled with cowardice and impatience, hiding <note>original: "couching"</note> from the blows of Fortune within the den of death.

<header>CHAPTER 24. Violent Despair.</header>

<margin>Spiritual blindness.</margin>
When someone has been ignorant of their own nature for a long time, and suddenly, by God’s secret judgment, is revealed to themselves, they become so heavily distressed that the more they look into their own soul, the more they become impatient with themselves. Their inner self <note>original: "inward face"</note> frightens them, and the sight of who they are is an intolerable horror. They think of themselves as such an outcast <note>original: "abject"</note> and an avowed enemy of God that they consider it too small a revenge to end their own life. Despair likewise results no less from the ignorance of God.

<margin>Other uncured diseases of the soul.</margin>
Incredulity, hardness of heart, callous impenitence <note>original: "dedolent impenitency"</note>, a spirit of spiritual lethargy <note>original: "slumber"</note>, self-love, hypocrisy, apostasy, impatience, unruly passions, a seared <note>original: "cauterized"</note> conscience, and discontentment all strongly contribute to bringing on this passion. For those who are affected in this way either die like senseless blocks—as Nabal did—or become desperate, as Cain, Saul, Ahithophel <note>original: "Achitophel"</note>, and Judas did.

<margin>A wounded spirit. Matthew 27; Acts 1; 1 Chronicles 10:13.</margin>
But above all, *a wounded spirit* that is not cured in time—especially in a person rejected by God <note>original: "reprobate"</note>—creates the strongest urge toward this sickness. Examples of this are Judas and Spira <note>Francesco Spira (1502–1548) was an Italian lawyer who died in a state of famous despair after recanting his Protestant beliefs</note>. This is even more likely if they have committed a capital crime, as Saul died in despair for the transgression he committed against the Lord—specifically against the word of the Lord, which he did not keep—and because he sought and asked counsel from a medium <note>original: "familiar spirit"</note>. In such cases, sorrow and fear are always present.

<margin>The foolish imagination of a weak mind defends self-murder.</margin>
Many are the foolish ideas <note>original: "fond conceits"</note> that enter a person's cowardly mind to provoke them to this rage. Some have died to escape illnesses, such as Pomponius Atticus, Tullius, and Marcellinus <note>original: "Martellinus"</note>. Cleanthes the philosopher died by willful starvation <note>original: "abstinence"</note> to rid himself of the maladies that tormented him. Others did so because their plans did not succeed, or because they would not fall into their enemies' hands—as did Cato and the whole town of Saguntum. Being oppressed by extreme famine (which led to the proverb "Saguntine hunger" <note>original: "Sanguntina fames"; referring to the desperate starvation during the Siege of Saguntum in 219 BC</note>) and surrounded and besieged by their enemies, they built a great fire. ### Signs and Symptoms.

---

<margin>His disposition.</note>
A person inclined toward despair is either passionate or pensive, possessing a hasty and weak spirit, and is prone to melancholy <note>In the 17th century, melancholy was viewed as both a physical disease and a spiritual state of sadness</note>. He sleeps too long and too deeply in sin before becoming frightened. He is hard-hearted, has a guilty conscience, is unbelieving <note>original: "incredulous"</note>, and feels no remorse <note>original: "dedolent"</note>. He has grown too much in self-love; he is either a blinded atheist or a false <note>original: "painted"</note> hypocrite—an apostate, or someone with a seared conscience.

<margin>*Thucydides.*</margin>
He is more foolish than Timocrates the Athenian, who, when his ship was about to sink, killed himself to avoid the fear of drowning <note>original: "death by water"</note>. He has a dejected mind and takes everything in a negative way.

He is like a sick person who, as long as he hopes to be cured, abstains from harmful <note>original: "noysome"</note> foods; but as soon as he understands himself to be incurable, he holds nothing back. So it is with the desperate person: as long as he sinned with moderation <note>original: "mediocrity"</note>, he had some hope of mercy; but at last, sinning defiantly <note>original: "with a high hand"</note> and with a presumptuous mind, he cares for nothing. <margin>Concerns regarding different dangers.</margin>
A reprobate <note>A person rejected by God and destined for damnation</note> cannot be truly cured. If he gets any ease, it is by some palliative treatment or by some devilish narcotic, whereby he is cast again into the spirit of slumber. If he is one of the elect <note>Those chosen by God for salvation</note>, or has ever given proof of his sincere faith, there is some hope for him. This disturbance is less dangerous for someone who is phlegmatic or sanguine; it is more perilous in one who is choleric or melancholic <note>These refer to the "Four Humors," a historical medical theory that one's temperament and health were determined by the balance of four bodily fluids: phlegm, blood, yellow bile (choler), and black bile (melancholy)</note>. The latter is dangerous because of his strong and sorrowful imagination; the former because of the frenzy of his passion. Despair is a double sin; and if it is final or total, it has no forgiveness <note>original: "remission"</note>.

This is one of the judgments of God, which he uses to plague the persecutors of his Church, as is shown in the examples of *Saul, Ahithophel, Judas,* and *Montanus* <note>Montanus was a 2nd-century heretic who, according to tradition, died by suicide.</note>.

<margin>A question regarding the salvation of the desperate answered.</margin>
The question may be raised: can any who lay violent hands upon themselves be saved? The answer is short and easy. If their deaths were so sudden that they could not have enough time <note>original: "leisure"</note> to wish for mercy in their hearts, then in that case the worst is to be suspected, because they die in sin and without repentance <note>original: "impenitency"</note>. If their deaths were a little more lingering, and yet beyond their power to recover after their attempt, during which time they might have had some moment in their hearts to cry for mercy, then charity <note>In this context, the Christian duty to hope for the best regarding another's soul.</note> may judge for the best. 

Several people have been rescued from the very act of hanging or drowning themselves who have confessed that as soon as they attempted the act—at that very instant—they both repented of their deed and cried for mercy in their hearts. If anyone lays desperate hands on themselves because of a frenzy, physical madness, or melancholy, and if they have previously given testimony of their spiritual rebirth <note>original: "Regeneration"</note>, we must make the best interpretation of it, considering that they do this not so much from the mind as from the body.

Even though you have spent your entire life in sin until your very end, do not despair. Let your end amend everything. God judges and values everyone, not according to their past <note>original: "bigane," meaning bygone</note> life, but according to their end. For as death finds us—either repentant or unrepentant—so shall it deliver us up again at the last day to be saved or condemned. The past life of the penitent thief was not remembered when he said to his Lord, "*Remember me when you come into your kingdom*"; to whom it was readily and sweetly answered, "*Today you shall be with me in paradise.*" Your sins are far below the mercy of God and the value of Christ’s ransom. God cannot receive a greater wrong, nor can we injure ourselves more, than to despair of forgiveness. Christ raised one dead person who had just passed away; another in a coffin; and a third who was already smelling in the grave—declaring that just as there is no degree of death so desperate that it is beyond help, so there are no sins so desperate (in number or in greatness) that they can be beyond mercy.

<margin>Against despair of a wounded spirit.</margin>

Compel yourself to some measure of prayer. Be grieved at sin; or at the very least, be grieved that you are *not* grieved, for that is a great beginning of repentance. Persuade yourself that your sins are pardonable. God's mercy is

And because no one can be under this calamity unless hardness of heart both procures and accompanies it: embalm your heart with the blood of the true **Scapegoat** <note>In the Bible, the scapegoat symbolically carried away the sins of the people; here it refers to Christ.</note>. <margin>Against despair arising from discontentment.</margin>
If any discontentment disturbs your heart with this passion, it is because of some perceived misery and present calamity. Consider your burden a common one; with patience, make use of your evils. The cross drives none but fools to desperation. Do not be ignorant of the fountain of crosses <note>The "cross" refers to life's burdens or sufferings.</note>. Run to the **Striker** <note>The "Striker" refers to God as the source of discipline; the author suggests seeking mercy from the one who allows the trial.</note> and plead for His mercy. Make a virtue of necessity. Sweeten your cross by curing your conscience. Turn your misery into a medicine, and your dejection into steps toward glory. Endeavor to have a sweet enjoyment of God, who alone is a thousand-fold felicity, fully eclipsing all those inferior sparks of misery.

<margin>Moderate passions.</margin>
Moderate your immoderate passions; beware of self-love. Divert your mind to other objects. Be always fully resolute to pull up when you should, like a well-bridled horse. Mortify your passions through Christ’s passions. Reverence God’s providence and His will in all things. If your **servile fear** <note>Fear based on the threat of punishment.</note> is great, let the **filial fear** <note>The healthy, respectful love a child has for a parent.</note> of God correct it, and use all the remedies against fear. If your sorrow is extreme, use all the antidotes that are prescribed against it. If it comes from a **melancholy humor** <note>In historical medicine, "melancholy" was an excess of black bile thought to cause depression; the author suggests medical treatment for physical causes.</note>, your body must first be physically cured. Use all means to be freed from the **spirit of slumber** and from a **cauterized conscience** <note>A conscience that has become insensitive or "numb" to right and wrong through repeated sin.</note>, lest you fall again into the same snare.

->The part affected<-

<margin>
Desire.
1 John 2:16.
</margin>
The part of the person affected is that primitive passion of desire, which stirs up the heart and mind to obtain what is thought to be necessary. If the desire is moderate and lawful, it does not harm the soul; but if it is unlawful or excessive, it becomes a sickness of the mind and the *lust of the eyes*. All those inferior and secondary good things cannot fill or fully satisfy the heart's desire. The heart of man is but one syllable, one word, a small substance; yet in its capacity, it is greater than the world. It is so infinite in desire that this universe and globe cannot fill the triangle of it <note>A common early modern metaphor: the heart is triangular and the world is circular; a circle cannot fill the corners of a triangle—only the Trinity can</note> until the time when, through virtue and grace, it is settled in true contentment. With things that are currently possessed, the heart cannot help but overreach and disquiet itself by seeking more. The thing that is present feels burdensome <note>original: "grievous"</note> and does not satisfy.

Examples.

A person’s natural temperament <note>term: "complection"—referring to the balance of the four humors in the body</note> stirs up the mind to be the more covetous. The melancholic person is the most greedy and the more cunning. The sanguine person <note>original: "sanguinian"</note> has more attractive ways to deceive and allure. The choleric person is more malicious and fiery in his purpose. The phlegmatic person is the greater miser <note>original: "niggard"</note>. Examples also move people to avarice: when someone sees another man has much, he immediately <note>original: "incontinent"</note> thinks to himself that he is a man as well, and must have as much as the other has. Not just one example is seen, but thousands...

"The love of money grows [as the wealth itself grows]." <note>original: *Crescit amor nummi, &c.*</note>

Avarice begets avarice, just as too much drink begets thirst in hydropics <note>term: "hydropickes"—people suffering from dropsy (edema), whose thirst was said to increase the more they drank</note>. Fire kindles fire, and covetousness kindles itself until it cannot be quenched. The more one has, the more he loves to have more. Avarice grows up with riches, just as ivy grows up with the oak. *Alexander* <note>Alexander the Great</note>, hearing *Anaxarchus* debating about the existence of infinite worlds, wept and said, "Do I not have cause to mourn, when out of so many worlds I have yet scarcely conquered one?"

<margin>
Neglect of salvation.
</margin>
The eye cannot look at both heaven and earth at once. It is impossible to serve two masters; it is most difficult to bend the mind to two things equally. The neglect of heavenly things makes men inordinate in their desire for that which is earthly. A man waxes in the one as he wanes in the other.

<margin>
Self-love.
</margin>
Self-love begets a powerful obsession in the mind, by which a man thinks that nothing can content him as much as the acquiring and beholding of his riches. Nature desires but little, but personal opinion desires that which is infinite.

<margin>
"But a large part of humanity, deceived by false desire, says 'Nothing is enough.'" <note>original: *At bona pars hominum decepta cupidine falso, nil satis est inquit.*</note> Horace, Satires, Book 2, Satire 1.

Horace, Satires, Book 1, Satire 1.
"The people hiss at me, but I applaud myself..." <note>original: *Populus me sibilat, at mihi plaudo, &c.*</note>

The majority of men are falsely deceived by desire and cannot say, "It is enough." The covetous man flatters himself when he beholds his riches. He fears all things as if they were mortal, but desires all things as if they were immortal. Just as he is never satisfied, he is also never at peace. The greater the gain, the greater the pain. ### Prognostics <note>A "prognostic" is a forecast of the likely course of a disease or condition</note>.

Avarice, once it has settled itself and been confirmed by habit <note>original: "custome"</note>, is almost incurable. It is a furnace that is never extinguished; a tyranny spread throughout the whole world; a sickness that goes through the veins and sticks fast in the bowels. When it has become deep-seated <note>original: "inveterate"</note> and cannot be rooted out, it is called avarice. It is more natural <note>original: "innate"</note> than wastefulness <note>original: "prodigality"</note>, for there are more who are greedy than those who are wasteful, and the latter are more easily cured than the former. When riches run out, wastefulness is gone. But avarice is more difficult to help; both the rich and the poor are subject to it. It grows with age: when lack of self-control, wastefulness, lust <note>original: "venery"</note>, and other vices cease, it begins. Many wasteful youths have become greedy <note>original: "covetous"</note> old men. Avarice is profitable to no one—no, not even to the greedy man himself. Wastefulness is profitable to many <note>as the money is circulated back into the economy</note>, and even if it is not honorable <note>original: "honest"</note>, it is still pleasant. It is a lingering disease, and it begins early in life.
<margin>
A rich man is either a wicked man or the heir of a wicked man <note>original: "Dives aut iniquus est, aut iniqui hæres."</note>.
</margin>

the Kingdom of God: He shall not inherit the Kingdom of God who is avaricious <note>original: "auaricious"; meaning greedy</note>.

->Cures and remedies.<-

<margin>
Contentment <note>original: "Contentation"</note>.
Self-sufficiency <note>original Greek: "αυταρκεια" (autarkeia)</note>.
2 Corinthians 9:8.
Philippians 4:11.
What it consists of.
Hebrews 13:5.
1 Timothy 6:8.
</margin>
Greed <note>original: "Couetouſneſſe"</note> should not even be mentioned among Christians (Ephesians 5:3), who should strive by all means to put it to death <note>original: "mortifie"</note> (Colossians 3:5), and to restrain and rule the impulses of desire through that worthy virtue of contentment <note>original: "contentation"</note>: Be content with what you currently have. Having food and clothing <note>original: "rayment"</note>, be satisfied with those things. Let that be sufficient for you which is appropriate for your social standing <note>original: "conuenient for thy eſtate"</note> (Proverbs 30:8). Let current things please you. Whatever lot in life falls to you, accept it graciously <note>original: "take it in good part"</note>, and find rest in that which God has given you.

<margin>
1. Effect.
1 Timothy 6:6.
2. Effect.
</margin>
Contentment makes up for the lack of those things we do not have; for godliness with contentment is great gain. It is nature's wealth: it provides an easy and short path to riches through a moderate disdain for wealth. Contentment will keep your possessions safe from risk, and allow you to more pleasantly and peacefully preserve and enjoy what you currently have—something the greedy man cannot do. For while he is seeking more, he either loses or despises what he already has.

<margin>
Motives for contentment.
It is necessary to become accustomed to little. <note>original Latin: "Necessarium est paruo aſſueſcere." - Seneca</note>
Socrates.
One must subtract from one's desires. <note>original Latin: "Cupiditatibus detrahendum." - Seneca, *On Morals*</note>
</margin>
Study contentment (Philippians 4:11). It is better than riches; it can provide the benefits of riches, but riches cannot provide contentment, nor can they always afford it. This virtue is far more easily attained than wealth. No man is so fortunate as to have everything, and no man is so unhappy as to lack everything. If you have enough for the present, it is best, and you should be willing to go without what is impossible or unlawful to obtain. If you cannot mold your circumstances <note>original: "estate"</note> to fit your mind, then mold your mind to fit your circumstances. Be poor in your desires, and you shall soon be rich: it is great wealth not to desire wealth. Let the necessities of nature and the sufficiency <note>original: "competency"</note> of your standing rule your desires, and consider only that to be your "good" which truly does you good.

<header>CHAPTER 25. Insatiable Avarice.</header>

Life is short; necessity is soon satisfied. He is rich enough who does not lack bread; he is dignified <note>original: "ſtately"</note> enough who is not forced to serve.

It is a great skill to know what is enough, and greater wisdom to care for no more than that which is sufficient.

<margin>
To those who seek many things, many things are lacking; it is well for him to whom God [has given enough]. <note>original Latin: "Multa petentibus, deſunt multa: bene eſt cui Deus, &c." Horace, Odes, Book 3, Ode 16.</note>

1 Timothy 6:6.
</margin>
Desire neither poverty nor riches, but only as much as may feed you with bread *appropriate* <note>original: "conuenient"</note> for you and for your social standing. Let the fear of God possess your heart, and you shall find *a little better than great treasures with trouble.* Seek God to be your portion, and godliness to be your greatest gain. The world is round, but the heart is triangular; a circle cannot fill a triangle—the corners <note>original: "nookes"</note> will remain empty. <note>This was a popular 17th-century metaphor: the circular world cannot satisfy the three-cornered human heart, which was created to be filled only by the Trinity.</note> The heart is a small thing, and "heart" is a short word, but it has more capacity than the world can contain. Place your heart before that infinite Good, so that it may be filled with Him, who is the only full contentment for everyone.

<margin>
Consider life and death.
</margin>
<margin>
He easily despises all things who always thinks he is about to die. <note>original Latin: "Facile contemnit omnia, qui ſemper cogitat ſe eſſe moriturum." Jerome.</note>
</margin>
Meditate upon your birth <note>original: "natiuity"</note> and death: naked you came, and naked shall you go. You were born poor, but you shall die even poorer. You were born to inherit something, but you shall die and leave all things behind. Do you not see all things perish with you? He easily despises <note>original: "contemne"</note> all things who always thinks he is about to die, when all that you are or have shall be divided into three: your body to worms, your soul to devils <note>A warning that the soul of the unrepentant greedy man belongs to the enemy.</note>, and your goods to spendthrifts <note>original: "waſters"</note>. Your life is short and death approaches; why is so much provision needed for someone who is departing? Live contentedly and die with a good conscience, so that you may carry a treasure with you within your burial shroud <note>original: "winding-cloth"</note> to your grave—a treasure which the world loses by seeking and keeping worldly trash. You shall be a thousand times richer under the earth than the worldling was above the earth. Despise the things you will not need when you are dead; and what you will need when you are dead, ask of God, so that He may provide them to you.

</margin>

### CHAP. 25. Insatiable Avarice.

<margin>
Matthew 6:33.

<margin>
Care: lawful and unlawful.
</margin>
Care <note>The author uses "care" to mean anxiety or intense worry.</note> is an immoderate preoccupation in seeking temporal things as our only goal, and beyond the limits of the necessity of our present life. If it is great, it is accompanied by fear, sorrow, and distrust; if it is small, it is joined with a false sense of security. In three respects, care is unlawful:
1. When temporal things are chiefly sought.
2. When the care of them tears the heart apart—from itself, from God, and from heavenly things.
<margin>
Anxiety <note>original Greek: Μέριμνα</note>
</margin>
3. When in seeking them, God is distrusted and the lack of necessary things is feared. Otherwise, care is lawful: when the purpose and the outcome are entrusted to God, and the ordinary, lawful means are diligently and well used.

<margin>
Romans 12:11, 2 Corinthians 7:12.
</margin>

Frugality <note>original Greek: Περίοια</note>. Luke 11:42, 1 Timothy 5:8.
</margin>
Godliness and frugality are the remedies for avarice; they go very well together. It is a lawful thing to use foresight and provision. *If there is anyone who does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an infidel,* so that they may have enough for themselves and may discharge that natural duty that the stork has taught man <note>Naturalists in the 17th century believed storks were uniquely dedicated to caring for their aging parents, a virtue called *antipelargosis*.</note>. Other remedies.
</margin>
If you are one of God's people, it becomes you to be without avarice. It is a great degradation <note>original: "deiection"</note> of the mind to tie the soul, created according to God’s image, to the world. The soul is worth more than all the world. All those secular riches can neither be true riches, nor truly yours. It is only grace that makes a person perpetually and properly rich. Be rich in God. Lay up treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:19). It is no profit to win the whole world and lose the soul. He who walks contentedly and without avarice shall dwell on high.

Luke 12:21, Matthew 6:19, Mark 8:36, Isaiah 33:15.

# C H A P. XXVI.

## The Tympany of Pride.

> 1 Cor. 4:18. *Some are puffed up.*
> Jam. 4:6. 1 Pet. 5:5. *God resists the proud.*

### Description.

<margin>
Pride called a Tympany <note>A "tympany" is an old medical term for a swelling of the abdomen that sounds like a drum when tapped; the author uses it here as a metaphor for an inflated ego.</note>.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial P with floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>Pride may be justly called a Tympany, not only because it is empty and sounds like a drum—and is like that worst sort of dropsy <note>original: "dropsie," an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid</note> called *Tympanites*—but also because it is an inflation and swelling of the mind. The proud man is aptly called high-minded, or one who has a high heart; for pride is like a vapor, ascending high, and then immediately vanishing away in smoke.

<margin>
1 Cor. 4:8, 18.
Puffing up <note>original Greek: φυσίωσις</note>. or
2 Cor. 12:20.
2 Tim. 3:4.
Swelling in mind <note>original Latin: Tumens animo</note>.
Psalm 101:5.
Description.
</margin>
It is an immoderate desire for dignity, power, honor, reputation <note>original: "estimation"</note>, and excellence: under which are comprised all ambition, vainglory, boasting, and arrogance.

<margin>
Manifest pride.
Covered pride.
</margin>
Pride is either manifest or covered. Manifest pride is that which is obvious and can be seen by everyone. But covered pride is more difficult to perceive because it is hidden behind humility, poverty, humanity, civility, honesty, or nobility: many make these things a pretext <note>An excuse or outward appearance used to hide a different reality.</note> for their more secret pride. Again, pride may be either
