<margin>
Glorious pride.
Base pride.
Pride under humble clothing.
</margin>
...is either called glorious <note>In this context, "glorious" refers to ostentatious boasting or vanity.</note> or base. *Socrates*, when he beheld *Antisthenes* the *Cynic* showing everyone the tear in his cloak, said: "Through the rift in your cloak, I behold your vanity." By this, he declared that pride disguised as ragged clothing was more offensive than the pride of wearing gorgeous apparel.

<margin>
Diogenes Laertius, Book 6.
Examples of both.
</margin>
The pride that exists under filthy clothing is viler than that which is covered with silks. *Plato* was proper and clean in his apparel, but *Diogenes* was filthy. Diogenes once trampled upon *Plato's* carpets and cushions, saying: "I trample upon *Plato's* pride." To which *Plato* quickly replied: "You trample indeed upon my pride, but with another kind of pride."

<margin>
Pride under humility.
</margin>
It happens, marvelously enough, that the human mind is more proud of false humility than if it were openly proud. It is a most distorted pride that lurks under signs of humility. Vile vices strangely hide under the appearance and shadow of virtue.

<margin>
Other examples.
Pride under poverty.
Salaconian pride <note>original Latin: Salaconia superbia; a reference to a type of ostentatious boasting named after the character Salacon.</note>.
Pride under courtesy <note>original: "humanity."</note>.
2 Samuel 15:5, 6.
</margin>
*Diogenes*, when he saw *Olympias* and her company gorgeously dressed, said with a laugh, "This is nothing but pride." When he later saw the *Lacedemonians* <note>The Spartans, famous for their austere and simple lifestyle.</note> dressed in dirty and lowly clothes, he said, "This is but another kind of pride." *Salacon*, though a poor man, was as proud as if he had been extremely wealthy. *Absalom*, in the midst of his greatest ambition—conspiring against his father and aspiring to his crown—was both humble and courteous, and so stole the hearts of the people.

<margin>
Arrogance.
Vanity <note>original Greek: χαυνότης.</note>.
Vainglory <note>original Greek: κενοδοξία.</note>.
Philippians 2:3.
Galatians 5:26.
</margin>
Arrogance is one of the worst sorts of pride, by which a man vaingloriously exalts himself above his merit to be thought better than he is. It is rightly called a "fungosity" <note>A spongy, air-filled swelling.</note> or a swelling up with wind. He thinks he has the thing that he does not have; or if he has it, he thinks he has more of it than he does; or he thinks he has it of himself, or by his own merits; or that he alone has it, or that he is to have it forever.

<margin>
Pride against God.
</margin>
The highest degree of pride is that which is directed against God, defiantly opposing Him, as *Pharaoh* did...

<margin>
Differences.
</margin>
Many people cannot recognize their own pride, let alone the pride of others. For there are many who seem to be humble and yet are very proud, and there are many who appear to be proud and yet are truly humble. It is most appropriate, therefore, to set down the differences between pride, modesty, and stateliness, as well as the contrary extreme, baseness. The main question concerns honor and reputation: how far should it be sought, or how far should it be neglected? What is the golden mean <note>The ideal moderate position between two extremes.</note>, and what are the extremes?

<margin>
Love of honor <note>original Greek: φιλοτιμία</note>.
Philippians 4:8.
Magnificence <note>original Greek: Μεγαλοπρέπεια</note>.
Magnanimity <note>original Greek: Μεγαλοψυχία</note>.
Aristotle, book 2, chapter 7.
Pride differs from modesty and honesty.
</margin>
There is a lawful desire for honor. If it concerns smaller degrees of honor, it is called *modesty*. If it concerns greater and higher degrees, it is called *magnificence*, or *magnanimity*, *stateliness*, or *nobility*.

<margin>
Romans 12:16.
Philippians 2:3.
1 Peter 5:5.
</margin>
Modesty is a virtue by which we desire, acquire, and maintain a good name, a sufficient reputation, or moderate honors, and we do so lawfully, appropriately, contentedly, and decently. (Here we use the word *modesty* somewhat more strictly, referring to the virtue that moderates the appetite for honor.) *Humility* is modesty's sister, by which we desire no greater honors or reputation than we either deserve or can conveniently obtain; and it is when we prefer ourselves to no one, but rather make ourselves equal to those of a lower status. Pride and ambition, as vices of excess, are opposed to modesty. And *baseness* <note>original: "Baseness"; here meaning a lack of proper self-regard or a total neglect of one's reputation.</note>, or the neglect of fame and proper reputation, is likewise its opposite in deficiency.

<margin>
Indifference to honor <note>original Greek: Ἀφιλοτιμία</note>.
Pride differs from stateliness.
Aristotle, Ethics, book 4, chapter 4.
Greatness of mind <note>original Latin: Magnitudo animi</note>. Cicero.
</margin>
As for *magnificence* or *magnanimity*, it is a lawful desire for great honors due to our virtues, together with an honorable acceptance and preservation of them. This virtue requires a mind that is great, and a heart that is...

...is full of spirit. Here the word *Magnanimity* is not used (as it sometimes is) to mean *generosity, patience, or fortitude*.

<margin>
The properties of true stateliness and magnanimity.
Nobility and goodness <note>original Greek: Καλαγαθία</note>.
Greatness in danger <note>original Greek: Μεγαλοκίνδυνος</note>.
Aristotle, Ethics.
</margin>
There is nothing more similar to pride than this virtue, and yet they are clearly distinguished. For he who is endowed with this virtue seeks honors that are truly great, yet lawful. He seeks to be honored by men who are truly great and good. He does not care about the slanders of the unworthy and thinks just as little of their opinion of him. He strives to possess all virtues and to be a person of absolute and complete integrity. He is moderate, generous, content, thankful, just, dignified, kind, slow to start a task, and even slower to finish it—being deliberate. He is strong in both good and bad fortune, strong and bold in dangers, and honest in expressing both his love and his hatred.

<margin>
Vanity <note>original Greek: Χαυνότης</note>.
Pride <note>original Latin: Fastus</note>.
Pettiness <note>original Greek: Μικροπρέπεια</note>.
Baseness.
</margin>
He is neither vengeful, nor a hypocrite, nor irritable, nor a flatterer. He is not a meddler, nor an excessive admirer of others, and he envies no one. His pace is slow, and his voice is dignified, stable, quiet, and constant. His temperament is a perfect mixture of "blood" and "melancholy" <note>In the medicine of the time, this refers to a balanced "sanguine" and "melancholic" personality</note>, without any irritable or sluggish dominance <note>original: bilious or phlegmatic</note>. It is a most difficult virtue, which may easily degenerate into pride. Yet it agrees very well with Christian humility; the very same man can be both politically stately and Christianly humble. One may magnificently maintain his dignity in an honorable position (especially in the office of a magistrate), and yet before God and his own conscience, he may be lowly, cast down, and humbled, and may "lick the dust" in God's presence. He may most humbly mourn his sins and acknowledge himself to be but earth and a most miserable worm, and not a man. Opposed to this noble virtue in excess is ambition or pride, by which we judge ourselves more worthy of honor than we actually are. Opposed to it in deficiency are baseness and the neglect of one's reputation, as has been said.

<page-num>396</page-num>
<header>CHAP. 26. The Swelling <note>original: Tympany; a medical term for a swelling or bloating, often used as a metaphor for being "puffed up" with pride</note> of Pride.</header>

->The Part Affected<-

<margin>
Desire.
1 John 2:16.
Pride is composed of six other emotions <note>original: affections</note>.
</margin>
Pride has the emotion of desire for its primary seat: for all that is in this world is as *the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life*. But because it is a complex evil, it also usurps a place in other emotions. For a person who is proud and ambitious hates and fears being considered lowly <note>original: base</note>. He envies that others should equal him; he is jealous of everyone. He likewise rejoices in the object and direction of his pride. He hopes and trusts confidently that he will reach his highest peak <note>original: Zenith</note>, to which he has most slavishly addicted both his heart and mind: the one to devise and approve all that he does or intends, and the other to choose those actions.

---

->Causes<-

<margin>
God.
Satan.
</margin>
The two universal and external causes of pride (which are common to all other sicknesses of the soul) are: first, God, a most just "deficient cause" <note>A theological term meaning that God causes the outcome not by direct action, but by justly withdrawing his grace and leaving a person to their own fallen nature</note>, leaving many to themselves; and second, Satan, who, as his own first sin was pride, never ceases to infect everyone with that same poison.

<margin>
Prosperity.
Isaiah 9:9–10.
Isaiah 28:1, 3.
Hosea 13:6.
Psalm 30:6–7.
Augustine, Sermon 31.
*Vice is common in prosperous circumstances.*
<note>original Latin: Vitium rebus solemne secundis</note>
Claudian, *On the Second Consulship of Stilicho*.
</margin>
Prosperity promotes pride, and pride feeds upon prosperity so that it may grow even prouder. *Ephraim and Samaria, in the pride and presumption of their hearts, said, "The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild it again with dressed stones."* Ephraim’s drunkenness in prosperity gave birth to the *crown of pride*. *They were filled, and their hearts were exalted.* *In my prosperity,* said David, *I shall never be moved.* Pride is the worm that breeds in riches; it is difficult for a rich man not to be proud, for pride is the vice of prosperity. When the heart is lifted up to its height (Ezekiel 31:10), a delusional hope that prosperity will last forever exalts pride (Isaiah 47:7). If beauty, strength, or any of nature’s or art’s gifts are also present, pride raises itself even higher.

<summary>This page analyzes the psychological structure of pride as a "compound evil" rooted in desire and identifies its primary causes as spiritual (God's withdrawal and Satan's influence) and material (prosperity and personal talents).</summary>

--- Page 415 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of pride, moving from its external causes (God and Satan) to the internal psychological triggers: comparing oneself to others, the role of self-opinion, and innate human corruption.</meta>

<page-num>397</page-num>
<header>CHAP. 26. The Swelling <note>original: Tympany; a medical term for a swelling or bloating, often used as a metaphor for being "puffed up" with pride</note> of Pride.</header>

<margin>
Comparing with others.
</margin>
Many compare themselves with others whom they consider worse than themselves, just as the proud Pharisee did with the humble tax collector <note>original: Publican</note>. Such a person thinks himself superior to another, whereas the other may actually be superior to him in many ways. He is not careful to examine what he lacks, but only what he has, and he triumphs over his own qualities as if no one else could match him. He is ignorant of his neighbor, but far more ignorant of himself.

<margin>
Madness of mind and opinion.
To think oneself to be something when one is nothing. <note>original Greek: Δοκεῖν εἶναί τι, μηδὲν ὤν</note>
Galatians 6:3.
1 Timothy 3:6.
1 Corinthians 8:1.
Boastfulness. <note>original Greek: Ἀλαζονεία</note>
Evil boasting. <note>original Greek: Καύχησις πονηρά</note>
James 4:16.
</margin>
One's own opinion gives birth to pride; great ambition proceeds from the opinion of an evil man. To seem to yourself to be something important is the very ground of pride. Self-love and self-satisfaction <note>original: complacency</note> deceive many, making them imagine themselves to be more and better than they are in reality, and to be greater in their own eyes than they are in the eyes of God or man. A young scholar is easily puffed up. The source of all pride is lying, gilded over with a coloring of truth. Ambition, like a wily serpent, creeps into the mind through a small hole; its mother is presumption. We imagine we have virtues that we actually lack, or we think we have them in a greater measure than we truly do. From this are born Pride's two daughters: **ostentation** before others (through writing, gestures, clothing, and when we speak too much good of ourselves) and **boasting** within ourselves.

<margin>
Innate corruption.
Erasmus, *Apophthegms*.
Mark 7:21, 22.
2 Corinthians 12:7.
Psalm 30:6, 7.
</margin>
Innate corruption <note>original: Natiue corruption; the theological concept of "original sin" or the fallen nature of humanity</note> is the closest and most direct cause of pride. It was the first sin in heaven, the first sin in Paradise, and the first sin that springs up within us. Even the greatest moralist cannot be free from it. *Socrates*, refusing to receive the magnificent gifts of the proud *Alcibiades*, said, "He sends these gifts out of ambition, and it is our own ambition to refuse them." In this way, everyone has their own inborn pride. Christ said, *From within, even out of the heart, proceeds pride.* Even the saints are hardly free of it, which gives rise to pride over one's own good deeds, marring the face of innocence and staining them with secret hypocrisy.

->Signs and Symptoms.<-

Pride buds (Ezekiel 7:10) and testifies to the face: a high heart has a proud look. It presents a grand appearance and a large shadow, but is lacking an honest mind—like a portrait of Hercules drawn upon the sands. The proud person pretends to be strict <note>original: precise; often referring to Puritan-like religious rigor</note> and plays the hypocrite in all respects. For his worst wine, he provides the fairest garland <note>This refers to the practice of hanging a garland outside a tavern to advertise wine; here it means using a beautiful exterior to hide a poor interior</note>. He is the imitator <note>original: Ape</note> of virtue and religion. He counterfeits gravity, modesty, and magnificence, but only in some external and ridiculous gesture, voice, and display. He is a fool who provides sport for wise men.

<margin>
Self-satisfaction <note>original: Complacency</note>.
</margin>
He delights in his own trifles, like the fisherman in *Theocritus* <note>A reference to Theocritus's Idyll 21, where a fisherman dreams of catching a golden fish</note> who satisfied his hunger with dreams of gold. He is full of self-satisfaction and self-opinion. He wants everything he does to be free from criticism. He excuses or lessens his own faults and lays the weight of them on everyone else. He thinks no one is able to match him—like *Zeuxis* <note>original: Zeuxes</note>, who, when he had finished the picture of *Atalanta*, admired his own work and wrote under it: *It is easier for painters to envy than to imitate what I have done.* <note>original Latin: "Invisere aliquis facilius quam imitari possit"</note>. He is like the peacock, glorying in his own feathers, and like a bubble of water, puffed up by the wind; or like an empty vessel—the emptier it is, the more noise it makes. He is mounted upon his own conceits and thinks, like *Antiochus*, that he is able to sail on the earth and walk on the seas. His attempts are beyond his power and status.

<margin>
Discontentment.
A seductive solicitor for dignities. <note>original Latin: Blanda conciliatricula dignitatum. Ambrose, Commentary on Luke, Book 3.</note>
</margin>
His spirit is ever stirring and unquiet. It is never settled nor content; it is always aspiring to a higher altitude. His ambition is a flattering solicitor for honors. *Alexander* answered the ambassadors of *Darius* (who pleaded for peace and offered his daughter in marriage) that *the heavens could not permit two suns, and the earth could not permit two Alexanders.* His heart was insatiable; when he heard the philosopher *Anaxarchus* speak, by the authority of...

<margin>

Bernard.

Pride is most difficult to cure, and especially when one is hardened in pride, as was King Nebuchadnezzar. Youth is more subject to it than the elderly. It is hard to humble the proud through power, and even harder through advice. For pride is a foolish evil, a secret venom, a hidden plague, a deviser of fraud, the mother of hypocrisy, the parent of envy, the moth of holiness, and the blinder of hearts; it produces diseases out of remedies and begets grief out of medicine.

Augustine, in his *Epistle*.
The element of evils <note>original: Elementum malorum</note>.

Pride was one of the mother sins of Sodom. The proud man is forsaken by God; he grows determined in wickedness. Jugurtha killed Hiempsal and Adherbal <note>original: Aherbal</note>, his brothers, so that he alone might be King of Numidia. Abimelech killed his seventy brothers all at once, so that he might be King of Israel. At first, in the Church, *devotion birthed wealth*; however, the daughter choked the mother and ate through her like a viper, and fathered the monster *Ambition* (a cursed offspring of a bastard mother), who in the end devoured her grandmother, *Religion*. Pride is the beginning, the end, and the cause of all evils. Avarice and ambition are the primary elements of evil. What wars has that insatiable lust for dominion kindled? Alexander the Great in Asia, Cyrus in Ionia. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> rose against the Athenians; they in turn against the Corinthians. The Carthaginians fought against the Romans. The Romans fought against all nations, and at last against their own kin <note>original: bowels</note>.

Ambrose on Luke, book 3.
Bernard, *On Consideration*, book 3.

</margin>

His mind frets; the desire for high rank is a rust <note>original: cankerredneſſe; likely referring to the Latin 'aerugo' (rust/corrosion) in the margin</note> to the mind. The more gold pride eats, the more blood it drinks; and the higher it climbs over other men's heads, the sooner it breaks its own neck. His pride shall deceive him, even if he dwells in the clefts of the rocks—he whose habitation is high and says, "Who shall bring me down to the ground?" Though he exalts himself like the eagle and makes his nest among the stars, God will bring him down from there. *God resists the proud*, and those who walk in pride He will humble, just as King *Uzziah’s* heart was lifted up to his own destruction.

### *Curation and remedies.*

<margin>
Occasions to be shunned.
</margin>
When external occasions are the chief causes for the heart to become proud, they should either be avoided or the mind should be diverted from them. *Plato* once mounted his horse and, judging himself to be a little moved by pride, immediately climbed down from his horse, lest he should be overtaken by loftiness <note>haughtiness or arrogance</note> while riding.

Know yourself.
Why should man be proud, whose conception is sin, whose birth is pain, whose life is labor, and whose death is inevitable? <note>original: "Vnde superbit homo, cuius conceptio culpa, nasci pœna, labor vita, neceſſe mori?"</note>

Consider what foul waste leaves your mouth, your nose, and the rest of the passages of your body, and you will see there is no more disgusting dunghill than your body is. Consider where you come from and be ashamed; where you are and lament; where you are going and be afraid. For what reason should a man be proud, whose conception is sin, his birth a pain, his life a labor, and his death a necessity?

When King Philip [of Macedon] boasted so much of his victories, Archidamus (the son of Agesilaus) wrote to him, saying that if he measured his shadow now after his victory, he would find it no larger than it was before, when he had been defeated.

Remorse for sin.
From the poisonous foam of dragons, the Bezoar <note>original: "Bezoardicum"; a stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, believed in early medicine to be an antidote to poison</note> is made; and thus chemists create the greatest remedy <note>original: "alexiterium"; a medicine used to ward off infection or poison</note> from the strongest poison.

Mix the sense and sorrow of them with your pride. Let the peacock’s tail be lowered at the sight of its black feet. Let the white swan look at its black legs. Consider what guilt and filthiness are within, and what a vile carcass your body is compared to all other animals. Your best qualities are far too lowly; they are not pure but mixed with many impurities. A single wasp is enough to poison a whole jar of preserves. Your sins and vices are pure and absolute evils, made worse by many evil circumstances.

</margin>

## CHAP. XXVII.
### The passion of Joy.
---

> Proverbs 14:13. *Even in laughing the heart is sorrowful, and the end of that mirth is heaviness.*

#### Description.

<margin>
Etymology: *Chara* <note>original: "χαρα"</note> because of the state and nature of the soul. It comes from *cheo* <note>original: "χεω"</note> (to pour) and *reo* <note>original: "ρεω"</note> (to flow).
</margin>
In joy, the heart, in a sense, runs out; and through the enlarged passages, the cordial spirits <note>In early modern medicine, "spirits" were thin fluids believed to carry life and emotion through the body</note> are poured out <note>original: "effunded"</note>. Because of this, sudden astonishment and even death sometimes follow.

<margin>
Description.
2 Corinthians 6:11.
Psalm 89:16.
</margin>
Joy is an emotion <note>original: "affection"</note> of the heart, arising from the perception <note>original: "opinion"</note> of some present or future good. In all joy, the heart is enlarged and lifted up.

<margin>
Joy internal, external.
</margin>
Joy is either internal and hidden, which does not appear, or else external, which appears in one's gestures, facial expression, laughter, or otherwise. Joy, again, is distinguished according to the diversity of its object. It is either for some good to ourselves, or for some good to our friends, or for some evil to our enemies.
<margin>
Joy <note>original: "χαρα"</note>.
Schadenfreude <note>original: "ἐπιχαιρεκακια"; joy at the misfortune of others</note>.
Job 31:29.
</margin>

<margin>
Joy natural, spiritual.
</margin>
Joy, in respect to those who rejoice and their manner of rejoicing, is either natural or spiritual. Natural joy is common and is either lawful or unlawful. Unlawful joys are either those that arise only from the pleasure of God's gifts, or from the pleasure of sin. Joy arising from God's gifts—such as food and drink, men or women, the subjection of spirits, the destruction of our enemies, or plea-
<margin>
Psalm 4:6, 7.
1 Corinthians 3:21.
Luke 10:20.
</margin>

<summary>This page defines joy as a physical and emotional expansion of the heart and begins categorizing joy into types, such as internal/external and natural/spiritual. It also warns that excessive joy can lead to physical shock or even death by over-extending the body's "spirits."</summary>

#### Causes.

<margin>

</margin>
There is no joy except in the attainment <note>original: "fruition"</note> of that thing which is enjoyed. Joy is the fulfillment <note>original: "expletion"</note> of love and desire for something that is esteemed to be good. In this, there are three things required:
1. A delighting good.
2. A union with it.
3. A knowledge and a feeling of that union.

<margin>

Euripides.
Proverbs 27:7.
Nature is always in a state of flux <note>original Latin: "Natura semper est in fluxu"</note>.
</margin>
The change of all things is delightful. We cannot stay but one day in one state. Nature delights to wander from vanity to vanity (as *Eve* did among the trees); what it has, it loathes; what sweetness it finds, it desires to change so that it may find more. It passes from pleasure to pleasure, seeking some complete pleasure—like one who reads a line and then goes to another line, and so forth, so that he may know the whole of what is written.

<margin>
Whatever is excessive is unpleasant <note>original Latin: "Quicquid nimium, iniucundum est"</note>.
</margin>
To look long upon one pleasant color dazzles the eyes; so the long enjoyment of one joy wearies the mind until it finds a new one. New objects, changed often with rarities, ravish the heart. Too much of anything is loathed.

Prosperity is one of the greatest captivators <note>original: "ravishers"</note> of the heart with joy; yet if it is sudden, it astonishes. If it is lingering and hardly attained or retained, the resulting anxiety counteracts the delight. Wealth always affords much opportunity for indulgence in wantonness. As the rich man <note>original: "Dives," the Latin word for "rich man" used as a proper name in the Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus</note> said to his *soul*, *“You have many goods laid up for many years; live at ease, eat, drink, and take your pastime.”* In such a state, no sinful joy is spared. *“It is a pastime to a fool to do wickedly,”* for he rejoices in doing evil.

<margin>
Calamity of enemies.
"That it is the mark of a lowly mind to exult in the misfortunes of others." <note>original Latin: "Quod abiecti esset animi, malis exultare alienis."</note> Suetonius.
</margin>
Calamity befalling our enemies, or those we hate, breeds joy in the heart. This is not because any evil can simply, or by its own nature, create joy, but as a consequence of our own self-love; we delight in that which benefits ourselves through the overthrow of our enemies. This is a most wretched and vile kind of joy, and is only found in weak and base spirits. For example, Phocion <note>An Athenian statesman and general (c. 402–c. 318 BC)</note> forbade the Athenians from offering sacrifices of celebration at the glad news of the death of their enemy, Philip of Macedon.

A jovial temperament <note>original: "complexion"</note>.
Prov. 15:21.
</margin>
A plethoric <note>meaning an overabundance of blood, according to the medical theory of the four humors</note> and jovial temperament <note>original: "complexion"</note>—characterized by healthy blood and a balance of all the bodily humors, along with a weaker wit and a stronger body—causes too much carnal joy by allowing insolent sensuality to predominate. When the body affects the mind in this way, and if outward temptations and inward, unbridled affections coincide without the restraint of reason or grace, the mirth of the mind becomes even more frantic. For *“foolishness is joy to him who is destitute of understanding.”*

<margin>

By a wound.
Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 3, Chapter 10.

Laughter proceeds from sudden delight <note>original: "delectation"</note>. It is the motion of the mouth and breast caused by the diaphragm <note>original: "midriff"</note>. The thing that moves this mirth must be recent, stirring up some wonder <note>original: "admiration"</note> and constricting the heart through some sudden suspense; immediately, the heart is enlarged again by delight. Through a certain struggle <note>original: "colluctation"</note> between the constricting and the expanding of the heart, the muscles of the breast and cheeks are moved with a specific vibration. So it is that when someone is wounded in certain parts near the heart, and those parts touch the diaphragm <note>original: "midriffe"</note>—causing them to twitch <note>original: "palpitation"</note>—the person will die laughing. Affected laughter is not natural; it is only in the mouth and not in the heart. Sardonic laughter is interpreted as either faked or deadly. For instance, when the elderly of Sardinia <note>original: "Sardon"</note> (those over seventy years old) were sacrificed to Saturn, they died laughing, scorning death and expecting a better life. Or it is so called from the Sardinian herb <note>original: "herbe Sardoa or Sardinia"</note>; if anyone eats it, they die looking as if they are laughing. Sanguine people <note>original: "Sanguinians"; those characterized by a cheerful, active temperament in the system of the four humors</note> are the quickest to laugh, but those with a melancholy temperament <note>original: "melancholians"</note> are slower to start and slower to stop.

## Curation and remedies.

<margin>
Spiritual joy, which is from God.
</margin>
Nothing is as well-suited to banish sinful joy and to temper all immoderate, natural, and sensual joys as that *spiritual joy* which is from God (Romans 15:13; 2 Corinthians 1:3; Isaiah 9:3). It is wrought in the heart by the Spirit (Romans 14:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:6 and 1:6; John 15:26). It belongs to those who seek the Lord (Psalm 105:3) and are upright in heart (Psalm 32:11), who "rejoice with trembling" (Psalm 2:11), and whose joy is furthered by the help of a minister <note>original: "miniſteriall helpe"</note> (2 Corinthians 1:24). It is joined with peace in believing (Romans 15:13). The Kingdom of God does not consist of food or drink, but of righteousness, peace, and this joy in the Holy Ghost (Romans 14:17), found in those who rejoice in serving God (Colossians 1:11).

<margin>In godly things</margin>
This spiritual joy must be focused on those things that pertain to God (Romans 15:17), such as God's holy name (Psalm 105:3; Isaiah 61:10; Philippians 4:4) and His mercy (Psalm 32:10, 11; 31:7; 89:16).

To see them agree (Philippians 2:2; 4:1; Acts 3:3 <note>Likely referring to unity in the early church</note>). And when all the land binds themselves to seek God by an oath (2 Chronicles 15:15), for the deliverance of the faithful (Psalm 35:27; Philippians 1:26). We should rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15; 2 Corinthians 2:3; 7:13). At a sinner's conversion, and when others believe (3 John 4 <note>original: "3. Ioh. 8. 4."</note>).

<margin>In God's gifts.</margin>
In all God's gifts (Deuteronomy 26:11) and all the works of His hands (Psalm 92:4) as so many tokens of His favor—and especially in His specific deliverances (Isaiah 9:3).

<margin>It must be both internal and external.</margin>
The joy of faith must be internal (Philippians 1:25; Romans 15:13; John 15:11; 17:13) and eternal (Hebrews 12:1 <note>This citation likely refers to the "joy set before" Christ mentioned in 12:2</note>; Matthew 25:21).

<margin>Use of this remedy.</margin>
This spiritual joy makes all other carnal and natural joys be esteemed as nothing (Galatians 6:14; Philippians 3:8; 1 Corinthians 7:30). The more one tastes of this heavenly joy, the more he detests all other joys.

<margin>Consider the following evils.</margin>
Consider all the evils that follow from sensual joy, as is described at greater length in the *Prognostics* <note>original: "Prognoſtickes"; likely a reference to a preceding section or a medical/theological diagnostic work</note>. Since we must necessarily be refreshed by some natural joys, so that they may be both more moderate and sanctified: let the conscience within and the life without correspond in goodness. For a good life makes all earthly joys good.
<margin>Ecclesiastes 3:12.</margin>

<margin>
Death (Ecclesiastes 11:8; 12:1).
</margin>
When you are either attempting or enjoying earthly delights, so that you may be sooner stopped and better tempered, remember death—and that all this life is but vanity. Think upon the Last Judgment. Let your mind be diverted to some other sorrowful subjects.

# CHAPTER XXVIII.

## The Passion of Gluttony.

->Philippians 3:19. *Whose God is their belly.*<-

### Description.

<margin>
Appetite is threefold:
Natural.
Animal.
Rational.
</margin>
Man's appetite is threefold. 1. Natural, which is shared with plants, by which it draws in nourishment without conscious thought. 2. Animal, which is shared with brute beasts, located in the brain and spread to other parts of the body; it feels a conscious desire for what it needs. 3. Rational, which is unique to man, desiring those things that are agreeable to reason; this is properly called *Will* <note>original: *Voluntas*</note>, just as the others may be called concupiscence <note>unregulated desire or lust</note>, or *pleasure* <note>original: *voluptas*</note>.

<margin>
Natural desire <note>original Greek: ἐπιθυμια φυσιχη (epithymia physike)</note>.
Common craving.
*Aristotle's Ethics, Book 3, Chapter 11.*
Gluttons/Belly-mad <note>original Greek: Γαϛρίμαργοι (gasterimargoi)</note>.
The same source as above.
Specific/Acquired craving.
Lovers of specific things <note>original Greek: φιλότοιοι (philotoioi)</note>.
</margin>
The craving <note>original: "lust"</note> for food <note>original: "meate"</note> is either more natural and common—where few people fail, except by taking too much—or the craving for food is more specific and acquired <note>original: "ascititious," meaning not innate but learned</note>, and more strangely stirred. This is seen in those who are lovers of specific things which they study and delight in, even when they are not necessary; or wanting more than others; or not as they should; or not for the right purpose. In this, there is an excess, not so much in the quantity of the food, as an excess in the quality, or rather a perversion of the vain appetite.

<margin>
Description of gluttony.
*Horace, Satires, 2.7.*
</margin>
Gluttony is an excessive desire for food, going beyond the limits of nature, whether it be in too great a quantity—*feasts sought without end* <note>original Latin: *Epulæ ſine fine petitæ*</note>—or in a vain variety:

### Part affected.

<margin>
Natural desire.
2 Peter 2:12.
Irrational natural beasts <note>original Greek: Ἄλογα ζωα φυσικά (aloga zoa physika)</note>.

The part affected is that common affection of natural concupiscence <note>strong desire or appetite</note> and desire, which is most focused on what agrees with the aspect of sensuality concerning food <note>original: "meate"</note>. If it is orderly and within measure—regarding both quantity and variety—it is natural and necessary. But if it exceeds these bounds, it is a passion that affects the soul. The seed-bed <note>original: "seminary"</note> and flame of it is founded in the stomach; it draws both the heart and the mind along with it, as if it were something very reasonable and worthily chosen. Those who are so corrupted yield themselves as slaves to the senses. The rational appetite is captured by the *animal* appetite. Those who are thus diseased are like irrational natural beasts.

<margin>
Satan.
Matthew 4:7.
1 Timothy 4:4.
1 Corinthians 8:10.
Revelation 2:20.
1 Samuel 14:32.
Acts 10:15.
Isaiah 5:20.
</margin>

He makes men think that what God calls lawful food is unlawful, and that what God calls unlawful is lawful (such as food sacrificed to idols). He causes some to believe that a lawful amount is unlawful, and that an unlawful amount is lawful—as "belly-gods" <note>those who make a god of their appetite</note> do. He pollutes what God has purified; he puts darkness for light, and light for darkness; he speaks good of evil, and evil of good.

Natural hunger.

And this moisture feeds upon the whole body; from its exhaustion <note>original: "exinanition," meaning a state of being emptied or weakened</note> and emptiness comes this natural hunger and desire for food. The lamp of life wastes the best sap and finest oil of our body. As the burning flame wastes the candle—which, if it is not supplied, soon comes to an end—so by this natural and imperceptible hunger, the veins suck the stomach until it is empty. <margin>

### Treatment and Remedies <note>original: "Curation and remedies"</note>

<margin>
Follow nature.

Seneca.
</margin>
Nature teaches moderation: she has given man a small mouth and a narrow throat. It is a shame to him that neither the earth, the sea, nor the heavens can satisfy it. And although the belly listens to no instructions <note>original: "heareth no precepts"</note>, being like an unthankful beast that only begs and seeks, it is not actually a demanding creditor. It will be content with very little, provided you give it what you *should* rather than all that you *could*. Satisfy nature, but do not overfill <note>original: "surfet"</note> it. As *Socrates* said to his friends at his modest supper: "If you are virtuous, this will be enough; if not, you are unworthy of it." You should eat only enough so that your strength is refreshed, not overwhelmed. You must eat to live, not live to eat. Satisfy your body only as much as is necessary for health.

<margin>
"One must eat to live, not live to eat." <note>original Latin: "Esse oportet ut vivas: non vivere ut edas"</note> Cicero, *Rhetoric*, Book 4.

Christian abstinence and the motivations for it.

Various kinds of abstinence.

Isaiah 58:8.
</margin>
Abstinence is an excellent virtue; it was the basis of the first law given in Paradise <note>referring to the restriction on eating the forbidden fruit</note>. It is the fuel for virtue and prayer. There are many types of abstinence: 
1. **Spiritual**, which is turning away from sin. 
2. **Medicinal**, involving a controlled diet for health. 
3. **Civil**, mandated by the King’s laws. 
4. **Gluttonous planning** <note>original: "Belly-wise"</note>, where one eats little now only so that much more may be eaten later. 
5. **Necessary abstinence**, found among the poor. 
6. **Miserly abstinence** <note>original: "Sordid and filthy"</note>, found in the greedy. 
7. **Hypocritical**, found in those who only pretend to be holy. 
8. **Christian**, proper to the born-again <note>original: "regenerate"</note>, who eat with a clean conscience and are moved to moderation because they partake in Christ.

<margin>
Jerome <note>original: "Hieron."</note>, in his *Letter to Paulinus*.
</margin>
He who eats that bread <note>the spiritual bread of Christ</note> is not obsessed with how much expensive food he turns into waste <note>original: "dung"</note>. Yet, just as eating should be moderate, so should abstinence. It is necessary to restrain your flesh, not to destroy <note>original: "extinguish"</note> it; to hold it back, not to crush it. This ensures that the body serves you and does not become unruly <note>original: "fierce"</note>—that it may be humbled rather than acting as the commander. Let the flesh be subject to the soul, and the soul to God. Let God command your reason; let reason command your soul; and let your soul command your body. Treat your soul like a King and your body like a donkey <note>original: "Ass"</note>. Give the body enough food so that it does not collapse, and give it a burden,

"Everything in excess is harmful; everything should be done in moderation." <note>original Latin: *Omne nocet nimium, mediocriter omne gerendum.*</note>
Plutarch, *Precepts of Health*.
Xenophon.
</margin>
Hunger is a fine seasoning <note>original: "pickle"</note>. A person who is full despises a honeycomb, but to a hungry soul, every bitter thing is sweet. *Socrates* mocked the gluttony of the Athenians with a similar saying: "The best cooks to make the finest appetizing sauces are these two proven recipes <note>original: "recall recipe’s"</note> of King *Alexander*: walking before daybreak and having a sparing dinner." The first serves as preparation for his dinner; the second as preparation for his supper. When *Ptolemy* <note>likely Ptolemy I Soter, a general under Alexander the Great</note> (who was almost starving during a journey) was given a morsel of bread, he thought nothing was more pleasant. The temperate man has a great advantage over the glutton. For through overeating, the glutton is made to loathe even the finest food, while the temperate man makes the worst food good and pleasant enough. Besides this, his temperance and strict diet digest many humors <note>term: humors: bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—once thought to determine a person's health and temperament</note>, cure many diseases, and prolong life. *Gorgias*, at 108 years old, was asked how he reached that age; he answered that he never ate nor drank for pleasure, but only for necessity. *Hippocrates’* counsel for the preservation of health was: let food, drink, sleep, and sex <note>original: "Venus"</note> all be moderate. "Do not overfill yourself with food, do not avoid labor, and preserve your vital substance: these three things are most healthy" <note>original Latin: *Non satiari cibo, non refugere laborem, feminis substantiam conservare: haec tria saluberrima sunt.*</note>. *Cyrus* said regarding his health: "I never sit down to the table unless I have an appetite; I never fill myself too full; what I have eaten, I digest well. This is why I am always healthy" <note>original Latin: *hinc est quod semper valeo*</note>. *Galen* lived a hundred and twenty years in health because he never rose from the table feeling full.

Musonius, *On Food*.
Suidas; Laertius, Book 2.

From him came the proverb, "More temperate than Zeno" <note>original Latin: *Zenone temperantior*</note>. Men before the Great Flood, for a period of 2,242 years, lived very temperately on the fruits of the ground, without any...

<margin>
Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, Chapter 6.

"They lived according to a strict diet." <note>original Latin: *Viuebant dieteticè.*</note>

Reading at Tables.
<term>Readers</term> <note>original Greek: *Ἀναγνῶσται* (Anagnostai)</note>.

1 Esdras 3:5.

Matthew 4.

Matthew 27.

...any use of wine or meat, which were introduced afterward. The Egyptian Kings fed only upon simple food; there was brought to their table only a heifer or a goose, together with a certain measure of wine. The Platonic, Pythagorean, and Diogenic suppers were frugal and learned; their provision was moderate and simple. They filled their minds more than their bellies; they did not take as much pleasure in the food as in the philosophical discourses. The next morning, they found neither headache nor indigestion <note>original: "cruditie of stomacke"</note>. To divert the mind further from the food, many great men had reading at their tables, as did *Pomponius Atticus* in Rome and *Carolus Magnus* <note>Charlemagne</note> the Emperor. This fashion thereafter came into monasteries and academies. Kings also used enigmatic questions and riddles at their tables, as *Darius* did in his great feast. Christ, the Prince of all the kings of the earth, who with one word multiplied the bread and the fishes, was himself the mirror of moderation. He permitted his disciples in his own presence to pluck the ears of grain <note>original: "corne"</note>, rub them with their hands, and eat them like beasts. He fasted forty days, and after such a great hemorrhage and loss of blood, and with such great pain in his greatest thirst, he was offered <note>original: "propined"</note> the bitterest drink. There is no bread so poor <note>original: "naughty"</note>, which will not become well-tasted if it is seasoned with a little of that vinegar that was given to Christ.

<margin>
Learn to detest this vice, and how.
</margin>
This more than beastly evil is in no way so well repressed as by a noble <note>original: "generous"</note> indignation conceived against the sin; this should be done either at leisure, as *Cicero* thought, or suddenly, as *Aristotle* thought. The outcome and end of this vice should be considered: what is eaten is, for the most part, filthily lost. Our bellies are the burials and graves of all other living creatures. One forest will suffice for many elephants, but both sea and land are not able to feed one man.

Instruction in the grace of God.
</margin>
Be instructed in the grace of God, which will teach you—

### CHAPTER XXIX.
## The Passion of Drunkenness.

->Ephesians 5:18. *Do not be drunk with wine, in which there is excess.*<-

---

->Description.<-

<margin>
Use of drink.
Titus 1:15.
1 Timothy 4:4, 5.
1 Timothy 5:23.
Proverbs 31:6.
Psalm 104:15.
John 2:7.
Nehemiah 8:10.
</margin>
Strong drink is the good creation <note>original: "creature" — here meaning anything created by God for human use</note> of God: pure to those who are pure. It serves:
1. **Naturally**, for the body’s nourishment and strength, to be used with sobriety.
2. **Medically** <note>original: "physically"</note>, for the strengthening <note>original: "corroboration"</note> of the body and the refreshing of the mind.
3. **Socially** <note>original: "civil"</note>, for the maintenance of friendship <note>original: "amity"</note> and as a sign of honest happiness.

<margin>
What drunkenness is.
Passion <note>original: Πάθος (Pathos) — meaning a disease or suffering</note>.
Drinking session <note>original: Πότος (Potos)</note>. 1 Peter 4:3.
Proverbs 23:30.
Isaiah 5:11.
Ephesians 5:18.
Luke 21:34.
Excessive wine-drinking <note>original: Οινοφλυγια (Oinophlygia) — literally "wine-swilling"</note>.
1 Peter 4:3.
</margin>
Drunkenness is not only when wine has banished wit (which may soon overtake a weak brain), but also when one sits for a long time at drink, even if their brain were ever so strong to bear it. Such a person *stays long at the wine, and goes and seeks mixed wine.* Drinking sessions are condemned just as much as stumbling drunkenness <note>original: "ebriety"</note>. Such drunkenness is called a boiling, a chafing, or a growing too hot with wine.

<margin>
Specific types.
Basil, *On Drunkenness*.
Augustine, *Sermons for the Times*, Sermon 131.
</margin>
Some delight to be drunk all alone; some provoke others to do the same. Some drink "by measure" (in which there is actually no measure). The drunkard says, "Match my drink" <note>original: "Do me reason" — a phrase used to challenge a companion to drink the same amount as a toast</note>, even though both his demand and the other’s agreement are completely without reason. All these types of people are affected by this malady and diseased with this vilest vice.

<summary>This page defines drunkenness as a "passion" or disease, distinguishing between the legitimate use of alcohol for health and social bonding and its abuse through long drinking sessions or peer pressure.</summary>
<keywords>drunkenness, sobriety, wine, Basil the Great, Augustine, Ephesians 5:18, temperance</keywords>

<header>CHAPTER 29. The passion of Drunkenness.</header>

->Part affected.<-

<margin>
Natural appetite.
Mark 7:21, 22, 23.
</margin>
The part affected is the same one that is affected in gluttony <note>original: "gulosity"</note>. And although both this and the other appear to be only external acts and vices, the hidden disease lies within, like a root in the heart from which they spring. Just as food <note>original: "meat"</note> is the object in the other vice, in this one it is drink—not that natural, common <note>original: "vulgar"</note>, or necessary drink brought forth for human use without human artifice, but that which intoxicates <note>original: "inebriates"</note>, whether it be wine, ale, beer, or similar drinks.

---

->Causes.<-

<margin>
Habit <note>original: "Custom"</note>.
Drunkenness arises from doubled lust <note>original: "Ebrietas geminata libidine surgit"</note>.
Ovid, *Metamorphoses*.
</margin>
Habit makes this disease contagious to many, for habit turns unnecessary excess into an urgent necessity. First, the drunkard drinks because of thirst, then for delight, at last for lack of restraint <note>original: "wantonness"</note>; and finally, without measure, driven by insatiable indulgence.

<margin>
Imitation.
Exodus 22:3.
Romans 12:2.
</margin>
Imitation bewitches the weak mind, which is easily drawn by the fashions of the crowd to do evil. Men conform themselves to the world and follow observed examples, such as those of Noah and Lot and others like them. However, an adulterer, murderer, or apostate might just as easily defend themselves using the examples of David and Peter <note>referring to their biblical moments of failure</note>.

<margin>
Drunkards.
Isaiah 56:12.
Habakkuk 2:15.
Proverbs 20:20.
1 Corinthians 5:11.
Ephesians 5:11.
</margin>
One drunkard causes another, saying: *Come, I will bring wine, and we will fill ourselves with strong drink; tomorrow shall be like today, and even more abundant.* The accused <note>original: "challenged"</note> drunkard claims that his companions forced him, using the phrase "either drink or depart" <note>original: ἢ πίθι ἢ ἄπι (Greek) / aut bibe aut abi (Latin)</note>, even though we are expressly forbidden from keeping company with drunkards and gluttons or having fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness.

<summary>This page argues that drunkenness is an internal disease of the heart fueled by intoxicants rather than natural thirst. It identifies habit and the social pressure to imitate others as the primary drivers of the vice.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER 29. The passion of Drunkenness.</header>

<margin>
A graceless heart.
</margin>
A graceless heart, turning the grace of God into wantonness <note>original: "wanton-neſſe"</note> and having a feeble and weak mind, allows sensuality to reign over reason and grace (Galatians 5:23; Jude 19 compared with verses 12, 16, 18). It is a corrupt and disorganized <note>original: "vncompoſed"</note> mind (1 Peter 4:2, 3 and 2:10, 12), filled with a false opinion of pleasure (2 Peter 2:13), foolishness (Ephesians 5:15, 17, 18; 1 Thessalonians 5:7), and a brutish, senseless blindness, like swine being fed for the slaughterhouse <note>original: "ſham-bles"</note>.

<margin>
Excuses.

Isaiah 5:22.
Ecclesiastes 10:17.
Plutarch.
</margin>
Drunkards (mad in their foolish conceit) forge for themselves imaginary excuses, thinking it lawful to drink as they please as long as they are not overcome by it. They do not consider that those who are "strong" enough to handle strong drink are cursed, or those who drink simply for the sake of drinking, or who attend drinking parties too often. They are (as Demosthenes said to King Philip) "sponges" who lack only a womb as wide as their unrestrained will to exceed the capacity of a barrel <note>original: "Caſke"</note>; in "overcoming" their drink, they themselves are overcome. Others think that drink is given by God not only for necessity but also for delight, believing they may indulge as they please. They do not consider that strong drink was given to man to cheer the heart and not to oppress it—to praise God for it, and not to offend Him.

<margin>
Hosea 2:15.
Drunkenness is not medicinal <note>original: "phyſicall"</note>.

"When the medicine is shameful, one should be ashamed to be cured" <note>original: "cùm turpis eſt medicina, ſanari pudeat"</note>.
</margin>
Some pretend that drunkenness is medicinal <note>original: "phyſicall"</note>; in this, they foolishly err, valuing the cause of a hundred illnesses as the medicine for one, and the poison of the soul as good medicine for the body. No physician of the body will recommend it, and no physician of the spirit will allow it.

---

->Signs and Symptoms.<-

<margin>
The character of a drunkard.
</margin>
A drunkard is like a leech that is always sucking and cannot be satisfied. His delight is in that wine which best satisfies all five senses, according to the word *Costa* <note>original: "Coſta." This was likely a mnemonic for the five qualities of wine: *Color, Odor, Sapor, Tactus, Auditus* (Color, Smell, Taste, Touch, Sound)</note>. When nature fails, he turns to artifice and skill <note>referring to the use of additives or complex recipes to stimulate a dulled palate</note>.

<summary>This page argues that drunkenness stems from a "graceless heart" and refutes common excuses, such as the idea that one can drink excessively without being "overcome" or that drunkenness can serve as a medical treatment.</summary>
<keywords>drunkenness, sensuality, Demosthenes, spiritual health, medical excuses, vices, five senses, Costa</keywords>

### Prognostics <note>The likely outcomes or symptoms of the condition</note>

<margin>
The drunkard's case.
Isaiah 5:11, 12.
</margin>
The drunkard is rarely cured; he finds his disease so pleasant and allows his malady to become habitual. He does not respect the work of the Lord, nor does he consider the works of His hands. He despises all corrections. <margin>Proverbs 23:35.</margin> *“They have stricken me,” he shall say, “but I was not sick; they have beaten me, but I did not know it. </margin>
Drunkenness is the mother of all vices. It is a faking fiend, a sweet poison, a pleasant sin. He who has it, does not have himself; he who commits it, does not just sin, but is altogether sin. In a state of drunkenness, *Alexander* <note>Alexander the Great</note> killed his friend *Clitus*; for which, when he was sober again, he attempted to kill himself. <margin>Proverbs 23:29, 31, 32.</margin> *To whom is woe? Although wine goes down pleasantly in the beginning, in the end it will bite like a serpent and hurt like a cockatrice <note>A mythical serpent said to kill with its breath or glance</note>.* It brings forth lust <note>original: "Venery"</note>. <margin>Jerome. Fomes libidinis."</note> Genesis 19:32. 2 Samuel 11:13.</margin> Never believe a drunken man to be chaste. ### *Treatment and remedies.*

<margin>
Caution.
</margin>
It is hard to cure a man who is addicted to drunkenness. It is difficult <note>original: "difficill"</note> to speak to the belly, which has no ears. It is folly to rebuke a drunken man. The best time to try to cure a drunkard is when the drink has left him.

<margin>
Plutarch, *Life of Cato the Elder*.
1 Samuel 25:36.
1 Samuel 25:37.
Avoid occasions.
</margin>
The occasions that lead to drunkenness should be avoided <note>original: "eschewed"</note>. *Lycurgus* <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>, to cure the people's drunkenness, ordered all the vines to be cut down; but he would have done better to have a well built in every vineyard, and in every cup to have "married a watery nymph to fiery Bacchus" <note>This is a poetic metaphor for diluting wine with water</note>. *Diogenes*, when he was pressured to drink excessively, poured the drink on the ground, saying, "If I drank all this, I would ruin myself rather than the liquor." The company of those who are afflicted with this "disease" should also be avoided.

<margin>
Consider the repulsive behavior of drunkards.
</margin>
The *Lacedemonians* (Spartans) scared their children away from drunkenness by showing them the repulsive behavior <note>original: "deformity"</note> of their drunken slaves. Considering the filthy manners of drunkards is a great protection <note>original: "preservative"</note> for an honest heart.

<margin>
Erasmus, *Apophthegmata*, Book 7.

### Description.

<margin>
Specific types:
Sexual assault <note>original: "Stuprum"</note>.

Adultery.
Incest <note>original: "Incestus"</note>.
</margin>
This is a rooted tree, growing up with many branches, such as: the deflowering of virgins; the ordinary abuse of the same concubine, which—when done once or seldom—is called *fornication*; and it is technically defined as sexual intercourse between two single persons <note>original: "soluticum soluta"</note>. If it is commonly practiced, it is called promiscuity <note>original: "scortation"</note>, or "whore-hunting." Adultery is when one or both of the parties are married; it is either single or double. Incest is when sexual intercourse occurs between parties who are within the prohibited degrees of blood relation <note>original: "consanguinity"</note> or relation by marriage <note>original: "affinity"</note>. As for other sorts of filthy lust that are against nature, they are unworthy even to be named.

</margin>

Almost all the emotions work together in forming and promoting lust: fear, sorrow, joy, anger, jealousy, trust, doubt, distrust, and others all conspire together (though in different ways) to kindle the sparks and increase the burning until it becomes a filthy flame. The reproductive <note>original: "generatiue"</note> spirits cause a bubbling up <note>original: "ebullition"</note>, which affects the physical senses and the imagination. The heart becomes so imprisoned by lust that no laws, reason, conscience, fear, or sense of honor <note>original: "honesty"</note> are able to restrain it.

->Treatment and remedies.<-

<margin>
Bad remedies.
Saran in the *Life of Perdiccas*.
Plutarch.
</margin>
The ancient non-Christian physicians skillfully analyzed this hidden disease, which they never noticed until they found it making the body waste away. *Hippocrates* observed *King Perdiccas* in a chronic sickness; after a long inquiry, he perceived that his wasting away arose from a mental disease <note>original: "spirituall disease"</note>, caused by the love he had for *Phila*, his father’s concubine. He suggested the cure was to arrange for *Phila* to meet with *Perdiccas*. *Erasistratus* the physician did the same with *Antiochus*, curing his lingering fever caused by his lust for *Stratonice*. And *Saluchus* did similarly by causing the father to give his wife to the son as a cure. These three physicians cured the body but killed the soul—a bad kind of healing. It would have been better if they had cured the lust itself first, so that the body might become healthy on its own. Evil should not have been done so that good might come of it; a Christian has many better ways to cure this passion.

<margin>
It wounds the conscience unto hell.

Jerome <note>original: "Hieron."</note> in his Letter to Salvinus.

"Not as they arrive, but as they depart" <note>original: "Non venientes, sed abeuntes"</note>.
"Pleasure bought with pain is harmful" <note>original: "Nocet empta dolore voluptas"</note>.

Committing it wounds the conscience and brings on God's wrath and all kinds of evils. The penance for it is too expensive for the pleasure it provides. That wound is to be avoided <note>original: "eschewed"</note> because it cannot be cured except with a salve of sorrow and grief. *Aristotle’s* advice was to look at pleasures not as they arrive with delight, but as they depart with pain. A thousand pleasures are not as perfect as one of those torments; but how much more do the torments of hell exceed them? There, for every single pleasure, there shall be a thousand torments—perfect, total, and final. Therefore, consider this beastly pleasure to be far too expensive, and shun the goods that are bought at such a high price. The memory of the burning fires of hell quenches the burning lust of sexual immorality <note>original: "luxurie"</note>.

# Chapter 31.

## The Leprosy of Ingratitude.

---

> 2 Timothy 3:2. *People shall be unthankful.*
> Luke 17:17. *Were there not ten lepers cleansed, but where are the nine?*

---

### Description.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop-cap "A" decorated with intricate scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>

As leprosy is a universal cancer <note>original: "Cancer (Canker)"</note> of the whole body, full of venom and infection <note>original: "contagion"</note>, arising from the foulest, darkest fluids <note>original: "putrid blackest humour"</note> of the body; so *ingratitude* is a universal sickness of the soul, proceeding from an inborn <note>original: "inbred"</note> and acquired corruption and a wicked <note>original: "vicious"</note> state <note>original: "constitution"</note> of the heart.

So that it may be better known, the opposite virtue of gratitude and thankfulness must be briefly touched upon.

<margin>
Benevolence.
Goodwill <note>original: "Ευνοια" (Eunoia)</note>. Aristotle.
Goodwill/Favor <note>original: "Ευδοκια" (Eudokia)</note>. Paul.
Beneficence.
Good deeds <note>original: "Ευεργεσια" (Euergesia)</note>.
</margin>

Benevolence is the parent of beneficence <note>the act of doing good</note>, and beneficence prompts another to feel gratitude. *Ingratitude* <note>original: "Ingratefulnesse"</note> receives the benefit, but disregards the generosity <note>original: "beneficence"</note> of the benefactor.

<margin>
The benefit.
A good deed or favor <note>original: "Ευεργετημα" (Euergetema)</note>.
</margin>

The benefit is the object of our desires. It may be taken from us, while the benefactor's generosity remains. Unforeseen events <note>original: "Accidents"</note> may rob us of the use of a gift, while the feeling of goodwill still maintains a connection <note>original: "relatiue subsisting"</note> in the mind. The benefit is only the impression <note>original: "print"</note> and...

<meta>catchword: character</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the concept of ingratitude as a "leprosy of the soul," defining it through its relationship to benevolence and beneficence. The author argues that while a physical gift may be lost, the goodwill of the giver should remain in the mind of the recipient.</summary>

<keywords>ingratitude, leprosy, benevolence, beneficence, Aristotle, Apostle Paul, gratitude, virtue, moral sickness</keywords>

--- Page 466 ---
<meta>This page continues the definition of beneficence (the act of doing good) as a remedy for or contrast to the "leprosy" of ingratitude. It transitions from describing the internal motivation (benevolence) to the external action (beneficence) and begins categorizing types of gifts.</meta>

<page-num>448</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 31. The Leprosy of Ingratitude.</header>

...character of the action of beneficence: and both of these are the streams from the fountain of benevolence.

<margin>Beneficence described.</margin>
**Beneficence** <term>the act of doing good or being charitable</term> is a willing effort in giving gifts to others for their benefit <note>original: "commoditie"</note>. Every instance of providing a benefit is not truly beneficence unless it comes from a willing mind. A stone, a beast, the earth, the sea, or even an enemy may provide benefits by chance; but they cannot be said to possess or practice beneficence. One person might profit another ignorantly or unwillingly, but that is to be considered neither a benefit nor beneficence. It is not enough to have benefited someone unless it was done willingly.

<margin>
Worthy beneficence requires 5 things.
"Swift favor is sweeter" <note>original Greek: "Ωκεια χαρις γλυκερωτερη"</note>.
"Often what is given is small, but what follows from it is great." — Seneca <note>original: "Sæpè quod datur, exiguum : quod sequitur ex eo, magnum est"</note>.
</margin>
**Beneficence** is either *worthy* or *unworthy*. A worthy beneficence requires five things:
1.  **A cheerful giver.**
2.  **The choosing of a fit receiver**, who is either worthy or in need <note>original: "indigent"</note>.
3.  **A convenient time**: the more timely, the better. Swift benefits are sweet; he gives twice who gives quickly.
4.  **A convenient place**: public places are appropriate for an honorable beneficence, while a private place is most suitable when someone’s necessity or poverty is being helped.
5.  **A fit matter**, appropriate in regard to the giver. A princely gift fits the hand of a prince, not the hand of a poor man; the widow’s mite <note>a reference to the biblical story of the "widow's mite," where a small gift from a poor person is highly valued</note> suits the hand of a poor widow, not the hand of a king. The matter must also be appropriate for the receiver, for his good and for his use. A benefit may be of little worth in itself, but great in its use and consequence. Often the thing that is given is small, but the good which follows from it is great.

<margin>
Psalm 119:71.
"Cut and burn, so that you may heal." — Seneca, *On Benefits*, book 5, chapter 20 <note>original: "Secare, urere, ut sanes"</note>.
</margin>
**Beneficence** must always aim at its own proper end, which is the well-being <note>original: "utility"</note> of the receiver, even if the beginning of the benefit is painful. As David says: *It is good for me, O Lord, that you have afflicted me, that I may learn your statutes* <note>Psalm 119:71</note>. A surgeon may cut and burn so that he may heal.

1. **Naked**, meaning it lacks any good deed or effort to perform it, having only a profession of goodwill and nothing...

Even if the receiver currently desires the benefit and values it, if the giver knows it will actually harm him, his act of generosity is worth nothing. Instead, it is a "cruel kindness" or a "smooth and friendly hatred." In such a case, withholding the gift would be a greater benefit than bestowing it. For what could an enemy do more than to ensnare someone he hates with a gift?

In that case, the poison became a medicine and the hatred became a remedy. This is not to be considered an act of generosity, nor a true benefit,

...it is little different from an injury. All these ways of doing good are unworthy of the name of beneficence and of the name of a "benefit." Just as a dead man may be called a "man" in name only <note>original: "improperly"</note>, so these may be called "unworthy beneficence" and an "unworthy benefit," because they lack the willing intention of the giver regarding the good and usefulness of the receiver.

<margin>
The grounds of gratitude are truth and equity.
</margin>
Gratitude is provoked by the worthy kindness and worthy benefit of another, and these are the sparks that kindle that flame. It is grounded on **truth** <note>original: "verity"</note> and **equity**. **Truth** acknowledges and declares the benefit by giving thanks to the benefactor, by announcing the benefit before others as well, and by the promise and purpose to repay it according to one’s power. **Equity** strives to make compensation as far and as soon as is possible. Both of these obligate the heart to thankfulness. **Gratitude** has three degrees: 1. In the heart. 2. In word. 3. In deed. These shall be described more fully hereafter in the section on remedies.

As for **unthankfulness**: Some are ungrateful only in part; some are merely and altogether unthankful.

<margin>
Gratitude that is faked, forced, or restrained.
</margin>
<margin>
They give thanks secretly, in a corner, and in the ear. Seneca, *On Benefits*, book 2, chapter 23. <note>original Latin: "Furtiuè agunt gratias, in angulo, & in aurem"</note>
</margin>
Faked <note>original: "fained"</note>, restrained, and forced thankfulness is a kind of ungratefulness. Some pretend to be thankful while they have no such feeling in their heart. Some are ashamed to publish their thankfulness; if they utter it at all, it is privately in a corner and whispered in the ear. They blush at the thought that anyone should know they are obligated debtors.

<margin>
He who owes against his will is ungrateful. Seneca, *On Benefits*, book 5, chapter 39. <note>original Latin: "Qui inuitus debet, ingratus est"</note>
</margin>
Some are forced to be thankful by shame, fear, necessity, imitation, or circumstance. These are not truly thankful in their hearts. They find themselves bound to a duty which is against their will, and so they willingly remain ungrateful. Others, again, are purely unthankful: 1. He who does not acknowledge within himself the benefit and the greatness of it. 2. He who does not declare it before others, or who disguises or denies it.

<margin>An evil conscience.</margin>
Just as there is nothing more powerful to make a man both speak the truth and do what is most just than a good conscience, so there is nothing more capable of making him forgetful of his duty, so ready to hide <note>original: "dissemble"</note> the giver's generosity <note>original: "beneficence"</note>, and so unrighteous as to never repay a favor, than an evil conscience—one that is either blinded, sleeping, dead, or seared <note>original: "cauterized"; a reference to a conscience made insensitive by repeated sin.</note>.

<margin>Self-love.</margin>
<margin>2 Timothy 3:2.</margin>
When men are too lenient in judging themselves, overestimating their own worth <note>original: "merit"</note>, they think they have deserved more from the giver’s hand. They feel the giver has valued them at too cheap a price. The receiver thinks he might have gained more if his efforts and labors had been bestowed upon anyone else. The self-lover, as he loves no one as much as himself, cannot love his benefactor as he should.

<margin>Avarice (Greed).</margin>
Greed <note>original: "Avarice"</note> makes a man ungrateful. There is no satisfying his greedy appetite. The more he gets, the more discontented he becomes (unless he gets even more). And if he receives no more, he thinks all he has already gained is nothing. He forgets what he has and considers it an injury if anything he craves is withheld. Greediness for things desired makes us forget what we have already received, and avarice is always ungrateful.

<margin>Envy.</margin>
<margin>"No one can both envy and give thanks." <note>original Latin: "Non potest quisquam, invidere, & gratias agere."</note> Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book 3, Chapter 3.</margin>
Envy enters with her comparisons, feeling indignant that others should have been treated as equals or preferred over the receiver in the giving of gifts. Envy disturbs the receiver's heart with these comparisons. He who envies suffers sorrow, but the grateful person rejoices. No man can both envy another and give him thanks.

<margin>Pride.</margin>
Ambition and pride permit no one to be thankful. The proud man does not remember his own humble beginnings <note>original: "baseness"</note>; he does not consider his current status, improved by the gift, which he once desired most. He does not look at...

<margin>Corruption of nature.</margin>
By nature, we are more sensitive to evil than to good. The pain of one finger is felt more than the health of the whole body. And by the corruption of nature, injuries make a deeper impression on the mind than benefits do, and these benefits slip out of memory sooner than the injuries. We are so poisoned by the venom of the inherent "body of sin and death" <note>A reference to Romans 7:24, describing the fallen human condition.</note> that we devise and invent excuses for unthankfulness. Those who have a perverse disposition are neither overcome nor changed by kindness. As it is said of the wolf, though kindly fed with milk: a benefit cannot change its nature.
<margin>It is the mark of a perverse heart to search for excuses for ingratitude. <note>original Latin: "Perversi cordis est, occasiones ingratitudinis investigare."</note> Bernard.</margin>

He despises the bounty of God, like the Gentiles who knew God and yet were not thankful. He never thinks of God except in times of trouble. He has a trained memory for wrongs and can name them all as easily as Cyrus could name his soldiers <note>Cyrus the Great was famous for knowing the name of every soldier in his army.</note>.

<page-num>457</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 31. The Leprosy of Ingratitude.</header>

There is no worse thing than an ungrateful man. He is always either devising evil or doing evil. He flatters himself and disparages others. Just as he hates all men, he values his benefactor only for the benefit received. The worse he grows, the more bold he becomes to commit any vice. Ingratitude is a monstrous sin and the breeding ground <note>original: "seminary"</note> for many vices. There is no virtue that is not blamed or criticized by someone, except only gratitude; and there is no vice that someone will not commend, except only ungratefulness. There is no vice so condemned by everyone, and yet so widely embraced by many. Serpents contain venom within themselves, which they release to hurt others, but the ungrateful person is tormented by his own venom. Nothing is a greater enemy to peace <note>original: "concord"</note> and human society than ungratefulness. <margin>You have said everything if you have said a man is ungrateful <note>original: "Omnia dixeris, si ingratum dixeris."</note>. 2 Timothy 3:2.</margin> It is the epitome of all vices. It is a vice that increases daily. For in the last days, perilous times shall come, and men will be unthankful. A gentle nature may pardon any wrong except unthankfulness; it is hard to stomach <note>original: "hardly digested"</note>. The laws of Persia, Macedonia, and Athens condemned the ungrateful to death. <margin>Proverbs 17:13. Endeavor to be thankful, either in:
**Affection.**
</margin>
*Answer:* Thankfulness exists either in **affection**, in **profession**, or in **action**. Thankfulness in **affection** is when we heartily accept the benefit, heartily consider ourselves indebted for it, and heartily endeavor to make a recompense, even if power, opportunity, and the occasion to perform the deed fail us. A person may be a skilled craftsman and yet can do nothing for lack of tools, or for want of fit material and subject to work upon. Likewise, he is thankful who can do no more than be willing to be thankful.

He is thankful in his conscience; he has no other witness but himself. We must not think that an idle "wish" is thankfulness, but rather he who wills and **endeavors**. An endeavor is often better than a greater recompense. The will must be accepted for the deed—the affection for the action—in such a person who has sought out every opportunity for repaying the favor and could not find one.

</margin>
Thankfulness in **profession** is when we are not only thankful in our hearts (affection) but also make a public declaration of the benefit, commending and praising the giver, and promising and vowing to repay them according to our power.

# CHAPTER 31. The Leprosy of Ingratitude.

...repay what we should, or what we can. To whom, when, where, and how must be decided as discretion thinks it appropriate. If the heart's treasure is filled with true and mutual benevolence, the hand will not be empty of real, repaying generosity <note>original: "beneficence"</note>.

Therefore, it should be the care of one who would be truly thankful to be so in all these three ways. To be so in **action** alone, or in **profession** <note>that is, in words or declarations</note>, without the affection of the heart, is mere hypocrisy. To be so in **affection** only, when no more is in our power, is true thankfulness; for such a heart always cares to profess and perform as far as we are able.

<margin>
Thankfulness symbolically <note>original: "hieroglyphically"</note> described.
</margin>
The Ancients have depicted thanks, thankfulness, and mutual favors symbolically <note>original: "hieroglyphically"</note> through three sisters fathered by Jupiter, to show that being thankful and bountiful is a divine virtue that comes from God. They are called the *Charites* <note>original Greek: "χάριτες"</note> or *Graces* <note>original Latin: "Gratiæ"</note>, because giving, receiving, and repaying should be done with mutual joy. There are three of them to represent those three actions of giving, receiving, and repaying. One of them has her face turned away from us, representing the giver, who should forget his own gift. But the other two have their faces toward us, to show that the receiver should remember what he has received and remember to repay it. They are naked, showing that in generosity and thankfulness there should be no hypocrisy, but only simplicity and sincerity. They are joined together because there should be reciprocal love and harmony <note>original: "concord"</note> between the giver and the receiver. They are merry and smiling because there should be cheerfulness <note>original: "hilarity"</note> among them. And they are young virgins because the memory of a kind deed should never grow old.

## CHAPTER 32.
### The Poisonous Tongue.

> James 3:8. The tongue is full of deadly poison.

---

->Description.<-

<margin>
Epiglottis <note>the flap of cartilage at the root of the tongue, which is depressed during swallowing to cover the opening of the windpipe</note>.
</margin>
<margin>
A description of the tongue.
</margin>
<margin>
James 3:5.
</margin>
The top of the throat and its cover [the epiglottis] create and adjust the voice. However, the instrument used to shape and articulate words is the *Tongue*. It is the messenger of the mind, the reflection <note>original: "character"</note> of a man, the storehouse <note>original: "buttery," referring to a room where provisions were kept</note> of reason, the shaper of words, and the judge of tastes. And although it is a small fire, it can ignite a great forest <note>original: "matter"</note> and boast of great things. In its physical substance, it is small; yet it consists of almost as many parts as there are letters in the alphabet. It has a bony root, with glands <note>original: "kernels"</note> on both sides and a significant amount of fat. On its underside, it is tied with a ligament <note>original: "bond"</note>, like a rein on a horse, to control its movement and rapid speech <note>original: "volubility"</note>. It has two large veins to provide nourishment, along with two arteries to give it life. Two nerves spread throughout it: one serving for movement and the other for tasting. It consists of nine muscles, with four on each side to move it in every direction. The ninth muscle is in the middle of the other eight; its purpose is to extend the tongue's length and draw it back in again (two opposite motions, a function unique to this muscle among all others in the body).

The substance of the tongue is a muscular and fibrous flesh, and it is entirely covered on the outside with a membrane and a skin. *It is like the pen of a ready writer* <note>original: "swift writer," citing Psalm 45:1</note>; and, like an eel, it can turn and twist itself into all shapes, and rotate through every kind of motion. It is one of the smallest body parts <note>original: "members"</note>, the most mobile, and the one that tires least easily. Through it, a person naturally pours out in language the very image of their life.

When Anacharsis <note>a Scythian philosopher</note> was asked what was the best and worst part of a human being, he answered, "The Tongue." If it is not controlled, it is the worst; if well-governed, it is the best. *Death and life are in the power <note>original: "hands"</note> of the tongue* <note>Proverbs 18:21</note>. One leads to life, if it is sound <note>original: "whole"</note> and used correctly; the other leads to death, if it is infected and abused. *A soothing tongue is a tree of life* <note>original: "wholesome," Proverbs 15:4</note>. And, *the tongue of the wise brings healing* <note>original: "is health," Proverbs 12:18</note>, to both himself and others. Speech (if the tongue is healthy and well-governed) is a remedy for sorrow, anger, and for a soul in distress <note>original: "sick soul"</note>.
