The disease of the tongue is a violent ailment, and whoever is afflicted by it can either never remain silent, or can never speak well. It is the devil’s carriage <note>original: "coach"</note> if it is not bridled, and a "most filthy sewer" <note>original: "channel"</note>, says Saint Chrysostom. By nature, it is (just as the lips are) uncircumcised <note>meaning unconsecrated or spiritually impure</note>, polluted, and unclean <note>Exodus 6:11–12; Isaiah 6:5</note>. It eventually becomes *an unruly evil, full of deadly poison* <note>James 3:8</note>. It is so inflamed by this that *it is set on fire by hell and sets on fire the whole course of nature* <note>James 3:6</note>. This poison makes the tongue so venomous that it is both poisoned itself and a poisoner of others. It is both passive and active: it is set on fire, and it sets others on fire. It is paralyzed when it comes to doing good, yet frantic in pursuit of all evil. It defiles the whole body and harms those who hear it, or those whom it speaks about, spitting out *the poison of adders from under their lips* <note>Psalm 140:3; Romans 3:13</note>. This is a disease both offensive <note>original: "noisome"</note> to others and as dangerous to the speaker himself as if he had sucked the *poison of asps* <note>Job 20:16</note>.

This poison of the tongue is not physical <note>original: "bodily"</note>, but spiritual. The tongue itself is not properly affected by this poison as if it were fixed and inherent within it. Neither is this disease *idiopathic* <note>original: *Idiopatheticke*; a medical term for a disease arising spontaneously from the part itself</note> and unique to the tongue, but *sympathetic* <note>original: *Sympatheticke*; a condition caused by the suffering of another part of the body</note> and occurring by association with the evil-disposed and poisonous soul. For, *out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.* And, *out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, false witness, blasphemies, etc.* The wicked heart provides no holy <note>original: "gracious"</note> employment for the tongue; instead, many foolish imaginations and godless passions are released.

The heart is wicked above all things and gathers iniquity to itself, with *grapes of gall and the gall of bitterness*. A heart laden with sin (Isaiah 1:4), like a full winepress and an overflowing vat <note>original: "fat"</note>, sends up the excess of many poisonous and corrupting thoughts to the tongue to be proclaimed to the world. Through this, it becomes full of deadly poison to itself and to others.

</margin>

### Signs and Symptoms.

<margin>
Psalm 15:3.
Isaiah <note>original: "Esa."</note> 56:10.
</margin>
The poisoned tongue accuses the servant to the master (Proverbs 30:10; 1 Samuel 22:9; 2 Timothy 3:4) with false accusations (Titus 2:3). It is set against God (Isaiah 3:8) and against man, acting as an arrow shot out (Jeremiah 9:8). In a bad servant, it "answers back" <note>original: "answereth againe," meaning to be talkative or argumentative when rebuked</note> (Titus 2:9), but in a rich man, it answers roughly (Proverbs 18:23). It babbles (Proverbs 9:13; Matthew 6:5, 7; Ecclesiastes 5:3, 7; Judges 5:28, 29, 30; Acts 17:18) about vain and profane things (1 Timothy 6:20) which lead to more ungodliness (2 Timothy 2:16; Acts 17:18). It backbites (2 Corinthians 12:20) and kills from further away than the basilisk <note>a mythical serpent or lizard whose gaze was said to be lethal</note> does with its eyes (Proverbs 30:14). It barks at people's persons but is silent <note>original: "dumbe"</note> about their sins. It is bent like a bow to shoot the arrows of bitter words (Psalm 64:3, 4; 57:4; 120:4; Jeremiah 9:4, 8). It bites like a serpent (Ecclesiastes 10:11). It is bitter (Ephesians 4:31; Romans 3:14). It blasphemes God and man (Ephesians 4:31; Colossians 3:8; 2 Timothy 3:2, 4; Titus 3:2; Revelation 13:6; Leviticus 24:15, 16). It blesses God, but only hypocritically; and it blesses a friend with a loud voice, which is eventually turned into a curse to itself (Proverbs 27:14). It boasts of mischief (Psalm 52:1) and of great things (James 3:5; 2 Timothy 3:2; Romans 1:30). It bubbles or belches out foolishness (Proverbs 15:2).

The righteous man also hates lying (Proverbs 13:5) as a fruit of our "old man" <note>original: "old man"; referring to the unregenerate or sinful nature before spiritual renewal</note> (Colossians 3:9). Properly speaking, three things make up a lie:
1. Speaking an untruth.
2. Speaking against our own thoughts.
3. Speaking to deceive.

And above all liars, the worst are those who have taught their tongues to speak lies (Jeremiah 9:5) and who "trim and plaster up" lies (Psalm 119:69; Job 13:4).

It multiplies words (Ecclesiastes 10:14), and for all its floods of words, it has scarcely one drop of reason. This multitude of words is not without sin (Proverbs 10:19), and in many words there are various vanities. The best that can be said of it is that it is like the reed <note>original: "tongue of a pipe"</note> of a pipe; if it is taken away, the pipe is of no more use. It is like an unskillful shoemaker who makes a large shoe for a tiny foot. It is mischievous and talks of mischief (Proverbs 24:2). It murmurs (John 4:1; Malachi 3:14; Jude 16). It is wicked <note>original: "naughty"; in the 17th century, this meant something seriously bad or morally corrupt</note> and worth very little; it is hurtful both to itself and to others (Proverbs 17:4). It either whispers abroad things that are true (Romans 1:30; Genesis 9), or it alters them by adding something or changing the meaning (Matthew 26:60). Or it surmises what is not true (Jeremiah 37:13), or it colors its tale-telling with prefaces of pity and sorrow—using pretenses of goodwill, or a "necessity" to speak, or a claim of being free from malice—and making protestations of secrecy about things it actually wants the whole world to know. It is tasteless, like the white of an egg (it is so foolish) (Job 6:6–7). It tattles like a busybody, speaking what it ought not (1 Timothy 5:13). It has sharpened teeth (Psalm 112:10) and is itself sharpened like a sword (Psalm 64:3–4). It whispers through secret railing <note>original: "rayling"; the act of using harsh or abusive language</note> and backbiting, and separates close friends; and it is itself separated from God (Proverbs 16:28 and 26:20, 22; 2 Corinthians 12:20; Romans 1:29). It is windy and proud (Job 8:2) with words of wind (Job 16:3 and 15:2), and it is like a north wind through stormy scolding (Proverbs 25:23). It bears false witness and is a maul <note>original: "mawle"; a heavy hammer or club used as a weapon</note>, a sword, and a sharp arrow (Proverbs 25:18; 1 Kings 21:13; Proverbs 19:5, 9 and 21:28). It wounds and can never heal the damage it causes (Proverbs 26:22 and 18:8). It provides fuel for the fire of contention (Proverbs 26:20). And in a word: the evil and poisoned tongue is a world of iniquity (James 3:6).

### Cures and Remedies

<margin>A purified heart.</margin>
The healing of the tongue is a tree of life (Proverbs 15:4), and the healed and healing, wholesome tongue is most profitable and comforting for itself and for others. Because the impure and poisoned heart—filled with secret venom through native and inherent corruption—produces both poisoned deeds (Deuteronomy 32:33) and poisoned and corrupt talk (Romans 3:13; Ephesians 4:29), the heart must first be purged. Nothing is more suitable for this than faith.

<margin>By faith.</margin>
For faith purifies the heart (Acts 15:9). By faith, we apply Christ crucified to our hearts to mortify <note>original: "mortification"; to kill or put to death sinful desires</note> sin and all our earthly members (Colossians 3:5), of which the tongue is one of the principal in its use. This also serves to quicken <note>original: "quickning"; to bring to life or revitalize</note> the *Inner man*. Those who belong to Christ crucify the lusts and affections that bud forth in those members, and especially in the tongue (Galatians 5).

<margin>Prayer.</margin>
Prayer is a suitable remedy to cure the poison of the tongue; if it is fervent, constant, and effective, it avails much (James 5:16). This is true in two respects:

1. It creates an acquaintance with God (Job 22:21) and habituates a person to "take words with him" <note>original: "take words with himself"; a reference to Hosea 14:2, where the prophet urges the people to "Take words with you, and return to the Lord."</note> when turning to God. This even includes that holy, secret speech (Isaiah 26:16; Job 15:4). Through time, he becomes so circumspect and holy in his talking with God that he is taught to be wise and grave in his speech with men.

2. By prayer, he becomes a begging petitioner. Because God can best cure and rule the tongue—for the answer of the tongue is from God (Proverbs 16:1), and the "tongue of the learned" to speak a word in season is from Him (Isaiah 50:4)—he entreats Him through prayer that He would set a watch before his mouth, and

<margin>Wisdom.</margin>
<margin>A lover of learning, not a lover of words. <note>original: "φιλολόγος non λογοφίλος." This phrase is attributed to Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note></margin>
Wisdom is most necessary for curing the tongue, especially that "wisdom that is from above" (James 3:17). Wisdom weighs words as men weigh gold and silver. The heart of the wise teaches and moderates their mouth (Proverbs 16:23). They have the key to their tongue, kept in the "cupboard" of their heart. Fools carry their hearts in their mouths, but a wise man carries his mouth in his heart. Just as he looks at his food before he eats, so he ponders the substance of his words before he speaks. He considers that God has given him two ears but only one tongue—walled in with teeth and lips to bar and bridle it (Ecclesiasticus 28:28 <note>original: "Eccleſ. 28. 28." Refers to the deuterocanonical book of Sirach, also known as Ecclesiasticus.</note>). He chooses rather to be a lover of knowledge than to be talkative and a lover of words.

<margin>Moderation. To bridle or lead with a bridle. <note>original: "χαλιναγωγεῖν" (chalinagōgein).</note> Refraining.</margin>
This moderation of the tongue restrains and directs it. The refraining of the tongue (Proverbs 10:19) is the "bridling" of it (James 1:26; Psalm 39:1) and the keeping of it from evil (Psalm 34:13; 1 Peter 3:10) through diligent observation and watchfulness. He who keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps his soul from trouble (Proverbs 21:23), and he who keeps his mouth keeps his life (Proverbs 13:3).

<margin>Silence.</margin>
<margin>Sparing of speaking.</margin>
This wisdom of restraining the tongue makes a person either conceal and hold their peace about things that should not be uttered—for a prudent man conceals knowledge, while the heart of fools proclaims foolishness (Proverbs 12:23, 15:2), and a man of understanding holds his peace while a tale-bearer reveals secrets (Proverbs 11:12–13)—or else it makes him slow to speak (James 1:19). He who has knowledge spares his words (Proverbs 17:27) and utters none except those he ponders well in his mind beforehand. He speaks sparingly of himself...

Pleasant words are like a honeycomb: sweet to the soul and health to the bones (Proverbs 16:24).

And as it is a fountain of life to depart from the snares of death (Proverbs 14:27), so it is a healing wellspring to cure the maladies of the tongue. <margin>Reverence of God,</margin>
Reverence depends upon true fear. We should learn to serve God with *reverence*, Hebrews 12:28, and religiously and reverently regard in our speech all those things which belong to God directly. <margin>And men.</margin>

In our speaking, we should preserve the reputation and good name of others, which is "better than precious ointment" (Ecclesiastes 7:1) and "better than great riches" (Proverbs 22:1). This right reverencing of God and man cures and amends in the tongue all blasphemy, taking God's name in vain, joking about the Scriptures, cursing, slandering, backbiting, railing, reviling, and the like.

<margin>Veracity.</margin>
The virtue of *veracity* <note>meaning: habitual truthfulness</note>, by which a man speaks the truth in his heart (Psalm 15:2), makes the tongue speak everything as it is, and just as the heart thinks it.

It is a fruit of the Spirit (Ephesians 5:9) and should be carefully sought (Philippians 4:8). It is the badge of a godly man who shall inherit the Kingdom of heaven (Psalm 15:2). It makes a person acceptable to God, for those who deal truly are God’s delight (Proverbs 12:22). The practice of this worthy virtue of *veracity* <note>truthfulness</note> must be so balanced with prudence that its freedom does not harm the virtue of 
<margin>Taciturnity and silence.</margin>
*taciturnity* <note>the habit of being reserved or silent</note>, nor reveal the secret caverns and mysteries of wise silence. 

We do not need to speak of things that are pointless, irrelevant, unnecessary, filthy, hateful, or harmful to God’s glory or to our neighbors. Nor should we speak things that are scandalous, offensive, secret, tedious, or the like, even if they are entirely true. We should not speak every truth before everyone indiscriminately; we must not cast pearls before swine, nor give what is holy to dogs (Matthew 7:6 and 27:14). Similarly, we should not answer a fool according to his folly, unless it is to prevent him from being wise in his own conceit (Proverbs 26:4–5 and 23:9). 

We should be hesitant to speak before the elderly (Job 32:6), before magistrates and honorable men, or those in authority (Titus 2:9, Acts 20:10), or in the hearing of angry, malicious, and deceptive <note>original: "dissembled"</note> persons. This virtue of *veracity* cures all lying, dissembling, flattering <note>original: "glozing"</note>, glossing over <note>original: "smoothing"</note>, and cheating <note>original: "cogging"</note>.

<margin>Peaceableness</margin>
Learn to be of a meek and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is of great value (1 Peter 3:4). This consists in striving to be quiet and for a man to mind his own business (1 Thessalonians 4:11). It means living in peace with all men, so far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18), and bearing with others in love (Ephesians 4:2). It involves tolerating the behaviors <note>original: "suffering men's manners"</note> of those you cannot change (Acts 13:18, by consequence <note>original: "ex conseq."</note>), covering sins with love (Proverbs 10:12), and—as one who is both prudent and peaceable—covering the shame of others (Proverbs 12:16). 

We should avoid all strictness and rigor, instead using moderation toward all people (Philippians 4:5) and avoiding all occasions of discord and strife (Genesis 13:7). The habit and practice of this virtue cures all scolding <note>original: "chiding"</note>, clashing <note>original: "jarring"</note>, false rumors, blasphemy, cursing, and all evil words that arise from discord and debate.

(peaceable)

<margin>Taciturnity.</margin>
Study the virtue of *taciturnity* <note>the habit of being reserved or silent</note> and wise silence. Through this, those things that are to be kept silent and secret, as well as things that are not necessary to be uttered, are not spoken. Those things that are necessary are spoken sparingly, and only so far as they may serve the good of others. This virtue cures garrulity <note>original: "garrulitie"; excessive talkativeness</note>, lack of restraint in speech, pointless talk <note>original: "futilitie"</note>, the revealing of secrets, flattery, slander, insults, reproaches, and the like.

<margin>Moderation of judgment.</margin>
Our judgment of others and of their actions should be neither too high nor too harsh. We should not show excessive admiration for people for the sake of personal gain (*Jude 1:16*). Neither should we condemn others too rashly or too severely when we think they have offended. Do not be suspicious where there is no ground for it, and do not judge things to be worse than they are, nor interpret them in the worst possible way by giving them a wrong construction (*Matthew 7:1*). 

As for those you respect, judge them truly according to what you certainly know. For those you dislike (whose actions or sayings you do not approve), either suspend your judgment of them or, where there is doubt, interpret it for the best. What you know and dislike in another, excuse it: either by his intent, which may be good; or by his ignorance and weakness, which is to be pitied; or by his inclination, which is common to many; or by his temptation, which may have been great; or by his necessity, which was inevitable; or by the circumstances of his action, which may lessen the fault; or by the hope of his repentance, which may be tomorrow; or by reflecting on yourself—that you may be at some other time just as he is now. This is the right sobriety and moderation in our judgment of others. It corrects the words of flattery and does not allow men to "bless with a loud voice" (*Proverbs 27:14*) nor to give "flattering titles" (*Job 32:2* <note>The author likely refers to Job 32:21–22, where Elihu refuses to give flattering titles to men.</note>). Much more, it corrects all backbiting, upbraiding, slanderous speech <note>original: "blaſpheming"</note>, and all such words that savor of rash judgment.

<page-num>483</page-num>
# CHAPTER 32. The Poisonous Tongue.

<margin>Meekness and patience.</margin>
Meekness and patience are perfectly suited for the curing of the tongue; both are put to the test by injuries <note>original: "iniuries"; here meaning wrongs, insults, or unjust treatment</note>. *Patience* calmly suffers the wrong, while *meekness* quietly moderates the anger felt because of that wrong. *Paul* prescribed these two virtues to *Timothy*, who had much to do with his tongue—to teach, to reason, and to dispute, as well as to reprove and answer those who greatly contradicted and opposed him. Lest he should be provoked <note>original: "exasperate"</note> into expressing his passions in words, Paul recommends to him the virtues and graces of patience and meekness, saying: "The servant of the Lord must be patient, in meekness instructing those who oppose themselves" (*2 Timothy 2:24-25*). He also tells him to remind everyone, following his example, to speak evil of no one and not to be brawlers; he wants them to be gentle, showing all meekness to all men (*Titus 3:2*). These two virtues joined together make the tongue silent (*2 Kings 18:36*), make the answers soft (*Proverbs 25:14-15*), and allay <note>diminish or soothe</note> the bitterness of words (*Proverbs 15:1*).

These two virtues allowed *Gideon* <note>original: "Gedeon"</note> to answer so softly and appease the angry *Ephraimites* (*Judges 8:3*), and *Abigail* to answer the angry and threatening *David* so sweetly (*1 Samuel 24:7*) <note>While the text cites 1 Samuel 24:7, the story of Abigail's intervention is found in 1 Samuel 25.</note>. Similarly, the patient and meek *David*, when faced with his enemies' insults, was like a deaf and mute man who did not open his mouth, and in whose mouth were no reproofs (*Psalm 38:13-14*). These virtues make men courteous, not returning evil for evil or insults <note>original: "railing"</note> for insults, but on the contrary, giving a blessing (*1 Peter 3:8-9*) and not cursing (*Romans 12:14*). These qualities make men defend their innocence with great moderation of words, as *Paul* did before the Council (*Acts 23:1*), *Hannah* <note>original: "Anna"</note> before *Eli* (*1 Samuel 1:15*), *Christ* before the *Jews* (*John 8:48-49*), *Daniel* before *Nebuchadnezzar* <note>Though the text mentions Nebuchadnezzar, the events of Daniel chapter 6 involve King Darius.</note> (*Daniel 6:22*), and *David* before *Saul*, who patiently commended his cause to God and said:
> Judge me, O God, for I have walked in my innocence (*Psalm 26:1*).
By these virtues also, reproofs are moderated, and those who fall are

# CHAPTER 32. The Poisonous Tongue.

...restored by those who have the spirit of meekness (*Galatians 6:1*). Reproofs are wisely wrapped up in some grave <note>serious or solemn</note> sentence, or with some preface and insinuation <note>original: "inſinuati-on"; a gentle or subtle introduction</note> of love, of pity, respect, and reverence. They may also be given with an application of the reproof to oneself (*1 Corinthians 4:6*), or with some exhortation or prayer (*1 Timothy 5:1*), and either in gentle words or in some sensible parable (*2 Samuel 12:1*). By these methods are cured all cursing, railing, sharp rebukes, "answering back," chiding, contention, gallings <note>original: "gallings"; speech meant to irritate, annoy, or cause resentment</note>, and all bitterness in speech.

<margin>Modesty and humility.</margin>
*Modesty* and *humility* make a man, when he seeks his own reputation, do it with great moderation (*Philippians 4:8*). Out of the sense of his own unworthiness, he arrogates <note>claims or takes for oneself without right</note> nothing too much to himself, nor does he derogate <note>takes away from or belittles</note> anything from another (*Ephesians 4:2; Colossians 3:12, 13*). He does nothing through strife or vain-glory, but in lowliness of mind, esteems others better than himself (*Philippians 2:3*). 

*Modesty* makes a wise man spare his words because he is of a cool spirit (*Proverbs 17:27*). He spares to speak any evil of another or of himself (*1 Timothy 1:13, 15; 2 Corinthians 15:9*). He even spares to speak any good of himself; or if he does it, he does it with a wise convoy <note>original: "conuoy"; here meaning a skillful manner or prudent way of conveying a message</note>, as if in the person of another (*2 Corinthians 12:2; John 19:26*). He chooses seemly words for unseemly things (*Genesis 4:1; 1 Samuel 24:4*). This virtue cures self-praise, boasting, vaunting, filthy speaking, and such like.

<margin>Fidelity.</margin>
Be faithful in words and promises: for those who deal truly are God's delight (*Proverbs 12:22*). He who speaks the truth from his heart, and swears to his own hurt and does not change, shall dwell in God's holy hill of eternal happiness (*Psalm 15:4*). 

Be slow to promise and swift to perform. Before you promise, foresee that the promise is both lawful to be made and possible to be performed.

<page-num>485</page-num>
### CHAPTER 32. The Poisonous Tongue.

This virtue and grace, joined with wisdom, preserves the tongue from making rash promises and makes a person careful to perform those that have been made.

<margin>Gravity tempering urbanity.</margin>
Let *gravity* <note>seriousness and dignity</note> temper your *urbanity* <note>original: "urbanitie"; refined social grace or wit</note> and *hilarity* <note>original: "hilarity"; cheerfulness or mirth</note> (Titus 2:2; Philippians 4:8; Ephesians 5:4). For just as there is a time to laugh with delightful words, they should not seem mad (Ecclesiastes 2:2) through excess or impertinence <note>irrelevance or inappropriate behavior</note>. Instead, your words should be suitable for your status, age, and calling <note>vocation or social position</note>. Merry words and jokes should not be offensive to others. Rather, because they are pleasant, playful, and sweet for the recreation of the mind (Proverbs 23:8), they must offend no one but instead edify <note>build up or encourage spiritually</note> (Ephesians 4:29; Acts 2:4, 6). They must be appropriate, timely, and used in moderate or neutral matters. If needed, and if your calling requires it, you may even wrap a sharp reproof <note>correction or criticism</note> within a merry joke (1 Kings 18:27). This *urbanity* of speech, tempered with gravity and wisdom, will cure all idle and hurtful jesting, taunting, girding <note>mocking or making biting remarks</note>, scorning, and unseemly or immoderate laughter and merriment.

<margin>The grace of regeneration.</margin>
Finally, because all the poison of the tongue flows from ungodliness and worldly lusts, endeavor to be a partaker of the *grace of God* which brings salvation to all people. It will teach you to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world (Titus 2:11–12). Consequently, you should refrain from all ungodly, vain, passionate, and idle words. Utter none but those that savor and smell of godliness, righteousness, and sobriety—or at least words that are not harmful or contrary to these virtues. Look for that blessed hope and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. He gave himself for us so that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a special people, zealous for good works and good words (Titus 2:13–14).

## CHAPTER XXXIII.
### The Deafness of the Ear.

---

> Isaiah 42:18. *Hear, you deaf.*
> Isaiah 43:8. *Bring forth the deaf who have ears.*

---

#### Description.

<margin>A description of the ear.</margin>
God has planted the ear (Psalm 94:9), and as it pleases him, he makes people deaf (Exodus 4:11). The hearing of the ear and the seeing of the eye—God has made them both (Proverbs 20:12). The ear is of an excellent design, set in the highest part of the body because sounds travel upward; they are always open so that we may hear more readily.

Within the ear there is a thin membrane called the *eardrum* <note>original: "Tympanum"</note>, with three little bones grown to it called the *anvil*, the *hammer*, and the *stirrup* <note>original: "incus, malleus, strapes" (modern: stapes)</note>, which marvelously serve to enable hearing. The ear tests <note>original: "tryeth"</note> words (Job 12:11 and 34:3). The ears are called the "daughters of music" <note>A biblical metaphor from Ecclesiastes 12:4 referring to the physical faculties of hearing.</note> because they delight in it. The ear is the gateway <note>original: "port"</note> of the royal road of reason and the gateway of faith (Romans 10:14). But unless it is "dug" or opened by God, it will never be sanctified <note>set apart for a holy purpose</note> for that use (Psalm 40:6).

<margin>What is spiritual deafness?</margin>
The deafness of the ear is either physical or spiritual:

<page-num>487</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 33. The Deafness of the Ear.</header>

...spiritual. Physical deafness, being involuntary, is to be pitied and cured rather than cursed (Leviticus 19:14 <note>The original text cites Leviticus 14:19, but the biblical prohibition against cursing the deaf is found in Leviticus 19:14.</note>). But spiritual deafness should be pitied and cured, otherwise it is accursed because it is voluntary; it is like the deafness of the cobra <note>original: "Adder"</note> that stops her ear, which will not listen to the voice of charmers, no matter how wisely they charm (Psalm 58:4). This is the "heavy ear" accompanied by a "fat heart" (Isaiah 6:10, Zechariah 7:11), and the "uncircumcised ear" <note>A biblical metaphor for an ear that is closed or unresponsive to God's word.</note> resulting from hardness of heart (Jeremiah 6:10 and 7:26).

<margin>It is two-fold: Natural and Acquired.</margin>
This spiritual deafness, this unwillingness to hear what is most profitable for the soul, is either *natural*—common to our corrupt human nature—or *acquired* by habit and time. This occurs when the heart is increasingly withdrawn from God and from His will. When, through the stubbornness of the heart and the stiffness of the neck, the ear is not inclined to listen to God (Jeremiah 7:24, 26), and the neck is made more and more stiff so that the ear cannot hear or receive instruction (Jeremiah 17:23). This is contrary to God's own direction, saying: *Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live* (Isaiah 55:3).

---
#### Part affected.
---

This deafness of the ear is not *idiopathic* <note>original: "Idiopatheticke"; a medical term meaning a condition arising primarily within the organ itself.</note> and proper to the ear itself, but *sympathetic* <note>original: "Sympatheticke"; a condition occurring in one part of the body due to an ailment in another—in this case, the ear being affected by the state of the soul.</note>, occurring in agreement with the evil-disposed and dead soul. The soul does not employ the ear for good uses, but rather withdraws it from hearing all things that are most profitable, and instead inclines it toward those things that are idle, vain, and harmful.

<summary>This page distinguishes between physical deafness and "voluntary" spiritual deafness, which the author attributes to a hardened heart and a soul that refuses to listen to God. It classifies spiritual deafness as a "sympathetic" condition where the physical ear is led astray by the spiritual state of the person.</summary>

---
#### Causes.
---

<margin>God deserting and punishing.</margin>
Just as God causes physical <note>original: "bodily"</note> deafness (Exodus 4:11), He also inflicts this spiritual deafness as a just punishment. He abandons <note>original: "deserteth"</note> the heart and does not incline it toward Him (1 Kings 8:58). He also abandons and does not incline the ear to listen and pay attention to what is His will. He says to the Prophet, "Make the heart of this people fat <note>A biblical metaphor for becoming spiritually insensitive or calloused.</note>, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn back and be healed" (Isaiah 6:10). For a long time, God gave the people of Israel many opportunities to see His works and to hear His Word; yet He did not give them a heart to perceive, eyes to see, or ears to hear (Deuteronomy 29:4).

<margin>Satan seducing</margin>
Satan injects all the evil he can to stop up both the heart and the ear. The Devil is called a "deaf spirit" (Mark 9:25) because he goes about trying to stop the ear from hearing God’s Word and from all godly and wise counsel.

<margin>External occasions.</margin>
External distractions <term>original: "auocaments"; things that call one away or divert attention</term> withdraw the ear from hearing God's advice. The rude guests claimed they could not come to the banquet because of other business (Matthew 22). Sometimes the ear is withdrawn because the person is physically absent; at other times, while the body is present, the ears are withdrawn and held back by other distractions.

<margin>Prosperity.</margin>
Men are reluctant to listen to the Word when they are surrounded by prosperity, as God says: "I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not hear'" (Jeremiah 22:21).

<margin>Foolishness.</margin>
The wisdom of the flesh (which is enmity against God, Romans 8:7) and the wisdom of this world (which is foolishness to God, 1 Corinthians 3:19), along with all the vanities of the mind (Ephesians 4:17) and the drowsiness of the heart, stop the ear from hearing the wisdom of God.

And again it is said: "The people refused to listen, and pulled away the shoulder, and stopped their ears, so that they should not hear. Yes, they made their hearts like an adamant stone <note>original: "Adamant stone"; a legendary substance of impenetrable hardness, used here to describe extreme spiritual obstinacy.</note>, lest they should hear the Law" (Zechariah 7:11, 12). They are called "a rebellious people, lying children, children that will not hear the Law of the Lord" (Isaiah 30:9). 

From this comes a stubborn refusal to hear God's Word (Jeremiah 13:8, 10), as they prefer the imagination of their own hearts over God's precepts (Jeremiah 13:10; 16:12; 17:23). When the preaching of the Word meets a "fat" <note>In a biblical context, "fat" refers to being spiritually calloused or insensitive.</note> and obstinate heart, it irritates the heart and makes it even harder. The "thundering" of the Word so dulls the ear that it is made heavy and deaf (Isaiah 6:10).

### *Signs and Symptoms.*

Just as David (though he otherwise naturally heard) was willingly deaf to his enemies' insults—Psalm 38:13–14—hearing them, he did not listen to them, and regarded them no more than if he had not heard them; so those who are spiritually deaf hear voices, words, and sentences, but do not pay attention to them, as if they were physically deaf. They have ears but do not hear, like idols, Psalm 115:6 <note>original: "Pſalm. 114. 6."; the author likely intended Psalm 115:6 or 135:17, which describe idols having ears that cannot hear.</note>. Though it is said to them, "This is the resting place," <note>original: "the refreshing"; see Isaiah 28:12</note> yet they will not hear, Isaiah 28:12. Even if they hear, they do not act according to what they hear; like fools, they build their house on the sand, Matthew 7:26. In hearing, they hear but do not understand, Isaiah 6:9, because they do not incline their ear to understand; their idle and vain hearing is merely "ear-labor" <term>original: "eare-labour"; physical hearing or the effort of listening without any mental or spiritual engagement.</term>.

<margin>Many sorts of deaf hearers.</margin>
Some hear and mock, Acts 17:32. Some delay their hearing until another time, Acts 24:25. Some gaze, some muse, some wonder, and some wander with their minds. Some simply applaud and hear gladly for a time, only as Herod did, Mark 6:20. Some are like the Athenians, itching for news <note>original: "newes"; referring to the Greek desire for intellectual novelty</note>, Acts 17:21. Some, like the Pharisees, watch for something to criticize and twist what is spoken, Luke 11:53–54. Some are curious to know all things so that they may be able to talk about them, Acts 17:18, 21. Some crave nothing but eloquence; some, a variety of topics, or whatever fits their mood. Some are too picky and sensitive; they will hear no one unless they please them well. In their spiritual famine, they refuse their food because they think a raven is the carrier of it—something Elijah would not have done, 1 Kings 17:6. Some hear as the path <note>original: "way-ſide"</note> received the seed: they do not understand what they hear; the wicked one comes and snatches away what was sown in their hearts. Some hear as the stony places received the seed: they hear the Word and immediately receive it with joy; but it has no root, it lasts for a while, and

<margin>The many evils that follow the deaf ear.</margin>

## CHAPTER 33. The Deafness of the Ear.

[...refuse to] hear, within the net of the Word. He who eats and does not keep his food in his stomach is in a physically bad state; but he who hears and does not keep the Word in his heart is in a far worse state spiritually. For he who does not receive the Word has someone who judges him; the Word shall judge him on the last day (John 12:48). To him, it becomes the aroma of death leading to death (2 Corinthians 2:15–16). <note>original: "savour of death"; in this context, the preaching of the Gospel, which should bring life, instead seals the condemnation of the listener.</note> And he shall be cut off because he does not listen to God (Hosea 9:17).

Against those who will not hear and obey, God calls upon the heaven and the earth to listen (Deuteronomy 30:19, 31:28, and 32:1). He prefers those naturally deaf creatures to men and women who are willfully deaf to His Word. He makes those mute and deaf creatures bear witness against human obstinacy and ingratitude (Isaiah 1:2 and 34:1; Jeremiah 6:19 and 22:29, etc.). As Joshua said to the people: "The great stone under this oak shall be a witness to us, for it has heard the words of the Lord which He spoke to us; it shall be a witness against you, lest you deny your God" (Joshua 24:27).

# CHAPTER 33. The Deafness of the Ear.

[...because they have brought the judgments of] God upon the deaf ear that would not hear His Word (1 Samuel 3:11, 2 Kings 21:12, Jeremiah 19:3). He threatens to send a famine in the land: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the Word of the Lord. And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the North even to the East; they shall run to and fro to seek the Word of the Lord and shall not find it (Amos 8:11–12). The people of Judah refused to hear, stopped their ears, and made their hearts like an adamant stone <note>original: "Adamant stone"; a legendary mineral of extreme hardness, used here to describe a heart that is completely impenetrable and stubborn.</note>, lest they should hear the Law; therefore, a great wrath came upon them. And just as God cried out and they would not hear, so they cried out and God would not hear; He scattered them with a whirlwind among the nations (Zechariah 7:11, 14). Those who willingly stop their ears when God speaks shall, against their will, both hear and feel His fearful judgments; and the deaf shall "feelingly" hear the words of the Book (Isaiah 29:18, 11, 12).

->*Cure and remedies.*<- <note>original: "Curation"; refers to the process of healing or treating a condition.</note>

<margin>Instruction.</margin>
Diligent instruction, together with private and public admonition, helps greatly to mend the deaf ear. It can turn an unwilling ear into a willing and ready one, and cause *the ears of the deaf to be unstopped* (Isaiah 35:5) and *the ears of those who listen* to be attentive (Isaiah 32:3). Then the deaf who have ears to hear the Word shall say, *"It is truth"* (Isaiah 43:8–9). It may be objected: "What is the need for preaching or teaching to deaf men?" It may be just as well answered: God may join such a blessing with instruction that those who are not only simply deaf, but even those in the grave (fully dead in sin), may be made to hear (John 5:28). The preacher must proceed in teaching and leave the success to God; the Word will serve either for conversion or for conviction. The deaf must be instructed, whether they will hear [or not...]

# CHAPTER 34.

## The Evil Eye.

> Mark 7:22, 23. *The evil eye, etc., comes from within and defiles the man.*

---

->Description<-

<margin>The dignity of the eye.</margin>
The Maker of the eye is God (Proverbs 20:12; Psalm 94:9; Exodus 4:11). Nature attends and serves as a handmaid. The eye (as some think), among the other organic parts of the body, is the first to begin forming and the last to be finished, because it is the smallest part in size and the greatest in variety; in its composition, it is more admirable than the rest. It possesses a lively, clear, and shining beauty because of the complexity <note>original: "subtility"</note> of its many small parts. It is more divine than any other part of the body.

<margin>It resembles the world. The Trinity. Aqueous (watery), Vitreous (glassy), Crystalline (lens), Adnata (attached), Cornea (horny), Uvea (grape-like), Crystalloid, Retiform (net-like), Hyaloid (glassy) <note>original: "Aqueus, vitreus, Cryſtallinus, Adnata, Cornea, Vuea, Cryſtalloides, Retiformis, Hyaloides"</note>. The visual spirits and rays.</margin>
It is a little globe, full of *visual spirits* <note>original: "viſory ſpirits"; in early medical theory, these were subtle fluids that enabled sight</note>, and it resembles the round, living <note>original: "animated"</note> world. Certain imprints of the invisible *Deity* and *Trinity* are as clearly seen in it as in any other creature (Romans 1:20). In one and the selfsame eye, there are three colors, three humors <note>original: "humours"; the primary fluids of the eye</note>, three common tunicles <note>original: "tunicles"; layers or membranes</note>, and three particular smaller membranes.

The eye is filled with *visual spirits*, produced and generated from the *animal spirits* <note>original: "animall ſpirits"; in Galenic medicine, these were refined from blood in the brain to enable sensation and movement</note>, which flow from the brain into the eye through the *optic nerve*. From those,

...proceed the visible and reflected rays in the eye, as in a mirror; which quickly form an image of the thing seen. This image is received in the crystalline humor <note>The lens of the eye</note>; and by the visual spirits <note>original: "viſory ſpirits"; in early medical theory, these were subtle fluids that enabled sight</note> through the optic nerve, it is sent into the brain to be considered by the common sense and imagination.

<margin>It excels the rest of the senses.</margin>
Of all the parts in the body, the eye is most precious. Its sense of *Seeing* is the most certain of all the senses regarding its object and sensation. It is more exquisite and more detailed than the rest, and it works upon the smallest and finest things that exist. It has the greatest number and variety of objects to feed and delight upon. It ranges through the world and pierces the skies, even to the fixed stars. It creates light to rejoice the heart and keep a man company when he is solitary; whereas darkness breeds fear in him, as he finds himself robbed of such an excellent guide (Proverbs 15:30). So it is that the sight of the eyes is better than the walking and wandering desires of the soul (Ecclesiastes 6:9). For the light is sweet, and it is a pleasant thing for the eyes to behold the Sun (Proverbs 15:30; Ecclesiastes 11:7).

<margin>It has the highest place.</margin>
It has the most conspicuous, the highest, and most royal place of the body, far above the rest of the senses, and it looks out as if through a window (Ecclesiastes 12:3).

Through the little hole of the eye, as through a gate <note>original: "Port"</note>, this great visible world and everything within it enter into the mind of this "little world" <note>The "microcosm," a common Renaissance concept that the human body reflects the structure of the universe</note> of our body. This happens through the apprehension of the likenesses <note>original: "similitudes"</note> of things, through *delight* <note>original: "oblectation"</note> in those abstract likenesses, and through *judgment* <note>original: "dijudication"</note> and discerning one from another. It is, of all the senses, the one most often put into action. It is also the swiftest, needing the least time and creating sight in a moment; most promptly, in an instant, it can grasp even the heavens themselves. It possesses a liberty (which other senses lack) of eyelids ready to open and shut, to see or not see, as it pleases. Whatever it perceives, it quickly imprints the form of it upon the imagination. If the eye is "single" <note>In the biblical context of Matthew 6:22, "single" means healthy, clear, or sincere</note>, it makes the whole body light (Matthew 6:22).

# CHAPTER 34. The Evil Eye.

<margin>
The mind dwells in the eyes (Pliny).
The eyes are the indicators of the mind (Cicero).
And indicators of character (Demosthenes).
<note>original Latin: "In oculis animus habitat, Pl. Oculi indices animi, Cic. Et morum indices, Demosth."</note>
</margin>

6.22. And by looks (as by a silent speech), the eye signifies our wills, thoughts, and affections to others. Other senses are merely passive; the eye is also active. The mind seems to dwell in the eye, so much does the eye reveal it. Men's hearts may be seen through their eyes; therefore, a beautiful <note>original: "good"</note> eye is quickly able to ravish the hearts of those who behold it, as in Song of Solomon 4:9. Likewise, those with weak spirits blush when their superiors look them in the eye.

The eye is so delicate by nature that, since it was the first sense that offended <note>A reference to Eve seeing the forbidden fruit in the Garden of Eden</note>, it is—as a fitting punishment—made subject to as many maladies as there are weeks in a year.

If the eye is well-disposed and rightly guided, it benefits the soul most; but if it is ill-disposed and misguided, it harms the soul most. It is said to be "evil" when it is a conduit to secretly convey much evil into the heart, and an instrument to stir up the heart to even more evil; it is also evil when it expresses and declares the bad passions of the mind. Evil eyes are the springs and streams of lusts (1 John 2:16). Their evil nature is well-represented by the fitting name they are given in the Holy Tongue <note>Hebrew</note>, where they are called "springs" (Proverbs 28:22, Psalm 87:7, compared with Song of Solomon 7:4). When, therefore, the eye is an instrument of sin, it may then be said that it is an **evil eye**, subject to an evil disease, which even the pagans acknowledged.

<margin>
Blinded in the eye.
<note>original Greek: "Πεπηρωμένη ὀφθαλμον" (pepērōmenē ophthalmon); Philostratus, *Lives of the Sophists*.</note>
</margin>
For example, Isaeus, when made to look at a most beautiful woman and asked if she was not most fair, answered: "I have ceased from being diseased in my eyes." <note>Isaeus was a Greek Sophist; his reply suggests he had disciplined his sight to no longer be "infected" by lustful Gazing.</note>

---

### Part Affected.

The part affected is the eye; however, the malady is not bodily, but spiritual. And just as in sorrow the eye affects the heart with weeping (Lamentations 3:49, 51), and the heart affects the eye with sorrow in a continuous cycle, so it is in this disease: the **evil eye** both affects the heart and is affected by the heart.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "evil eye" introduced on page 501, moving from the eye's role as a mirror of the mind to its moral corruption. It explores how the eye acts in concert with a sinful heart and lists the external triggers that turn sight into a tool for sin.</meta>

# CHAPTER 34. The Evil Eye.

The eye itself is not primarily affected by this evil (as if the evil were fixed and inherent within the organ itself), nor is it entirely *idiopathic* <term>arising spontaneously or from within the organ itself</term> and specific to the eye alone. Rather, it is *sympathetic* <term>acting in harmony or shared feeling with another part of the body</term>, occurring in agreement with the evil heart; for "out of the heart proceed evil thoughts... an evil eye" <note>Matthew 15:19–20</note>. It is to be called "evil" when it is an unsanctified <note>original: "un-sanctified," meaning not made holy or set apart for God's use</note> organ and member of the body. It does not only yield itself to the heart (as "a weapon and instrument of unrighteousness for sin" <note>Romans 6:12, 13, 19</note>), but it also seduces the heart through its own observations, whereby "the heart walks after the eye" <note>Job 31:7; Genesis 3:6; Numbers 15:39</note>.

---

### Causes.

<margin>
Objects.
</margin>
External objects presented to the eye by chance, sought out by sensual appetite, or shown to it by Satan's schemes, stir up this evil disposition of the eye. These cause it to look upon the deceiving vanity found in visible things, which kindles the "lust of the eye" toward the things it delights in <note>1 John 2:16</note>. For example, when the woman <note>Eve</note> saw (with the eyes of her mind) that "the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes" (of the body), she "took of the fruit and ate it" <note>Genesis 3:6</note>. Similarly, "the sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful" <note>Genesis 6:2</note>. And when Ham <note>original: "Cham"</note> saw the nakedness of his father <note>Noah</note>, he told his two brothers outside <note>Genesis 9:22</note>. David also, from the roof, saw a woman who was very beautiful washing herself <note>2 Samuel 11:2</note>. This is not a simple looking at an object, but a looking with *lusting*, as Christ says: "Whoever looks on a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery" <note>Matthew 5:28; see also 1 John 2:16</note>.

<margin>
Drunkenness.
</margin>
Drunkenness, just as "it makes the eye red" <note>Genesis 49:12</note>, so it makes the mind mad and causes the eyes to "behold strange women" <note>Proverbs 23:33</note>. And it leads to many more enticing vanities in the world.

The author cites several biblical examples, such as Eve, Ham, and David, to show how sight can trigger sinful desires.</summary>

<margin>
Foolishness.
</margin>
As wisdom is seen in the face (and eyes) of one who has understanding, so the eyes of a fool are in the corners of the world, hunting for every vanity, and not in his head as the *wise* man's eyes are <note>Proverbs 17:24; Ecclesiastes 2:14</note>. A shallow wit and a wandering, unstable mind create a rolling eye, which is quickly and recklessly drawn to every object, gazing idly at everything and turning hastily from one thing to another.

<margin>
A wicked heart.
</margin>
An evil heart creates an evil eye: for the evil disposition of the eye comes from the heart and defiles a person <note>Mark 7:22–23 compared with Matthew 6:23, 20:15, and 5:28</note>. The heart leaves a strong impression on the eye, and much of a person's heart can be seen in their eyes. Just as an honest heart has a good eye, so a wicked heart has an evil eye to serve it and reflect it.

<margin>
Passions.
</margin>
*Passions* make the eyes look like themselves. *Lust* within creates lustful eyes on the outside <note>1 John 2:16</note>. *Pride* has a proud look <note>Psalm 101:5</note>, lofty eyes <note>Psalm 131:1; Proverbs 6:17</note>, and haughty <note>original: "high-looking"</note> eyes <note>Isaiah 2:11</note>. *Envy* is visible in the eye; it makes the eye unable to look patiently upon the good fortune <note>original: "good hap"</note> of another <note>Proverbs 23:6 and 28:22</note>. A merciless and malicious heart has eyes set even against the poor <note>Psalm 10:8</note>. A scornful heart has a mocking eye <note>Proverbs 30:7</note>. The greedy <note>original: "avaricious"</note> heart has covetous eyes <note>Jeremiah 22:17</note>, and the lecherous heart looks out through the windows of adulterous eyes <note>2 Peter 2:14</note>.

<margin>
Desertion.
</margin>
When God deserts a person, their eyes and the rest of their senses are surrendered to their heart and lusts. Their heart is then handed over to Satan to be misguided at his pleasure, so long as that *strong* man <note>Satan, referencing the "strong man" parable in Matthew 12:29</note> keeps the whole castle <note>representing the human body or soul</note>, until he is overcome and cast out by the power of *regeneration* <term>spiritual rebirth or the process of being made new by God</term>.

<summary>This page describes how internal moral failings—such as folly, pride, envy, and greed—manifest outwardly through the eyes. It concludes by explaining that when God withdraws His grace, the senses and heart become vulnerable to Satan's influence until spiritual rebirth occurs.</summary>
<keywords>Evil Eye, Folly, Wicked Heart, Passions, Envy, Lust, Spiritual Desertion, Regeneration, Satan</keywords>

## Signs and Symptoms.

<margin>
General.
</margin>
People's actions are like their eyes and like the things they see. Just as *Jacob's* sheep, by looking at the rods, gave birth to sheep that looked like the rods rather than themselves <note>original: "Jacob's sheep," referring to the biblical story in Genesis 30:37–43</note>. What is looked upon rashly and recklessly <note>original: "retchlessly"</note> cannot easily be abandoned, and the heart likes best whatever pleases the senses most. For where lust is fixed, the eye is also fixed. Silent, wicked thoughts are expressed through the eyes, and perverse passions are easily discovered in one's looks. The evil eye misguides the heart <note>Job 31:7</note>, does not have the fear of God before it <note>Psalm 36:1</note>, and is the eye of vanity <note>Psalm 119:37</note>.

<margin>
Special.
</margin>
There are many specific symptoms of the evil eye. For instance, the eyes of a fool are in the ends of the earth <note>original: "corners of the world"</note>; that is, they are foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> and gaze after unprofitable and unnecessary things while ignoring more important matters <note>Proverbs 17:24</note>. The evil eye delights in seeing and beholding sin, which is completely contrary to God, who has pure eyes and cannot look upon evil or behold wickedness <note>Habakkuk 1:13</note>.

<margin>
Proud eyes.
</margin>
A proud man has eyes like himself: proud, haughty, lofty, and high-looking eyes <note>Psalm 101:5; Proverbs 6:17, 21:4, and 30:13; Psalm 131:1; Isaiah 2:11</note>. Sometimes they are even painted, as *Jezebel’s* were <note>2 Kings 9:30; compare with Jeremiah 4:30 and Ezekiel 23:40</note>.

<margin>
Covetous.
</margin>
The covetous eye is cast upon that which is "nothing"—that is, riches <note>Proverbs 23:5</note>. He who has an evil eye hastens to be rich <note>Proverbs 28:22</note>, and his eye cannot be satisfied with wealth <note>Ecclesiastes 4:8</note>. Whatever it looks upon and likes, it must have; just as *Ahab* looked upon *Naboth's* vineyard and coveted it. Such an eye is never satisfied and is like hell <note>Proverbs 27:20; Jeremiah 22:17</note>.

<margin>
Lecherous.
</margin>
The lustful eye longs for many things <note>1 John 2:16</note>. The eye of the adulterer waits for the twilight and says, "No eye shall see me" <note>Job 24:15</note>. Such was the eye of

### Prognostics <note>A "prognostic" is a forecast of the likely course of a disease or situation; here, it refers to the spiritual and physical symptoms or outcomes of an evil eye.</note>

<margin>
The evils of an evil eye.
</margin>
"As the eye is, so is the whole body," said Hippocrates <note>an ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine"</note>; but far better says Christ: "The light of the body is the eye: if the eye be single <note>meaning sincere, healthy, or focused on God</note>, the whole body shall be light; but if the eye be wicked, then all the body shall be dark; and if that light be turned to darkness, how great is that darkness?" Matthew 6:22–23. From the first evil eye (which saw the tree in the Garden of Eden as fair and beautiful), came the first and greatest harm to all mankind. God has therefore wisely and justly made the eye subject to more diseases than any other part of the body and, above all other parts, to sympathize most in sorrow with the heart. There is no part of the body that starts more sins with less cause than the eye, Ezekiel 23:16. In the eye, there is a great ease for sinning: an impudent eye needs someone to watch over it, and do not wonder if it trespasses, Ecclesiasticus 26:11.

The evil eye is easily deceived by objects: "My appearance," said Judith, "has deceived Holofernes <note>original: "Olophernes"</note> to his destruction," Judith 13:16. Her sandals ravished his eyes, and her beauty took his mind prisoner to lust, Judith 16:9. The evil eye defiles the whole man, Mark 7:22–23. And the offending eye (that is, the eye that causes a person to sin) causes a person to be cast into hell, Matthew 18:9. And Samson, who fed his eyes too much by flirting <note>original: "dallying"</note> with Delilah <note>original: "Dalila"</note>, had his eyes put out, Judges 16:21 <note>The original text mistakenly cites Judges 26:21; the Book of Judges only has 21 chapters</note>. Zedekiah, who offended God so greatly with his eyes, had his sons slain before his eyes, and then had his own eyes put out (2 Kings 25:7).

The eyes that are so insolent and so ready to offend God, He makes them fail through sorrow (Deuteronomy 28:65; 1 Samuel 3:2; Job 17:5). The Lord hates haughty eyes (Proverbs 6:17) and they are detested by men (Psalm 101:5); the lofty looks of man shall be humbled (Isaiah 2:11 and 5:15). As for the eye that mocks his father and despises the instruction of his mother: let the ravens of the valley pick it out, and the young eagles eat it (Proverbs 30:17). And wandering eyes are threatened with shame and sorrow (Isaiah 3:16).

It is only just that the evil eye is deprived by God of the objects in which it sinned and delighted itself—even the very "pleasure of the eyes" (Ezekiel 24:16, 21, 25). Or else, if He spares the object, He makes them become "pricks in the eye" to vex a person (Numbers 33:55), or else a source of resentment <note>original: "grudging"</note> and of wonderful discontentment, so that the eye shall be evil toward one's brother, wife (or husband), and children, through the extremity of God's plague (Deuteronomy 28:54).

David's remedy: prayer.

Lift up your eyes with tears to Him (John 11:41; Job 16:20). Entreat Him earnestly, as David did, that it would please Him, by His special grace and the power of His Spirit, to sanctify both the heart and the eyes so that they may be turned away from looking at worthless things <note>original: "vanity"</note> (Psalm 119:37). <margin>
Job's remedy:
A covenant
with the eyes.
</margin>
Make a covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1). That is, rule your spirit and eyes (Proverbs 6:32), imperiously imposing a law and commandment upon the eyes so that they do not offend. To "make" this covenant (in the sacred tongue <note>The "sacred tongue" refers to Hebrew.</note>) is literally "to cut a covenant." This is because those who made a covenant first took an oath, and then they passed between the parts of an animal that had been cut in two. This act symbolized their agreement: "Let them be cut asunder, as this beast is, who shall break this covenant," as seen in Jeremiah 34:18 and Genesis 15. Even so, the covenant with the eyes must be so resolutely kept that before the eye should offend, it should rather be cut in pieces. The basis of this covenant and the resolution to guard the eyes is the fear of God and His judgments, as well as a conscience mindful of God's all-seeing and all-sufficient knowledge. As Job gives the reason that moved him to make this covenant, he says: The portion from God is destruction to the wicked, and God sees all our ways and counts all our steps (Job 31:1–2; compare Psalm 36:1).

<margin>
Christ's remedy:
To pluck out
the eye.
</margin>
Christ’s medicinal <note>original: "physicall," meaning related to the art of healing or "physick."</note> counsel for the evil eye is that if one's right eye offends him, it must be plucked out (Matthew 5:29). It is called the "right" eye, presupposing that even if it were ever so excellent or dear to us, it should not be spared. It is called *our eye*, as it is of our own sinful and unregenerate nature; and it is said to "offend" because it acts as a rock or a stumbling stone in the way of God’s service, in which we are walking, by causing us to fall. If it is plucked out and cast from us, it is certain it will never offend us anymore. 

<margin>
"Our own, which is truly from us, when the will persistently introduces a less than chaste intention." Bernard, Sermon 2; Augustine. <note>original: "Noſter, qui verè à nobis eſt, dum voluntas minus caſtam importunè ingerit intentionem. Bern. ſ.2.d. Aug."</note>
</margin>
If it is objected that this is a most difficult remedy—to pull out the eye—and who can follow such advice? The answer is: just as Christ commands us to forsake all that we have (Luke 14:26, 33) and to hate father, mother, brother, and sister, and our own life also (John 12:25), so also is the plucking out of the offending eye commanded. Although these commands are strictly proposed and necessary to be obeyed under the pain of

eternal condemnation); yet they are not to be taken literally and simply, but understood metaphorically <note>original: "tropically," from the word 'trope' meaning a figure of speech</note> and comparatively. As Christ explains himself, saying: "He who loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than me, is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10:37). We must rather "hate" father or mother than Christ; and we should rather pluck out the eye before we offend God with it.

Christ in that passage explains the seventh commandment and shows that adultery is committed in three ways: by *lusting*, *looking*, and *lying* with a woman. He does not condemn simply looking at a woman, but looking with lust for her—even a *lustful look* with the intent to lie with her. If the eye is made an instrument <note>original: "Organe"</note> of sin, it is an abuse of the eye and a breach of the seventh commandment. Either this abuse of the eye—looking at a woman to lust for her—must be abandoned (and thus "plucked out" of the eye) to avoid <note>original: "eschewing"</note> the everlasting fire of hell, or else the eye itself must be plucked out. But nature abhors the plucking out of the eye; therefore, the *abuse* of the eye must be plucked out, which is what the Law commands.

<margin>
This, however, will happen if you do not consent, if you resist, and through the cutting off of your own will.
— Bernard <note>original: "Hoc autem fiet, si non consentias, si resistas, & in abscissione propriæ voluntatis." Referring to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux.</note>
</margin>
So, Christ’s remedy against the "evil eye" is to always remember the fire of hell, which will befall the whole person if the eye is abused for lust. The consideration of hell, that everlasting fire, and the worm that never dies should restrain the eye from being an instrument <note>original: "Organe"</note> of iniquity and a transgressor of the Law. In this way, it may no longer be *our* (unsanctified) *right eye* (dear to our corrupt minds), but rather a simple eye—the *eye of God's Spirit* and the eye of a new creature in *Christ*.

True wisdom.
</margin>
Learn to be truly wise—not with that wisdom which is earthly, natural, and devilish, but with the wisdom from above that is pure (James 3:17). This wisdom makes the "wise man’s eyes to be in his head" (Ecclesiastes 2:14). That is, he circumspectly and prudently notices, finds out, and tests all things, so that he may embrace and do those things that are good, while forsaking and avoiding <note>original: "eschewing"</note> all things...

He will use his eyes discreetly. Do the same with all the rest of your passions: crucify them with Christ and put them to death through His death.

Remove all such tempting objects from your sight and say with David, "I will set no wicked thing before my eyes" (Psalm 101:3). Shut your eyes from seeing evil, and you shall "dwell on high" (Isaiah 33:15–16). Do not be like Ham <note>original: "Cham"</note>, who fixed his eyes upon his father’s nakedness, but rather like Shem and Japheth, who covered the nakedness of their father while keeping their faces turned away (Genesis 9:23 <note>Note: The original text cites Gen 9:33, but the event occurs in verse 23.</note>). Thus, we must either keep the object away from our eyes or withdraw our eyes from the object.

Just as those who are runners in a race will not wander with their eyes this way or that, but will carefully set their eyes upon the right path to stay moving straight ahead; even so, let your eyes behold what is right, and let your eyelids direct your way before you (Proverbs 4:25). Let your eyes take pleasure in the ways of God and be ready to serve the soul in all things where the soul should serve God. Give your heart to Him who made it, as that essential Wisdom <note>original: "essential Wisdom"; referring to Christ or the personification of Wisdom in the Book of Proverbs</note> says: "My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes delight in my ways" (Proverbs 23:26).

And just as light naturally brings joy to the eye, God Himself—that perfect Light (1 John 4:8 <note>While 1 John 4:8 states "God is love," the author attributes the quality of "perfect Light" to God here, likely echoing 1 John 1:5.</note>)—shall graciously enlighten, clear, and cure your evil eye. He will sanctify it so that it may be a blessed organ for the soul’s good and for God’s glory. Then you may say confidently with Job: "I know that my Redeemer lives, and that He shall stand at the last day upon the earth; and though worms eat up this skin, yet in my flesh I shall see God. I shall see Him for myself, and my eyes shall behold Him and not another, even though my heart <note>original: "reins"; literally kidneys, but used biblically to refer to the seat of emotions and the innermost soul</note> is consumed within me" (Job 19:25–27). And so, in the resurrection of the just, you shall obtain from God a crown of righteousness.
